papers.title: Mapping transcriptional responses to cellular perturbations with RNA fingerprinting
papers.abstract: RNA fingerprinting is a statistical framework that infers causal regulators from single-cell experiments by mapping their transcriptional responses onto reference perturbation dictionaries.

papers.title: Lymphatic constraint of germinal centers optimizes protective antibody responses
papers.abstract: Lymphatic vessel networks remodel during infection to regulate antigen and immune cell dynamics, yet whether these changes impact humoral immunity remains unknown. Mudianto et al. demonstrate that lymph node lymphangiogenesis encapsulates activating germinal centers to constrain their size, which enhances clonal selection and protective antibody responses, establishing lymphatic vessels as structural determinants of germinal center fitness.

papers.title: Single-cell analyses of global cohorts outline determinants of immune aging and link the ratio of GZMK+ to GZMB+ Tem cells to health trajectories
papers.abstract: Terekhova et al. assemble a single-cell PBMC atlas of 8 datasets, 2,609 individuals, and over 12 million cells to dissect variable and conserved features of human immune aging. CD8+ Tem GZMK+ to GZMB+ ratio distinguishes healthy from disease-associated trajectories and predicts mortality risk. This work provides a clinically relevant marker for monitoring human aging.

papers.title: 40S ribosome remodeling triggers 18S rRNA U-tailing and DIS3L2-dependent decay
papers.abstract: Translational perturbations trigger ubiquitination and turnover of 40S ribosomes, yet how these events are coupled remains unclear. Shah et al. reveal that RIOK3 remodels ubiquitinated 40S subunits, exposing the 3′ end of 18S rRNA for uridylation and subsequent DIS3L2-mediated degradation. These findings link ribosomal protein ubiquitination to selective rRNA turnover.

papers.title: Oligo(uridine) tailing and exonucleolytic decay drive 40S ribosome degradation in response to stress
papers.abstract: 40S ribosomes are degraded in diverse stress conditions. Diehl et al. find that in response to stress, TUT7 is recruited to ubiquitylated 40S ribosomes and adds 3′ oligo(U) tails to the 18S rRNA. Iterative uridylation and 3′-5′ decay by the exonuclease DIS3L2 drive 18S rRNA and ultimately 40S ribosome degradation.

papers.title: Pectin alleviates alcohol-associated liver disease partly through cell-type-specific aryl hydrocarbon receptor signaling in female mice
papers.abstract: Hu et al. demonstrate that conditional deletion of AhR in hepatocytes or intestinal epithelial cells exacerbates alcohol-induced liver disease (ALD), whereas AhR deficiency in dendritic cells or Rorγt+ cells does not further worsen ALD. However, pectin remains effective in ameliorating ALD across all these cell-specific AhR knockout mouse models.

papers.title: Early infiltration of ischemia-conditioned Tregs attenuates BBB damage via suppressing neutrophil extracellular traps in ischemic stroke
papers.abstract: “Right time, right place, right people equal success.” Li et al. demonstrate that physiological delayed Treg arrival after stroke permits neutrophil-mediated BBB injury, but timely Treg awakening (ICTreg) and deployment into the brain curbs neutrophils and safeguards the barrier.

papers.title: Oxidative DNA damage drives centromere fragility and chromosome instability
papers.abstract: Thompson et al. show that centromeric oxidative DNA lesions disrupt DNA replication, destabilize CENP-A chromatin, and generate centromeric DNA breaks. The outcome depends on cell-cycle timing and checkpoint status, with centromeric damage promoting cell-cycle arrest and senescence in checkpoint-proficient cells but chromosome instability and whole-arm translocations when p53 is lost.

papers.title: The urgent challenge of gastroesophageal cancer
papers.abstract: Gastric and oesophageal cancers caused more than 1 million deaths worldwide in 2024. Cancer Grand Challenges has launched two targeted challenges to address this unmet need, inviting global interdisciplinary teams to apply for up to US $34 million in funding from the Torrey Coast Foundation and Cancer Research UK and move the dial towards the prevention of gastroesophageal cancer. Gastric and oesophageal cancers caused more than 1 million deaths worldwide in 2024. In this Comment, Cancer Grand Challenges explain how they have launched two targeted challenges to address this unmet need, inviting global interdisciplinary teams to apply for up to US $34 million in funding from the Torrey Coast Foundation and Cancer Research UK and move the dial towards the prevention of gastroesophageal cancer.

papers.title: Skeletal muscle enhancer programming of intrinsic cardiorespiratory fitness
papers.abstract: Cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) is a heritable trait associated with improved metabolic health and longevity. Integrating 546 transcriptomic and epigenomic profiles from skeletal muscle of 128 genetically heterogeneous rats selectively bred for high and low running capacity (HCR and LCR), a model that mirrors CRF-associated traits in humans, we identify a distributed enhancer architecture underlying their divergent transcriptomes. Line-divergent alleles were concentrated in distal enhancers: those more active in HCR were enriched for ETS-family transcription factor motifs and positively linked to hundreds of mitochondrial oxidative metabolism and angiogenesis genes, whereas those more active in LCR were enriched for Mef2 motifs and negatively linked to these genes. In 426 genotype, gene expression, and chromatin accessibility profiles from an independent HCRxLCR F2 population (n=147), we validated thousands of these genetic effects. Thus, heritable CRF reflects many enhancers cumulatively tuning energy metabolism and oxygen delivery, providing a molecular basis for variation in CRF.
affiliations: University of Michigan (corresponding author)

papers.title: Design of Orthogonal Far-Red, Orange and Green Fluorophore-binding Proteins for Multiplex Imaging
papers.abstract: Fluorescent proteins have transformed biological imaging, yet their limited photostability and brightness restrict their applications. We used deep learning-based de novo protein design methods to design binders to three bright, stable and cell-permeable dyes spanning the imaging spectrum: JF657 (far red), JF596 (orange-red) and JF494 (green). We obtain highly specific dye-binding proteins with low nanomolar affinities for the intended target; a crystal structure of one binder confirms close resemblance to the design model. Simultaneous labeling of mammalian cells expressing three dye-specific binders at different subcellular compartments demonstrates the utility in multiplex imaging. We further expand the functionality of the binder by incorporating an active site that carries out nucleophilic aromatic substitution to form a covalent linkage with the dye, and develop split versions which reconstitute fluorescence at subcellular locations where both halves are present towards monitoring in-cell protein interactions and chemically induced dimerization. Our designed high affinity and specificity dye binders open up new opportunities for multiplexed biological imaging.
affiliations: University of Washington (corresponding author)

papers.title: Dysfunctional effector programming in Foxp3-ΔE2 Tregs promotes enhanced CD8+ T cell responses
papers.abstract: Regulatory T cells (Tregs) prevent autoimmunity through suppressive functions largely programmed by the transcription factor FOXP3. Humans express two major alternatively spliced isoforms of FOXP3: a full-length version containing all coding exons (FOXP3-FL) and a version lacking Exon 2 (FOXP3-{Delta}E2). Sole FOXP3-{Delta}E2 expression causes lethal IPEX syndrome, indicating that FOXP3 Exon 2 is essential for full Treg function. Here, we used Foxp3-{Delta}E2 mice to determine how Foxp3 Exon 2 impacts the functional differentiation of Tregs at homeostasis and during inflammation. Analysis of central and effector Foxp3-{Delta}E2 Treg populations revealed dysfunctional effector Treg programming, including reduced expression of IL-2 receptor subunits, CTLA-4, and tissue-homing chemokine receptors. During influenza infection, reduced IL-2 regulation by Foxp3-{Delta}E2 Tregs and decreased Foxp3-{Delta}E2 Treg localization to the T cell zone during priming contributed to enhanced acute and memory CD8+ T cell responses. Thus, dysfunctional effector Treg programming by the Foxp3-{Delta}E2 isoform impairs suppressive function, resulting in failure to restrain CD8+ T cells and aberrant immune responses.
affiliations: Center for Fundamental Immunology, Benaroya Research Institute; Seattle, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: Combined High Fat and Viral Insults in Pregnancy Disrupt Specific Placental Nutrient Transporter Systems in Mice
papers.abstract: The placenta adapts to support nutrient transport to meet the demands of the growing fetus. Maternal obesity and viral infection are associated with adverse fetoplacental development. How co-exposure affects placental morphology and nutrient transport across gestation remains unclear. We hypothesise that co-exposure would have a greater impact on placental morphology and nutrient transporter expression than either of the exposures alone. C57BL/6J mice were fed a control (CON) or high-fat (HF) diet before and throughout pregnancy and exposed to poly(I:C) or vehicle at gestational days (GD) 12.5, 15.5, or 18.5. Placental morphology, folate and fatty acid transporter mRNA expression and localisation were evaluated by haematoxylin and eosin staining, immunohistochemistry (reported as % immunoreactivity (ir)-area stained), and qPCR, respectively. At GD12.5, HF diet associated with reduced junctional zone (JZ) area and increased maternal blood space, followed by reduced fetal blood space at GD15.5 and increased JZ and labyrinth zone (LZ) area size by GD18.5. HF diet and viral infection independently associated with increased placental Fat/Cd36 mRNA expression at GD12.5. However, HF diet and infection associated with increased ir-FR- while HF diet alone decreased ir-PCFT at GD12.5. By GD15.5, HF diet associated with reduced placental ir-FR- but increased ir-PCFT. At GD18.5, infection associated with reduced Rfc1 mRNA expression. HF diet and infection associated with greater prevalence of SGA and LGA fetuses, particularly at GD18.5. Obesity and infection independently and jointly disrupted placental morphology and nutrient transporter expression in a zone- and gestational age-specific manner, with consequences for fetal growth across gestation.
affiliations: Carleton University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Structural features and conservation of the lncRNA HOTAIR in primates
papers.abstract: Long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) regulate diverse cellular processes and are frequently implicated in disease, but their functional mechanisms often remain elusive. One such lncRNA, HOTAIR (Hox transcript antisense intergenic RNA), is a ~2.1 kb mammalian transcript whose overexpression promotes invasion and metastasis in breast cancer. However, the mechanisms by which HOTAIR influences gene regulation in cancer are poorly understood. To approach this problem through a structural lens, we predicted the full-length in cellulo secondary structure of HOTAIR using chemical probing in a metastatic breast cancer cell line. The resulting structure shows that HOTAIR adopts a multidomain architecture and has local structural features unique to the cellular context. Comparison between in vitro and in cellulo chemical probing identifies regions of differential accessibility that may indicate context-dependent molecular interactions or folding. Conservation analyses further reveal that HOTAIR is conserved across primates with evidence of structural covariation in specific domains. Together, these results provide a roadmap for future mechanistic studies of structure-function relationships in HOTAIR and its contribution to gene regulation in cancer.
affiliations: Yale University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Synthetic genetic circuits that count developmental cues in plant roots
papers.abstract: Plants explore soil environments through their roots, which branch repeatedly to access water and soil-borne nutrients. In many plants, root branches are generated by repeated developmental programs and molecular analyses have not identified markers that distinguish primary from later root branches. Consequently, efforts to engineer plant roots for improved water or nutrient acquisition are limited to changes that affect the entire root system. Here, we developed synthetic genetic circuits to count repeating root development cues and enable differential gene expression in successive root branches of the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana. The circuits use a root primordium-specific promoter to express large serine recombinases, which irreversibly invert segments of DNA each time a new lateral root is initiated. This converts repeating rounds of root formation into distinct, heritable DNA states. Because root branch specification and outgrowth occur over a ~2 day period, we tested circuit designs for their ability to count long-duration input pulses and developed an architecture that produces distinct fluorescence outputs in primary, secondary, and tertiary roots. By linking repeated developmental cues to distinct genetic outputs, synthetic genetic circuits that count enable root system engineering at the resolution of individual branches and offer a general strategy for dissecting developmental processes that rely on repeated signals.
affiliations: Stanford University / Howard Hughes Medical Institute (corresponding author)

papers.title: Molecular sterics guide tmRNA translocation on the ribosome
papers.abstract: Translation of defective mRNA transcripts can lead to the formation of stalled ``non-stop'' ribosome complexes. To rescue these ribosomes, bacteria have evolved a mechanism called trans-translation that is mediated by transfer-messenger RNA (tmRNA) and small protein B (SmpB). During the translocation step of trans-translation, the stalled mRNA is ejected and the reading frame found in the mRNA-like domain (MLD) of tmRNA is loaded into the mRNA channel. The ribosome then translates the new template, thereby tagging the nascent protein for degradation. While structures of tmRNA-SmpB on the ribosome have been available for years, little is known about the molecular factors that govern the dynamics of tmRNA translocation. Here, we use an energetically smooth model (i.e. SMOG) to simulate translocation of tmRNA-SmpB, which reveals that the structure of the ribosome gives rise to a preferred sequence of conformational substeps. Specifically, the tRNA-like domain (TLD) translocates, then the MLD loads, and finally the C-terminal tail of SmpB rearranges. These steps are interdependent and associated with a range of sterically-induced barriers that regulate the kinetics. This provides a structural and energetic framework for understanding, and ultimately controlling, the dynamics of trans-translation.
affiliations: Northeastern University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Amide I kurtosis maps cardiac amyloid in human tissue by ultrabroadband multiplex coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering (CARS) microscopy
papers.abstract: Cardiac amyloidosis is caused by deposits of misfolded proteins in the heart and can lead to heart failure. Histological confirmation typically involves staining tissue sections with Congo red and examining them under polarized light for apple-green birefringence; however, achieving an interpretable, label-free, and observer-independent assessment remains challenging. Here we show that Pearson kurtosis of channel intensities within the amide I window provides an interpretable, fitting-free contrast for cardiac amyloid in unstained human cardiac tissue sections from ten participants imaged by ultrabroadband multiplex coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering (CARS). In a discovery participant, high-kurtosis regions corresponded with Congo red-positive tissue in two CARS-histology pairs of adjacent sections (descriptive spatial AUCs, 0.79 and 0.73). Across 15 fields from nine additional participants, field-level kurtosis values did not overlap between severe-deposition and Congo red-negative tissue fields. Among the descriptors examined, kurtosis showed the largest standardized participant-level separation. Exploratory multivariate curve resolution yielded a deposit-associated component with aromatic-residue features shared with reagent transthyretin. In one field from the discovery participant, the second harmonic generation (SHG) signal, acquired simultaneously with CARS, showed a broadly inverse spatial pattern relative to the amide I kurtosis map, revealing distinct tissue-architectural contrast. Together, these findings support a potential label-free approach to detecting cardiac amyloid deposits that combines amide I kurtosis derived from broadband CARS with SHG-derived architectural contrast.
affiliations: Graduate School of Science and Technology, Keio University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Potassium modulates Phytophthora zoospore motility and flagellar beating through dose-dependent effects
papers.abstract: Biflagellate zoospores are critical agents in the spread of Phytophthora spp., plant pathogens causing major agronomic and economic losses worldwide. These motile cells navigate soil water films toward plant roots using taxis triggered by environmental cues. Here, we investigate how potassium modulates zoospore motility by analyzing trajectory and flagellar beating parameters across KCl concentrations. Using high-speed imaging, we apply kymograph analysis and Fourier transform of the cell body direction over time to quantify flagellar dynamics, while low-speed imaging provides trajectory characteristics. Our results demonstrate that increasing potassium concentration significantly reduces swimming speed while enhancing directional changes. We establish a direct correlation between altered swimming speed and changes in flagellar beating parameters. Our findings indicate that potassium differentially affects anterior and posterior flagella beating. Furthermore, potassium exerts multiple effects, influencing beat amplitude, wave propagation speed and direction- change frequency. This reveals potassium as a key modulator of zoospore motility, triggering a shift from exploratory swimming to confined, reoriented movement. By uncovering the biomechanical responses of zoospores to potassium, this study advances our understanding of how surrounding signals regulate pathogen dispersal in the environment.
affiliations: Universite Cote d'Azur, CNRS (corresponding author)

papers.title: STRUCTURAL AND MOLECULAR DYNAMICS ANALYSIS OF HUMAN β-DEFENSIN 1 VARIANTS REVEALS DISTINCT PERTURBATION SIGNATURES
papers.abstract: Human {beta}-defensin 1 (hBD-1) is a small, disulfide-constrained antimicrobial peptide produced predominantly in the kidney and urogenital tract, where it contributes to epithelial innate defense. Genetic variation in the gene encoding hBD-1 has been associated with altered expression levels and susceptibility to infections, including infection following solid organ transplantation, yet the molecular consequences of coding substitutions in the active, mature form remain largely undefined. Here, we integrate conventional genomics, protein bioinformatics, structural modeling, and molecular dynamics to investigate the molecular consequences of 93 human-observed hBD-1 missense variants. Evaluation of hBD-1 missense variants across sequence-, structure-, and dynamics-based dimensions reveals variant-specific molecular perturbation signatures that complement conventional and static biophysical predictions. By treating naturally occurring substitutions as a perturbation series across a compact defensin scaffold, this study identifies multiple molecular routes through which sequence variation can remodel an endogenous antimicrobial peptide and prioritizes variants for direct structure-function testing. These findings provide a mechanistic framework for investigating how naturally occurring hBD-1 variation may influence peptide behavior and, ultimately, antimicrobial function.
affiliations: Mayo Clinic (corresponding author)

papers.title: Cross-linker binding strength influences actin assembly microstructure and myosin II driven remodeling
papers.abstract: The actin cytoskeleton is a self-assembled material that acts as the mechanical scaffold of the cell. Within the cell, protein cross-linkers organize actin filaments into assemblies with various microstructures that support distinct physiological functions. These protein cross-linkers differ in structural features. To decouple the role of individual cross-linker properties in actin assembly microstructure and mechanics, we synthesize programmable cross-linkers using a DNA linker coupled to binding domains. We find that high affinity cross-linkers induce actin bundling, while low affinity cross-linkers form actin networks. Myosin II motors remodel and contract all cross-linked networks tested in distinct ways from uncross-linked networks. We find that networks with high affinity cross-linkers have different myosin induced dynamics than networks with low affinity cross-linkers. This research expands our understanding of how cells regulate their mechanics and microstructures, while also providing insight towards the structure-property relationship in complex soft materials.
affiliations: Clemson University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Synthesis and characterization of NIR fluorescent BODIPY-Xanthene hybrid dyes
papers.abstract: The development of NIR fluorescent dyes with favorable optical properties is of great importance especially for applications within the field of optical imaging. In this study, we report the design, synthesis and photophysical characterization of novel BODIPY-Xanthene hybrid dyes obtained via Knoevenagel condensation between an asymmetrical BODIPY core and the functionalized xanthene aldehydes intermediates. The synthesized dyes ex-hibit absorption (667 nm) and emission bands (720-722 nm) within the NIR region. Detailed UV-Vis and fluo-rescence studies were performed and molar extinction coefficients and stokes shifts also calculated. Moreover, findings highlighting the influence of structural modifications on the optical behavior of the hybrid dyes and their potential utility in optical imaging applications are reported.
affiliations: Institute of Chemical Biology, National Hellenic Research Foundation, 48 Vassileos Constantinou Avenue 11635, Athens, Greece (corresponding author)

papers.title: Quantification of cellular contributions to multi-cellular pattern formation
papers.abstract: Multi-cellular pattern formation is a key process in organism development, regeneration, and disease. Such multi-cellular patterns include, for instance, cell density and gene expression patterns. Here, we develop a cell-track-based method that quantifies how much individual cellular processes contribute to the emergence of large-scale patterns. These cellular processes include changes in cellular expression levels, cell motion, cell divisions, and apoptosis. We validate our method using synthetic data, before demonstrating it on two sets of experimental data. Our method is purely geometric and does not require any mechanistic assumptions about the underlying pattern-forming processes, making it very generic and robust. It thus enables unbiased, data-driven study of the mechanisms driving pattern formation across a broad class of systems.
affiliations: Cenetr for Theoretical Physics (CPT), French National Center for Scientific Research (CNRS) (corresponding author)

papers.title: Microscopic collisions govern macroscopic aerotactic spreading through emergent transport coefficients
papers.abstract: Collective migration is often attributed to complex cell-cell communication, yet coordinated multicellular dynamics can also emerge in organisms lacking social interactions. Continuum descriptions successfully capture such behaviors but generally rely on phenomenological transport coefficients whose microscopic origin remains elusive. Here we show that these coefficients emerge from cell-cell collisions and can be independently determined from experiments. We investigate the aerotactic dispersal of confined colonies of the solitary amoeba Acanthamoeba castellanii, in which oxygen consumption continuously reshapes the local environment to generate self-organized guidance cues. Combining quantitative videomicroscopy, oxygen mapping with phosphorescent sensing films, and oxygen-controlled microfluidics, we directly measure both the oxygen landscape and the aerotactic response governing colony expansion. We then develop a Patlak-Keller-Segel (PKS) -type drift-diffusion model whose transport coefficients are entirely determined from independent experiments and microscopic-to-macroscopic modeling approach, without adjustable parameters. The model quantitatively reproduces the observed dynamics, including the coexistence of a fast ballistic front and a trailing transient accumulation band. We show that both diffusion and aerotactic transport are modulated by the same collision-controlled mechanism through density-dependent changes in cell persistence. More generally, our results establish transport coefficients as measurable emergent properties bridging microscopic cell dynamics and macroscopic collective behavior, providing a predictive framework for oxygen-guided migration in living active matter.
affiliations: University Lyon 1 CNRS (corresponding author)

papers.title: A deep learning-generated hASIC1a miniprotein inhibitor confers neuroprotection in stroke
papers.abstract: Ion channels remain notoriously recalcitrant drug targets despite their extensive pathophysiological significance. Acid-sensing ion channels (ASICs) are proton-gated cation channels that cause neuronal death when excessively activated, such as during ischaemic stroke. This acidosis-driven injury pathway remains unchallenged by existing therapeutics. Here we generate two de novo designed hASIC1a-specific miniproteins by developing a platform that integrates computational miniprotein design, high-throughput automated patch clamp screening, biophysical and structural characterisation, and in vivo validation. We identify a subtype-selective hASIC1a inhibitor, Denasin1, which achieves near-complete inhibition with nanomolar potency. Denasin1 is disordered in solution but adopts the computationally predicted helix-turn-helix fold when bound to the extracellular acidic pocket of hASIC1a. Crucially, Denasin1 reduces infarct volume by > 50% in a murine model of ischaemic stroke. We thereby establish our de novo design platform as a route to develop potent and selective ion channel modulators.
affiliations: University of Copenhagen (corresponding author)

papers.title: Structural Insights into the Expanded Substrate Scope of a Cysteine-Dependent Hydrolase from Rhodococcus opacus for Polyethylene, Polypropylene, and Polystyrene Biodegradation
papers.abstract: Microplastic pollution from homopolymers such as polypropylene (PP), polystyrene (PS), and polyethylene (PE) poses growing health and environmental concerns, highlighting the need for robust polymer-degrading biocatalysts. We previously identified a naturally occurring cysteine-dependent hydrolase (CsdH) from Rhodococcus opacus, featuring a unique Cys160-Lys127-Asp39 catalytic triad and providing a novel mechanism for polyethylene terephthalate (PET) degradation. In this study, we have determined crystal structures of CsdH in complex with PP, PS, PE, and styrene and demonstrated the potential of the enzyme to directly degrade these homopolymers into their respective low molecular weight degradation products using LC-MS. Structural analysis reveals that the enzyme retains a conserved principal access tunnel while undergoing subtle substrate-dependent changes to accommodate different substrates. The enzyme exhibited broad plastic degradation activity with the highest weight loss observed for PE, followed by PP and PS. SEM analysis reveals surface roughness, cracks and grooves, confirming polymer degradation. Further, these results corroborate through FTIR and TGA analysis. These findings establish a strong foundation for enzyme engineering and aim at developing efficient microplastic degradation.
affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee, Roorkee 247667, (corresponding author)

papers.title: A transient third metal ion shapes the catalytic cycle of a group I intron ribozyme
papers.abstract: The self-splicing group I intron ribozyme from Tetrahymena thermophillia (THr) is a prototypical example of how RNA overcomes its limited chemical repertoire to form complex, negatively charged junctions and catalyze chemical reactions. Despite over 30 years of biochemical and structural characterization, questions still remain regarding the requirements for THr catalysis that may inform structure based drug design against group I introns, as well as the use of THr as an RNA editing tool. Recent cryo-EM structures have provided an unprecedented window into the first and second steps of splicing, enabling detailed mechanistic investigation at the atomistic level. In this work, we leverage solvation theory, molecular dynamics, alchemical free energy simulations, and machine learning accelerated QM/MM to probe outstanding questions related to 1) the role of a possible third Mg2+ binding in the active site, 2) differences in catalytic requirements between Gexo cofactors and between the first and second steps of splicing, 3) the potential role of an acid or base, and 4) restrictions on the identity of the 5' exon splice site nucleotide, U(-1). We propose that a transient, cofactor dependent, interaction with a third metal participates in the first step, while a higher affinity interaction with this third ion is required in the second step. We also propose that the presence of a phosphate on the Gexo in the first step, and analogously the G{omega} in the second step, forms a metal ion binding site not present when guanosine is bound. Finally, we propose and computationally test design modifications of G22 (isofunctional substitutions of 2,6-diaminopurine that tune the pKa at the N1 position) that we predict will enable the accommodation of C(-1) in a crucial wobble-like pair at physiological pH. This design would provide a potential strategy for expanding the sequence space accessible to programmable trans-splicing ribozymes in RNA editing applications.
affiliations: Laboratory for Biomolecular Simulation Research, Institute for Quantitative Biomedicine and Department of Chemistry and Chemical Biology, Rutgers University, Pi (corresponding author)

papers.title: Physical Basis Of pKa Shift For Ionizable Lipids In An LNP-like Environment
papers.abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are a leading drug delivery platform for mRNA or other nucleic acid-based therapeutics. LNP platforms are typically composed of ionizable aminolipids, phospholipids, sterols, and lipids tagged with polyethylene glycol. The ionizable aminolipids are typically cationic at low pH, allowing them to encapsulate negatively charged mRNA. The pH at which the ionizable head groups change charge states, the apparent pKa, is crucial to understand the characteristics and formulation of LNP. However, this is difficult to measure as the apparent pKa differs from the pKa of the aminolipids in bulk solution due to the complex chemical and charge environment. In this study, we use molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with alchemical free energy perturbation to calculate the pKa shift as a function of lipid composition, treating LNP-like and vesicle-like environments. Our results show that the pH-dependent structure of the systems affects the trends in pKa shifts in complex ways, driven by factors including surface electrostatics and lipid internalization. Our all-atom simulation protocol allows us to efficiently estimate the apparent pKa of LNP-like models formed with novel ionizable aminolipids and estimate how it will change with composition.
affiliations: University of Rochester Medical Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: Crowding governs resistance confinement and guides the improvement of adaptive therapy in a 2D melanoma model system
papers.abstract: The emergence of treatment resistant mutants is one of the primary contributors to therapy failure in cancer. Evolution-based adaptive therapies aim to exploit the competition between sensitive and resistant cells to prolong therapeutic control. However, in the densely packed tissues of solid tumors, competition is not only determined by cell-intrinsic factors but also a result of local physical interactions between neighboring cells. The successful development of physics-informed adaptive therapies therefore hinges upon the bottom-up integration of tissue mechanics and experimentally grounded models of tumor evolution. Here, we show how population-level treatment response emerges from mechanical interactions between individual cells. Combining genetically tailored therapy-mimicry experiments in spatially structured 2D melanoma colonies with mechanistic, particle-based tissue simulations as digital twins in a real-to-sim-to-real framework, we reveal how treatment-induced changes in mechanical crowding shape a cascade of resistance expansion, spatial competitive escape, and consequent therapy failure. We then link these underlying physical mechanisms to population-level observables in an abstracted mathematical model for reinforcement-learning-based therapy optimization and a distilled treatment-decision-heuristic, which we test experimentally. Together, our results identify mechanical crowding and escape as governing principles of resistance-mediated therapy failure in solid tumours and provide a basis for mechanistically informed, evolution-based treatment strategies.
affiliations: Max-Planck-Zentrum fuer Physik und Medizin (corresponding author)

papers.title: Grow2Fold: mapping heterogeneous developmental growth to human brain folding
papers.abstract: Cortical folding emerges through complex developmental processes, yet what organizes these processes into the characteristic folding patterns of the human brain remains unclear. Here, we developed an imaging-informed whole-brain modeling framework, Grow2Fold, that integrates developmental cortical regionalization, quantitative growth characterization, and mechanics-guided simulation to investigate how cortical growth shapes brain folding patterns. Using 836 fetal and neonatal MRI sessions from 747 participants spanning 21-45 postmenstrual weeks, we identified a reproducible and hierarchical spatiotemporal organization of cortical expansion characterized by coordinated regional growth trajectories. Rapid expansion occurs earlier around peri-central territories and progressively shifts toward frontal, parietal, and temporal association cortices. We encoded these imaging-derived trajectories into region- and age-specific growth laws and incorporated them into anatomically realistic whole-brain mechanical models. The resulting simulations recapitulate major sulcal landmarks and characteristic folding development across global and regional morphological measures. Comparing regional and uniform growth, we find that differential growth drives cortical instability, while heterogeneous developmental growth organizes this instability into anatomically recognizable folding patterns. Combined with subject-specific anatomy, these population-informed growth laws reproduce individualized longitudinal folding trajectories. Together, our results identify spatiotemporally patterned developmental growth as a key spatial constraint on cortical morphogenesis and establish a quantitative bridge from developmental imaging, through mechanical instability, to anatomically organized folding.
affiliations: University of Georgia (corresponding author)

papers.title: CryoFAST: A Fab-Aided Cryo-EM Workflow for High-Resolution Structure Determination of Sub-50-kDa Protein Targets
papers.abstract: Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) plays an increasingly important role in structure-based drug discovery (SBDD) by revealing target protein-ligand interactions at the molecular level, but its application has largely focused on large- and medium-sized protein complexes. Many therapeutically important targets are smaller than 50 kDa and remain highly challenging for cryo-EM analysis because of low signal-to-noise ratios and difficulties in particle alignment. Here, we describe cryoFAST, an integrated workflow that couples ligand-compatible Fab discovery and structure-guided computational maturation with biochemical triage, fiducial-complex assembly, and single-particle cryo-EM. Through phage-display screening and/or AI-guided design, we developed high-affinity Fab binders of approximately 50 kDa that stabilize the target without disrupting ligand-target interactions and then assembled Fab-target complexes for cryo-EM analysis. Using the therapeutically relevant extracellular domain (~20 kDa) of interleukin-4 receptor (IL-4R) as a proof of concept, we determined its cryo-EM structure at 2.74 Angstrom resolution and established a framework for elucidating ligand-binding modes. This workflow provides a practical, efficient, and potentially broadly applicable route to the structural characterization of small protein targets that are otherwise challenging to study. By extending the applicability of cryo-EM to high-value but technically challenging small targets, cryoFAST may open new opportunities for structure-based drug discovery.
affiliations: Cryo-EM Platform, VIVA Biotech, Shanghai, China (corresponding author)

papers.title: Structural Basis for Near Infrared Absorption and Noncanonical Photoisomerization in Neorhodopsin
papers.abstract: In retinal proteins, light absorption leads to a double bond isomerization of the chromophore, followed by conformational relaxations that drive functional protein rearrangements. The balance between photoisomerization and radiative or non-radiative decays of the excited state is adjusted to the demands of the respective photoreceptor function. The molecular determinants controlling the excited state processes remain poorly understood and are the focus of this combined crystallographic, spectroscopic, and theoretical work on the recently discovered neorhodopsin (NeoR). NeoR exhibits a highly red-shifted and fluorescent dark state and selectively photoisomerizes from all-trans to 7-cis. We show that the local electrostatic environment reduces the negative charge density near the Schiff base and suppresses torsional motion around the canonical C13=C14 isomerization site of microbial rhodopsins. Instead, the chromophore-binding pocket permits only low-efficiency C7=C8 isomerization, accompanied by polyene inversion, {beta}-ionone ring displacement, and Schiff base deprotonation. Consequently, unlike other retinal photoreceptors, NeoR undergoes structural changes localized near the {beta}-ionone ring.
affiliations: Humboldt University of Berlin (corresponding author)

papers.title: Tolerance to Lung Infection in TWIK2 K+ Efflux Mediated Macrophage Trained Immunity
papers.abstract: Alveolar macrophages (AM{phi}) are essential for innate immune function in the lungs. It is now apparent that macrophages can be trained to become better at attacking infections. Although trained immunity is thought to result from metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we report that AM{phi} can be trained by extracellular ATP, which is ubiquitously released during inflammation. ATP ligates the canonical Purinergic Receptor 2 subtype X7 receptor (P2X7) to mediate endosomal Two-pore domain Weak Inwardly rectifying K+ channel 2 (TWIK2) translocation into the plasma membrane (PM). This endows the cells to transit to a ready state for microbial killing in two directions: first, K+ efflux via PM-TWIK2 induces NLRP3 inflammasome activation, which further activates metabolic pathways; second, upon bacterial phagocytosis, PM-TWIK2 internalizes into phagosome membrane with proper topological orientation, where TWIK2 mediates K+ influx into phagosomes to control pH and ionic strength favoring bacterial killing. Therefore, the enhanced association of TWIK2 in phagosomal and plasma membranes signaled by danger-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), such as ATP, mediates trained immunity in AM{phi} and enhances the microbiocidal activity.
affiliations: University of Illinois at Chicago (corresponding author)

papers.title: An ancestral tRNA maturation enzyme repurposed for cytoplasmic non-coding RNA processing
papers.abstract: Ribonuclease Z enzymes remove 3' trailers from precursor tRNAs. In human cells, ELAC2/RNase ZL matures nuclear and mitochondrial pre-tRNAs, whereas the cytosolic short paralog ELAC1/RNase ZS repairs ANKZF1-cleaved tRNAs, but its broader substrate repertoire remains unclear. We investigated ELAC1 function using transcriptome profiling, small RNA sequencing, CLIP-seq, and biochemical reconstitution. ELAC1 was dispensable for canonical tRNA processing but associated with structured RNA polymerase III transcripts, prominently Y RNAs and vault RNAs (vtRNAs). Purified ELAC1 cleaved all four human vtRNAs near their 3' ends, with high-resolution mapping identifying a conserved cleavage position within the 3' extension. Efficient cleavage required structural features of the vtRNA terminal region. In contrast, ELAC2 showed little or no vtRNA cleavage under the conditions tested and displayed stricter substrate and cleavage-site selection on pre-tRNA. Loss and re-expression of ELAC1 altered structured ncRNA abundance and small-RNA end profiles. These findings identify vtRNAs as direct ELAC1 substrates and support functional specialization of human ELAC paralogs, with ELAC2 favoring precise pre-tRNA maturation and ELAC1 exhibiting broader RNA substrate specificity.
affiliations: Department of Biochemistry, School of Medicine, University of Patras, 26 504 Patras, Greece (corresponding author)

papers.title: Perturbation of the replication stress-ATR axis accelerates human erythroid differentiation but blocks terminal maturation
papers.abstract: Replication stress (RS) can act as an input to differentiation: in erythroid and myeloid cells it is sufficient to accelerate commitment. Yet genotoxic chemotherapy, which imposes replication stress on the bone marrow can cause anemia; a frequent dose-limiting toxicity whose deficit of mature red cells is often attributed to progenitor depletion rather than to any effect on differentiation itself. Here, we ask how RS-induced accelerated commitment gives rise to impaired red cell output, using in vitro erythroid differentiation of cord-blood CD34+ progenitors perturbed with clinically relevant chemotherapy agents. We find that treated erythroblasts differentiate faster than controls but fail to mature, measured by lack of enucleated cells. Inhibition of ATR, but not ATM or DNA-PK, reproduces this phenotype. Mechanistically, single-cell profiling of drug-treated cells shows convergence on a transcriptional program, marked by loss of MYB and MYC activity. Treated cultures also accumulate aberrant late erythroblasts depleted for globin and heme programs and enriched for p53 and proteotoxic stress signatures. Together, these results propose that defective maturation is an alternative mechanism for chemotherapy-induced anemia, in addition to depletion of progenitors.
affiliations: University of Basel (corresponding author)

papers.title: A synthetic xeno-free extracellular matrix surrogate supports robust human induced pluripotent stem cell maintenance and multilineage differentiation
papers.abstract: Animal-derived surface coatings present the gold standard in stem cell culture. However, they come with major drawbacks such as lot-to-lot inconsistency and an ethically problematic production. Approaches to develop synthetic coating alternatives have largely failed to recapitulate biological functions essential to PSC-self renewal and differentiation. In this study, we have investigated the suitability of a fully synthetic, chemically defined extracellular matrix-mimicking coating named BIOINSTRUCT for hiPSC culture. BIOINSTRUCT was employed during maintenance culture of IMR90-4 cells, as well as directed differentiation of HIHCNi008-A, ACTN2-GFP, and UKKI-011-A cells. BIOINSTRUCT preserved hiPSC characteristics over the experimental period of 10 passages similar to Matrigel. Spontaneous differentiation resulted in the formation of ectodermal, mesodermal and endodermal derivatives, confirming the retention of pluripotency. Directed differentiation on BIOINSTRUCT enabled the generation of neuronal, cardiac and pancreatic endocrine cells. Altogether, our data underscore BIOINSTRUCT as a promising alternative to animal-derived extracellular matrix coatings.
affiliations: Translational Center Regenerative Therapies TLC-RT, Fraunhofer Institute for Silicate Research ISC (corresponding author)

papers.title: XPO1 controls VDR localization and activity in triple-negative breast cancer cells
papers.abstract: The association of cytoplasmic localization of VDR in TNBC tumors and disease aggressivity prompted investigation of its regulation by XPO1. In TNBC cell lines, the XPO1 inhibitors selinexor and eltanexor increased nuclear VDR localization. Their effects were particularly strong when combined with vitamin D treatment. Similarly, XPO1 knockdown increased nuclear VDR levels, both alone and in combination with vitamin D. These results identify XPO1 as an important regulator of VDR subcellular distribution. XPO1 inhibition also enhanced vitamin D-dependent VDR transcriptional activity. Indeed, selinexor, eltanexor, and XPO1 silencing increased vitamin D-dependent CYP24A1 reporter activity and the expression of genes such as CYP24A1 or CDH1. RNA sequencing showed that XPO1 modulation markedly reshaped the vitamin D transcriptional response. The affected genes were mainly involved in metabolism, cell-cycle regulation, protein localization, and cellular organization. Functional analyses demonstrated that cytoplasmic VDR promoted TNBC cell proliferation. Conversely, nuclear VDR was required for the antiproliferative effects of vitamin D. Accordingly, XPO1 inhibition or depletion potentiated vitamin D-mediated growth suppression. This finding suggested functional cooperation between XPO1-dependent export and VDR activity. Finally, high VDR expression was associated with poor disease-free or overall survival only in tumors with high XPO1 expression. Overall, XPO1 negatively regulates VDR nuclear localization and vitamin D responsiveness in TNBC. Targeting XPO1 may therefore enhance the therapeutic potential of vitamin D-based strategies in TNBC.
affiliations: INSERM, U1194 (corresponding author)

papers.title: Inflammation-driven cellular selection impacts X-linked mosaicism in the epidermis
papers.abstract: In eutherian females, the choice of which X chromosome gets embryonically inactivated is thought to be random. Somatic tissues are thus assumed to comprise cells with a 50:50 ratio of maternal:paternal X active. However, a phenomenon known as X-skewing has been observed, wherein tissue composition shifts to be dominated by cells expressing one X or the other. On a gross level, such X-skewing is phenotypically silent except in the case where one X-chromosome carries a disease mutation. Here, by leveraging a mouse model of an X-linked disease called Incontinentia Pigmenti, caused by heterozygous mutations in the NF-kB effector, Nemo, we explore how X-linked cellular dynamics shape progenitor biology in the epidermis. Lineage tracing with X-linked reporters shows that at birth, the epidermis is unexpectedly skewed toward mutant cells. Within a week, as inflammation emerges, these dynamics reverse leaving surviving animals with almost entirely wild-type epithelium. The shift is driven by loss rather than growth since mutant cells adopt an aberrant fate and die at higher rates than their wild-type neighbours; proliferation rises in both populations. Notably, wild-type proliferation scales with local tissue composition, suggesting these cells calibrate their response to the extent of the mutant burden to compensate appropriately for tissue loss. Depleting macrophages, the principal TNF- source, attenuates inflammation, mutant cell death and ultimately is expected to preserve the mutant population. Altogether, our results identify inflammation as a selective force capable of resolving deleterious mosaicism, not only in the context of an X-linked disease, but within any dynamic, clonally heterogeneous epithelium.
affiliations: University of Vienna / Max Perutz Labs (corresponding author)

papers.title: Progressive Actomyosin Remodeling Defining a Structured Podocyte Injury Response in Nephrotic Syndrome
papers.abstract: Nephrotic syndrome, the leading cause of chronic kidney disease worldwide, is associated with injury and eventual loss of podocytes, the specialized epithelial cells that form the final layer of the kidney's filtration apparatus. The progression from injury to loss is largely irreversible. However, some forms of nephrotic syndrome undergo remission, suggesting that injured podocytes may retain a capacity for repair, the structural basis of which remains unknown. Podocytes respond to injury by the stereotypical morphological change known as foot process effacement (FPE), which can be visualized using transmission electron microscopy. Using modified ultrastructure expansion microscopy (U-ExM) protocol combined with super-resolution microscopy, we discovered that injured podocytes exhibit a three-stage progression of FPE maturation, with kinetics determined by the degree of actomyosin contractility. Through longitudinal study of adriamycin-induced nephropathy in mice, we identified three sequential stages of actomyosin reorganization within the sarcomere-like structures (SLSs) that define the injury response: focal infiltration of myosin IIA into synaptopodin-rich foot processes (Stage 1), disordered intermingling of synaptopodin/myosin IIA (Stage 2), and the formation of highly organized periodic contractile arrays oriented perpendicular to the direction of capillary blood flow (Stage 3). Longitudinal quantification revealed predictable temporal dynamics, with mature Stage 3 predominating by day 7-9 post-injury. To determine whether this sequence is conserved in human disease, we analyzed kidney biopsies from patients with minimal change disease, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, membranous nephropathy, and diabetic nephropathy. The same three stages were present across all four diseases, and their distribution tracked disease course: acute podocytopathies exhibited heterogeneous early-stage patterns, whereas chronic injuries converged on uniform, mature SLS organization. These findings demonstrate that podocyte injury is a graded, potentially reversible process rather than a binary switch. They identify structured actomyosin remodeling as a conserved wound response across mechanistically distinct kidney diseases and suggest that therapeutic strategies targeting specific stages of this progression could alter the trajectory of diverse glomerular diseases.
affiliations: University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: Compressive stress couples calcium signalling to translational control and proteostasis
papers.abstract: Compressive stress is a pervasive feature of solid tumour growth, and mechanical loading is known to activate calcium signalling through the mechanosensitive channel Piezo1. How this signal is converted into changes in cellular biosynthetic capacity, however, remains unclear. Here we show that compressive stress engages a Piezo1-dependent calcium checkpoint that reduces translational output with increasing mechanical load, independently of mTORC1 and the integrated stress response. Compression triggers Piezo1-dependent release of endoplasmic reticulum Ca2, activating eEF2 kinase to slow translational elongation. This same Ca2 signal drives mitochondrial remodelling and reactive oxygen species production, which reinforce translational repression through redox-dependent oxidation of the translation initiation factor eIF2{beta}. In parallel, Ca2-dependent AMPK activation triggers autophagic ribosome degradation, alleviating compression-induced macromolecular crowding and restoring cytoplasmic rheology despite sustained mechanical load. These mechanisms act at distinct levels of translational control: initiation, elongation and ribosome abundance; yet converge to limit biosynthetic output under compression. Consistent with a role for this pathway in tumour adaptation to mechanical constraint, eEF2K expression correlates with poor overall survival in a public PDAC patient dataset. Together, these findings define a mechano-metabolic checkpoint through which cells actively tune biosynthetic capacity to their physical environment.
affiliations: Istituto di Genetica Molecolare, Consiglio Nazionale delle Ricerche (IGM-CNR), Via Abbiategrasso 207, Pavia, Italy (corresponding author)

papers.title: Chronic ER Stress Disrupts Mitochondrial-Associated ER Membrane Integrity in Corneal Endothelial Cells.
papers.abstract: Purpose: Fuchs endothelial corneal dystrophy (FECD) is an age-related degenerative disease of the corneal endothelium cells (CEnCs), affecting 4% of the US population over 40. While Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and mitochondrial stress have been independently associated with FECD pathogenesis, few studies have examined ER-mitochondrial interactions/ER-mitochondrial contact sites/mitochondria-associated ER membrane (MAM), or MAM proteins, and their contribution to ER and mitochondrial stress in FECD. This study aims to characterize alterations in MAMs and identify key MAM proteins associated with ER and mitochondrial stress in FECD. Methods: Human corneal endothelial cell line (HCEnC-21T) and Fuchs corneal endothelial cell line (F35T) were cultured and subjected to ER stressor tunicamycin for 6 and 24 hours. MAM proteins were isolated by subcellular fractionation, and key ER and mitochondrial-damage-sensor proteins, such as PERK and Parkin, respectively, were identified by immunoblotting. ER-mitochondrial contact sites were quantified using the MAM plasmid and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) in normal and Fuchs cell lines, as well as in human tissues under chronic ER stress. Results: ER-mitochondrial contact distance significantly increased in Fuchs tissues compared with normal tissues, and a similar increase was observed in 21T cell line after tunicamycin treatment. There was a significant increase in the intensity of the MAM plasmid upon tunicamycin treatment at 6 hours in the 21T cell line compared to the non-treated control. However, MAM plasmid intensity significantly decreased at 24 hours compared to 6 hours post-tunicamycin treatment in 21T cell line. Analysis of MAM function by quantifying phosphatidylserine synthase 1 (PSS1 [gene PTDSS1]) expression in 21T cells showed a reduction in PTDSS1 expression after 24 hours of tunicamycin treatment. ER stress protein PERK and mitochondria damage sensor protein (Parkin) significantly increased in the MAM fraction after tunicamycin at 24 hours in 21T cell. Conclusions: Fuchs cell lines and tissues demonstrate decreased ER-mitochondrial interactions/MAMs, which are also seen in 21T cell line after chronic ER stress. Under chronic ER stress, ER and mitochondrial stress mediator proteins are translocated to MAM. This study highlights the importance of MAMs as a potential mediator of ER-mitochondria crosstalk in degenerating corneal endothelial cells for FECD.
affiliations: Eye and Vision Research Institute, Department of Ophthalmology and Pharmacological Sciences, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, New York, USA. (corresponding author)

papers.title: A Novel Role for FSTL-1 in Hematopoietic Stem Cell Homeostasis and Post-injury Regeneration
papers.abstract: Background: The ability to repopulate all lineages of blood cells from a single hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) requires a constant balancing between maintenance of quiescence/self-renewal and the need for differentiation and adoption of specific lineage phenotypes. A classical interpretation suggests that during homeostasis, long- and then short-term HSCs differentiate into multipotent progenitors (MPPs), which then lack self-renewal capacity but can still differentiate into all downstream lineages. While much is known about the intrinsic and extrinsic regulators that promote HSC homeostasis, less is known about factors which influence HSC behavior following significant bone marrow (BM) injury, such as sublethal irradiation (SLI). Methods: Conditional knock-out of follistatin-like 1 (FSTL-1) was achieved by breeding mice with floxed Fstl1 sites to mice expressing CreERT2 under control of the ROSA locus, followed by systemic tamoxifen administration. ELISA and RT-PCR quantitated protein and RNA level loss of FSTL-1, respectively. HSC populations were assessed by flow cytometry under multiple conditions. Sublethal irradiation induced BM injury and blocking polyclonal FSTL-1 antibodies were used to recapitulate results seen with genetic ablation. Finally, single cell RNA sequencing defined both cell-specific expression of Fstl1 within the BM compartment, but also identified transcripts and pathways upregulated in the absence of FSTL-1. Results: These studies delineate a novel role for FSTL-1 in regulating HSC biology. In addition to selective expression of Fstl1 within HSCs, genetic deletion of Fstl1 increases Lineage negative;Sca-1+c-Kit+ (LSK) cell number and alters HSC homeostasis. These findings are further amplified in the BM in the context of recovery from sublethal irradiation. Importantly, the post-irradiation increase in BM cellularity seen with Fstl1 deletion is replicated by treatment with anti-FSTL-1 polyclonal antibodies. Finally, single cell RNA sequencing reveals distinct Fstl1 expression in specific LSK subpopulations, including HSCs and proliferating cells, and identifies a novel relationship between decreased FSTL-1 levels and enrichment of canonical metabolic pathways including oxidative phosphorylation, fatty acid metabolism, and glycolysis. Conclusions: Taken together, these results highlight a novel role for FSTL-1 in promoting HSC homeostasis. They also unlock an innovative way to promote HSPC recovery following BM injury, knowledge predicted to be of significant therapeutic value.
affiliations: University of Minnesota (corresponding author)

papers.title: A tissue-targeted auxin-inducible degradation toolkit for C. elegans embryogenesis
papers.abstract: Many proteins required for embryogenesis are expressed in multiple tissues and across developmental time, often with tissue- and stage-specific roles. To resolve where and when proteins function, we developed a tissue-targeted auxin-inducible degradation toolkit for C. elegans embryogenesis. We generated a plasmid set compatible with single-copy insertion or high-copy extrachromosomal array generation that employs tissue-specific promoters (active in the germline, intestine, muscle, pharynx, neuroblasts, neurons, sensory neurons, epidermis, and pan soma) to drive an operon expressing an optimized auxin-dependent plant F-box factor TIR1 and, in most cases, a fluorescent histone. Using a ubiquitous nuclear envelope marker as a test substrate, we identified single-copy insertions and arrays that exhibit efficient auxin-dependent, tissue-specific target degradation. We also establish a workflow that ensures all functionally important isoforms of a target are tagged and that degradation reproduces the loss-of-function phenotype prior to tissue-specific analysis. Applying the toolkit to the broadly expressed Rho kinase LET-502, we find that degradation in the epidermis, but not in other embryonic tissues, disrupts elongation. Unexpectedly, temporal analysis revealed that LET-502 is required for late as well as early elongation.
affiliations: University of California San Diego (corresponding author)

papers.title: CDX2 Drives Divergent Regional Programs During Intestinal Development and Redeploys Them During Regeneration
papers.abstract: Region-specific transcription factors (TFs) establish small intestinal and colonic identity, yet what activates their region-specific expression during development is unresolved. Moreover, discrete fetal gene sets reactivate during post-injury regeneration, but their full scope, and what reactivates the programs required to restore regional identity and tissue structure, remain unclear. By determining CDX2 and partner TF binding, enhancer activity, and gene expression dynamics across intestinal regions, in stem and differentiating cells, and through development and adult regeneration, here we show that CDX2, despite uniform expression across the fetal and adult intestinal epithelium, organizes a hierarchical enhancer network. This network cooperates with partner factors such as CTCF to establish a shared, plastic fetal enhancer landscape, which resolves into region-specific programs upstream of regional TFs. During regeneration, rather than reactivating a general fetal state, CDX2 selectively rebinds many region-specific and common enhancers for genes associated with fetal cell-motility and tissue-morphogenesis signatures along with a more recently active adult stem-cell program, each deployed across distinct crypt tiers. CDX2 thus functions as a central, context-responsive regulator, deploying fetal, adult stem-cell differentiation, and regenerative programs as tissue context requires.
affiliations: University of Southern California (corresponding author)

papers.title: Exploring the substrate specificity and catalytic mechanism in a PAPS independent ASST from Salmonella typhimurium
papers.abstract: Sulfation plays an important role in many metabolic processes such as substrate detoxification, solubilization or activation. The enzymes responsible for these reactions, sulfotransferases, occur in all domains of life and can be classified in two major, evolutionary independent groups, PAPS dependent and PAPS independent or arysulfate sulfotransferases (ASST) enzymes. Besides the fact that they play key roles in biological functions, sulfotransferases can be interesting enzymatic tools to selectively sulfate specific positions of various metabolites. To this end we need to understand the relation between sequence, structure and function. Actually, eukaryotic PAPS dependent sulfotransferases have extensively been studied, while we largely lack knowledge about the diversity of bacterial PAPS-independent ASSTs. We have conducted a multidisciplinary study of a bacterial sulfotransferase from Salmonella typhimurium, revealing the importance of active site residues for activity and guiding substrate specificity. Based on the crystal structure in complex with substrate, we used molecular docking combined with Quantum Mechanics/Molecular Mechanics (QM/MM) free energy calculations to investigate the reaction catalytic mechanism with a focus on the role of specific active site residues in substrate specificity. Our results show that the catalytic mechanism involving three conserved histidines is common with previously determined ASSTs, and highlight a specific pair of aromatic residues, Phe174 and Tyr557, that play an important role in defining the substrate specificity in ASST clade 5. These findings enhance our general understanding of how substrate specificity is attained and has the potential to guide further enzyme engineering to expand the acceptor scope of ASSTs.
affiliations: Nantes University, CNRS, US2B, UMR 6286, F-44000 Nantes, France (corresponding author)

papers.title: Photobiocatalytic Diastereo- and Enantioselective Synthesis of Non-Canonical Amino Acids Bearing Challenging Stereochemical Dyads and Triads
papers.abstract: Catalyst-controlled stereodivergent synthesis of acyclic molecules bearing multiple stereogenic centers remains a longstanding challenge in asymmetric catalysis, particularly through intermolecular radical C-C coupling. Here, we report the directed evolution of pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP)-dependent biocatalysts for the stereodivergent synthesis of non canonical amino acids bearing either skipped , {gamma}-stereochemical dyads or contiguous , {beta}, {gamma}-stereochemical triads. Starting from a thermophilic tryptophan synthase {beta}-subunit, protein engineering generated complementary enzyme variants that selectively construct three of the four possible , {gamma}-stereoisomers through biocatalyst-controlled reversal of both remote {gamma}-stereochemistry and proximal -stereochemistry. These engineered enzymes catalyzed intermolecular radical C-C bond formation with a broad range of secondary alkyltrifluoroborates, affording , {gamma}-disubstituted amino acids in excellent yields and stereoselectivities. Furthermore, directed evolution enabled efficient {beta}-dehydroxylative radical coupling of the non-native threonine-derived aminoacrylate intermediate, providing amino acids bearing contiguous , {beta}, {gamma}-stereochemical triads with up to 96:4: 99:1 e.r.. To further demonstrate the synthetic utility of this platform, the stereochemically enriched amino acids were transformed into valuable {gamma}-chiral amines through engineered PLP dependent tryptophan decarboxylases, establishing a dual PLP enzyme based biocatalytic cascade for the enantiodivergent synthesis of privileged amine scaffolds. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that enzyme controlled {gamma}-stereoselectivity originates from active-site remodeling that modulates {pi}-{pi} interactions and steric contacts governing the facial selectivity of the radical addition step. This work expands the synthetic capabilities of radical biocatalysis by enabling catalyst-controlled stereodivergent assembly of complex acyclic stereochemical arrays and establishes engineered PLP enzymes as versatile catalysts for the synthesis of stereochemically complex amino acids and chiral amines.

papers.title: Repurposing dopamine D3 receptor fluorescent ligands for D2 receptor
papers.abstract: The dopamine D2 receptor is a principal target of antipsychotic and antiparkinsonian drugs, yet well-characterized fluorescent ligands for the D2 receptor remain scarce compared with its relative, the D3 receptor. Here we show that fluorescent ligands developed for the D3 subtype can be repurposed as tools for studying the D2 receptor pharmacology. Using a machine-learning-assisted, live-cell fluorescence microscopy assay, we screened twelve fluorescent probes and identified eight ligands that bound specifically to the D2 receptor at 10 nM. Four ligands exhibited classical saturable binding, yielding Kd in the nanomolar range, whereas the remaining probes displayed unsaturated, time-dependent binding profiles. Kinetic analyses revealed substantial differences in association and dissociation behavior, highlighting the importance of time-resolved measurements. Competition binding with dopamine and haloperidol yielded affinity estimates consistent with literature values. These results expand the toolkit of validated D2 receptor fluorescent probes and support cross-receptor repurposing as a strategy for fluorescent ligand development.

papers.title: KRAKEN: A provenance-tracked knowledge graph for multiomic and wellness research
papers.abstract: Existing general-purpose biomedical knowledge graphs tend to focus on disease mechanisms and drug repurposing, leaving multiomic and wellness-relevant content underrepresented. KRAKEN (Knowledge Research & Analysis Kit for Evidence Networks) addresses this gap by integrating existing graphs (including Translator KG Open, RTX-KG2, and ROBOKOP) with specialized sources such as RefMet, LIPID MAPS, NIH Common Data Elements, Polygenic Score Catalog, and derived wellness measures including biological age and biological BMI. The resulting graph spans ~26M nodes and ~121M edges across 62 entity types. KRAKEN adopts the Biolink Model as its semantic layer, ensuring compatibility with standardized resources emerging from the NIH NCATS Biomedical Data Translator program. A lightweight, modular build system rebuilds the full graph (including entity resolution), with peak memory consumption under 48 GB, and supports flexible inclusion or exclusion of sources, allowing the user to scope the graph to a domain of interest. Built-in analytical tools include multi-hop reasoning, subgraph extraction, text, vector and hybrid entity search, and enrichment analyses, all accessible through an interactive web interface, a REST API, and a Model Context Protocol server, the last enabling direct consumption by agentic and LLM-based systems. KRAKEN is freely available at https://app.krakenkg.com.
affiliations: Phenome Health (corresponding author)

papers.title: A permeable G310 constriction limits K+ flux in the activated KCNQ2 pore and is disrupted by the encephalopathy variant G310S
papers.abstract: KCNQ2 (Kv7.2) subunits contribute to the channels that carry the neuronal M-current, and variants in KCNQ2 cause epilepsies that range from self-limited neonatal seizures to developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE). Structures of KCNQ2 bound to PIP2 and cannabidiol show a widened activation gate, yet it has remained unclear which point of the activated pore limits K+ flux and how DEE variants at that point act. We simulated the KCNQ2 pore domain (PDB 8J01) in a POPC bilayer under an applied field of about 565 mV, restraining only the terminal residues of S5 and S6 so that G310 and S314 were free. The activated pore conducted K+ at 4.3 pS (95% CI 2.5-6.9; 17 net filter crossings in 1120 ns over four replicas), while the closed-state pore (PDB 7CR3) conducted none in 560 ns. Conduction proceeded by knock-on through a filter that was doubly occupied in 84-92% of frames. Along S6 the narrowest position of the activated pore was not the canonical gate residue S314 but the glycine of the Pro-Ala-Gly motif, G310: activation widens S314 by 0.37 nm but G310 by only 0.07 nm, and restraining G310 to its closed-state width in one replica abolished gate crossings. The DEE variant G310S reduced conduction about six-fold (G310S/wild-type ratio 0.16, 95% CI 0.02-0.66; p = 0.003). Its serine hydroxyls project into the constriction and halve the water column in the G310 plane (8.7 to 4.7 waters), an effect reproduced in CHARMM36m (9.9 to 4.3). The first coordination shell of a K+ ion at the constriction was, however, conserved (6.3 vs 6.5 oxygens), because the serine hydroxyls replace the waters they displace. The hydroxyls did not retain the ion: contacts lasted tens of picoseconds, and ions were instead turned back at the serine ring, fewer reaching the gate plane (45 vs 79 excursions per microsecond) and fewer of those crossing it (5% vs 23%). In mixed tetramers carrying one or two variant subunits the effect on the water column was additive, each subunit removing about a quarter of it (f = 0.22 and 0.58 of the full effect). These results identify G310 as the flux-limiting constriction of the activated KCNQ2 pore in our simulations and point to a permeation defect as one component of G310S loss of function.

papers.title: Adaptive motility and feeding strategies of deep-branching predatory protists
papers.abstract: Heterotrophic flagellates play a major role in nutrient recycling and shaping aquatic microbial communities. Many motile species have evolved diverse predatory strategies to exploit microbial prey, from bacteria to small eukaryotes. Excavates, deep-branching eukaryotic lineages with distinctive biflagellate morphology and conserved cytoskeletal features, exhibit varied feeding behaviours, including grazing, raptorial feeding, and filter-feeding. However, the temporal dynamics of their motility, feeding, and spatial distribution in relation to bacterial population density remain under-explored. Here, we quantify the behavioural ecology of excavates using high-resolution, single-cell tracking and quantitative analysis. Focussing on two Discoba species - the marine Jakoba libera and freshwater Reclinomonas americana - we identify different behavioural patterns: J. libera swims, forages and feeds, while R. americana swims and feeds. Prey availability differentially affects motility: J. libera increases the number of swimming cells when food is scarce, while R. americana shows the opposite trend. Spatial statistics reveal fundamental differences in their feeding and redistribution strategies. J. libera acts as an active forager, whereas R. americana behaves as a strict filter feeder. A third species, the anaerobic Kipferlia bialata (from a different clade), adopts a foraging strategy similar to J. libera. Together, these results elucidate the adaptive relationship between prey availability, feeding modes, and motility in bacteriovorous excavate flagellates, offering new insights into the ecological and evolutionary dynamics of microbial predators.

papers.title: Direct visualization of lysosome-mediated intracellular transport and membrane anchoring of TNF-α in human T cells
papers.abstract: Tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-) represents a major pro-inflammatory cytokine associated with chronic inflammation. Enhanced understanding of intracellular trafficking of TNF- enables the identification of drug targets that modulate TNF- secretion at the cellular source. However, conventional cytokine assays provide only bulk measurements of secreted TNF- or static measurements in fixed cells and therefore cannot provide mechanistic information. Here, we report a fluorescence imaging platform to visualize and quantify intracellular TNF- trafficking in human T cells. Using a Jurkat T cell line stably expressing TNF- fused to mStayGold as a model system, we revealed through single-particle tracking (SPT) that T cell activation increased the motility of TNF- vesicles and that microtubule perturbation disrupted this increased motility. 3D structured illumination microscopy uncovered spatial associations between TNF- vesicles and lysosomes, and SPT further demonstrated their coordinated transport. Using total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy, we captured the sub-second splitting of single TNF- vesicles into multiple puncta that subsequently separated, suggesting delivery of TNF- from the vesicle to the plasma membrane. Confocal-based super-resolution microscopy further resolved TNF- vesicles fusing with the plasma membrane and transmembrane TNF-. Together, these imaging capabilities for tracking and super-resolving the intracellular transport and membrane delivery of TNF- in live T cells enable mechanistic studies of TNF- trafficking and release.
affiliations: University of Illinois Chicago (corresponding author)

papers.title: Membrane Filtration Removes Lipids and Compromises the Acoustic Stability of Nanobubbles
papers.abstract: Nanobubbles (NBs) have been widely investigated as ultrasound contrast and therapeutic agents, yet whether submicron gas bubbles can directly generate measurable ultrasound signals remains controversial. Because acoustic scattering scales with bubble size, several studies have recently attributed nanobubble echogenicity primarily to larger bubbles. A recent Science Advances publication, attributed the loss of ultrasound signal after filtration to the removal of residual larger bubbles [1]. This interpretation assumes that filtration acts solely as a size-selection process. Here, we show that filtration also alters the shell properties and stability of lipid-coated NBs, independent of size. Filtered NBs (F-NBs) show significant lipid loss and accumulation on the filters themselves, resulting in decreased bubble stability and greater susceptibility to destruction under acoustic excitation. To decouple size from processing effects, we generated NB populations size-matched to filtered samples using increased centrifugation (IC-NBs), a comparatively gentler separation method. Despite comparable size distributions, IC-NBs retained sustained ultrasound scattering, whereas filtered NBs showed significantly reduced acoustic persistence. Filtration through 5 m pores, ~5-fold larger than the largest bubbles, preserved acoustic persistence but still reduced bubble concentration by ~30%, suggesting that membrane contact may contribute to bubble loss beyond size exclusion. Complementary lipid and gas-content assays provided further evidence of filtration-induced changes. The 0.45 m filtration removed substantially more total lipid than could be attributed to free-lipid removal alone, while the lipid associated with the larger bubbles removed during filtration accounted for only ~5% of the additional lipid loss. Encapsulated gas content remained comparable to that of size-matched centrifuged controls, suggesting that the reduced acoustic stability of filtered NBs is more closely associated with changes in lipid content than with loss of the gas core. These results indicate that membrane filtration is not a purely size-selective process: it removes substantially more lipid than size exclusion predicts and yields bubbles that are less stable under ultrasound, most likely through changes in shell lipid content or in the surrounding lipid reservoir, underscoring the importance of processing-induced effects in interpreting nanobubble echogenicity.
