papers.title: Anneal-MaxCal: kinetic ensembles from a Markov model learned along a solute-tempering ladder
papers.abstract: A full characterisation of a molecular system requires its metastable states, their populations and their interconversion rates. Molecular Dynamics can in principle provide this characterisation but is limited by sampling and by force-field inaccuracies. Enhanced sampling addresses the first problem, but typically requires prior knowledge of reaction coordinates or metastable states and often sacrifices the kinetics, while maximum-caliber reweighting by Brotzakis, Vendruscolo and Bolhuis [Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A., 118(2):e2012423118, 2021] has been implemented to that matter on reweighting continuous pathways by imposing rate constants as kinetic constraints in two-state protein folding. Here, we introduce Anneal-MaxCal, which tackles both problems by imposing rate constants or time-resolved data on a Markov model learned along an annealed solute-tempering ladder spanning softer to physical interactions. MBAR assigns physical free energies to all 160 cells of a slow TICA subspace, against 79 visited at the physical coupling. The square-root approximation (SqRA), a discretised diffusion on this free-energy landscape, converts these populations into a detailed-balance rate matrix. Its prefactors, which act as a position-dependent diffusivity across each cell face, are learned from transitions at the softer couplings and extrapolated log-linearly to the physical coupling. This yields rates and a committor across the TICA space, although the physical rung contains a single barrier crossing. For alanine dipeptide, 665 ns of simulation give a relaxation time of 5430 {+/-} 996 ps against 4413 {+/-} 446 ps from 15.4 s of unbiased dynamics, whereas a constant prefactor is 2.5 times too slow. Maximum caliber then minimally perturbs this prior, with the posterior populations following from a generalised Doob transform. A synthetic time-resolved density with a tenfold slower back-transition lowers {Delta}F from 5.191 to 2.885 kBT , raises the product-basin population from 0.0055 to 0.0529 and slows relaxation 9.47-fold, leaving the reactant basin unchanged. Forward and backward rates accelerated 3 and 20-fold raise {Delta}F by 1.892 kBT and shorten relaxation from 4818 to 289 ps.

papers.title: Blockiness as Determinant of Liquid Phase Formation by Polypeptide-Like Polymers in Stickers-Spacers Paradigm
papers.abstract: Liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) driven by intrinsically disordered protein regions underlies the formation of membraneless organelles. The role of these structures in cell biology is an active area of research, yet their physical understanding remains less developed than that of protein assemblies with well-defined, rigid tertiary structures. The amino acid composition of disordered regions, particularly the abundance of charged residues, is known to modulate phase behavior. These factors govern accessible conformations, the assembly of compact sticker clusters, and the porosity of the resulting polymer networks. In contrast, the spatial distribution of side-chain volumes remains a comparatively understudied sequence determinant. Here, we employ a model that captures the patterning of side-chain volumes and interaction strengths without specifying chemical identity to show how sequence blockiness modulates the phase-nucleation propensity, connectivity, and compactness of polypeptide-like polymer assemblies. Using a library of polymers with identical composition but permuted residue arrangements, we show that clustering of bulky residues generates cooperative sticker domains and identify the threshold blockiness required to stabilize polymer networks. Coarse-grained simulations and mean-field theory reveal that this effect arises from an interplay among steric repulsion, solvent entropy, and higher-valency interactions, whereby blocky patterns promote the formation of multi-node percolated networks. Segregation of stickers and spacers is therefore one of the sequence parameters governing LLPS which may be useful for interpreting the evolution of disordered protein sequences, high-throughput proteome screening, and engineering of stimuli-responsive biomaterials. These rules may be exploited to predetermine condensate stability, viscoelasticity, and molecular exchange rates without altering chemical functionality.

papers.title: Mathematical Modelling of Stochastic Gene Expression Quantifies mRNA Heterogeneity in Cancer Cell Populations with Extrachromosomal DNA
papers.abstract: Oncogene amplification on circular extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA) has been linked to poor prognosis and higher treatment resistance in multiple types of human cancer. ecDNA are mobile genetic elements lacking centromeres that are partitioned unevenly into daughter cells at mitosis. While random segregation of ecDNA contributes to gene-copy-number heterogeneity among tumour cells, how ecDNA contribute to phenotypic heterogeneity, via mRNA and proteins, and how this affects targeted therapy outcomes is still not understood. In fact, cancer cell populations with ecDNA show remarkable heterogeneity in mRNA concentrations, which is not explained by gene-copy-number heterogeneity alone. In this paper, we use a stochastic model of gene transcription to mathematically model mRNA production and decay in cancer cells with ecDNA, extending a method that has been used to study phenotypic heterogeneity in eurokaryotic and prokaryotic cells. Using our model, we explore the space of possible mRNA distributions from a given ecDNA distribution, under different model parameter regimes. Our model is able to produce realistic mRNA distributions and we use it to estimate transcriptional parameters from single-cell measurements of ecDNA and mRNA counts in cell-line data. We discover a remarkable similarity in estimated parameters across cell lines and amplification types, indicating similar processes underlying transcription in ecDNA and chromosomal amplifications. We also model genotoxic therapy and use our model to predict the mRNA composition of persisting cells, showing the usefulness of such a modelling framework to understanding the origins of treatment resistance in ecDNA-containing cancers.
affiliations: Queen Mary University of London (corresponding author)

papers.title: PIK-75 suppresses an SREBP-centred sterol programme in PIK3CA-altered small-cell lung cancer cells, but attribution to p110α remains unresolved
papers.abstract: Abstract: Background. Class IA PI3K isoforms are candidate therapeutic targets in small-cell lung cancer (SCLC). The transcriptional consequences of isoform-directed inhibitors in SCLC cells have not been compared genome-wide. Methods. We re-analysed GEO series GSE40564: PIK3CA-altered NCI-H69 cells treated for 24 h with vehicle, PIK-75 (p110-directed) or TGX-221 (p110{beta}-directed), three arrays per group (Affymetrix HG-U133 Plus 2.0). Differential expression used limma, with re-processing from raw files and spike-in-anchored normalisation as sensitivity analyses. Gene sets were assessed by effect size, competitive and rotation tests, and size-matched random-set nulls. Isoform dependency was examined in DepMap CRISPR screens. A PIK-75 response score was tested in 81 primary SCLCs against random-signature nulls. Results. PIK-75 reduced SREBP-controlled sterol- and lipid-synthesis genes (SQLE, HMGCS1, HMGCR, LDLR, SCD; log2 fold-change -1.1 to -1.6). Cholesterol, mTORC1, hypoxia and glycolysis gene sets fell far more than size-matched random sets. E2F-target and homologous-repair genes fell more modestly, including BRCA1 (-0.91). The response was broad: 11,645 of 17,458 genes changed at FDR < 0.05, but only 316 decreased and 20 increased significantly beyond two-fold, an asymmetry that persisted under spike-in-anchored normalisation. TGX-221 changed 358 genes, none two-fold. Its set-level effects were four- to nine-fold smaller and depended on two of three replicates. PIK-75 did not induce canonical FOXO targets, and it inhibits kinases other than p110, so the response cannot be attributed to p110 alone. In DepMap, SCLC lines depended more on PIK3CA than on PIK3CB (median Chronos -0.38 vs -0.15), as did other lineages. In patients, the response score was not associated with survival or subtype beyond what random gene signatures achieve (empirical p = 0.14 and 0.11). Conclusion. PIK-75, but not TGX-221, suppresses an SREBP-centred anabolic transcriptional programme in NCI-H69 cells. Attributing this to p110 requires confirmation with selective inhibitors or genetic perturbation.
affiliations: Mashhad University of Medical Sciences (corresponding author)

papers.title: Epstein-Barr virus co-opts ADAR1 to evade PKR activation of the integrated stress response in nasopharyngeal carcinoma
papers.abstract: Viruses generate immunogenic double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) during their life cycle, necessitating mechanisms to evade host innate immune detection. Protein kinase R (PKR) is a pattern recognition receptor (PRR) that senses viral dsRNA and activates the host integrated stress response (ISR) by phosphorylating eukaryotic initiation factor 2 (eIF2) on its alpha subunit, causing global mRNA translation arrest. Viruses evade activation of the ISR and translation shut-down to facilitate replication. Adenosine deaminase acting on RNA 1 (ADAR1) is uniquely positioned to support viral replication due to its ability to convert adenosine (A) into inosine (I) inside dsRNA, thereby disrupting base-pair matching and preventing PKR activation. Here, we discovered that Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), the oncogenic driver of nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC), requires ADAR1 both to maintain latent infection and for lytic reactivation by preventing PKR-mediated ISR activation. EBV lytic reactivation stimulated viral protein expression, which was attenuated in the absence of ADAR1. Importantly, lytic reactivation or treatment of synthetic dsRNA in the absence of ADAR1 induced phosphorylation of eIF2 by PKR, stress granule formation, and caused cancer cell lethality without the production of virion progeny. Together these findings support a strategy for EBV lytic induction therapy in NPC without viral dissemination by exposing EBV to endogenous PRRs through ADAR1 inhibition.
affiliations: Cancer Research Malaysia (corresponding author)

papers.title: Pheno-MYCN maps the morphological footprint of MYCN amplification in paediatric neuroblastoma
papers.abstract: MYCN amplification and segmental chromosomal abnormalities have long been prognostic markers in paediatric neuroblastoma, and are often accompanied by morphological changes that portend high-risk disease. Yet quantitative morphological assessment is limited to countable features, such as the mitosis-karyorrhexis index. Other high-risk features, such as nuclear size, pleomorphism and anaplasia, lack formal criteria. This leaves a gap: current simple pathology metrics cannot capture, or localise, the full morphological landscape of high-risk biology, such as disease driven by MYCN. Seeking high-risk cases that standard criteria may miss, we developed Pheno-MYCN, a weakly supervised framework linking slide-level MYCN prediction on 189 H&E whole-slide images to interpretable phenotypic sub-populations that expert review mapped to neuroblastoma morphologies. The aim is not a stronger classifier, but to reveal the morphological basis of MYCN prediction. Cell-level profiling found MYCN-associated differences across sub-populations. Amplified tumour was densely cellular but disorganised, with less connected networks, lower cellular diversity and greater abundance of haemorrhagic and acellular necrotic regions. MYCN-amplified-like tissue was identifiable per slide from these features alone (AUC 0.93-1.00, leave-one-slide-out) and traced as a continuous gradient within tumours. Thus MYCN amplification leaves a concrete, interpretable footprint, readable and localisable on routine H&E.
affiliations: The Institute of Cancer Research (corresponding author)

papers.title: Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus Whole-Genome Diversity Reveals Divergence of Contemporary Populations in the United States
papers.abstract: Porcine epidemic diarrhea virus (PEDV) was introduced into the United States (USA) in 2013 and has circulated ever since. PEDV causes significant losses in the swine industry, with the greatest impact observed during the first years following its introduction into the country. However, the evolutionary dynamics of the virus remain underexplored. Recently, analyses of the Spike protein subunit S1 suggested that the PEDV population currently circulating in the USA represents a fraction of its historical diversity and comprises only two clades restricted to specific geographic regions. These observations were based on a limited set of S1 sequences. Furthermore, our understanding of evolutionary dynamics at the genomic level is even more limited, as complete PEDV genomes have not been generated since 2017. Here, we characterized the evolutionary dynamics of PEDV populations in the USA using complete genomes and assessed the contribution of different evolutionary mechanisms to shaping population structure. We analyzed 338 complete genomes, of which 25 were obtained in this study, together with 623 Spike S1 sequences, of which 41 were obtained in this study. All sequences obtained in this study were assigned to the non-S-INDEL strain. No S-INDEL sequences were recovered in this study, although these viruses continue to circulate in the country. Our analyses revealed that most sequences sampled after 2023 formed a monophyletic clade divergent from sequences collected in previous years, suggesting an ongoing temporal population structuring. Population structure analyses further supported evidence of population differentiation over time. Recombination analyses indicated that sequences belonging to the contemporary clade shared a single recombination event, suggesting that this clade may have emerged through recombination. Time-scaled S1 phylogenies were consistent with previous findings, supporting the circulation of only two contemporary clades; however, one of these clades was detected for the first time outside its previously reported geographic range. Our findings document temporal genetic differentiation in US PEDV populations, consistent with continued viral evolution, and broaden the known geographic distribution of contemporary S1 clades. These results highlight the value of continued genomic surveillance to monitor changes in PEDV diversity and distribution and provide sequence data to inform vaccine research.
affiliations: University of Minnesota (corresponding author)

papers.title: MacroH2A1 and H3K27me3 target cGAS to facultative heterochromatin to restrain innate immune activation
papers.abstract: The DNA sensor cGAS is largely sequestered on chromatin in an inactive form, but how this state is regulated remains unclear. We show that cGAS preferentially binds nucleosomes containing the histone variant macroH2A1 (mH2A1) marked by H3K27me3 and H3K9me3. Cryo-EM reveals that cGAS selectively engages the mH2A1/H2B acidic patch within heterotypic nucleosomes. Depleting mH2A1.1 or blocking H3K27me3 deposition releases cGAS from chromatin and activates the cGAS-STING-IRF3 pathway. Genome-wide profiling reveals two cGAS-bound chromatin compartments: chromosome-arm sites co-occupied by mH2A1.1, methylated CpG islands, and CTCF, where cGAS and mH2A1.1 binding are interdependent; and centromeric regions (14% of peaks), which lack DNA methylation and mH2A1.1 dependence. These findings establish mH2A1 and H3K27me3 as determinants of cGAS chromatin tethering, linking nuclear cGAS regulation to facultative heterochromatin and opening new avenues for modulating cGAS-STING signaling.
affiliations: Institut de Genetique Humaine, Laboratoire de Virologie Moleculaire CNRS Universite de Montpellier, Montpellier, France (corresponding author)

papers.title: SatelliteQ: an open-source workflow for multidimensional, object-based quantification of centriolar satellites
papers.abstract: Centriolar satellites are membrane-less organelles that store, modify and traffic proteins, in particular those of the centrosome and the primary cilium, and their deregulation is linked to ciliopathies, neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorders. Satellite number, size, intensity and spatial distribution vary with cell type and cell state, yet satellites are usually quantified by a single readout, the pericentrosomal fluorescence intensity in maximum-projected images, which cannot distinguish changes in satellite number, size and position. Here we present SatelliteQ, an open-source Fiji and Python workflow for object-based quantification of satellites in 2D, 3D and time-lapse images. SatelliteQ segments satellites, detects centrosomes or primary cilia in the same cells, and reports satellite number, size, intensity, distance to the centrosome, shape and spatial distribution per satellite and per cell, with interactive graph and spatial viewers. Its measurements correlate closely with Imaris-based quantification; absolute values depend on segmentation settings and analysis mode, whereas the biological differences tested here were preserved across matched settings. Using SatelliteQ, we resolved distinct spatial signatures of satellite dispersal induced by microtubule depolymerization and by disruption of weak hydrophobic interactions, quantified differences between cell types and the scaling of satellite number with cell size, captured PCM1 granule dynamics in living cells, and compared satellite organization between ciliated and unciliated cells. Depletion of the ciliopathy-associated satellite protein CEP290 altered satellite abundance and pericentrosomal organization, while patient-derived cells carrying CEP290 mutations displayed divergent satellite phenotypes that were not explained by ciliation alone. SatelliteQ thus establishes satellite properties as a multidimensional cellular phenotype and provides an accessible framework for exploring satellites as an organelle-level readout in disease.
affiliations: Koc University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Force Induces a Collective Inactivity in Dyneins to Auto-Regulate Bidirectional Transport of Vesicles
papers.abstract: The back-and-forth (bidirectional) motion of Endosomes and Phagosomes along microtubules is fundamentally important for nutrient absorption, receptor recycling, pathogen degradation and many other downstream cellular pathways. Bidirectional motion requires opposing force from the kinesin and dynein motors, causing intermittent Tug-of-Wars (ToWs) followed by runs where winning motors drive their cargo until the next ToW. Dynein displays a counter-intuitive behaviour of catch bonding tightly to the microtubule against opposing force, but why such a response is needed remains unknown. Here we force dynein to catch-bond using an optical trap when dynein-teams are transporting phagosomes in-vitro and inside cells. An unexpected form of collective inactivity emerges, where larger dynein-teams remain inactive for longer after they have been catch-bonded. Kinesin exhibits a high probability of reversing the cargo during such periods of inactivity of dyneins. Therefore, the inactivity of dyneins allows cells to auto-regulate the effect of opposing molecular forces for the purpose of achieving bidirectional motion of endosomes/phagosomes. We propose that an inactivating conformational change is induced when dynein detaches against strain from its catch-bonded state. Collective inactivity follows because each inactive dynein exerts an entropic force on the other to delay the entire team from being activated. We capture the dynamics of this process through a statistical model of Entropically Constrained Reactivation, obtaining predictions in excellent agreement with experimental data. The emergent behaviour observed here possibly prevents a runaway dynein situation inside cells, its simple entropic origin suggesting broader relevance to catch-bonded receptor ligand interactions operating under conditions of cellular crowding.
affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology Bombay (corresponding author)

papers.title: A cellular atlas of Astyanax mexicanus embryogenesis reveals principles of developmental microevolution
papers.abstract: The evolution of development is the primary mechanism by which morphological and functional diversity is generated. Comparing the developmental trajectories of single cells in entire embryos across species can reveal how gene expression is conserved and varies, as well as the molecular mechanisms underlying how cell- and tissue-specific changes in developmental regulation generate phenotypic differences. However, this perspective has not addressed the mechanisms of small-scale developmental microevolution, i.e, in closely-related species or even within a single species. The fish Astyanax mexicanus, which comes in two forms adapted to distinct environments - the eyed, river-dwelling morph and the eyeless, cave-adapted morph - is a remarkable model with which to investigate the evolution of gene regulation in a single species. Here, we generated and analyzed a single-nucleus RNA-seq atlas of the development of the two Astyanax morphs, from gastrula to swimming larva. Despite extensive changes in gene expression observed in the eight examined stages, for both ubiquitously-expressed and tissue-specific genes, and in both embryonic and extra-embryonic tissues, the temporal progression of cavefish and surface fish cells was similar in ordinal regression-based pseudotime models using 20-100 core genes. However, transcriptome-wide comparisons of gene expression waves revealed massive heterochronic shifts. In cavefish, some tissues had a majority of genes lagging behind in their transcriptional dynamics (e.g. the optic region), while in others, a majority of genes had accelerated dynamics (e.g. the mesoderm), or else, an equivalent number of genes were found in either category (e.g. the endoderm). Furthermore, cell fate acquisition and differentiation were variably affected in different cavefish lineages, with delays of ~6 hours in the retina, ~2 hours in the axial mesoderm and ~none in the extra-embryonic enveloping layer. Thus, cavefish embryos progress as a mosaic of different tissues, or modules, each following its own transcriptional tempo. Because gene expression differential regulation and time shifts were more prevalent in the early stages and gradually diminished throughout development, we propose that cavefish embryos initially undergo strong decanalisation before becoming re-canalized in line with the shared Astyanax developmental program.
affiliations: Paris-Saclay Institute of Neuroscience, CNRS and University Paris-Saclay (corresponding author)

papers.title: The Batten disease gene product CLN6 is a glycerophosphoglycerol epimerase that establishes S,S-BMP stereochemistry
papers.abstract: Bis(monoacylglycero)phosphate (BMP), a lysosomal phospholipid essential for lipid catabolism and cholesterol clearance, has a noncanonical S,S glycerol configuration found in no other mammalian phospholipid, a feature necessary for its stability in the lysosome. How cells invert glycerol stereochemistry to build S,S-BMP has remained unexplained since this configuration was discovered five decades ago. Here, we show that the endoplasmic reticulum-resident Batten disease protein CLN6 is a Ca2+-dependent epimerase that isomerizes glycerophosphoglycerol (GPG) from R,S-GPG to S,S-GPG. CLN6-deficient cells, mouse tissues, and patient samples predominantly contain R,S-GPG, S,R-lysophosphatidylglycerol (LPG), and R,S-BMP instead of their S,S counterparts, with a net depletion of BMP. Purified CLN6 catalyzes GPG epimerization in vitro, an activity abolished by a pathogenic substitution in its substrate-binding pocket. Consistently, exogenous S,S-GPG restores BMP synthesis and relieves lipid storage in CLN6-null cells. Our work establishes stereochemical commitment upstream of acylation, placing CLN6, CLN8, and CLN5 in sequence in BMP biosynthesis and unifying the lipid defect across these neurodegenerative disorders.
affiliations: Stanford University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Cancer-associated mutations reconfigure dynamical responses in EGFR kinase
papers.abstract: The epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is a tyrosine kinase receptor that plays a fundamental role in regulating cellular proliferation, survival, and differentiation. EGFR's kinase domain catalyses the autophosphorylation that drives downstream signalling and is a known hotspot for cancer-associated mutations. Such substitutions often enhance receptor activation, driving oncogenesis and therapeutic resistance, with major implications for prognosis and treatment choice; consequently, a detailed understanding of this domain's functional dynamics, and how mutations reshape them, is essential. Here, we apply dynamical-nonequilibrium molecular dynamics (D-NEMD) simulations to probe how changes at the ATP-binding site are transmitted throughout the kinase domain, ultimately shaping the behaviour of distal regions in the wild-type protein and in two of the most clinically observed non-small cell lung cancer variants, L858R and L858R+T790M. D-NEMD reveals previously uncharacterised communication networks linking the ATP pocket to key functional motifs, including the P-loop, C-helix, hinge region, activation loop, and F-helix, showing the intricate allosteric connectivity within this domain. Notably, numerous cancer-related mutation sites, despite being distant from the ATP site, map onto or lie close to these communication pathways, indicating that D-NEMD simulations can identify functionally relevant allosteric positions and potential mutation sites in EGFR. Our simulations further reveal that the two variants rewire EGFR's internal signal propagation network in distinct ways: L858R diminishes the transmission of structural changes to distal regions of the C-lobe, whereas introducing T790M in addition to L858R partially restores wild-type-like behaviour through compensatory rerouting of early-stage dynamical pathways.

papers.title: Single-molecule reaction chambers reveal intramolecular protein kinase activation
papers.abstract: Many protein kinases, ubiquitous signal transducers across all kingdoms of life, are activated by phosphorylation of one or more conserved residues in their activation loops. This reaction is widely considered to be intermolecular (trans) in nature, dependent on the transient dimerization of two kinase domains. However, since the substrate, product and reaction chemistry are identical, bulk solution kinase assays cannot distinguish between intra- and inter-molecular reactions. Discriminating between these two mechanisms is crucial because they impose different requirements on the cell for acute, high-fidelity signal transduction. Using single-molecule reaction chambers fabricated from DNA origami, we show that the paradigmatic insulin receptor kinase (IRK) undergoes intramolecular (cis) autophosphorylation with kinetics indistinguishable from those in free solution. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the bacterial serine/threonine kinase protein kinase B (PknB) undergoes intramolecular autophosphorylation, allosterically stimulated by intermolecular (trans) interactions. Our findings establish that intramolecular activation loop autophosphorylation is not only possible, but likely an ancient and conserved feature of protein kinase signaling. More broadly, our work provides new tools for single-molecule enzymology.

papers.title: A Practical Assay for Assessing Mean Red Blood Cell Age Using the Protein 4.1a/4.1b Ratio
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: The protein 4.1a/4.1b ratio is an intrinsic molecular marker of mean red blood cell (RBC) age resulting from progressive deamidation of protein 4.1b during RBC circulation. Despite its potential for estimating mean RBC age from a single blood sample, its application has been limited by labor-intensive RBC membrane preparation, and its interindividual variability has not been characterized in a large human population. METHODS: We developed a low-volume method for direct RBC membrane isolation from whole blood using saponin permeabilization and differential centrifugation without prior RBC washing. Membrane proteins were separated by SDS-PAGE, and protein 4.1a/4.1b ratios were determined by densitometric analysis with Gaussian peak fitting. Assay conditions, sample-volume requirements, membrane protein recovery, and analytical reproducibility were evaluated. The method was subsequently applied to 114 anonymized residual samples from routine diagnostic testing selected for complete blood count parameters within the corresponding laboratory reference intervals. RESULTS: The optimized procedure used 50 uL of whole blood, 0.06% saponin, and centrifugation at 9000 g, although protein 4.1a/4.1b remained measurable from starting volumes as low as 5 uL. Mean within-subject CVs were 3.90% for electrophoretic/densitometric determination and 5.39% for membrane protein recovery; whole-procedure CVs in 3 subjects were 1.40% to 3.50%. In the population analysis, the mean protein 4.1a/4.1b ratio was 1.428 (SD 0.146), with an observed range of 1.052 to1.799 and a central 95% interval of 1.151 to 1.695. Ratios did not differ significantly between females and males (P=0.246) or among females aged 18 to 50 years, females aged >50 years, and males (P=0.151). The ratio showed modest positive correlations with chronological age in females (Spearman p=0.26, P=0.047) and males (p=0.33, P=0.015), while substantial interindividual variability remained across the age range. CONCLUSIONS: Direct isolation of RBC membranes from small volumes of whole blood enables reproducible determination of the protein 4.1a/4.1b ratio using a simplified workflow. Application of the assay to a comparatively large human population revealed substantial interindividual variation in this molecular marker of mean RBC age that was not explained by sex or chronological age alone. The method provides a practical approach for investigating biological variation in mean RBC age and its potential contribution to laboratory measurements influenced by RBC survival.

papers.title: Biohybrid toggle switches: leveraging bistability in muscle-actuated machines
papers.abstract: Tissue-engineered skeletal muscle offers robotics unique advantages in energy density, adaptability, and self-repair, but current biohybrid machines couple muscle directly to artificial skeletons, limiting net force output and requiring continuous stimulation maintain mechanism positions. Here, we introduce a biohybrid bistable switching mechanism that converts antagonistic muscle contractions to snap-through actuation of an elastomeric four-bar flexure, maintaining stable positions without energy consumption. We decouple passive muscle pre-tensioning from flexure operation with thin-film elastomer resistance bands, enabling fine tuning of spring stiffness and force to match muscle mechanical output envelopes. Leveraging mesoscale additive manufacturing, spin coating, and replica molding techniques, components are integrated into a millimeter-scale linear stage to axially align muscles with artificial components. Our prototype achieves reversible toggling between bistable states with a 130 ms switching time, establishing skeletal muscle actuators as viable electromechanical switches, and broadening biohybrid robotics towards novel applications such as grippers, valves, and mechanical computers.

papers.title: Scalable fold-change estimation from microbial metagenomics
papers.abstract: Microbial sequencing data are subject to sample-specific and species-specific distortions that complicate inference about true microbial abundances. Recent work established assumptions under which relative fold-differences in microbial abundances can be estimated from sequencing data, accompanied by an estimation and testing method called radEmu. While radEmu has excellent error rates, its computational cost can be prohibitive for large-scale analyses. Here we introduce fastEmu, a scalable approximation to radEmu's testing methodology. fastEmu uses a small, data-driven subset of taxa to approximate the computationally expensive test statistic. In a metagenomic analysis, we show a reduction in per-taxon runtime from 4-8 hours to 0.5-45 seconds, and simulations illustrate no adverse impact on estimation error or Type I error rate control. fastEmu enables testing differential abundance for thousands of microbial taxa while retaining clear parameter interpretation and error rate control.

papers.title: Anti-target chemical-space coverage of Indian medicinal plant phytochemicals
papers.abstract: Computational safety evaluation of phytochemical libraries commonly relies on models trained on experimentally tested compounds and applied to much larger and chemically diverse collections. An important but often overlooked question is whether predicted compounds are adequately represented within the experimental chemical space underlying these models. Here, we examined this question for the Indian Medicinal Plants, Phytochemistry and Therapeutics (IMPPAT) database using experimentally characterized datasets for three anti-target endpoints: hERG blockade, cytochrome P450 (CYP) inhibition, and pregnane X receptor (PXR) induction. After structure standardization, 14,956 unique IMPPAT compounds were compared with 8,877 hERG, 4,905 CYP, and 4,138 PXR reference compounds using consensus nearest-neighbor similarity based on Morgan and atom-pair fingerprints. At a Tanimoto similarity threshold of 0.80, only 0.92%, 0.30%, and 0.46% of IMPPAT compounds had close measured analogs in the hERG, CYP, and PXR datasets, respectively. Relative to the internal nearest-neighbor distributions of the reference datasets, a typical IMPPAT compound lay near the 1st percentile, indicating substantial chemical-space separation. Compounds with close experimental analogs also showed distinct molecular characteristics, with descriptor-based logistic regression yielding cross-validated AUC values of 0.77-0.80. Plant-level enrichment was markedly reduced after excluding widely distributed metabolites and was further restricted when the nearest measured analog was required to have pIC50 or pEC50 [≥] 5. The remaining signals were concentrated in a limited number of taxa, including Rauvolfia, Sinopodophyllum/Dysosma, Cinchona, and Catharanthus roseus. Overall, most IMPPAT phytochemicals lack close structural representation among currently measured anti-target compounds. Computational safety predictions for these molecules should therefore be interpreted as extrapolations and accompanied by explicit measures of structural support. Absence of a close experimental analog should be regarded as a gap in available evidence rather than evidence of safety.

papers.title: SCKAnalyzer: A Web Tool for Single-Cycle Kinetics Analysis and Simulation
papers.abstract: Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) and biolayer interferometry (BLI) are well-established label-free analytical technologies used to determine biomolecular interaction rates (ka, kd) and equilibrium constants (KD). While assays historically rely on multi-cycle kinetics (MCK), this approach requires intermediate surface regeneration, risking sensor degradation and increasing reagent consumption. Single-cycle kinetics (SCK) avoids regeneration by sequentially injecting increasing analyte concentrations. However, implementing SCK workflows on biosensor platforms like the OctetRR8 BLI instrument (Sartorius) remains a challenge due to the lack of built-in or online data analysis tools. To address this, we introduce SCKAnalyzer, a free, user-friendly web application designed for processing and fitting SCK datasets. SCKAnalyzer accepts column-based text files and native raw BLI data (.frd format) from Sartorius instruments, performing data pre-processing and non-linear fitting to a 1:1 interaction model. Additionally, it offers advanced simulation capabilities that allow variable association and dissociation durations across sequential injection steps, a feature absent in existing platforms such as BiacoreTMSimul8. The performance of SCKAnalyzer was experimentally validated using a 3-step SCK method (SCK3) for DNA/RNA duplex formation on a Biacore T200, as well as 4-step (SCK4) and 5-step (SCK5) methods for DNA/DNA duplex formation on an OctetRR8 BLI instrument. Binding parameters (ka, kd, KD) derived from SCKAnalyzer showed excellent agreement with values from established proprietary softwares such as Biacore T200 Evaluation Software v3.2.1 and BIAevaluation v4.1.1. SCKAnalyzer provides a practical alternative to MCK, reducing probe consumption and extending SCK utility across biosensor platforms. SCKAnalyzer is available at sck.iecb.u-bordeaux.fr (source code: github.com/synthaze/sckanalyzer).

papers.title: Senescence-induced Spatio-temporal Re-organization of the Nuclear Lamina Dynamic Landscape at Single-molecule Level in Live Human RPE Cells
papers.abstract: A defining hallmark of cellular senescence is the extensive remodeling of the nuclear lamina (NL) in both structure, composition, and its interactions with lamina-associated genomic domains. However, how such senescence-induced changes could quantitatively impact the spatio-temporal dynamics of NL interactions at the single-molecule level remain poorly understood. Herein, using human retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells as model system, we establish a robust, chemically inducible cellular senescence model capable of recapitulating key signatures of the senescence-associated phenotype. Senescent RPE cells exhibit distinct alteration patterns in the expression of various NL components, including lamin B receptor (LBR) and emerin, two key mediators of NL-chromatin interactions. Importantly, live-cell diffusion measurements via imaging FCS reveal globally enhanced mobility for both LBR and emerin, indicative of weakened NL anchoring in senescent cells. Single-molecule tracking and super-resolved STAR mapping further unveil distinct, multi-modal re-organization of their NL-binding dynamics in both space and time (especially in the form of LBR binding "hotspots" where multiple stable binding events cluster to effect more extended and prolonged interaction), in line with their respective expression-level alterations and differential lamin interactions. Moreover, correlative mapping uncovers a strong spatial coupling between reduced LBR mobility and highly condensed constitutive heterochromatin domains at the NL, which become dispersed during senescence. Collectively, these findings demonstrate the re-organization of NL dynamic landscape at single-molecule level as a critical and previously under-explored facet of senescence-induced NL remodeling, and point to a synergistic interplay between physical de-anchoring, dynamic attenuation of stable NL-binding and spatial restructuring of chromatin architecture in modulating NL-heterochromatin contacts to potentially effect global changes in senescence-associated gene expression.
affiliations: National University of Singapore (corresponding author)

papers.title: Single molecule Grb2 dynamics reveal spatiomechanical modulation of RTK signaling across length scales
papers.abstract: Extracellular matrix (ECM)-mediated cell adhesion and tension regulate development and disease through crosstalk with Receptor Tyrosine Kinases (RTKs). RTKs stimulate proliferation, survival, and metabolic reprogramming via Ras/ERK and PI3K/Akt signaling. Emerging evidence identify the biophysical and biochemical integration of integrin-mediated adhesions with RTK signaling, however, the molecular mechanisms regulating this phenotype remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that ECM stiffness potentiates ligand-mediated epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) signaling at scales ranging from the single adaptor protein, Grb2 upward to multicellular spheroids and tissues. We show that ECM stiffness-driven RTK signaling is mediated by integrin adhesions that reshape the membrane to induce the formation of RTK signaling hotspots distributed globally across the cell membrane. A parsimonious computational model and biochemical membrane perturbations causally implicate membrane curvature and topography in tension-dependent integrin-EGFR crosstalk. The results demonstrate how the mechanical properties of the ECM direct molecular recruitment and confinement of signaling molecules to regulate growth factor-dependent RTK signaling. Given that many RTK-driven solid tumors develop a stiff stroma, the findings could explain why many therapeutic tyrosine kinase inhibitors develop clinical resistance. The findings suggest clarifying how tension regulates transmembrane receptor signaling could identify unique force-dependent molecular regulators towards which new antitumor therapies could be applied.
affiliations: Purdue University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Sample-efficient time-resolved X-ray crystallography with serial small wedges
papers.abstract: Time-resolved crystallography can be inaccessible for membrane proteins and other difficult-to-crystallize targets for which suitable crystals are scarce. Here we present an acquisition strategy that records consecutive diffraction images during a small crystal rotation synchronized to a single activation pulse. Matching image segments are merged across crystals to reconstruct successive time windows, enabling a single crystal ensemble to capture an extended structural trajectory. Using the Mesh&Collect workflow at a synchrotron, we obtained ten consecutive 7.5-ms time windows at 2 [A] resolution from 1,255 microcrystals of a bacteriorhodopsin triple mutant at room temperature. An additional 790 crystals extended the observation window to 500 ms. Rotation-based processing, retrospective time binning and dose control maximize information extracted from each crystal, while compatible measurements can be pooled across acquisitions. This approach makes millisecond time-resolved crystallography practical for crystal-limited targets at synchrotrons, with further development potentially extending the temporal resolution down to 1 ms.

papers.title: Pdk1-dependent metabolic heterogeneity promotes aggressive colorectal cancer through cell-intrinsic interferon signaling
papers.abstract: Tumor heterogeneity is a major determinant of tumor progression and therapeutic resistance, yet the contribution of metabolism to intratumoral heterogeneity still remains poorly explored. Here, we find that pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase-1 (Pdk1) expression defines metabolically distinct cancer cell populations in colorectal tumors. Image-based spatial single-cell phenotyping shows that Pdk1-high cells are associated with tumor progression in orthotopic models of colorectal cancer (CRC). Genetic ablation experiments demonstrate the role of Pdk1-high cells in tumor growth, 5-fluorouracil chemoresistance and tumor relapse. Mechanistically, we identify a link between Pdk1-driven metabolic states and specific cell phenotypes, where Pdk1-high cancer cells exhibit an EMT, stem cell-like phenotype characterized by increased interferon (IFN) signaling. Mitochondrial remodeling in Pdk1-high cells leads to the release of mitochondrial DNA to the cytosol and activation of IFN pathways, promoting Pdk1-driven phenotypes. Inhibition of IFN signaling impairs the tumorigenic and aggressive features of Pdk1-high cancer cells, thus establishing a functional connection between metabolic heterogeneity, cell-intrinsic IFN signaling and aggressive CRC.
affiliations: University of Barcelona (corresponding author)

papers.title: Regional reproducibility of immune expression programs in glioblastoma and implications for single-biopsy assessment
papers.abstract: Tissue immune measurements can guide immunotherapy only if one biopsy represents the rest of the tumor. We quantified this in a secondary analysis of public data from 75 magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-localized glioblastoma (GBM) biopsies from 19 patients. Fourteen transcriptomic modules scored supportive, inhibitory, and checkpoint programs. The intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) gave the share of variance between patients rather than regions, before and after removing the component explained by a 12-gene leukocyte composite. An ICC of 1 indicates no variation in module scores among biopsies within each patient, whereas an ICC of 0 indicates that biopsies from the same patient are no more similar, on average, than biopsies from different patients. Two hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cohorts and a microdissected GBM atlas served as comparisons. CD8 had the lowest unadjusted ICC among abundance scores (0.42; 95% patient-bootstrap interval, 0.10 to 0.68; leukocytes, 0.65). Within patients, CD8 correlated with supportive and inhibitory modules alike (unadjusted mean r, 0.37 and 0.36) but not with major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I; r = 0.06). Leukocyte adjustment lowered the median module ICC from 0.56 to 0.34 but interferon (IFN) only from 0.74 to 0.70. IFN had the highest adjusted ICC and ranked first in 86% of patient-bootstrap resamples (post hoc). MHC-I was second (0.47) and not separable from IFN (difference 0.23; interval, -0.04 to 0.43); after purity residualization in 67 biopsies, IFN and MHC-I were similar (0.66 and 0.62). Median adjusted ICCs were 0.34 in bulk GBM, 0.62 and 0.74 in HCC, and 0.08 in microdissected GBM. In bulk GBM, only IFN, and MHC-I after purity residualization, had adjusted ICC point estimates above 0.5. The data support multiregion sampling with CD8, IFN, MHC-I, and checkpoint readouts from the same regions.

papers.title: Tumour-stroma signaling drives a reversible program with neural-like features in cancer-associated fibroblasts
papers.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is one of the most aggressive cancers, in part due to a dense and highly plastic tumor microenvironment dominated by cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs). In previous work, we identified a CAF population expressing a neural-associated NES+SOX4+NOTCH1+ program that increased with disease progression. The signals driving this state and the mechanisms regulating it remained unclear. Here, we investigated how tumor-derived signals activate this program and whether it represents a stable fibroblast identity or a reversible state. Using spatial transcriptomic data spanning normal pancreas to invasive carcinoma, we identified EGF, FGF2 and BDNF as candidate tumor-to-fibroblast signals associated with disease progression. Functional experiments in patient-derived CAFs and human fibroblast cell lines showed that EGF and FGF2 are sufficient to induce the NES+SOX4+NOTCH1+ program. Growth factor withdrawal reversed the NES+SOX4+NOTCH1+ program at both the protein and transcriptional levels, indicating that this state is dynamic and environment dependent. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis further revealed a multi-phase response involving early loss of fibroblast-associated features, transient activation of neural-associated genes, and a later stress-associated state. Regulatory analyses identified ETS-family transcription factors as key regulators of the program, while phosphoproteomic profiling and inhibitor studies showed that MAPK/ERK signaling plays a central role in its transcriptional activation. Finally, pan-cancer single-cell analysis showed that this state is enriched in CAFs and increases from normal to tumor tissue across multiple cancer types. Together, these findings define a reversible, growth factor-driven CAF program and identify signaling mechanisms that may provide opportunities to selectively modulate tumor-supportive fibroblast states.

papers.title: Certified Design Regions under Parametric Plant Uncertainty with Application to Antithetic Integral Feedback
papers.abstract: Kinetic parameters in engineered biomolecular circuits are typically known only within intervals and are not precisely tunable; controller synthesis is therefore naturally posed over sets of gains rather than at a single nominal design. We formulate robust controller tuning under parametric plant uncertainty as a universally quantified set-inversion problem: given a plant-parameter box, compute the controller gains that stabilize every plant in the box. Robust stability is decided by Hurwitz sign conditions, which are bounded over the joint gain-parameter domain using validated range enclosures, yielding machine-checkable certificates of local exponential stability of the deterministic equilibrium. Numerical experiments show that the certified region depends strongly on the range enclosure. For an antithetic integral feedback (AIF) controller acting on a two-species gene-expression cascade, a tensor-product Bernstein enclosure certifies 83.2% of the design plane at bisection tolerance epsilon=0.05 with 324 terminal boxes, whereas four baseline enclosures certify between 50.9% and 58.9% on the same paving. For a fifth-order loop, the certified fraction increases from 34.4% to 73.8%, and the certified and excluded terminal boxes confine the robustly stabilizing area to a window of about 2.1 percentage points. Finally, for a refining variant of the algorithm in which the plant box is refined alongside the design box, the undecided area satisfies |U(epsilon)|=O(epsilon) under a non-degeneracy assumption on the stability boundary.

papers.title: A Multilayer Human Skin Diseasome Links Molecular Architecture, Clinical Co-occurrence, and Drug-Reversal Signatures
papers.abstract: Abstract Background: Immune-mediated skin diseases frequently co-occur, but the molecular architecture connecting clinically distinct disorders, and the extent to which molecular proximity predicts shared therapeutic opportunity, remain incompletely defined. We constructed a multilayer skin diseasome integrating transcriptomic overlap, pathway enrichment, protein-interactome topology, curated disease associations, real-world clinical co-occurrence, and drug-perturbation signatures across psoriasis (PS), atopic dermatitis (AD), hidradenitis suppurativa (HS), vitiligo (VL), and chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU), using sodium lauryl sulfate-induced irritant contact dermatitis (SLS-ICD) as a mechanistically distinct barrier-injury comparator. Methods: Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were derived from publicly available NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus datasets and compared using exclusive pairwise and higher-order intersections. Gene Ontology biological-process enrichment characterized shared and condition-specific programs. Interactome-based network separation (S_AB) quantified the relative topological proximity of disease modules. DisGeNET enrichment generated candidate disease +associations, a selected subset of which was examined descriptively for patient co-occurrence in TriNetX. Candidate compounds were ranked by reversal of disease-associated expression signatures against LINCS L1000 perturbation profiles. Results: The largest exclusive DEG intersection occurred between PS and HS (2,060 genes), followed by AD-PS-HS (490), VL-PS (464), AD-PS (402), and VL-PS-HS (379). Fourteen genes were shared across PS, AD, HS, VL, and CSU but not SLS-ICD. Neutrophil-associated processes recurred across the immune-mediated conditions, whereas SLS-ICD was dominated by keratinization and epidermal-differentiation programs. PS and HS had the lowest observed network-separation value (S_AB = -0.594); SLS-ICD had positive S_AB values in all five comparisons, although this separation did not persist once module sizes were harmonized. DisGeNET linked the index conditions to diverse immune, cardiovascular, neurologic, and neoplastic categories; 42 of these candidate diseases were observed to co-occur with an index condition in the queried TriNetX cohorts. Drug-signature overlap was greatest between PS and CSU, despite their marginal interactome separation, indicating that interactome proximity and predicted pharmacologic reversal capture different dimensions of disease relatedness. mTOR/PI3K-pathway inhibitors were prominent among the psoriasis reversal candidates, while methotrexate and mycophenolate mofetil emerged from both the CSU signature and the curated gene set associated with HIV infection. Conclusion: Multilayer integration identified a connected molecular core among five immune-mediated skin diseases and a distinct SLS-ICD injury module. The discordance between interactome proximity and drug-signature overlap suggests that no single layer adequately defines disease relatedness. These findings provide a hypothesis-generating framework for prioritizing disease links and repurposing candidates, but controlled epidemiologic analyses and experimental validation are required before clinical or therapeutic inference.
affiliations: University of Cincinnati (corresponding author)

papers.title: tRNA-derived second messengers confer bacterial immunity
papers.abstract: Bacterial small-molecule messengers that function in diverse immune signaling pathways have been thought to derive strictly from biosynthesis using nucleotide and cofactor substrates. Here we report a nuclease-driven immune signaling pathway in which tRNA cleavage generates a specific small molecule that triggers cell death in response to RNA-guided transcript recognition in prokaryotes. We identify a class of type VI-B CRISPR systems in which the RNA-guided nuclease Cas13 and its accessory transmembrane protein, 2TM{beta}, are co-encoded in an operon and are jointly required for bacteriophage defense. Upon target RNA recognition, Cas13 activates 2TM{beta} by producing mono- and dinucleotide messengers bearing 2',3'-cyclic uridine phosphate ends by tRNA cleavage. Activated 2TM{beta} destroys infected cells by forming a multimeric complex that disrupts cell membranes to mediate cell death. These findings demonstrate RNA-programmed tRNA cleavage for second-messenger biogenesis, revealing a new logic for prokaryotic immune signaling.
affiliations: Innovative Genomics Institute, University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, CA, USA; Department of Molecular and Cell Biology, University of California, Berkel (corresponding author)

papers.title: Spatiotemporal Mapping of Glomerular Endothelial Regeneration Identifies Apold1 as an Intrinsic Regulator of Repair
papers.abstract: Abstract Endothelial cell (EC) injury is central to the pathogenesis of various renal disorders, highlighting the critical importance of vascular repair for restoring organ health. However, due to limited access to human tissue during active regeneration, the exact reparative processes remain largely unknown. This study aimed to investigate regeneration mechanisms specifically within the glomerular microvasculature by utilizing a selective endothelial cell injury (ECI) model in mice.Lineage tracing identified the origin of regenerating ECs. To uncover the transcriptional dynamics driving these reparative changes, we combined single-cell RNA sequencing and Xenium spatial transcriptomics (ST), mapping distinct glomerular EC (gEC) subpopulations across different phases of injury and recovery. Apold1 emerged as a key regulatory candidate within this process. To functionally validate this gene's specific role during the regenerative phase, Apold1-deficient (Apold1-/-) mice underwent the ECI model. After showing that gECs regenerate primarily from local, pre-existing renal ECs, our transcriptomic analysis identified 10 distinct gEC subpopulations and revealed a complex temporal pattern of regeneration. This process begins with the expression of genes associated with inflammation, followed sequentially by endothelial cell (EC) migration, the activation of immediate early genes, vascular remodeling and cellular proliferation. Within this dynamic process, the EC-specific gene Apold1 was identified as a key regulatory candidate. Apold1-/- mice exhibited impaired endothelial regeneration, characterized by increased endothelial activation and greater immune cell infiltration seven days post-ECI. To our knowledge, this is the first study to elucidate the spatiotemporal mechanisms of glomerular endothelial cell regeneration. By identifying local gECs as the primary source of repair, and stablishing the change in their expression pattern during regeneration, as well as identifying Apold1 as an intrinsic regulator, we have laid the groundwork for future research on renal microvascular disorders.

papers.title: Combining AlphaFold 3 with microscale thermophoresis for aptamer optimisation
papers.abstract: Although use of AI-based tools has gained ground in molecular biology research, their reliability remains a matter of debate. Here, we combined AlphaFold 3 modelling with microscale thermophoresis to investigate the interactions between glucan-binding protein C and the biofilm-inhibiting aptamer and its five derivatives. Structural modelling identified a binding motif on the aptamer and suggested a mechanism of action; however, the predictions were only partially supported by the experimental results. The AlphaFold generated confidence metrics did not correlate directly with the measured binding affinities, indicating that confidence scores can help identify plausible interaction interfaces, but they are not reliable predictors of binding strength. These results highlight the importance of integrating structural prediction with biophysical validation to dissect aptamer-protein recognition.
affiliations: Department of Molecular Biology, Institute of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Semmelweis University (corresponding author)

papers.title: A quick and efficient method enabling lncRNA functional studies in the marine diatom Phaeodactylum tricornutum using a multiplexed CRISPR-Cas9 editing approach
papers.abstract: Background: Long non protein coding (lnc)RNAs are ubiquitous transcripts known to be major regulators of cellular processes in eukaryotes. In diatoms, specific lncRNA expression is tightly correlated to nutrient fluctuations, which suggests function, but their biological relevance remains to be established. In order to fill this knowledge gap, we sought to design a protocol to generate diatom lncRNA knockout mutants by CRISPR-Cas9 enabling subsequent functional studies to shed light into their mechanistic roles. Since lncRNAs do not contain open reading frames that can be targeted by point mutations for the generation of functional knockouts, we designed a multiplexed CRISPR-Cas9 plasmid harboring two independent gRNA for the specific ablation of lncRNA loci in P. tricornutum. As proof of concept, we used our plasmid-based system to target three phosphate depletion responsive lncRNAs. Results: Using the golden gate based uLoop system, we assembled a single plasmid containing all the necessary components to generate CRISPR-Cas9 large genomic ablations of lncRNAs in P. tricornutum using bacterial conjugation. Three intergenic lncRNAs (Linc91, Linc77 and Linc24) responsive to phosphate fluctuations were selected and independently targeted. Around 32% of the exconjugants presented a monoallelic ablation of the targeted loci and 11% presented a biallelic ablation on the first PCR-screening round. Mutated lines, harboring biallelic lncRNAs ablations for each lncRNA targeted, were successfully generated for each of the targeted lncRNAs. Additionally, a first line of phenotypic analysis revealed significant growth rate differences for one of the mutants ({Delta}Lnc24) under both full and phosphate depleted conditions, suggesting its involvement in cell division regulation under nutrient fluctuations. Conclusions: This work provides a simple and efficient method for the generation of lncRNA knock-out mutants in P. tricornutum. Furthermore, this approach can be easily adapted to other microalgae amenable to transformation, enabling the enhancement of our understanding of these important cellular regulatory transcripts in the marine environment.
affiliations: IBENS/UPEC (corresponding author)

papers.title: Functional and molecular profiles of the neuroretina and retinal pigmented epithelium-choroid in response to aging and Nrf2 deletion
papers.abstract: Purpose: Age is the leading factor for age-related macular degeneration (AMD), in which retinal pigmented epithelium (RPE) atrophy is a hallmark. The nuclear factor-erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2), a major anti-stress transcription factor, decreases in AMD, suggesting bioenergetic stress interacts with age during AMD pathogenesis. We profiled visual function and gene expression of the retina and RPE-choroid with Nrf2 deletion and aging. Methods: We tested 3mo and 14mo Nrf2 null (Nrf2 KO) and Nrf2 WT mice for optokinetic tracking (OKT) and dark-adapted electroretinography (ERG) responses. Eyes were harvested for retina outer nuclear layer (ONL) thickness analysis and retina and RPE-choroid cup RNA isolation for RNAseq profiling. Results: Visual acuity was reduced with aging with lower values in the Nrf2 KO vs Nrf2 WT comparison at 14mo. We observed aged-related reduction of a-, b-, and c-wave ERG amplitudes in both WT and KO mice. Age-related c-wave decline was exacerbated by Nrf2 loss. By RNAseq, two-way ANOVA of RPE-choroid samples revealed differentially expressed genes (DEGs) with age and genotype main effects, as well as DEGs with age and genotype interaction effects. Age DEGs were over-represented in pathways related to inflammation and phagocytosis. Genotype DEGs were associated with alterations in antioxidant and inflammatory processes. Retina RNAseq showed age and genotype DEGs. Conclusions: Ablation of Nrf2 exacerbates age-related declines suggesting that decrease in Nrf2 with aging has functional consequences for inflammation/resiliency. We provide retina and RPE-choroid bulk-RNAseq datasets from the same cohort of mice that can be interrogated to better understand degeneration of retina/RPE-choroid.
affiliations: University of Oklahoma Health Campus (corresponding author)

papers.title: Network fixation expansion microscopy
papers.abstract: Expansion microscopy (ExM) physically magnifies preserved biological specimens by using a specimen-permeating hydrogel to pull biomolecules, such as proteins, apart from each other. ExM protocols exhibit a tension between the need to initially fix proteins to each other during sample preservation, to retain proteins and their nanoscale organization, and the need to separate proteins from each other isotropically, to achieve physical magnification. We here propose to address this tension by fixing proteins directly to the hydrogel network itself, which then serves as a common substrate for both initial fixation and final separation. We equip proteins with chemical handles, then form a specimen-permeating hydrogel that binds the handles, in a ~15-minute chemical process conducted entirely at -20oC. This network fixation ExM (nfExM) procedure enables excellent epitope retention and nanoscale organization preservation, in cultured cells. nfExM may help support ultrastructural investigations of protein complexes and interactions.

papers.title: Chronic nanoplastic exposure causes size-dependent cytotoxicity and ANGPTL4 induction in human kidney cells
papers.abstract: Nanoplastics (NPs) are widespread environmental contaminants, yet most toxicity studies rely on short-term, single-dose exposures that poorly reflect daily human exposure. The kidney, particularly the proximal tubule, is a likely site of repeated NP exposure given its role in filtration and reabsorption, but chronic exposure effects are largely unexplored. Here, a long-term in vitro model was developed in which human proximal tubule (HK-2) cells were continuously exposed to 20 nm or 100 nm carboxylated polystyrene NPs (100 {micro}g/mL) over 12 days. Continuous 20 nm NP exposure caused progressive loss of viability whereas 100 nm NPs left viable cell numbers largely unaffected. RNA-sequencing showed 20 nm NPs drove extensive, time-dependent transcriptional dysregulation (1,548 differentially expressed genes at day 6, rising to 4,431 at day 9), far exceeding the minimal alterations in gene expression (35 genes) caused by 100 nm NPs. Cell-cycle analysis and pathway enrichment revealed KRAS pathway activation and S-phase arrest in 20 nm-treated cells, with ANGPTL4 the most upregulated gene. Validation with qRT-PCR confirmed increased ANGPTL4, HMOX1 and FN1 expression, genes implicated in renal fibrosis and chronic kidney disease. These findings show that continuous, size-dependent NP exposure elicits progressive cytotoxic and transcriptional responses in kidney proximal tubule cells and indicate ANGPTL4 as a candidate early biomarker of NP-induced renal stress.

papers.title: Kcs1-dependent inositol pyrophosphates promote DNA double-strand break repair via Pho80-Pho85 in budding yeast
papers.abstract: The cleavage of membrane-bound phosphoinositides produces inositol polyphosphates (IPs) and pyrophosphates (PP-IPs), small water-soluble signaling molecules that are highly conserved in eukaryotes and play a critical role in cell metabolism. Loss of the inositol pyrophosphate kinase (PP-IPk) Kcs1 and its mammalian ortholog IP6K1 was previously shown to cause hypersensitivity to genotoxic stress and reduced homologous recombination (HR) repair. To identify the mechanism linking PP-IPs to DNA double-strand break (DSB) repair, we combined quantitative proteomics with biochemical, genetic, and cell-cycle analyses in budding yeast. We found that loss of Kcs1, but not the PP-IPk Vip1, caused increased sensitivity to the radiomimetic drug zeocin. kcs1{Delta} cells displayed persistent Rad53 signaling and elevated {gamma}-H2A levels, remaining arrested in G1/S during treatment and accumulating in G2/M for hours after damage removal. Unexpectedly, Kcs1-dependent PP-IPs promoted DSB repair independently of the core HR machinery and of cell-cycle stage. Quantitative proteomics revealed increased levels of PHO pathway proteins in zeocin treated kcs{Delta} cells, and deletion of the CDK inhibitor PHO81 substantially rescued zeocin hypersensitivity, indicating that constitutive inhibition of the Pho80-Pho85 cyclin-dependent kinase underlies the DNA repair defect caused by Kcs1 loss. This function of Pho80-Pho85 was mechanistically distinct from its canonical role in phosphate homeostasis, and partially independent of its connections to Ku80 regulation. Together, our findings identify Kcs1-dependent PP-IP signaling as a new upstream input controlling Pho80-Pho85 activity during the DNA damage response, establishing an HR-independent axis for genome maintenance and linking PP-IP metabolism to the DNA damage response in eukaryotic cells.

papers.title: Carbonic anhydrase inhibition rescues heart function in the Tg2576 Alzheimer's mouse model by ameliorating cardiac amyloid-β pathology and neurotrophic signaling impairment.
papers.abstract: FDA-approved carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (CAIs) have shown robust efficacy in reducing amyloid- beta pathology, neurodegeneration, and cerebrovascular dysfunction in Alzheimer disease (AD) and cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) models, highlighting carbonic anhydrases (CAs) as a promising, previously untapped therapeutic target for AD and the vascular contribution to dementia. We have recently shown that amyloid- beta aggregates disrupt neuro-signaling and deplete neurotrophic factors (particularly BDNF) in the heart of AD mouse models and human subjects. In this study, we present the first in-depth examination of CAI therapy (acetazolamide, ATZ) in Tg2576 mice, a well-established model of AD and CAA. We confirm that progressive cardiac fibrosis and amyloid- beta deposition in 13-month-old mice severely impair the cardiac neuro-signaling system, marked by a drastic decrease in BDNF and reductions in adrenergic fibers and regenerating nerve endings (TH and GAP-43 markers), leading to significant declines in ejection fraction and fractional shortening compared to age-matched WT littermates. Critically, this study demonstrates that long-term ATZ treatment in Tg2576 mice significantly reduces cardiac amyloid- beta burden, prevents adverse neuro-signaling remodeling, and restores heart physiological function, as assessed via speckle tracking strain echocardiography. These in vivo findings were corroborated in human cardiomyocytes, in which CA inhibition reduced human amyloid- beta40 oligomer-dependent disruption of CREB signaling, thus preserving BDNF expression. Together, these results reveal a previously unrecognized cardio-neuroprotective role for CAIs in preventing amyloid- beta-induced cardiovascular remodeling and neuro-signaling disruption in the Tg2576-AD model. Given the established benefits of CAIs on cerebrovascular function and cognition, our findings further support advancing repurposing efforts into clinical trials. CAIs such as ATZ could offer a dual-action therapy approach, addressing both the central nervous system and cardiac pathologies associated with AD and, potentially, the systemic effects of amyloidosis.
affiliations: Temple University Lewis Katz School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Fluorescence-based sorting of extracellular vesicles enables detection and omics
papers.abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are nanosized, lipid bilayer-enclosed particles that mediate intercellular communication and hold considerable promise as biomarkers and therapeutic agents. However, their functional heterogeneity remains incompletely understood, largely due to the absence of reliable methods for isolating specific EV subpopulations. Here, we established a Nanoscale Flow sorting (NanoFACS) workflow and evaluated its potential for EV detection, sorting, and molecular characterization. We assessed critical parameters, including fluorescent staining and labeling approaches, background signal discrimination, dilution and flow-rate effects, and scatter triggering. We achieved high-purity sorting of CFSE-stained and antibody-labeled EVs, preserving vesicle integrity and sufficient RNA yields for small RNA sequencing of sorted populations. We identified EV subtype-specific small RNAs despite partial cargo overlap in single-marker sorted populations. Our results establish a reproducible antibody-based NanoFACS workflow that defines key operational parameters for reliable EV detection and sorting, with potential adaptability across conventional and spectral flow cytometry platforms. By reducing background and non-EV-associated events, the workflow enables the isolation of phenotypically defined EV subpopulations suitable for downstream molecular analysis, providing a practical approach to investigate EV heterogeneity.

papers.title: Rab35 drives epidermal wound closure by promoting lamellipodial protrusions and membrane vesicle transport
papers.abstract: In response to tissue damage, the epidermal barrier must be restored immediately to prevent excessive blood loss and infections. How cells coordinate actin-driven protrusions and membrane transport during reepithelialization is poorly understood. Here, we identified Rab35 as an important driver of epidermal wound closure in Drosophila. Endogenous Rab35 positive vesicles are directed to the wound edge and in protruding lamellipodia. Suppression of Rab35 function results in striking lamellipodia defects and an accumulation of PIP2-positive vesicles. Depletion of Fascin, a known Rab35 effector phenocopies rab35 knockdown. Upstream of Rab35, we identified CG18659 as potential Rab35-GEF protein, which physically interacts and colocalizes with Rab35. Suppression of Rab35 GEF CG18659 or overexpression of Rab35 GAP Whacked results in strong wound healing defects. We propose model in which Rab35 drives epidermal wound closure by promoting Fascin-stabilized actin-driven protrusions and vesicle transport required for cell membrane expansion and local PIP2 delivery at the wound site.

papers.title: Hierarchical TPR:ZC3HC1 interactions drive stepwise assembly of nuclear basket extensions projecting into vertebrate cell nuclei
papers.abstract: The nuclear basket (NB) is a fibrillar scaffold anchored to the nuclear pore complex (NPC), with protein TPR constituting its structural backbone. Recently, ZC3HC1 was identified as an additional structural NB component interconnecting TPR subpopulations. However, it had remained unclear how ZC3HC1 and TPR engage each other and how the resulting TPR:ZC3HC1 ensembles are arranged relative to the NB. Here, we uncover a hierarchy of sequential interactions between distinct ZC3HC1 and TPR domains, resulting in NB-appended ZC3HC1:TPR ensembles that extend beyond the NB dimensions traditionally considered prototypic. Consistent with a modular organisational principle, we furthermore find copy numbers of NPC/NB-associated TPR to be far higher than commonly anticipated. Together with sufficient ZC3HC1 copy numbers, our data define a model in which alternating recruitment of ZC3HC1 and TPR extends the NB's spatial and functional reach into the nuclear interior.

papers.title: An Inducible Model of RPE-Associated Hydroxyapatite Mineralization with Relevance to Drusen Formation in Age-Related Macular Degeneration
papers.abstract: A cardinal feature of nonexudative age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is the accumulation of drusen between the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and Bruch's membrane, yet the mechanisms that initiate and promote drusen formation remain to be fully understood. Hydroxyapatite (HAP), a calcium-phosphate mineral identified within human drusen, has been proposed to contribute to drusen nucleation and is associated with increased likelihood of RPE atrophy. However, mechanistic studies providing insight into RPE-associated mineralization have been limited by a lack of easy-to-use and manipulatable culture models. Here, we established a rapid, inducible ARPE-19-based model of HAP mineralization. We found that ARPE-19 cells cultured in minimum essential media (MEM) supplemented with nicotinamide (NIC), sodium phosphate, and ascorbic acid (NaPAA) reproducibly formed HAP positive deposits, whereas mineralization was not observed while using standard DMEM/F12 medium, DMEM/F12 with NaPAA, MEM-NIC medium, or MEM-NIC medium with alternative osteogenic supplements (such as beta-glycerophosphate, ascorbic acid, and dexamethasone). Scanning electron microscopy with energy dispersive X ray spectroscopy demonstrated that the formed deposits were enriched in calcium (Ca) and phosphorus (P) with Ca/P ratios comparable to drusen-associated HAP deposits from AMD donor tissue. ARPE-19-based HAP deposits were also closely associated with neutral lipid-rich material, staining positive for BODIPY around their core structure. Bulk RNA sequencing of mineralized ARPE-19 cells revealed extracellular matrix, angiogenic, inflammatory, and metabolic transcriptional changes in the absence of strong enrichment of canonical osteogenic pathways. Co-treatment of mineralizing cells with either pyrophosphate, EDTA, or sodium citrate significantly reduced mineral deposition, but these approaches were not able to reverse it. Together, these findings establish a tractable RPE mineralization model that recapitulates key features of AMD-associated HAP and provides a platform for investigating mechanisms of drusen-associated mineral formation.
affiliations: University of Minnesota (corresponding author)

papers.title: Generative inverse design steers human hematopoietic cell fate in vitro
papers.abstract: Inverse design has advanced the discovery of molecules and materials. Yet it remains largely unexplored for steering cell fate, where inputs are continuous, combinatorial culture conditions and outputs are distributions of cell states. Human hematopoiesis, in which combinations and doses of growth factors steer stem cells toward each blood lineage, is a demanding test case. While forward models can evaluate discrete conditions, the vast combinatorial space renders searching for a specific, target-producing design an intractable inverse problem. Here, we introduce LabCompass, an inverse-modeling framework that optimizes experimental designs toward candidates expected to produce specified target cell states, using a flow-matching generative model guided by cellular phenotypes predicted by a forward surrogate. We applied LabCompass to primary human CD34+ in vitro cultures, where continuous cytokine and small-molecule parameters govern hematopoietic cell fate. In a lab-in-the-loop setting, we experimentally validated model-driven designs and used these measurements to update the model across four successive loops. LabCompass recovered established lineage-inducing designs, improved predictions with new data, and enriched target populations across lineages. Incorporating new parameters expanded the design space and enriched rare populations beyond initial reach. Across loops, we generated a 78-million-cell spectral flow cytometry dataset and identified distinct culture conditions converging on the same target cell states. Our results establish generative inverse modeling as a compelling paradigm for navigating high-dimensional, continuous experimental spaces, and demonstrate that virtual cell models should be judged not only by how accurately they predict cellular responses, but also by how effectively they guide experiments toward desired biological outcomes.

papers.title: Active maintenance of accessible chromatin at poised meiotic promoters by the NFYA-NURF axis is required for meiotic entry in mice
papers.abstract: Developmental genes often acquire accessible chromatin prior to their activation, yet the mechanisms regulating this permissive state remain poorly understood. During spermatogenesis, many meiotic gene promoters display this poised state in spermatogonia, characterized by accessible promoters and paused RNA Pol II occupancy before their activation during meiosis. Here, we identify the NURF chromatin remodeling complex, comprised of SMARCA5 and its accessory subunit BPTF, as a key regulator of this process. We demonstrate that the transcription factor NFYA interacts with SMARCA5 and is required for its occupancy at poised meiotic gene promoters. Approximately one-third of poised meiotic gene promoters is co-occupied by NFYA, SMARCA5, and BPTF. Germline deletion of Smarca5 disrupts chromatin accessibility at poised meiotic promoters, impairs transcriptional program required for mitosis-to-meiosis transition, resulting in developmental arrest at meiotic entry. These findings identify NFYA-NURF as a key regulatory axis that regulates accessible chromatin at developmentally poised meiotic genes and primes them for activation later during meiosis.
