papers.title: Co-occurrence network multicollinearity artefacts using centered log-ratio transformation
papers.abstract: Next-generation sequencing data is compositional in nature and ignoring this fact can significantly impact downstream data analyses. This is especially true in co-occurrence (correlation) networks because compositional data is prone to many false negative correlations. The centered log-ration (clr) transformation is a commonly used compositional data analysis (CoDA) approach that converts compositionally constrained data into real number space. The clr transformed values can subsequently be used in machine learning and statistical analyses such as Spearman or Pearson correlations used to generate co-occurrence networks. Here we show that the necessary zero substitution performed prior to clr transformation can create numerous multicollinearity artefacts. We also show that a newer CoDA approach called the robust centered log-ratio (rclr) eliminates these artefacts in correlation-based network analysis.
affiliations: San Diego State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: DancE: A DNA-Activated Bacterial cGAS-like Enzyme in Antiphage Immune Defense
papers.abstract: Vertebrate cGAS senses DNA and synthesizes cyclic GMP-AMP to launch an immune response through the adaptor protein STING. Bacterial cyclic oligonucleotide-based signaling systems (CBASS) are evolutionarily related to the metazoan cGAS-STING pathway, but the molecular cues triggering bacterial cGAS activation remain poorly understood. Here, we identify a cGAS-like enzyme, termed DancE (DNA-activated di-nucleotide cyclase in Escherichia), that is activated by binding to double-stranded DNA. DancE is repressed by the bacterial chaperone DnaK, which prevents DNA binding by DancE. We further identified lambda phage prohead protease gpC that activates DancE through its protease activity. These results provide an example of a bacterial cGAS-like enzyme that is activated by DNA but through a guard-like mechanism that normally suppresses DNA sensing, suggesting that DNA sensing by cGAS family proteins is an ancient antiviral strategy conserved across kingdoms of life.
affiliations: University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: Characterization of two Martinezella spp. species: M. legmii sp. nov. and M. ivanii sp. nov., from tropical legume trees in Costa Rica
papers.abstract: Four rhizobial strains isolated from root nodules of tropical leguminous plants in Costa Rica were characterized. Strain LEGMi-135b was isolated from Lonchocarpus felipei root nodules, LEGMi-12c from Cojoba arborea, LEGMi-198b from Calliandra haematocephala and Rhizobium altiplani LEGMi-166a from Mimosa pigra. Phylogenetic analyses based on the 16S rRNA gene and four concatenated housekeeping genes (recA, atpD, GATase and gyrB) placed these strains within the genera Martinezella (LEGMi-12c, LEGMi-135b, and LEGMi-198b) and Rhizobium (LEGMi-166a). Genome-based analyses showed that strain LEGMi-135b exhibited an average nucleotide identity (ANI) value of 94% and a digital DNA-DNA hybridization (dDDH) value of 53.2% compared with its closest related species, Martinezella hainanensis CCBAU 57015T, supporting its classification as a distinct species. LEGMI-12c exhibited ANI and dDDH values of 98% and 87%, respectively, compared with Martinezella hainanensis CCBAU 57015T. LEGMi-198b showed the highest similarity to Rhizobium cerradonense CNPSo 3464, with ANI and dDDH values of 98% and 81.4%, respectively; however, this taxon has not been validly published. LEGMi-166a exhibited ANI and dDDH values of 100% and 99.3%, respectively, compared with Rhizobium altiplani BR 10423, confirming its assignment to this species. Additionally, differentiation of strains LEGMi-135b and LEGMi-198b from their closest phylogenetic relatives was supported by phenotypic, physiological, and biochemical analyses. Based on the combined genomic, phenotypic, and biochemical evidence, we propose the establishment of the novel rhizobial species Martinezella legmii sp. nov., with strain LEGMi-135b designated as the type strain (LEGMi-135b), and Martinezella ivanii sp. nov., with strain LEGMi-198b designated as the type strain (LEGMi-198b). This study expands our understanding of rhizobial diversity associated with nitrogen-fixing symbioses, particularly among tropical leguminous plants from Costa Rica
affiliations: Universidad de Costa Rica (corresponding author)

papers.title: Species Distribution, Antifungal Susceptibility, and Machine Learning-Based Prediction of Optimal Therapies Against Candida Species
papers.abstract: Invasive candidiasis has become more common in recent decades, particularly within ICUs. Identifying specific Candida spp., and testing their sensitivity to antifungal drugs is crucial for effective treatment that helps healthcare providers to detect potential treatment challenges early. This study aimed to identify Candida spp. at their spp. level present in blood, assess their susceptibility to antifungal agents, and apply a random forest classifier to predict the best antifungal drug for a given species. The isolates were classified at the species complex level through MALDI-TOF MS. The strains' susceptibility to antifungal agents such as AMB, FLZ, VOZ, ITZ, POZ, CAS, MFN, and ANF was assessed using CLSI guidelines. Out of the 354 Candida spp. isolated from blood, C. utilis was found to be the predominant species, followed by C. tropicalis, and C. albicans. This study demonstrated that MFN and ANF exhibited high potency, with an impressive MIC90 of 0.12 {micro}g/mL against all isolates, surpassing CAS, which had a slightly higher overall MIC90 of 0.25 {micro}g/mL. FLZ exhibited the highest MIC90 value among the azoles at 16 {micro}g/mL, while VOZ, ITZ, and POZ all had MIC90 values of 0.5 {micro}g/mL. AMB MIC90 values were 2 {micro}g/mL against all isolated Candida species. The Random Forest AI/ML model showed perfect overall prediction, with the actual and predicted best antifungal drugs matching for all fungal species. This study is particularly essential because rare Candida spp. becoming more common and exhibiting higher MICs to AMB and FLZ and required suitable remedies for controlling the infection.
affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology (BHU) Varanasi (corresponding author)

papers.title: A Bispecific Biologic That Robustly Reverses HIV-1 and SIV Latency
papers.abstract: Antiretroviral therapy suppresses HIV-1 replication but cannot eliminate the latent viral reservoir persisting in memory CD4 T cells. Existing latency reversal candidates have yet to achieve robust viral reactivation at tolerable doses. We engineered T4IL15{triangleup}, a bispecific biologic that selectively delivers IL-15 signaling to memory CD4 T cells, with minimal off-target stimulation. T4IL15{triangleup} reactivated latent virus in 94% (48/51) of clinical samples ex vivo, 75% (15/20) of administrations in HIV-1-infected and ART-suppressed humanized mice, and 100% (6/6) of SIV-infected and ART-suppressed rhesus macaques at doses well tolerated. We also found that off-target stimulation of non-CD4 cells hindered HIV-1 reactivation ex vivo. T4IL15{triangleup} provides a robust reactivation platform that could complement other reservoir-elimination strategies toward an HIV-1 cure.
affiliations: Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons (corresponding author)

papers.title: Subpopulations of Pseudomonas aeruginosa inflict distinct tissue damage during infection
papers.abstract: P. aeruginosa is a Gram-negative, ubiquitous, opportunistic pathogen that can colonize open wounds and the respiratory airways and is particularly problematic for patients suffering from cystic fibrosis (CF) where it can cause chronic infections. One factor contributing to P. aeruginosa diversity during infection is phenotypic heterogeneity. Phenotypic heterogeneity is the ability of bacteria to express different levels of selected pathways, giving rise to multiple bacterial subpopulations in the same environment. The prevalence and relevance of this phenomenon have been poorly characterized in infection models. In this study, we developed strategies to detect these subpopulations via single cell reporters, flow cytometry and fluorescence microscopy, in simple infection models and a physiologically relevant, transwell-based model of the bronchial epithelium. Next, we optimized cell sorting coupled to low input proteomics approaches to characterize the physiological state of the identified subpopulations, and genetically manipulated P. aeruginosa to lock them in ON or OFF states of expression of phenotypically heterogeneous pathways. We identify that type IVc/Tad pili are expressed in a subset of P. aeruginosa cells and inflict damage to the host tissue, while type Tad pili-negative subpopulations express other virulence factors instead. Lastly, we validated the heterogeneous expression of this machinery across clinical strains. Our findings uncovered the diversity of strategies employed by P. aeruginosa for pathogenesis, where distinct bacterial subpopulations use different virulence factors to damage respiratory epithelia.
affiliations: Biozentrum, University of Basel (corresponding author)

papers.title: High-fidelity long-read metagenomics reveals the metabolic functions of dominant termite gut bacteria
papers.abstract: Many termites digest lignocellulosic wood using diverse gut microbiota, yet functions are rarely linked to specific symbionts because complete genomes are scarce. We used PacBio HiFi long reads to reconstruct circular single-contig bacterial metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) from the gut microbiota of the wood-feeding termite Nasutitermes takasagoensis. From 13.9 Gb of HiFi data, we obtained highly contiguous assemblies, including 11 Breznakiellaceae (Spirochaetota), two Candidatus Fibrimonas (Fibrobacterota), and one Chitinispirillaceae genome, three dominant lineages in this gut ecosystem. The reconstructed genomes encoded extensive carbohydrate-active enzyme repertoires and anaerobic fermentation pathways consistent with lignocellulose degradation. They also carried genes for essential amino acid biosynthesis, while nitrogen-fixation capacity was present in representatives of all three lineages but varied among closely related strains. One Breznakiellaceae genome possessed a complete Wood-Ljungdahl pathway potentially supporting reductive acetogenesis in the presence of external formate, whereas related strains carried incomplete variants likely involved in anabolic C1 metabolism. Differences in CAZymes, C1 metabolism, and nitrogen fixation among closely related strains reveal functional diversification that fragmented MAGs would not resolve. The mapping of metatranscriptomic reads from three biological replicates of the fiber-associated community to the reconstructed genomes provided independent evidence that key predicted metabolic functions are transcriptionally active. Our results demonstrate the power of HiFi metagenomics to recover highly contiguous genomes from complex insect microbiomes and uncover lineage-specific metabolic roles of dominant termite gut symbionts.
affiliations: Biology Center CAS (corresponding author)

papers.title: Sketching the SRA: experiment-wide similarity search across 4.8 million metagenomes
papers.abstract: Recent efforts have demonstrated that systematic analysis of the millions of metagenomes in the Sequence Read Archive (SRA) enables groundbreaking biological discoveries. However, SRA-scale comparison of whole metagenomes has remained elusive. Here, we introduce the most comprehensive resource to date for experiment-to-experiment analysis of all SRA metagenomes, comprising FracMinHash sketches (470GB), hypergen sketches (19GB), and an all-pairs Jaccard similarity matrix (90GB), which we release online at https://github.com/RolandFaure/SRA-metagenome-sketches-databases. These resources enable a wide range of analyses, which we demonstrate with several applications. First, we use the FracMinHash sketches to uncover temporal trends, finding that the amount of newly discovered microbial sequence continues to grow, rather than saturate or shrink. Second, we use the hypergen sketches, which enable nearest-neighbor search, to identify co-assembly candidates and thereby improve assembly quality. Third, we use the similarity matrix to analyze all SRA metagenomes, identifying duplicated submissions and over 50K candidates for metadata correction. Together, our resources unlock systematic analysis of metagenomic data at unprecedented scale.
affiliations: The Pennsylvania State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Cross-species convergence of surface polysaccharides shapes the virulence of an atypical carbapenem resistant uropathogenic Escherichia coli clone
papers.abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Escherichia coli (CREC) is an emerging global health threat associated with limited treatment options and increased mortality. Here, analysis of 20,331 E. coli genomes from urinary tract infection (UTI) and urine samples identifies phylogroup A sequence type 361 (ST361) as an emerging CREC clone associated with UTI. Phylogenetic and phylodynamic analyses reveal two dominant ST361 clades that emerged in Asia around 2006 and subsequently disseminated intercontinentally. ST361 exhibits near pan-drug resistance, with blaNDM-5 conferring carbapenem resistance. In silico capsule and O-antigen typing reveals a highly conserved Klebsiella-like surface polysaccharide serotype in 95.9% of ST361 genomes, which we show contributes to virulence in UTI and catheter-associated UTI mouse models. Analysis of the mobile genetic elements harbouring blaNDM-5 in ST361 and other CREC further reveals a dynamic interplay between plasmid transfer and insertion elements that contributes to blaNDM-5 dissemination. Together, these findings identify ST361 as an emerging UTI-associated CREC clone and reveal the convergence of clonal expansion, virulence-associated surface architecture and mobile genetic elements in its spread.
affiliations: Institute for Molecular Bioscience, The University of Queensland (corresponding author)

papers.title: Lung FDG-PET is an early pharmacodynamic biomarker of antiviral efficacy in preclinical influenza
papers.abstract: Background. Influenza remains a major cause of global morbidity and mortality. Pharmacodynamic biomarkers that quantify treatment response within the lung could accelerate influenza therapeutic development. We evaluated [18F]-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography ([18F]-FDG-PET) as a non-invasive biomarker of antiviral efficacy. Methods. Serial [18F]-FDG-PET was evaluated in two murine H1N1 influenza models using mouse-adapted PR8 strain and CA-09 clinical isolate following treatment with favipiravir, baloxavir marboxil, or ribavirin. PET measures were compared with pulmonary viral burden, inflammatory cytokine expression, computed tomography (CT) imaging, and respiratory function measured by whole-body plethysmography (WBP). Results. Antiviral treatment in PR8 infection model reduced lung [18F]-FDG uptake by 27-49% and metabolic lung volume (MLV) by 40.5-74.6% (both p < 0.001). Antiviral response was detectable as early as 3 days post-infection, when uptake decreased by 28.7-53.2% and MLV by 33.8-75.0%. Lung uptake also strongly correlated with MLV (r = 0.93, p < 0.001) and with pulmonary viral burden and inflammatory mediators. These findings were reproduced in a model of pandemic H1N1/CA-09, where baloxavir reduced uptake by 37.4% (p = 0.02) and MLV by 67.5% (p < 0.001) at day 3. In both models, changes in [18F]-FDG-PET parameters preceded improvements in lung CT and respiratory function. Conclusions. Lung [18F]-FDG-PET provides an early, quantitative measure of antiviral response in experimental influenza, supporting its further evaluation as a translational pharmacodynamic endpoint.
affiliations: Duke-nus Medical School (corresponding author)

papers.title: Global genomic epidemiology of multi-carbapenemase Enterobacterales
papers.abstract: Enterobacterales pathogens that encode multiple carbapenemase genes are an emerging public health threat. The genomic and plasmid context of the multi-carbapenemase producers has not yet been explored at scale. We analysed 1501 publicly-available global genomes that encoded two or more genes from the five prevalent carbapenemase families (IMP, KPC, NDM, OXA-48-like, and VIM). We observed 241 distinct allelic combinations, with NDM/OXA-48-like (25.6%), multiple KPC (25.3%), KPC/NDM (18.8%), and multiple NDM (10.9%) being the most common groups. We found that many genomes were part of high-risk lineages (48.0%). Most genomes carried carbapenemase genes on two plasmids (59.2%) or one plasmid (23.5%), and most genomes encoded different carbapenemase families (56.2%) rather than copies of the same allele (36.2%). We observed multiple mechanisms of multi-carbapenemase evolution including plasmid co-integration, convergence with virulence, and generation of novel allele diversity through duplication. Multi-carbapenemase plasmids had more AMR genes that conferred resistance to more AMR classes compared to plasmids encoding a single carbapenemase. The proportion of cross-class combinations (KPC/NDM and NDM/OXA-48-like) increased significantly over time, with NDM-5/OXA-181 (3.3-fold) and NDM-4/OXA-181 (8.9-fold) combinations enriched. These findings provide valuable insights into the genomic features of multi-carbapenemase Enterobacterales to support the development of effective surveillance programmes.
affiliations: Nuffield Department of Medicine, University of Oxford, Oxford, United Kingdom (corresponding author)

papers.title: Development of a CRISPR-Cas12a Assay for Detection of the PnimBG Mutation Associated with Heme-Dependent Metronidazole Resistance in Clostridioides difficile
papers.abstract: Objective Heme-dependent metronidazole (MTZ) resistance has emerged in Clostridioides difficile and is primarily mediated by a T-to-G single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) in the promoter of nimB (PnimBG). We aimed to develop a CRISPR-Cas12a-based assay for rapid detection of the PnimBG mutation associated with MTZ resistance. Methods A series of primers and CRISPR RNAs (crRNAs) were designed and optimized to identify the most effective combination for discriminating between PnimBG (MTZ-resistant) and PnimBT (MTZ-susceptible) alleles. Detection was evaluated by visual fluorescence using blue-light and UV imaging systems, as well as by quantitative fluorescence measurements. Results The CRISPR-Cas12a assay accurately differentiated PnimBG and PnimBT alleles in C. difficile. In a collection of clinical isolates, the assay correctly identified all 11 MTZ-susceptible isolates carrying the PnimBT allele and all 10 MTZ-resistant isolates carrying the PnimBG allele. Fluorescence signals were readily detected both visually and quantitatively. Furthermore, colony PCR using crude colony lysates yielded results comparable to those obtained with purified genomic DNA, enabling rapid colony-based detection without conventional DNA extraction. Conclusions The CRISPR-Cas12a assay enables rapid molecular detection of the PnimBG mutation associated with heme-dependent MTZ resistance in C. difficile. This approach could complement conventional susceptibility testing for MTZ resistance detection.
affiliations: University of Waterloo (corresponding author)

papers.title: Reply to: Structural polymorphism of amyloid fibrils in ATTR amyloidosis revealed by cryo-electron microscopy
papers.abstract: In the paper by Nguyen et al, published in Nature Communications in 2024, we describe structural polymorphism in fibrils extracted from patients with ATTR amyloidosis. ATTR amyloidosis is characterized by deposition of transthyretin amyloid fibrils across multiple organs, resulting in marked phenotypic variability. Previous studies on ATTR suggest its phenotypic variability may be linked to differences in fibril structure, as demonstrated in amyloid diseases such as AA amyloidosis, tauopathies, or synucleinopathies. Thus far, most ATTR fibrils adopt a strikingly similar fold across patients and affected organs. The most notable exception is described in the study by Nguyen et al., where we report the identification of two co-existing polymorphs in cardiac fibrils from three patients with the ATTRv-I84S variant. These cardiac polymorphs differ in conformation of the segment Gly57 to Gly67, termed the gate, which regulates access to a central polar channel within the fibril core. In one polymorph, the gate adopts an open conformation, exposing the channel, whereas in the other it is closed, shielding it. Whether these polymorphs extend beyond cardiac tissue remains unknown. Here, we address this question by extending our analysis to additional organs from a fourth patient with ATTRv-I84S amyloidosis.
affiliations: UT Southwestern Medical Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: Growth-state as a determinant of in vivo virulence of Mycoplasma pneumoniae
papers.abstract: Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a leading cause of community acquired pneumonia and bronchitis in people, particularly children and young adults. Like many bacterial pathogens, M. pneumoniae can grow in biofilm towers on both biotic and abiotic surfaces. Current models indicate that planktonic M. pneumoniae are simply individual cells that are dispersed from biofilm towers due to physical shear forces, and do not represent a bona fide planktonic growth state. However recent data indicate that these fractions may be physiologically distinct and may differentially influence disease outcome. We observed that experimental infection of mice with inoculum containing both adherent and non-adherent fractions of M. pneumoniae produced more severe lung pathology than inoculum prepared from M. pneumoniae adherent biofilms alone. Direct comparison of experimental infection with titer matched non-adherent (P-Mp) and adherent (B-Mp) fractions revealed that P-Mp produces more severe lung pathology compared to infection with B-Mp. Furthermore, experimental infection with a lower dose of P-Mp resulted in similar lung pathology relative to B-Mp infected mice. This increase in pathology was not associated with differences in bacterial burden, bacterial dispersal during inoculum preparation, nor due to differences in the phenotype of host immune responses. Comparative proteomics revealed that certain known and putative virulence factors associated with immune evasion are upregulated in P-Mp, potentially explaining the difference in virulence between the two fractions. Furthermore, comparative proteomics revealed distinct metabolic phenotypes between the two fractions, consistent with distinct planktonic and biofilm growth states, indicating that P-Mp likely represents a bona fide planktonic growth state. Collectively, these data implicate the growth state of M. pneumoniae as a determinant of in vivo virulence for this atypical human pathogen.
affiliations: University of Connecticut (corresponding author)

papers.title: Machine learning classifies subcellular Golgi morphology from imaging flow cytometry during inflammatory activation: an exploratory study
papers.abstract: Inflammatory activation remodels the Golgi apparatus to meet increased secretory demand, yet whether these structural changes carry computationally accessible information about immune cell state has not been explored. Here we show that machine learning applied to imaging flow cytometry images of the Golgi can distinguish lipopolysaccharide (LPS) treated from control cells. We trained models on Golgi images from human THP-1 monocytes before and 16 h after LPS stimulation in vitro, and from circulating myeloid cells of mice 24 h after intratracheal LPS or saline in vivo. In each dataset, the best-performing model was a deep learning model trained directly on images rather than a classifier using predefined morphometric features. Cross-domain performance varied with the model, transfer direction and use of labelled target data: several deep learning models trained on mouse images classified THP-1 cells above chance without changing model parameters. Grad-CAM highlighted regions within or adjacent to the GM130 fluorescence pattern. These findings indicate that GM130 images carry information associated with LPS treatment that supports classification within and across the two datasets. To our knowledge, this is the first application of supervised deep learning to imaging flow cytometry images of a subcellular organelle for inflammatory phenotyping, establishing organelle level image analysis as a potential complement to molecular assays for immune cell classification.
affiliations: University of Alabama at Birmingham (corresponding author)

papers.title: InfluProto: Predicting Cross-Species Transmission of Influenza A Virus via Prototype Learning
papers.abstract: Zoonotic influenza A viruses pose constitute a significant persistent threat to global public health, yet quantitative approaches for assessing their cross-species transmission potential remain limited. Here, we present InfluProto, a deep learning model that introduces prototype learning into host prediction for influenza A virus, framing conceptualizing host adaptation as a continuous process rather than a discrete outcome. InfluProto embeds viral sequences into a continuous representation space anchored by human, swine, and avian prototypes, using cosine distances as a quantitative measure of host adaptation. InfluProto accurately discriminated among the three host classes, achieving recall and precision exceeding 0.97, and substantially outperformed conventional classification models models--particularly on challenging zoonotic strains, including the 2009 pandemic H1N1 (pdm09) lineage. Beyond host classification, the learned representations captured biologically meaningful host-adaptive signatures,; notably, with pdm09 viruses occupying occupied an intermediate position between human and swine clusters, consistent with their evolutionary origin. Analysis of simulated reassortment further revealed that the introduction of human-origin segments into swine influenza viruses reduced their distance to the human prototype, indicating that InfluProto can detect reassortment-associated shifts in host adaptation. To facilitate broad public useaccess, we have developed an interactive web service for InfluProto. Collectively, our work establishes a continuous framework for characterizing host adaptation and evaluating zoonotic risk in influenza A viruses, with potential implications for pandemic surveillance and preparedness.
affiliations: Beijing Institute of Genomics, Chinese Academy of Sciences (corresponding author)

papers.title: Insights from a mobile healthcare clinic in Madagascar: Diversity and dynamics of viruses from febrile individuals in rural subsistence communities
papers.abstract: Communities living in biodiversity hotspots are at increased risk of pathogen exposure and spread due to insufficient access to nutrition, clean water, and sanitation. Viruses, in particular, have high epidemic and spillover potential, and widespread health impacts, yet, viral diversity and dynamics remain understudied in many high-risk regions. In Madagascar, a hotspot with unparalleled biodiversity, socioeconomic constraints, and a heavy burden of infectious diseases, ongoing healthcare initiatives provide opportunities to survey circulating viral diversity. Here, we used a metagenomic workflow to characterize the viromes of oral/nasal swabs from febrile individuals visiting a mobile healthcare clinic in southeastern Madagascar, of which 49% were malaria-positive (Plasmodium falciparum). We characterized sequences of human-infecting viruses from twelve families (Adenoviridae, Anelloviridae, Orthoherpesviridae, Papillomaviridae, Polyomaviridae, Astroviridae, Coronaviridae, Matonaviridae, Orthomyxoviridae, Paramyxoviridae, Picornaviridae, and Sedoreoviridae). These viral sequences generally showed high similarity to known lineages circulating globally, but multiple viruses considered rare or emerging were identified (e.g. enterovirus C105, enterovirus C117). While we did not detect a significant association between malaria status and pathogenic virus presence, younger individuals had higher odds of having a pathogenic virus. Nonpathogenic viruses in Anelloviridae were prevalent and diverse with richness ranging from 0 to 70. Individuals with P. falciparum or a pathogenic virus tended to share more anelloviruses. We also detected viruses that are protist-associated, plant-infecting, or with unknown hosts. Overall, our work documents extensive viral diversity in Madagascar, highlighting how metagenomic workflows can be used to build viral genomic resources for pathogen surveillance in regions with high infectious disease burden.
affiliations: Arizona State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Reliable extraction of clinical-trial evidence with provenance, verification, and targeted review
papers.abstract: Reliable extraction of trial characteristics and outcomes is essential for systematic reviews, yet incorrect values can alter evidence synthesis and are difficult to detect without clear source evidence. We evaluate EviSearch, a clinical evidence-curation system that links extracted values to source passages, independently verifies cited evidence, and prioritizes higher-risk cells for review. Using ten trial publications, a 133-column schema, reference annotations, and consistent scoring across model families, we assess answer quality, inter-reading agreement, evidence reproduction, targeted review, and evidence modality. In the Qwen evaluation, EviSearch achieved 91.70% accuracy, cited 100.0% of admitted values, and reproduced 98.9% independently. Reviewing 15.6% of cells increased accuracy to 95.22%.
affiliations: Arizona State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Position-wise Fold-Switch Prediction in Metamorphic Proteins: A Comparison of Handcrafted and Language Model Features
papers.abstract: In this work, we focus on predicting fold-switching phenomena observed in certain protein structures. Proteins that undergo fold-switching are called metamorphic proteins. We model fold-switch prediction in proteins as a position/residue-wise classification task. We use various features extracted from a protein's sequence as well as structure to train the classifiers. We propose a novel class of handcrafted parametrised features that encode the structural context of a residue. We also use embeddings from existing protein language models (PLMs) to train the classifiers. We train binary and 3-class classifiers, with the 3-class classifiers providing granular information on the type of fold-switch. In our computations, higher classification performance is achieved for binary prediction as compared to 3-class granular prediction. The handcrafted features perform comparably with the PLM embeddings on our standard test set. A rigorous error analysis by us during the review period revealed a critical data-leakage vulnerability in the metamorphic protein test data. This analysis also revealed that the PLM-based classifier suffers sequence-memorisation bias and fails to generalise to novel fold-switching sequences. On the other hand, one of our domain-informed handcrafted feature based classifier detects fold-switching without relying on sequence memory.
affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology Bombay (corresponding author)

papers.title: Continuous Integration and Software Quality in Scientific Software: A Large-Scale Empirical Analysis of GitHub Repositories
papers.abstract: Bioinformatics software plays a central role in biological research, yet many academic projects lack robust testing and continuous integration (CI) practices. This absence can compromise reproducibility, accessibility, and long-term maintainability. In this study, we conduct an empirical analysis of GitHub repositories spanning bioinformatics and other scientific software domains to examine the relationship between CI, software testing, and software quality. Repository discovery was performed using domain-specific search terms via GitHub's Application Programming Interface (API). This was followed by a layered data extraction pipeline, which included a Large Language Model (LLM) validation step, that connected repositories to published works, institutions, authors, funding, and citation counts. By integrating repository activity, community engagement, and backlog health into a composite Repository Quality Index (RQI), we find that the presence of CI and software tests is significantly associated with higher repository quality. Additionally, repositories with higher academic citation counts tend to cluster in higher RQI tiers, suggesting that software quality, which is driven by proper testing and integration, is associated with academic impact and funding status. These results demonstrate that adopting industry-standard development practices, such as CI and software testing, is a tractable path toward more sustainable and impactful academic software and funding opportunities.
affiliations: University of Arizona (corresponding author)

papers.title: CBFA2T3-GLIS2 establishes transcriptionally permissive enhancer hypermethylation associated with venetoclax response in pediatric AML
papers.abstract: CBFA2T3-GLIS2 (C/G) defines a high-risk pediatric AML subtype in which de novo enhancer rewiring sustains an aggressive leukemic transcriptional state. The early epigenomic mechanisms reinforcing this program and linking it to leukemic survival remain incompletely defined. Here, we identify enhancer-proximal hypermethylation as a noncanonical, transcription-permissive feature of C/G AML. Using primary C/G-positive AML samples and a developmentally relevant C/G-transformed cord blood hematopoietic stem/progenitor cell model, we integrated DNA methylation, chromatin state, fusion occupancy, and gene expression across early and leukemia-stage contexts. Early C/G-associated hypermethylated regions localized near H3K27ac/H3K4me1-marked active or primed cis-regulatory elements, were enriched for ERG/ETS-like motifs, and showed related architecture in leukemia-stage contexts. DNMT3B was prominently increased in C/G contexts, and its loss selectively altered methylation-associated gene expression without measurably changing global 5mC. Genetic DNMT3B loss increased venetoclax sensitivity in vitro, while pharmacologic DNMT3B inhibition with Nanaomycin-A similarly enhanced venetoclax response. During venetoclax treatment, DNMT3B-deficient xenografts showed reduced disease burden and prolonged survival. To assess whether this interaction extended to clinically used hypomethylating agents, azacitidine or decitabine plus venetoclax induced apoptosis-related transcriptional programs and mitochondrial depolarization. These findings identify hypermethylated active cis-regulatory elements as C/G-associated states linked to transcriptional dysregulation and venetoclax response.
affiliations: University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences (corresponding author)

papers.title: Parabens Impair Mouse Antral Follicle Growth and Alter Ovarian Hormone and Gene Expression Similar to Phthalates
papers.abstract: Benzyl paraben (BzP) and butyl paraben (BuP) are used as preservatives and antimicrobial agents in cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, and foods. BzP and BuP have been detected in urine, placental tissue, and ovarian follicular fluid and are understudied with regards to their endocrine activity, raising concerns on their impact to the reproductive system. We tested the hypothesis that BzP and BuP are toxic to the ovary and behave similarly to other structurally similar endocrine disrupting chemicals, such as phthalates and terephthalates, by altering hormone levels and impacting cell growth and gene expression in vitro. Untreated mouse antral follicles were exposed to vehicle, 0.1, 1, 10, or 100 g/mL BzP, BuP, or the BuP analog monobutyl terephthalate (MBuTP) for 96 hours. The highest dose of BzP and BuP were cytotoxic to follicles, suggesting that medium chain length hydroxybenzoates are more cytotoxic to the ovary than corresponding terephthalic acids. BzP significantly increased levels of estradiol and testosterone compared to control. BuP decreased follicle growth and disrupted expression of cell cycle regulators, similar to phthalates. The peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARg)-transcriptionally controlled gene Fabp4 was significantly upregulated by both BzP and BuP, whereas MBuTP upregulated all four PPAR target genes and decreased follicle growth. Overall, BzP, BuP, and MBuTP disrupted hormone levels, follicle growth, and cell cycle progression, suggesting similarities in toxicity to phthalates and potential endocrine disruption. Further study should be done on the reproductive toxicity and endocrine disrupting effects of chemicals similar in structure to phthalates to reduce exposure to endocrine disruptors and inform design of safer replacements.
affiliations: New Jersey Institute of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Immune determinants of leuprolide-associated cardiovascular risk in prostate cancer
papers.abstract: Leuprolide, a widely used androgen-deprivation therapy (ADT) for prostate cancer (PC), has been associated with increased cardiovascular events (CVE), although the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Through integrated spatial transcriptomic analyses of murine heart and immune-stromal profiling in patient blood, we identified immune programs linked to leuprolide-associated CVE risk. Spatial analyses revealed the distinct organization of lymphoid (T+B cells) aggregates and inflammatory macrophages in the plaque following leuprolide exposure that accompanied by ventricular hypertrophy, relative to normal vasculature. Parallel profiling of circulatory soluble and cellular components in patients demonstrated CD8+T cell enriched pattern in ~44% of patients, including memory and type 1 cytotoxic subsets that linked to treatment-induced CVE, such as ventricular dysfunctions, but no contribution of adipocytokines. These translational findings highlight the stratification of leuprolide-associated CVE risk in PC patients based on circulating T cell profiling and could guide the risk mitigation with alternative ADT agents.
affiliations: Emory University School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Mutational fitness landscapes of diverse human influenza H1N1 neuraminidases
papers.abstract: While neuraminidase (NA) is emerging as a promising influenza vaccine target, it evolves rapidly and undergoes antigenic drift. However, our understanding of its evolutionary constraints remains limited. Here, we systematically quantified the replication fitness effects of >6,000 mutations for each of three antigenically diverse H1N1 NAs using deep mutational scanning. Moderate correlations among H1N1 NA fitness landscapes revealed mutations with strain-dependent replication fitness effects. Additionally, cross-subtype comparison between N1 and N2 NAs uncovered similar epistatic effects that were enriched in the C-terminal interprotomer interface. We also showed that NA mutational fitness strongly correlated between in vivo and in vitro. Characterization of 40 individually constructed NA mutants further demonstrated that NA mutational fitness depended more on its surface protein expression than on its total protein expression or endoplasmic reticulum stress induction. Overall, the large dataset generated in this work provides critical insights into the evolutionary constraints of NA.
affiliations: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (corresponding author)

papers.title: Hepatitis C virus NS5A is not an effective antagonist of the canonical PKR-eIF2α pathway
papers.abstract: Protein kinase R (PKR) is an antiviral sensor that induces translational shutdown and stress granule (SG) formation through the phosphorylation of eIF2. Although previous studies have proposed that hepatitis C virus (HCV) non-structural protein 5A (NS5A) inhibits PKR dimerization, other studies consistently observe PKR activation and SG formation during HCV infection. To address this discrepancy, we interrogated the ability of NS5A from different genotypes and strains to regulate canonical PKR-eIF2 activation in a variety of cell culture models. Regardless of the genotype or strain tested, HCV NS5A failed to inhibit PKR dimerization or dsRNA-induced PKR activation, nor did it rescue downstream steps in the PKR-eIF2 pathway, such as translation halt and SG formation, in contrast to known viral PKR antagonists. Similarly, NS5A did not antagonise PKR activation when expressed in the context of other HCV non-structural proteins. We also tested the role of the host factor cyclophilin A (CypA), which interacts with both NS5A and PKR. However, the absence of CypA did not affect downstream PKR signaling or the activity of viral PKR antagonists or NS5A. Collectively, these findings indicate that NS5A does not effectively antagonise the PKR-eIF2 pathway and further support previous findings that HCV replication occurs in the presence of an active PKR response.
affiliations: Queen's University (corresponding author)

papers.title: High-titer convalescent serum from cats recovered from severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome protects SFTSV-infected mice
papers.abstract: Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS) is an emerging, tick-borne zoonosis caused by severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV) and is associated with high case-fatality rates in humans and cats. No vaccines or antiviral drugs are currently available for the prevention or treatment of feline SFTS. Because cats with SFTS often develop blood viral RNA loads exceeding those in severe human cases, we hypothesized that some naturally recovered cats develop strong neutralizing antibody responses and may serve as a potential source of antibody-rich serum for passive immunotherapy. We compared 80% plaque-reduction neutralization test (PRNT80) titers in convalescent sera from six human SFTS survivors and 14 cats that had recovered from naturally acquired SFTS, then evaluated the therapeutic efficacy of convalescent cat serum in SFTSV-infected, interferon receptor-deficient AG129 mice. Some SFTS-recovered cats showed high PRNT80 titers. Passive administration of high-titer convalescent cat serum early after infection protected SFTSV-infected mice. A single dose given at 2 or 3 days post-infection completely protected mice, whereas treatment at 4 days post-infection resulted in 40% survival. Administration on two consecutive days was associated with lower late-phase viremia in surviving mice. Sera from three independent SFTS-recovered cats improved survival, with greater effects observed for sera with higher neutralizing antibody titers. These findings indicate that some cats recovering from SFTS can develop high neutralizing antibody titers and their sera can exert therapeutic effects in an SFTSV-infected mouse model. These findings support further evaluation of passive immunotherapy as a treatment strategy for feline SFTS.
affiliations: University of Miyazaki (corresponding author)

papers.title: Redundancy relocated: the distributed metaparalog pool of an Arctic Pelagibacterales population
papers.abstract: The presence of metaparalogs (related genes diverging in function) has been proven to be extensive in the pangenomes of streamlined Pelagibacterales genomes. Here by leveraging a large number of complete genomes from an Arctic population we have been able to establish their universality and mechanistic origins. The diversity of some metaparalog families was as high within a single population than comparing with another (Mediterranean) population/species, which points to an ancient diversification of metaparalog families predating genomospecies separation. Metaparalog families provided diversity for transport and envelope diversity which would provide vast capacities to degrade substrates within DOM and interact with other cells or viruses or other subcellular entities (like EVs). The pool does not saturate at fifteen genomes. Our results highlight the immense importance of the pangenome in understanding the biology of bacteria in natural environments and how critical is the study of population genomics for the future of microbiology.
affiliations: Universidad Miguel Hernandez (corresponding author)

papers.title: Genome-wide within-host evolution during prolonged SARS-CoV-2 infection in a person with advanced HIV infection
papers.abstract: Within-host evolution during prolonged SARS-CoV-2 infection can be extensive in immunocompromised individuals, but the consequences of mutations that emerge and change in frequency over time remain difficult to predict. We characterized an XBB.1.5.10 infection lasting nearly 90 days in a person with advanced human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection. Genome-wide tracking of allele frequencies in samples collected on study days 43, 48, and 70 revealed a Spike N-terminal domain (NTD) deletion spanning residues 138-145 at frequencies of 33%, 80%, and 96%, respectively. A receptor-binding domain (RBD) deletion-insertion spanning residues 373-378 was detected on days 43 and 48 but not on day 70, while nsp12 C464Y was detected at approximately 8% on day 48 and 86% on day 70. We reconstructed representative Spike and non-Spike mutation profiles from the longitudinal samples and tested their effects on cell entry and viral RNA replication. The representative Spike construct for days 43 and 48 increased entry relative to XBB.1.5. Comparison with a matched construct lacking the receptor-binding domain deletion-insertion showed that the deletion-insertion enhanced entry, although it was not detected in the day 70 sample. The day 48 non-Spike profile supported the highest RNA replication among the tested replicons. Together, allele-frequency tracking revealed both transient mutations and mutations detected at progressively higher frequencies across the sampled time points. Functional testing showed that increased entry or RNA replication in vitro did not necessarily predict persistence in vivo.
affiliations: J. David Gladstone Institutes, San Francisco, California, USA | Department of Bioengineering and Therapeutic Sciences, University of California, San Francisco, (corresponding author)

papers.title: Rv2061c, a Putative F420-Dependent Oxidoreductase, is Required for Tolerance to Malachite Green and Other Antimicrobials and Oxidative Stress Protection in Mycobacterium tuberculosis
papers.abstract: The pathogenicity of Mycobacterium tuberculosis relies on its ability to withstand hostile host environments. Coenzyme F420 is critical for redox metabolism in Mycobacterium tuberculosis an organism distinguished by its abundant use of this low-redox-potential cofactor and a repertoire of F420-dependent enzymes. While F420-dependent mechanisms are known to confer protection against antimicrobials and oxidative stress, the specific enzymes responsible remain largely unidentified. In this study, using the F420-dependent detoxification of malachite green as a phenotypic marker, we performed a genome-wide screen in Mycobacterium tuberculosis using transposon mutagenesis and whole genome sequencing. The results of transposon mutagenesis and whole genome sequencing revealed that, among the 28 genes encoding F420-dependent enzymes, only mutations in fgd (essential for F420H2 re-generation) and Rv2061c, a gene encoding a putative F420-dependent oxidoreductase, were highly susceptible to malachite green. Subsequent experiments confirmed that Rv2061c and its homolog MT2120 are required for detoxifying malachite green and crystal violet. Furthermore, the Rv2061c mutant exhibited increased susceptibility to isoniazid and pretomanid; as well as menadione-induced oxidative stress. We also identified mutations in the transcriptional repressor Rv0678 as a key determinant of resistance to malachite green and crystal violet. This study establishes Rv2061c as a pivotal F420-dependent oxidoreductase that protects Mycobacterium tuberculosis from malachite green and other antimicrobial compounds as well as oxidative stress and further supports Rv0678 as a master regulator of multidrug resistance. These findings expand our knowledge of Mycobacterium tuberculosis defense mechanisms and highlight F420-dependent pathways as a potential target for new drug development.
affiliations: Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Epidemiology and virological characteristics of the emerging SARS-CoV-2 variant PJ.2.1
papers.abstract: SARS-CoV-2 continues to circulate globally at high levels and to evolve into new variants. Recently, a new saltation variant harbouring a highly mutated spike protein, PJ.2.1, emerged in North America. Here, we provide a brief epidemiological and virological characterization of PJ.2.1 and cocirculating variants. We report that PJ.2.1 is spreading in the USA, Canada, and Spain and mainly infects individuals aged 60 years and older, as do most other variants, with the exception of BA.3.2, which preferentially infects individuals aged 0-9 years. PJ.2.1 was less susceptible to inhibition by an antibody against ACE2 than were the other variants, indicating increased ACE2 binding. In contrast, PJ.2.1 did not show augmented evasion of antibodies from vaccinees who had received the LP.8.1-adapted vaccine compared with most other variants analysed. These results suggest that augmented ACE2 affinity rather than increased antibody evasion might drive the current, rapid spread of PJ.2.1.
affiliations: German Primate Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: Fu Ling (Wolfiporia cocos) Fungal β-Glucan in Combination with Bacillus coagulans Improve Colitis-Related Outcomes and Cecal Fermentation in DSS-Treated Mice
papers.abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease challenges modern gastroenterology due to high relapse rates. This study evaluated the effects of medicinal fungal sclerotium Fu Ling (Wolfiporia cocos), its derived {beta}-1,3-1,6-Glucan, Bacillus coagulans GBI-30, 6086, and their combinations in dextran sulfate sodium-induced colitis in male BALB/c mice. The {beta}-glucan-B. coagulans combination significantly improved body weight, disease activity index, colon length and architecture, mucus secretion, and cecal fermentation over single ingredient. Consistently, this combination increased total short-chain fatty acids production, particularly acetate, improved gut tight-junction organization and reduced myeloperoxidase accumulation. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing indicated that this combination reshaped the gut microbiota, notably enriching Anaeromassilibacillus sp., which associated with improved clinical feature. These findings highlight the potential of fungal-derived {beta}-glucan and probiotic combinations as functional food ingredients for mitigating intestinal inflammation and supporting barrier repair.
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong (corresponding author)

papers.title: Bacteria hyperpolarize in response to oxygen drop
papers.abstract: Aerobic microbes use oxygen as a terminal electron acceptor to establish an electrochemical gradient across their cell membranes. While this membrane potential ({triangleup}{Psi}) is essential for multiple cellular processes, it is unknown if and how it is maintained in bacteria during shifts in oxygen availability. We find that bacteria hyperpolarize in response to drops in oxygen. Focusing on Bacillus subtilis and guided by modeling, we report that hyperpolarization magnitude scales with the degree of electron acceptor deprivation. We find that potassium efflux contributes to the response. Surveying mutants, we uncover genes involved in potassium homeostasis and oxygen stress that contribute to hyperpolarization. We show that hyperpolarization scales with faster growth rates resulting from nutrient type and colony spatial heterogeneity. Finally, we demonstrate that oxygen shift increases susceptibility to antibiotics. Our results demonstrate a conserved link between {triangleup}{Psi} and oxygen stress, suggesting a common mechanism for responding to shifting oxygen availability.
affiliations: Boston University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Chromosomal integration of blaCTX-M redefines the evolutionary trajectory of antibiotic resistance in E. coli through lineage-structured expansion
papers.abstract: The global CTX-M pandemic is considered a plasmid-driven phenomenon, yet chromosomal integration of blaCTX-M has been reported in various settings. Screening 451,174 publicly available E. coli genomes and retaining 2,269 CTX-M-E. coli long-read or hybrid assemblies, we found that 33.5% carried at least one chromosomally integrated blaCTX-M. Chromosomal integration was strongly structured by E. coli lineage and CTX-M variant, reaching 68.5% in ST38 and 43.9% in ST131. In the latter, integration rates varied between subclades with modelling, suggesting recent acceleration within the ST131-C2 subclade. Additional resistance genes were frequently co-integrated with blaCTX-M (33%), with architectures largely inherited from plasmid-borne structures. Integrations were mainly ISEcp1- or IS26-mediated (77.3% and 18.9%, respectively) and occurred across the entire E. coli chromosome without spared zones. blaCTX-M chromosomal integration is a widespread, lineage-structured component of the CTX-M pandemic, providing stable vertical inheritance that complements or may supplant plasmid-mediated dissemination in successful ESBL-E. coli clones.
affiliations: Assistance Publique - Hopitaux de Paris (corresponding author)

papers.title: Genetic analyses reveal distinct functional roles of Eut microcompartment shell proteins in ethanolamine metabolism in Salmonella
papers.abstract: Ethanolamine utilization is an important metabolic capability of enteric bacteria and has been associated with bacterial fitness and adaptation within diverse host environment. In Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium, ethanolamine is metabolized within the bacterial microcompartment (Eut MCP), which is composed of five shell protein subunits. Deciphering how self-assembled shell proteins spatially organize the pathway, retain metabolic intermediates and create proper environment for catalysis is crucial for understanding role of Eut MCP in cellular metabolism and pathogenesis. Through genetic mutant construction, growth and metabolic assays, microscopy, and metabolite quantification, we demonstrate that each shell protein fulfills a distinct role to the functioning of the Eut MCP. Our findings provide mechanistic insights into the structural organization and functional dynamics of the bacterial microcompartment organelle.
affiliations: CSIR-National Chemical Laboratory (corresponding author)

papers.title: Distinct metabolic states of yeast and pseudohyphae differentially prime innate immune responsiveness
papers.abstract: Pseudohyphal growth in skin-associated fungi is often considered a morphological response to environmental stress, but whether it represents a coordinated metabolic state that influences host immunity remains unclear. Using Malassezia furfur, we combined synchronized morphogenesis, temporal metabolomics, stable-isotope tracing, targeted metabolite measurements, transcriptional profiling, and functional immune assays to compare yeast and pseudohyphal states. Yeast cells maintained an active tryptophan-aldehyde metabolic program that partitioned carbon between oxidative and reductive branches associated with redox balance and methylation potential. Pseudohyphal cells attenuated this program and instead underwent sequential metabolic remodeling, characterized by early changes in one-carbon and amino acid metabolism followed by sulfur-pathway remodeling and increased glutathione biosynthesis. These distinct fungal states generated extracellular environments that altered THP-1 innate immune responsiveness without directly inducing canonical macrophage polarization. Yeast-conditioned cells responded preferentially to tissue-repair signals, whereas pseudohypha-conditioned cells displayed enhanced responses to inflammatory stimuli. Individual metabolites did not reproduce these effects, suggesting that immune conditioning depends on the integrated extracellular milieu. Together, these findings identify pseudohyphal growth as an organized adaptive metabolic state and establish a framework linking fungal morphogenetic potential to context-dependent host immune responses.
affiliations: Case Western Reserve University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Protein response to deleterious episodes of GC-biased gene conversion in mammals of different Ne
papers.abstract: GC-biased gene conversion (gBGC) is a widespread recombination-associated process that favours the fixation of GC alleles independently of their fitness. In coding regions, it can oppose purifying selection and favour the accumulation of deleterious AT to GC mutations. In mammals where recombination hotspots are predominantly determined by PRDM9, the deleterious effect of gBGC is expected to be episodic due to the rapid turnover of hotspots. The deleterious impact of gBGC episodes on proteins has been well documented, particularly in rodents and primates. However, the evolutionary response of the affected proteins after the episodes end has been scarcely investigated. Theory predicts that a decline in gBGC intensity should trigger a compensatory response that enables previous damage to be repaired. Recently, we reported evidence for pervasive compensatory evolution following gBGC episodes in Hydromyini rodents. Here, we aimed to investigate whether this post- gBGC compensation is widespread among mammals in which gBGC is episodic. Using a phylogenetic approach, we analysed substitution patterns in coding exons from five mammalian taxa spanning a range of effective population size (Ne): Murini, Rattini, Cetacea, Cercopithecidae and Hominoidae. We detected thousands of gBGC episodes, characterised by an increased rate of non-synonymous AT to GC substitutions. We found evidence for compensatory evolution in non-primate taxa, and a lack of signal in Primates. Although the influence of Ne remains unclear, our study highlights both the evolutionary significance of post-gBGC compensation and the methodological challenges in detecting it.
affiliations: Universite de Paris Saclay, INRAE, CNRS, AgroParisTech (corresponding author)

papers.title: COPD Preferentially Disrupts Constitutive Redox Support Relative to Inducible Antioxidant Defense
papers.abstract: Redox homeostasis requires both inducible antioxidant defense and constitutive machinery that continuously regenerates cellular reducing capacity. How these systems are altered across lung cell populations in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) remains unclear. We integrated donor-level single-nucleus lung transcriptomes with smoke-exposure models, independent cohorts, and large-scale pharmacologic perturbation data. Both redox programs were reduced in established COPD, but constitutive redox support showed the greater loss, concentrated in fibroblasts and lymphatic endothelium. In fibroblasts, PGC-1 target-program output showed the most negative effect among 515 regulator programs despite preserved PPARGC1A expression. Smoke exposure activated inducible antioxidant defense across experimental models, whereas this adaptive program was reduced in established COPD. Pharmacologic perturbations further separated the two arms of redox homeostasis, with redox-directed interventions producing larger transcriptional responses in inducible defense and a distinct set of compounds increasing constitutive support together with PGC-1 target output and movement away from an independently defined COPD fibroblast state. These findings identify a cell-selective loss of constitutive redox support in COPD and implicate reduced PGC-1 target-program output in the fibroblast redox phenotype.
affiliations: Florida International University (corresponding author)

papers.title: RNA3D-Decoy: A Large-Scale Benchmark Dataset of AI-Generated RNA Structure Models for Quality Assessment
papers.abstract: Recent advances in AI- RNA structure prediction have increased the availability of candidate models, but their accuracy remains variable. Developing reliable quality assessment (QA) methods requires datasets that represent contemporary prediction errors across diverse targets and molecular contexts. Here, we present RNA3D-Decoy, a large-scale benchmark dataset comprising 103,549 decoys for 677 experimentally determined targets, including 416 RNA-only structures,117 RNA structures with metal ions, and 144 RNA-protein complexes. Decoys were generated using five biomolecular predictors: AlphaFold 3, ESMFold2, Protenix, Chai-1, and Boltz-2.Each decoy is evaluated against its experimental reference us-ing TM-score, lDDT, and RMSD, with global and local quality annotations where applicable. DockQ scores additionally characterize RNA-protein interface quality. Target grouping incorporates both RNA and protein sequence relationships to support dataset partitioning. Analyses reveal distinct quality distributions across dataset levels and target-dependent differences among predictors, with each predictor contributing the highest-TM-score model for a subset of targets. Broad pooled score distributions also coexist with limited within-target score variation, particularly for RNA-protein complexes, emphasizing the importance of target-level characterization. By combining AI-generated decoys, standardized quality labels, and structured metadata, RNA3D-Decoy provides a resource for developing and evaluating methods for global quality estimation, local error prediction, and candidate-model ranking. The data set and accompanying code are available at: https://github.com/HamiltonChenLab/RNA3D-Decoy.
affiliations: Hamilton College (corresponding author)

papers.title: STAVelo: deciphering spatiotemporal cellular dynamics via spatial RNA velocity inference from spatial transcriptomics data
papers.abstract: RNA velocity is a powerful tool for deciphering cellular transcriptional dynamics from transcriptomics datasets. However, existing methods have several limitations: some do not model cellular spatial location information, some rely on cell-agnostic constant transcriptional kinetic rates, and some have not been validated for generalization across a wide range of datasets. To this end, we present STAVelo, a graph attention encoder-decoder framework that models spatial information in spatial transcriptomics (ST) data and infers RNA velocity from neural representations of transcriptional kinetic parameters. In quantitative comparisons of multiple datasets from diverse species and platforms, STAVelo outperforms previous methods in capturing cellular migration and development dynamics. In human and mouse brain datasets from different platforms, STAVelo accurately inferred the inside-out migration pattern of neurons across cortical layers. Analysis of mouse kidney and chicken heart datasets captured organ-specific developmental gradients during organ development. Analysis of mouse embryo and placenta datasets with multiple time points uncovered spatiotemporal dynamics from existing states to newly established states. In short, STAVelo provides a spatial view of cellular state transitions and deeper insights into spatiotemporal cellular dynamics in complex tissue structures.
affiliations: Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science (corresponding author)

papers.title: SIMORGH: Ensemble-Aware Geometric Deep Learning for Apo-State and Cryptic Ligand Binding Site Prediction
papers.abstract: Most computational methods identify protein-ligand binding sites from ligand-bound (holo) protein structures, where the binding pocket is already preorganized. Although convenient for benchmarking, this setting differs from the practical drug discovery scenario, in which binding sites must be inferred from ligand-free (apo) proteins. In fact, binding-competent conformations may represent only a subset of the accessible structural ensemble, while transient and cryptic pockets can emerge through conformational fluctuations. Consequently, prediction from a single static structure is often insufficient. Here we present SIMORGH, an ensemble-aware SE(3)-equivariant geometric learning framework that predicts ligand binding sites by integrating information across protein conformational ensembles. SIMORGH employs a two-stage architecture consisting of a structure-level equivariant encoder that learns geometric representations from individual conformations and a lightweight ensemble-level aggregation module that combines them into residue-level binding predictions while scaling near-linearly with both protein and ensemble size. We evaluate SIMORGH across multiple complementary settings, including the PLINDER apo benchmark, molecular dynamics trajectories spanning more than 200 cryptic-pocket proteins, and established community benchmarks. SIMORGH consistently outperforms existing static and dynamics-aware methods under the challenging ligand-free setting, while identifying cryptic binding pockets, maintaining strong prediction consistency between paired apo and holo structures, and scaling efficiently to large multi-chain complexes. To facilitate reproducible, transparent, and accessible use, Simorgh is available through the Galaxy Europe server (https://usegalaxy.eu).
affiliations: Universite de Lorraine, Inria, F-54000 Nancy, France (corresponding author)

papers.title: mzQC: a versatile way to communicate quality information for biological mass spectrometry
papers.abstract: Reliable quality control (QC) is essential for reproducible biological mass spectrometry, yet QC information is still typically stored in tool-specific, poorly interoperable formats that hinder comparison, reuse, and transparent reporting. We present mzQC, a community-developed standard from the HUPO Proteomics Standards Initiative for the compact, machine-readable representation of QC metrics and their associated metadata across mass spectrometry workflows. mzQC is implemented in JSON, organized to support both individual mass spectrometry acquisitions and collections thereof, with formal QC metrics definitions supported by controlled vocabularies to ensure unambiguous metric interpretation and semantic consistency. The format is supported by validation tools and reference libraries in Python, R, and Java, facilitating integration into existing software ecosystems. We demonstrate the utility of mzQC across diverse analytical modalities and QC settings, spanning longitudinal instrument monitoring, acquisition-method evaluation, study-level quality assessment, repository-scale data characterization, and spatially resolved mass spectrometry imaging. Together, these use cases show that mzQC provides not merely a file format, but a shared foundation for interoperable QC reporting, large-scale data assessment, and more rigorous, reproducible, and reusable mass spectrometry-based research.
affiliations: Bioinformatics Solution Center, Institut fuer Informatik, Freie Universitaet Berlin, Takustr. 9, 14195 Berlin, Germany (corresponding author)

papers.title: Exploration of ligand (un)binding trajectories with Rosetta
papers.abstract: Ligand transport through proteins underlies many aspects of molecular function, but its detailed mechanisms remain largely inaccessible to direct observation. Molecular dynamics simulations could close this gap, but are computationally too demanding for practical purposes, including filtering stages of enzyme design pipelines. Simplified docking-based approaches might be informative, but sometimes the oversimplifications required for high throughput applications might lead to unreliable predictions. Here we present RosettaLigand PathFinder (RLPF), a fast and practical tool explicitly built to ensure conformational continuity of the ligand trajectory, protein and ligand flexibility, and robustness of every run. Built using a flexible RosettaScripts XML interface, it enables fine-grained control over all simulation parameters and adaptability for a wide range of use cases. Applied to several representative systems, RLPF reproduced established transport features and mutation effects, highlighting its ability to produce biologically relevant insights and serve as a filter in enzyme design campaigns. Wide customizability and well-defined scope of RLPF make it a useful addition to the family of tools to study the dynamics of interactions between small molecules and proteins.
affiliations: Institute for Drug Discovery, Leipzig University, Leipzig, Germany (corresponding author)

papers.title: Expression trajectories in the aging male mouse colon transcriptome
papers.abstract: Characterizing temporal dynamics during aging is crucial to understanding the course of aging-related events. The transcriptome is extensively remodeled with age, but the temporal trajectories of these changes, particularly through midlife, remain poorly defined in many tissues. Here, we address this gap in the male mouse colon. Using a dataset of 83 RNA-Seq samples from five time points during adult mouse lifespan, we show that colon aging is characterized by multiple gene-expression trajectories unfolding in parallel, with a major shift occurring during a mid- to late-life transition marked by a collapse of the unfolded protein response (UPR). Moreover, we report widespread non-monotonic trajectories, including genes that peak or dip in midlife and would be missed by comparisons limited to young versus old ages. We further describe age-dependent dynamics of transposable element-containing transcripts and a nonlinear course of transcriptomic entropy across the lifespan. Importantly, we identify a small set of genes that track chronological age and use only three of them to construct a compact transcriptomic clock, which we validate using an independent RNA-seq dataset and qPCR data. Together, our results indicate that nonlinear patterns dominate the aging colon transcriptome and underscore the value of high temporal resolution for identifying key transitions during aging.
affiliations: Leibniz Institute on Aging - Fritz Lipmann Institute (FLI) (corresponding author)

papers.title: CCT2 expression marks a translation-activated state in sporadic ALS motor neurons and is associated with functional decline
papers.abstract: Sporadic disease accounts for about 90% of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) cases, and its biological heterogeneity is a major contributor to the failure of trials that enroll patients under a single diagnosis. Because sporadic ALS lacks a shared genetic anchor, identifying biological signals is critical for effective patient stratification. We analyzed induced pluripotent stem cell derived motor neurons from 619 AnswerALS participants using transcriptomics, proteomics, and whole-genome sequencing and identified CCT2 as the first single-gene marker of a molecular state within sporadic ALS, providing a measurable basis for trial enrollment according to biology. We first anchored the analysis in known ALS genotypes. C9orf72 and SOD1 motor neurons did not converge on a common signature but retained genotype-specific differences that bulk postmortem tissue compresses. Scoring 391 sporadic patients along three transcriptomic axes (bioenergetic stress, cell cycle, and inflammation) resolved three states. One state was marked by CCT2, a TRiC chaperonin subunit, which distinguished it from the quiescent state with an area under the curve of 0.892. CCT2 was also elevated at the protein level and associated with the rate of ALSFRS-R decline, although this association weakened after adjustment for culture composition. Upstream regulator analysis placed this state downstream of MYC and mTORC1 activation. No germline test across 360 whole genomes explained these states. Validation using Target ALS data showed that the relationship between CCT2 and the cell cycle program was also present in postmortem cortex enriched for layer 5b projection neurons.
affiliations: Department of Computational Biomedicine, Cedars Sinai Medical Center, CA, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: Interchain base-stacking and spermine bridges govern ssDNA condensation and reentrant transitions
papers.abstract: Polyvalent-cation-induced condensation and reentrant transition in double-stranded DNA are classically described by backbone electrostatics. Whether the same principles govern single-stranded DNA, whose solvent-exposed bases can interact within and between chains to form complex phases, is unknown. Here, we employ simulations and experiments to show that the tetravalent cation spermine (Spm4+) drives two equilibrium transitions in poly(dT) and poly(dA). The onset of phase separation, resulting in thermodynamic equilibrium between the dispersed low-density phase and high density coacervate, occurs at a low sequence independent Spm4+ concentration and is primarily driven by charge balance between phosphate groups and Spm4+. Strikingly, the condensed phases are stabilized by at most 1.5 (poly dT) and 2.5 (poly dA) bridging Spm4+ per chain. The ssDNA chains condense to form fluid-like networks without chain collapse. The fluidity of chains in the dense phases is confirmed by fluorescence recovery after photobleaching experiments. Both simulations and experiments show that the range of spermine concentration over which phase coexistence persists is sequence dependent and nearly threefold wider in poly(dA). At higher sequence dependent spermine concentrations, a reentrant phase, characterized by dissolution of the coacervates, emerges. The transition to the reentrant phase occurs when the number of bridging Spm4+ molecules vanishes at high sequence dependent spermine concentration. The combination of experiments and simulations show that the two phase transitions in ssDNA are driven by an interplay of stacking and electrostatic interactions.
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin (corresponding author)

papers.title: Efficient detection of cryptic pockets on challenging drug targets using MD-free co-vibrational modes
papers.abstract: Allosteric and cryptic binding sites provide unique opportunities in drug discovery for achieving selectivity, reducing toxicity and unlocking challenging therapeutical targets. Yet, cryptic pockets are particularly elusive in that they are difficult to capture with experimental methodologies, and therefore often remain undetected. Computational approaches for flexible cryptic site detection traditionally involve extensive unbiased molecular dynamics simulations, or more efficient but computationally still highly demanding biased MD alternatives that make use of enhanced sampling along low-frequency motions of the protein structure. Here we utilize a new variant of the recently introduced and orders of magnitude faster, MD-free COVIB algorithm to identify cryptic pockets efficiently in two challenging targets, the KRAS oncoprotein and the N-terminal domain of the STAT5B transcription factor. Using experimental and AI-modelled structures, respectively, we identify numerous cryptic sites, some of which have not yet been reported. The sites are prioritized and validated with our pharmacophore optimized photoaffinity-tagged fragment library via MS-based peptide mapping and NMR spectroscopy. Besides identifying new, targetable regions on the surface of these important oncotargets, we have established a protocol combining COVIB-based cryptic pocket detection and photoaffinity-based experimental peptide mapping as a robust approach for exploring unique and tractable cryptic pockets.
affiliations: Flagship Pioneering, Pioneering Intelligence, 55 Cambridge Pkwy, Cambridge, MA 02142, U. S. A. (corresponding author)

papers.title: The Dilated Cardiomyopathy E525K Mutation Stabilizes the Cardiac Myosin Interacting-Heads Motif While Activating the Isolated Motor Domain
papers.abstract: Mutations in {beta}-cardiac myosin are a common cause of inherited cardiomyopathies. The dilated cardiomyopathy E525K mutation alters both thick filament regulation and motor activity, yet the structural basis for these effects has remained unclear. Here, we combined cryo-EM and MD simulations to determine how E525K affects the conformational landscape of cardiac myosin in both its autoinhibited interacting-heads motif (IHM) and isolated myosin head states. E525K-mutated myosin exclusively adopted a single S2 conformation in IHM, in contrast to the conformational heterogeneity observed in wild-type myosin. Structural and electrostatic analyses revealed that the mutation increased positive charge density at the blocked-head (BH) - S2 (subfragment-2) interface, strengthening interactions with negatively charged residues within S2. 3D variability analysis and MD simulations of the E525K IHM demonstrated reduced S2 mobility, consistent with strengthened BH - S2 interactions, and decreased conformational flexibility, providing a structural mechanism for stabilization of the IHM state. To investigate the isolated myosin head, we determined cryo-EM structures of wild-type and E525K subfragment-1 (S1). The mutation induced local conformational rearrangements in the activation-loop and Loop 3 region, the SH3-like domain, and the essential light chain of S1, revealing structural changes that support the enhanced motor activity previously reported for isolated E525K myosin motors. These findings show that E525K stabilizes the autoinhibited IHM through electrostatic stabilization of the BH - S2 interface while inducing structural changes consistent with activation of the isolated motor domain, providing structural insights into how a single DCM mutation differentially regulates cardiac myosin S1 and IHM structure and function.
affiliations: University of Massachusetts Chan Medical School, Worcester, MA, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: A Minimal Model of Functional Redundancy as a Route to Enzyme Specialisation
papers.abstract: Functional overlap among enzymes could permit individual proteins to specialise while maintaining organismal reaction performance. We examine this possibility in a minimal origin--fixation model in which weak generalists jointly supply 120 reactions and fitness depends on aggregate catalytic capacity. Pleiotropic mutations act on loop-local activity profiles subject to a tunable structural incompatibility constraint. No gene duplication occurs during evolution. A factorial sweep combines five initial redundancies, two mutation kernels, and four incompatibility values, with five replicates per combination and 250 fixed substitutions per simulation. Across all 40 parameter combinations, effective protein breadth decreases and the strongest function accounts for a larger share of activity. Mean breadth reductions range from 1.59 to 3.97 under the loss-biased kernel and from 6.32 to 8.16 under the symmetric kernel. Specialisation therefore does not require a mutational bias towards biochemical loss. Higher redundancy generally buffers weakest-reaction performance under loss-biased mutation, while structural incompatibility has a non-monotonic effect on specialisation. Total activity increases, but is not conserved by the model and does not measure a conservation-based efficiency gain.
