Complementary analysis of tumour-proximal cell populations revealed that multiple immune populations were associated with longer survival, whereas two fibroblast populations were associated with shorter survival. Integrating these analyses revealed that survival-associated tumour-intrinsic gene expression was correlated with the abundance of neighbouring immune and stromal populations that were themselves associated with survival. Pairwise Cox regression demonstrated substantial overlap in the prognostic information captured by these features, while analysis of individual gene-cell combinations showed that survival associations differed according to the abundance of neighbouring populations. Consensus clustering further identified four patient groups with distinct combinations of tumour-intrinsic expression and microenvironmental composition, broadly separating patients with longer and shorter survival. Together, this cohort-scale spatial analysis identifies tumour-intrinsic and microenvironmental features associated with HGSOC survival and reveals how their correlated patterns and combined associations relate to patient outcome.
affiliations: Harry Perkins Institute of Medical Research, QEII Medical Centre and Centre for Medical Research, The University of Western Australia, Nedlands, Perth, WA 6009, (corresponding author)

papers.title: KSHV upregulates the long non-coding RNA PURPL via p73 to suppress p53
papers.abstract: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) are a class of regulatory RNAs with lengths exceeding 200 nucleotides. The lncRNA PURPL (p53 upregulated regulator of p53 levels) is a p53-regulated gene. PURPL is an oncogenic lncRNA that represses p53 function; it is upregulated in many tumors and promotes cancer cell proliferation. Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV) is the causative agent of all forms of Kaposi sarcoma (KS) and is tightly associated with primary effusion lymphoma (PEL). We found upregulation of PURPL in both de novo and chronically KSHV-infected cells. We found that p73 (a p53 homolog) associates with the PURPL promoter and upregulates PURPL expression. Previously, it has been shown that KSHV-encoded latency-associated nuclear antigen (LANA) stabilizes p73. We found that ectopic expression of LANA increased both p73 protein levels and PURPL expression. p73 knockdown abrogates PURPL upregulation following KSHV infection. Antisense oligonucleotides (ASO) targeting PURPL reduced PEL cell proliferation and increased acetylated p53 levels. In contrast to p53, p73 is not repressed by PURPL RNA. In summary, our study reveals how an oncogenic virus can utilize p73 to upregulate the oncogenic lncRNA PURPL as an additional way to repress p53. Moreover, we propose another mechanism by which p73 may promote tumor growth.
affiliations: Azrieli Faculty of Medicine in the Galilee, Bar-Ilan University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Revisiting AXL as a therapeutic target in soft tissue sarcoma: dubermatinib and bemcentinib effects are largely independent of AXL inhibition
papers.abstract: Soft tissue sarcomas (STS) are a heterogeneous group of mesenchymal malignancies with generally poor prognosis, raising a continued interest in novel therapeutic targets. The TAM-family receptor tyrosine kinase AXL has been proposed as a therapeutic target across several cancer types, including STS. Here we revisit the clinical relevance of AXL in STS by combining in silico analyses with functional and transcriptomic characterisation of two representative AXL inhibitors, dubermatinib and bemcentinib, in the HT-1080 and SK-LMS-1 STS-derived cell models. STS ranked among the tumour types with the highest median AXL mRNA expression across The Cancer Genome Atlas, yet AXL expression was not associated with patient survival. Both dubermatinib and bemcentinib reduced cell viability and induced apoptosis but, unexpectedly, shRNA-mediated AXL knockdown failed to reproduce the antiproliferative effect of either inhibitor and did not modify cellular sensitivity to drugs treatment. Transcriptomic profiling after AXL genetic knockdown showed weak correlation with drug-induced transcriptional changes, with the large majority of drug-regulated genes being AXL-independent and largely specific to each cell line. Our data indicate that although dubermatinib and bemcentinib show clear antitumour activity in STS models, this activity is largely independent from AXL inhibition, suggesting the rationale for AXL-directed therapy may be reconsidered.
affiliations: Spanish National Research Council (corresponding author)

papers.title: Mechanistic Decoding of Pharmacodynamic Intratumoral Heterogeneity: A Pan-Cancer Regulatory Framework
papers.abstract: Intratumoral heterogeneity (ITH) drives therapy failure through divergent drug response propensities among coexisting subclones - a phenomenon we term pharmacodynamic intratumoral heterogeneity (PharmITH). While single-cell technologies have catalogued transcriptional heterogeneity, which molecular programs shape differential drug responses remains unresolved. Here we decode PharmITH by linking single-cell transcriptomes from 1,279 samples across 24 cancer types with drug-response profiles for 1,218 compounds. We identify 425 hub genes consistently associated with predicted treatment-response heterogeneity and with potential therapeutic relevance and perform multi-omics network analysis in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) integrating transcriptional regulation, somatic mutations, cell-cell communication (CCC), and alternative splicing. This analysis identifies four classes of candidate regulatory associations observed in the LUAD case study: 3 transcription factors establishing pre-existing drug-response programs, 41 genomic alterations amplifying pathway signaling through intermediate networks, 5 ligand-receptor pairs coupling microenvironmental cues to intracellular circuits, and 8 genes producing opposing isoforms via differential splicing. These findings converge on 6 core pathways, revealing that PharmITH arises from tumor-intrinsic mechanisms. Experimental validation and an online platform PharmITH for pan-cancer therapy enable state-resolved drug-response analysis and candidate-gene exploration. This approach transforms ITH from descriptive phenotyping to mechanistic dissection, providing actionable targets to overcome therapy resistance.
affiliations: Joint Research Center for Occupational Medicine and Health of IHM and School of Public Health, Anhui University of Science and Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Metabolic rewiring induces a viral mimicry-mediated quiescence in glioblastoma
papers.abstract: Glioblastoma is a highly aggressive brain tumour driven by therapy-resistant glioblastoma stem cells (GSCs) that switch between dormant and proliferative states through poorly defined programs. In this study, we identify SAT1, encoding the rate-limiting polyamine-catabolic enzyme SSAT1, as enriched in quiescent GSCs, linking metabolic rewiring to dormancy. Pharmacologic induction of SSAT1 with the polyamine analogue N1,N11-Diethylnorspermine (DENSpm) triggers a chemoprotective, reversible growth arrest in patient-derived GSCs, independent of stemness, differentiation or senescence. SAT1-induced dormancy coincides with reduced eIF5A hypusination and global protein translation, and a marked rise in double-stranded RNA that activates type I interferon signalling. Knocking down the mitochondrial antiviral-signalling protein, essential for antiviral innate immunity, partially reverses this growth arrest, establishing viral mimicry as functionally required for dormancy. Single-cell and cohort analyses across GSCs and neural stem cells demonstrate that susceptibility to metabolically induced quiescence is set by an intrinsic inflammatory tone and lysosomal dependency, defining a context-dependent metabolic-immune axis which can be targeted to prevent GBM progression.
affiliations: The Hospital for Sick Children (corresponding author)

papers.title: PWK genetic background reprograms heterochromatin and malignant epithelial states in Neu-driven mammary tumors
papers.abstract: Genetic background can alter the latency and behavior of cancers initiated by the same oncogenic driver, but how inherited variation reshapes the regulatory landscape that permits tumor development remains poorly understood. The PWK genetic background accelerates mammary tumor onset in the NeuT model. We compared PWK NeuT and BALB NeuT tumors using tumor-level RNA-seq, histone ChIP-seq, and single-cell multiome profiling. PWK tumors exhibited broad transcriptional reprogramming characterized by reduced immune-associated expression and increased epithelial differentiation and neuronal-like programs. Chromatin remodeling was spatially redistributed rather than uniformly increased or decreased. PWK tumors showed expansion of H3K9me3- and H4K20me3-associated chromatin, while both marks were depleted across many expressed genes and concentrated within selected intergenic and repeat-rich territories, revealing coordinated redistribution of constitutive heterochromatin. Single-cell multiome profiling showed that broad epithelial representation remained similar between strains, yet specific malignant states were strongly strain biased. Integrated RNA and accessibility analyses identified concordant strain-selective regulatory programs and candidate loci, while trajectory analysis revealed distinct epithelial state transitions between PWK NeuT and BALB NeuT tumors. Together, these findings indicate that inherited genetic background reshapes transcriptional programs, heterochromatin organization, and malignant epithelial state trajectories in NeuT mammary tumors, providing a regulatory framework for understanding strain-dependent differences in tumor onset.
affiliations: Wayne State University School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Precision Targeting of Heparan Sulfate Proteoglycans Broadly Dysregulates Survival Signaling and Metabolic Adaptation in Pancreatic Cancer
papers.abstract: Treatments for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) often fail because of the cancer's ability to adapt its signaling and metabolic pathways to circumvent treatment mechanisms. PDAC hallmarks that promote treatment resistance (increased fatty acid metabolism, survival signaling, desmoplasia, and macropinocytosis) are extensively regulated by heparan sulfate proteoglycans (HSPGs) and their binding partners. The pro-tumor functions of HSPGs are controlled by site-specific cleavage of their heparan sulfate chains by mammalian heparanase; however, cleavage by bacterial heparinase III (HepIII) represses these functions and prevents downstream, pro-tumor signaling. Using tumor-targeting, attenuated Salmonella typhimurium (strain YS1646), we have limited HepIII transgene expression to tumor tissue. Degradation of tumor cell heparan sulfates by HepIII resulted in decreased macropinocytosis, reduced survival signaling, lipid storage depletion, and decreased expression of translational machinery. This tumor-targeting treatment has the potential to improve the efficacy of several approved pancreatic cancer therapies, which is predicted to increase patient survival.
affiliations: Beckman Research Institute, City of Hope (corresponding author)

papers.title: Designing enzymes for new-to-nature chemistry and non-natural substrates with AlphaProtein Novo
papers.abstract: Creating highly active enzymes for arbitrary reactions is a transformative goal for the molecular sciences (1). Traditional protein engineering (2,3) is constrained by a reliance on existing natural starting points, which are often challenging to discover. De novo design offers the potential to overcome this by creating enzymes from first principles (4), but has yet to achieve practically relevant catalytic properties. Here we present AlphaProtein Novo (AP Novo), a machine-learning pipeline that demonstrates, for the first time, that de novo enzyme design can outperform natural sequence mining in addressing challenging chemistry. We used AP Novo to design new-to-nature nitrene transferases to synthesise the pharmacophore piperidine with unprecedented product selectivity, and to create enzymes that degrade the environmental toxin DEHP under conditions that denature natural enzymes. We also obtained state-of-the-art catalytic efficiencies on two well-studied model reactions, and through iterative design and analysis found that key enablers of success were mechanism-inspired metrics based on AlphaFold 3 predictions and sequence-ensemble-based scoring of designed backbones. Our results show that de novo design has become a powerful complement to natural enzyme diversity for discovering catalysts for a range of applications.
affiliations: Google DeepMind (corresponding author)

papers.title: Organizing principles of the cellular electron economy
papers.abstract: Life runs on electron flow. Cells extract electrons from nutrients and transfer them through metabolism, coupling carbon use to energy conservation, biosynthesis and redox homeostasis. Yet how and even whether electron flow is organized at the system-level across metabolism remain unknown. Here we formalize the concept of the cellular electron economy: a quantitative, genome-wide, reaction-resolved representation of electron generation, transfer and disposal. This electron-centric perspective reveals a quantitative relationship governed by two distinct organizing factors: the carbon source sets the baseline and maximal rate of electron flow, whereas the capacity to dispose of electrons to terminal sinks determines where within this range the system operates. Carbon uptake can even increase as net electron flux falls. This system-level organization is shown to apply to five microorganisms with different intracellular electron routing pathways and predicts graded physiological responses to oxygen supply across carbon sources and respiratory architectures. The cellular electron economy thus links reaction-level redox chemistry to whole-cell metabolic organization and reveals how the same organizing principles govern electron flow across diverse metabolic architectures.
affiliations: TBI, Université de Toulouse, CNRS, INRAE, INSA, Toulouse, France (corresponding author)

papers.title: Assay coverage reshapes metabolic diagnosis and the interpretation of pathway disturbance
papers.abstract: Metabolic profiles are used to quantify disturbance, classify disease and infer biochemical function, yet these endpoints retain different information. We combine secondary analysis of 386 metabolites in six Arabidopsis thaliana mutation accumulation lines, known-disease classification in 129 public human metabolic-disease profiles, and an analytically solvable kinetic model. A conditional occupancy model separates annotation-bin breadth from hit count and measured bin sizes: the plant low-versus-high fitness comparison changes from a two-sided exact permutation p = 0.10 to p = 0.30 after calibration. Unsigned metabolite profiles achieve mean macro recall of 0.911 and 0.895 in separate EDTA and heparin subsets, compared with 0.624 and 0.382 for a burden baseline. However, controlled loss of 50% of held-out measurements reverses representation ranking in heparin, giving signed profiles a recall advantage of 0.108 with a conditional bootstrap interval of 0.063-0.155. A spectral decomposition identifies the within-pathway contrasts attenuated by smoothing. The kinetic model then shows that lower concentration and faster relaxation can coexist with reduced desired product flux, while a null-space criterion states when observations identify a metabolic task. The results connect assay coverage, diagnostic information and functional identifiability. Human performance is internally validated, and the kinetic predictions remain uncalibrated to patients.
affiliations: Moscow State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Scalable and semi-automated Boolean network inference from multi-condition single-cell transcriptomes with scBOLT
papers.abstract: Predictive logical models have made substantial contributions to biomedical research by facilitating the identification of regulatory mechanisms driving biological processes. Yet, their construction remains a major bottleneck, as it typically relies on extensive prior knowledge at the genome scale. The emergence of high-throughput omics technologies has opened new opportunities for data-driven logical model construction by providing high-resolution observations of biological states. In parallel, formal constraint-based approaches have emerged, reformulating executable model inference as a constraint-satisfaction problem. However, transforming omics observations into biologically meaningful Boolean state abstractions and dynamical constraints suitable for logical synthesis engines remains challenging, particularly for poorly understood biological systems and multi-condition experimental settings. To address these challenges, we introduce scBOLT, a semi-automated framework for Boolean constraint engineering and logical model inference from multi-condition single-cell transcriptomes. Beyond these methodological contributions, scBOLT substantially improves computational tractability, enabling the inference of Boolean networks comprising several hundred components within practical runtimes.
affiliations: Univ. Bordeaux, CNRS, Bordeaux INP, LaBRI, UMR 5800, F-33400 Talence, France (corresponding author)

papers.title: Mucosal architecture, microbiota resilience and metabolic disruption reveal holobiont dynamics during bovine respiratory disease
papers.abstract: The gut-airway axis is increasingly recognised as an important determinant of respiratory health in livestock. However, the interactions among respiratory infections, microbial communities, mucosal barrier function, and microbial metabolism that underpin this axis remain poorly understood. Here, we combined longitudinal immunological, mucosal, microbiological, and metabolic analyses to characterise host-microbiota interactions during antibiotic treatment and experimental bovine respiratory disease (BRD). We found that the bovine respiratory tract is organised as a hierarchically structured mucosal ecosystem, with compartment-specific mucin expression patterns associated with distinct microbial communities. Within this framework, increasing respiratory pathogen loads were associated with greater clinical severity, oxidative stress, acute inflammation, and targeted alterations in mucosal regulation and microbial composition, while serum amyloid A emerged as the host biomarker most closely reflecting infection intensity. Although infection altered host and microbial states, antimicrobial treatment represented the dominant ecological perturbation. Antibiotic exposure reshaped both respiratory and intestinal microbial communities, reducing diversity, increasing community drift, and driving coordinated ecological transitions across the gut-airway axis that exceeded the effects of infection alone. Importantly, these compositional changes were accompanied by profound reductions in acetate, propionate, butyrate, and valerate, identifying short-chain fatty acids as a major functional consequence of gut microbiota disruption. Integrative multi-omics analyses revealed that mucosal organisation, microbial diversity, microbial metabolism, and immune activity were embedded within a highly structured gut-airway network. Together, these findings support a holobiont view of BRD in which disease outcomes emerge not only from pathogen-host interactions but also from ecological disturbances that propagate across interconnected mucosal compartments. Notably, antimicrobial treatment affected ecosystem structure and function more than infection itself, highlighting potential trade-offs between pathogen control and microbiota stability. Preserving microbial resilience and its metabolic functions may therefore represent an important component of future strategies to improve respiratory health and disease resilience in cattle.
affiliations: Univ Toulouse, ENVT, INRAE, IHAP, Toulouse, France (corresponding author)

papers.title: A quantitative interactome map reveals affinity tailored hijacking of human cellular functions by resident and pathogenic bacteria
papers.abstract: Bacteria employ molecular mimicry to hijack host cellular functions for their own benefit. Despite the wealth of data mapping human-bacteria interactions, a comprehensive view of how these networks are fine-tuned remains elusive. In particular, there have been no large-scale screenings measuring human-bacterial protein-protein binding affinities to explore their role in functional and pathological outcomes. Here, we report the largest quantitative interactome to date between the family of human PDZ domains and C-terminal PDZ-binding motifs (PBMs) in effectors from pathogenic and resident gut bacteria. We show that bacteria tailor effector sequences to bind PDZ domains with similar or higher binding affinities than human PBMs to hijack their associated cellular functions. For a subset of the dataset, we validate PDZ-PBM interactions with the corresponding full-length proteins and show that for pathogenic E. coli effector NleA, its C-terminal PBM is necessary for interactions with proteins involved in intracellular transport and membrane organization, probably impacting the host glycocalyx to favor infection. Finally, we show that motifs overlapping with effector PBMs target interaction modules other than PDZ domains, adding an additional layer of complexity to the host-microbe molecular dialogue.
affiliations: Architecture et Fonction des Macromolecules Biologiques, UMR7257 CNRS-Aix-Marseille Universite, 13288 Marseille Cedex 9, France (corresponding author)

papers.title: Standard-GEM supports reproducible development of genome-scale metabolic models
papers.abstract: The field of metabolic modelling at the genome scale continues to expand, with increasing numbers of models being reconstructed, shared and curated. This expansion creates a need to adopt common principles regarding transparency and versioning, in addition to standardisation of file formats, annotations, and model testing. Here, we present a repository standard and template for Git-based genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs) supporting both newly reconstructed and actively curated models, following FAIR principles (findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability), and incorporating research software best practices. Standard-GEM exposes GEMs across web services and platforms in the metabolic modelling field and enables automatic validation of GEMs. The use of this template for new models and its adoption reduces the effort required to share, validate and reuse GEMs.
affiliations: Department of Life Sciences, Chalmers University of Technology, Gothenburg SE-41258, Sweden (corresponding author)

papers.title: ProteomeScout v4: An open-source, harmonized, ecosystem for post-translational modifications
papers.abstract: There are many databases of post-translational modifications, but each has different protein and PTM coverage, making the current state of post-translational modifications difficult to obtain, assess, or harmonize. ProteomeScout has been a relational database that harmonized a myriad of resources to address this challenge. In this update, we wished to create a lightweight, sustainable open source resource for the community that retained the power of harmonization, protein visualization, and Python tools for interacting with the database. ProteomeScout-v4 presents an ecosystem of open-source tools for aggregating and updating proteins and post-translational modifications and presenting the web-based and code-based access tools for interacting with the data. ProteomeScout has moved from using a complex relational database to a flat-text file format. The database file update is version controlled on FigShare and all features have processes for continuous updating, including migrating PTMs to updated protein records, when external databases are updated. The open-source nature and flexibility allow for user-based control and community-based feature integration. Fast and easy analysis is possible with the API, with example analyses provided here.
affiliations: University of Virginia (corresponding author)

papers.title: A synthetic PGC1α co-activator reprograms microglial immunometabolism to preserve cone function in retinal degeneration
papers.abstract: Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is genetically heterogeneous, yet initiating mutations converge on primary rod degeneration followed by cone dysfunction and loss. Activated microglia are implicated in this secondary phase, but whether selective immunometabolic reprogramming of microglia preserves retinal function remains unknown. In human iPSC-derived microglia and retinal CD11b cells, PGC1 induction suppressed LPS-driven interferon signaling and cytokine release, yet Seahorse analysis and isotopologue tracing showed that energy metabolism remained altered. We therefore fused PGC1 to a multivalent p65-HSF1 module, yielding ~2.5-fold higher nuclear receptor output than native PGC1 and coordinated engagement of oxidative and anti-inflammatory programs in mouse retinal CD11b cells. Microglia-restricted expression in humanized RHOP347L mice preserved photopic responses through six months, increased retinal thickness and promoted ramified subretinal IBA1 morphology. Microglial immunometabolism thus represents a potentially genotype-independent neuroprotective target in RP, and engineered PGC1 co-activators provide a means to sustain oxidative metabolism under inflammatory pressure.
affiliations: Department of Ophthalmology, Columbia University, New York, NY, United States (corresponding author)

papers.title: Lipocalin-2-expressing red pulp macrophages link ischemic stroke to systemic immune reprogramming in mice and humans
papers.abstract: Background Acute ischemic stroke (AIS) triggers profound systemic immune alterations that contribute to post-stroke infections. The spleen is a key peripheral immune organ affected by AIS, but the molecular mediators linking cerebral ischemia to splenic immune dysfunction remain incompletely understood. Lipocalin-2 (LCN2) is an acute-phase protein implicated in neuroinflammation and host defense, yet its peripheral regulation, cellular sources and immune-modulatory actions after AIS remain unclear. Methods Male, 10-12-week-old C57BL/6J mice underwent transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO) or sham surgery. Spleens were collected 24 hours, 3 days, or 7 days post-stroke for 3-MACE-Seq transcriptomics, multiplex cytokine profiling, RT-qPCR, immunoblotting, and immunofluorescence. Murine T cells and monocytes were magnetically isolated, stimulated with recombinant LCN2 protein or vehicle, and analyzed using (i) RT-qPCR of LPS-induced proinflammatory cytokines (Il1b, Il6, Tnf), (ii) LCN2-driven T cell chemotaxis, (iii) FACS-based phenotyping, (iv) FACS-based phagocytosis of pHrodo-labeled E. coli bioparticles, and (v) FACS-based quantification of reactive oxygen species (ROS) using DHR-123. Human plasma samples and post-mortem spleens from three patients with ischemic stroke and one non-stroke control were analyzed for LCN2 expression and cellular localization. Untouched human monocytes from healthy donors were exposed to recombinant LCN2 and assessed by flow cytometry for antigen-presentation, co-stimulatory markers, phagocytosis and ROS production. Results Transcriptomics revealed robust, biphasic splenic Lcn2 upregulation at 24 hours and 7 days after tMCAO. LCN2 localized predominantly to F4/80+ red pulp macrophages (RPMs), and accumulated at RPM-associated CD3+ contact sites. AIS induced a broad suppression of splenic innate and adaptive cytokine networks. Recombinant LCN2 induced T cell hyporesponsiveness, suppressed Il6 and Tnf induction, and impaired CCL5-directed chemotaxis. In monocytes, LCN2 promoted a shift toward Ly6Clow phenotypes, enhanced phagocytosis of E. coli, and uncoupled phagocytosis from ROS production. In human ischemic stroke spleens, LCN2 was detected in CD68+ RPMs and at RPM-associated immune-cell contact sites, consistent with the murine splenic phenotype. In line with the murine findings, human monocytes exposed to LCN2 displayed increased E. coli uptake but reduced ROS, alongside reduced HLA-DR, CD80, CD206, and CD11b expression. Conclusions AIS induces a conserved splenic LCN2-expressing RPM niche in mice and humans. Recombinant LCN2 is sufficient to reprogram T cells and monocytes toward hyporesponsive, tolerogenic and phagocytosis-ROS-uncoupled states, thereby linking cerebral ischemia to systemic immune dysfunction. These findings identify LCN2-expressing RPMs as a translationally relevant immunoregulatory niche after AIS and nominate receptor-specific LCN2 signaling as a candidate pathway for future studies aimed at mitigating post-stroke immunodepression and infection susceptibility without compromising antimicrobial host defense.
affiliations: Goethe University Frankfurt, Institute of General Pharmacology and Toxicology, Pharmazentrum Frankfurt, 60590 Frankfurt am Main, Germany (corresponding author)

papers.title: Protective near-germline antibodies to malaria elicited by RTS,S/AS01E vaccination in African infants
papers.abstract: Malaria is a leading cause of childhood mortality, yet infant immune responses to vaccination remain poorly understood. Here, we characterize 88 monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) directed against the Plasmodium falciparum circumsporozoite protein cloned from African infants immunized with the RTS,S/AS01E malaria vaccine, identifying potent antiparasitic mAbs exhibiting molecular features resembling those observed in adults and minimal somatic hypermutation. Importantly, germline-reverted variants of four mAbs inducing sterile protection in vivo maintained high binding affinity and Fab-dependent parasite killing. Structural analyses revealed that a few amino acid replacements drive homotypic helical assemblies, fine-tuning parasite inhibition and protective efficacy. Thus, despite maturational constraints of early life, infants can generate potent antimalarial antibodies in a near-germline configuration, informing next-generation vaccine development for this vulnerable group.
affiliations: ISGlobal, Barcelona, Spain (corresponding author)

papers.title: Fluorescent proteins misreport ribosome abundance under translation inhibition
papers.abstract: Fluorescent proteins are widely used as quantitative reporters of protein abundance in living cells. Here we show that this relationship can break down under translation inhibition: the cellular ribosomal abundance can increase while fluorescence intensity remains unchanged or even decreases. Using fluorescent reporters of ribosome abundance in Escherichia coli and Bacillus subtilis, we find that cellular fluorescence intensity quantitatively tracks ribosome abundance, inferred by RNA-to-protein ratio, under nutrient-limited growth but that is no longer true during chloramphenicol treatment. In E. coli, the discrepancy occurs with transcriptional and translational reporters and with both ribosomal protein and ribosomal RNA promoters. To distinguish changes in fluorescence output per reporter from changes in reporter abundance, we constructed a fluorescent protein-LacZ dual reporter in which fluorescence and an independent enzymatic estimate of reporter abundance are obtained from the same protein. Under translation inhibition, LacZ-derived reporter abundance increases whereas fluorescence intensity remains approximately constant, showing that fluorescence output per unit reporter abundance decreases. In a companion study, Bakshi and colleagues demonstrate that the effect extends to other fluorescent proteins and other translation inhibitors, indicating that it is not specific to a particular fluorescent protein or translation inhibitor. Our results show that fluorescent-protein calibration can be condition-dependent and cannot be assumed to transfer across physiological perturbations.
affiliations: University of California, San Diego (corresponding author)

papers.title: LGR5-high colorectal cancer defines a Wnt-active stem-like state with multimodal therapeutic vulnerabilities
papers.abstract: Leucine-rich repeat-containing G protein-coupled receptor 5 (LGR5) marks a stem-like colorectal cancer population but is difficult to target directly because of its expression in normal intestinal stem cells. Here, we integrated transcriptomic, somatic mutation, and copy-number data from 396 colorectal tumors to define the LGR5-high molecular state and identify therapeutic vulnerabilities through modality-matched tractability analysis. LGR5-high tumors displayed a coordinated Wnt-active, stem-like transcriptional program associated with extracellular matrix remodeling, APC mutations, and IGF2 amplification, yet lacked selective genetic dependencies among the identified genes. We therefore assessed candidate targets across three complementary dimensions: surface accessibility, structural ligandability, and biomolecular condensate behavior. ENPP3 emerged as the strongest candidate for antibody-based delivery, combining tumor-associated expression, an accessible ectodomain, internalization capacity, and clinical antibody-drug conjugate precedent. PLCB4 showed the strongest structural ligandability, with independent algorithms identifying its catalytic site and additional predicted cavities. NKD1 lacked conventional ligandable pockets but formed RNA-stabilized condensates and partitioned into DVL2-AXIN1 assemblies, reducing AXIN1 self-association and DVL2-AXIN1 contacts in molecular simulations. Together, these findings define LGR5-high colorectal cancer as a therapeutically tractable molecular state and establish a modality-matched framework for translating tumor-associated signatures into experimentally testable therapeutic hypotheses.
affiliations: Department of Physical Chemistry, Universidad Complutense de Madrid, Av. Complutense s/n, Madrid 28040, Spain (corresponding author)

papers.title: Exploring the activation mechanism of the Mic60 subcomplex governing mitochondrial crista junctions
papers.abstract: Crista junctions (CJs) are narrow infoldings of the inner mitochondrial membrane, serving as entry points into the cristae microenvironment. The mitochondrial contact site and cristae organizing system (MICOS) complex is a highly conserved protein machinery controlling CJ biogenesis and architecture, but its assembly mechanism driving CJ formation has remained unclear. By determining a crystal structure of a Chaetomium thermophilum Mic60-Mic19 complex and combining it with modelling and mutagenesis studies, we identify an extended helical region (EHR) of the Mic60 mitofilin domain and a further Mic19 helix as crucial elements of complex formation. In vitro cross-linking data and hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry resolve domain assembly and conformational dynamics of the Mic60 Mic19 subcomplex and point to the EHR as a molecular switch controlling Mic60 transition from a closed dimer to a Mic19-bound hetero-octamer. Our data provide a structural model for Mic60 activation and therefore MICOS assembly as a prerequisite for crista junction formation.
affiliations: Max-Delbrueck-Center for Molecular Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Monomeric TDP-43 binds GU-rich RNA via its NTD but only its oligomers block cryptic exon inclusion
papers.abstract: TDP-43 aggregation is a pathological feature of several neurodegenerative diseases, resulting in nuclear loss of function and RNA dysregulation, including cryptic exon derepression. TDP-43 comprises two RNA recognition motifs required for canonical RNA binding, a low-complexity domain implicated in phase separation, and an N-terminal domain (NTD) that mediates oligomerization. While NTD-driven oligomerization is critical for TDP-43 splicing function, some studies suggest a direct interaction of NTD with RNA. Here, we investigated RNA binding by the NTD and its functional interplay with oligomerization. We show that the NTD preferentially binds UG-rich RNA via residues located at the oligomerization interface. The NTD engaged RNA only on monomeric TDP-43, as RNA binding and oligomerization compete for the same interface and rely on similar interaction modes. By disentangling these competing activities, we demonstrated that oligomerization, but not NTD-RNA interaction, is essential for TDP-43-dependent alternative splicing and repression of cryptic exons. Our findings uncover a previously unappreciated RNA-binding activity within the TDP-43 NTD that directly competes with oligomerization and establish oligomerization as a key determinant of TDP-43 cryptic exon repression.
affiliations: University of Zurich (corresponding author)

papers.title: Calcium-independent biosensors for multiplexed in vivo imaging of extracellular lactate dynamics
papers.abstract: Extracellular L-lactate reports cellular metabolism, but resolving its dynamics alongside intracellular metabolism and neuronal activity remains challenging. Here we develop eLACCO3 and R-eLACCO3, green and red cell-surface lactate biosensors with Ca2+-independent responses and faster response and recovery kinetics in cultured cells. Selected variants provide larger fluorescence responses than their predecessors in brain cells, slices, and living mice and improve detection of glucose-evoked extracellular lactate oscillations. Combining R-eLACCO3 with GCaMP6f enabled imaging of extracellular L-lactate simultaneously with odor-evoked activity in anesthetized mice and cortical activity in awake mice. These biosensors enable multiplexed measurements of extracellular lactate dynamics in relation to intracellular metabolism and neuronal activity.
affiliations: Academia Sinica (corresponding author)

papers.title: Ciliary neurotrophic factor curbs palmitate-induced inflammatory and metabolic changes in NPY/AgRP hypothalamic neurons
papers.abstract: Introduction: In both humans and experimental animals, obesity is associated with hypothalamic inflammation and neuronal metabolic dysfunction, which contribute to disrupting body energy homeostasis. Although ciliary neurotrophic factor (CNTF) is a neuroprotective cytokine with recognized anti-obesity effects in peripheral metabolic tissues, its role in obesity-associated hypothalamic dysfunction is still poorly characterized. We investigated whether CNTF exerts any direct effects on mHypoE-N41 (N41) hypothalamic neurons and whether it modulates the effects induced by palmitate (PA), an established model of obesity-associated neuronal metabolic dysfunction. Methods: N41 cells were administered CNTF alone or combined with PA to assess whether CNTF affects PA-induced lipotoxic stress. Gene and protein expression was assessed by qRT-PCR, western blotting, and immunofluorescence analysis. Results: In N41 cells, CNTF activated the STAT3, ERK and AMPK signaling pathways. It also upregulated genes involved in mitochondrial metabolism and fatty acid oxidation, including Ucp2, Cpt1 and Pgc1, as well as the proliferation-associated markers Ki-67 and PCNA. PA treatment induced inflammatory and endoplasmic reticulum stress responses and impaired insulin signaling. In PA-treated N41 cells, CNTF significantly attenuated the expression of pro-inflammatory markers Tnf, Mcp1 and Nfkb, restored insulin-induced AKT phosphorylation, and partially reversed PA-induced changes in the expression of metabolic genes Ucp2 and Cpt1. Conclusions: Collectively, these findings indicate that CNTF exerts direct protective metabolic effects on hypothalamic N41 neurons subjected to lipotoxic stress and supports a role for it in the preservation of neuronal metabolic function under obesogenic conditions.
affiliations: Center of Obesity, Marche Polytechnic University-United Hospitals, Ancona, Italy. (corresponding author)

papers.title: The RNA helicase KREH2 directly binds the RESC1-RESC2 complex in trypanosomatid mitochondrial RNA editing
papers.abstract: Trypanosomatids are medically important single-celled eukaryotic protists with exceptional RNA biology. They display highly unusual RNA biogenesis pathways, notably mitochondrial RNA editing, an essential post-transcriptional process transforming cryptic primary transcripts into functional mRNAs. Large multiprotein assemblies coordinate the RNA editing process, in which small guide RNAs (gRNAs) anneal to the pre-mRNAs and serve as templates for uridine insertion or deletion. Kinetoplast RNA Editing Helicases (KREHs) are important components of the RNA editing process that modifies large portions of pre-mRNA via the sequential annealing and dissociation of multiple gRNAs. However, how KREH helicases interact with components of the editing machinery, and which subunits mediate these interactions, remain unresolved. Here, we examined an association between the DEAH/RHA RNA helicase KREH2 and the RESC1-RESC2 protein heterodimer using proximity labeling and co-immunoprecipitation coupled to quantitative mass spectrometry in vivo. We reconstituted a minimal trimeric KREH2 peptide-RESC1-RESC2 complex in vitro and characterized novel direct binding of a KREH2 peptide to RESC1 using cryo-electron microscopy. These results establish a mechanistic link between the RNA helicase KREH2 and the RESC1-RESC2 module at the 5'-end of gRNAs, providing new avenues for studying the orchestration of RNA remodeling in trypanosomatid mitochondrial RNA editing.
affiliations: EMBL (corresponding author)

papers.title: A contact-mediated transfer mechanism directs in cis localization and spread of Xist RNA
papers.abstract: X chromosome inactivation in mammals is driven by the long non-coding RNA Xist, which localizes and spreads across the chromosome from which it is transcribed. Although several factors required for Xist localization have been identified, the underlying mechanism remains unclear. Here, we combine Nuclear-BRITE, a method for visualizing and quantifying the dynamics of individual Xist RNA molecules, with acute depletion of key localization factors. We find that Xist molecules remain constrained throughout interphase, consistent with continuous association with chromatin. Building on this observation, we identify a contact-mediated transfer mechanism in which 3D chromosome dynamics promote handover of Xist molecules between chromosomal sites. We further show that the Xist-binding proteins SPEN and HNRNPU play distinct roles in this process by promoting Xist - Xist and Xist - chromatin interactions, respectively. Together, our findings define a mechanism for Xist RNA spreading and provide a framework for understanding its unique chromosome-wide localization.
affiliations: University of Oxford (corresponding author)

papers.title: A Structural Model of Transcriptional Activation by Mediator
papers.abstract: Mediator integrates regulatory signals from transcription factors (TFs) and controls RNA polymerase II (Pol II) activity in eukaryotes. Its Tail module serves as the primary hub for TF activation domains (ADs), but the mechanistic logic coupling this distal engagement to transcriptional output is unclear. Here we model an extensive set of human AD-Tail interactions with AlphaFold 3 and infer how they may influence the architecture of the Mediator-Pol II complex. Across the ensemble, ADs recurrently engage a restricted set of surfaces spanning multiple Tail subunits, revealing several previously unrecognized sites. The ensemble map recovers established activator-binding regions and is consistent with prior biochemical and structural data. Our modeling suggests how multivalent AD binding modulates the conformational landscape of the Tail to favor an initiation-competent Pol II state, providing a structural framework for tunable gene activation through Mediator.
affiliations: Stanford University School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Arc represses gene expression in IS605-family transposons
papers.abstract: Bacterial insertion sequences (IS) are compact transposable elements that encode proteins required for their mobility and maintenance, yet many also encode accessory proteins with poorly understood functions. For example, IS605-family elements often encode a transposase called TnpA and an RNA-guided nuclease called TnpB that supports transposon maintenance, alongside an additional ribbon-helix-helix protein named Arc. Though the roles of TnpA and TnpB have been extensively studied in recent years, the enigmatic function of Arc has not been investigated. Here, we show that Arc acts as a transcriptional repressor to directly bind the transposon's native promoter sequence regulating TnpA and TnpB gene expression. By systematically testing Arc-containing IS605 elements, we identified a conserved binding pattern at intergenic transposon sequences neighboring protein-coding genes through chromatin immunoprecipitation and sequencing analyses. We then used fluorescence reporter assays and demonstrated that these intergenic sequences function as strong promoters, and that the presence of Arc dramatically reduces their gene expression. Together, these findings identify Arc as a transposon-encoded transcriptional repressor, revealing a regulatory layer that may promote long-term persistence of IS605-family elements by keeping their activity in check. The widespread association of Arc homologs with diverse mobile elements and cellular genes suggests that these compact regulators may more broadly restrain the expression of neighboring genetic machinery across varied genomic contexts.
affiliations: Columbia University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Fast single molecule localization microscopy in 3D
papers.abstract: Super-resolution methods, such as single molecule localisation microscopy (SMLM), can determine the distribution of specific proteins at the nanometre scale. However, three-dimensional (3D) SMLM is typically limited to thin sections and requires prohibitively long acquisition times to image complete cells. Here we introduce a 3D SMLM imaging modality, Intrinsic3D, that combines the speed and optical sectioning of oblique plane microscopy (OPM) with the nanometre resolution of SMLM to determine the position of single molecule emitters throughout complete volumes more than an order-of-magnitude faster over regular DNA-PAINT. By scanning the oblique light sheet across the volume and combining localization information from two or more adjacent planes, an emitter's x, y and z position is determined, eliminating the need for post-processing steps to stitch multiple image stacks together. We demonstrate resolution and speed by imaging nuclear pore complexes in U2OS cells and Drosophila egg chambers. As a proof-of-concept, we map the 3D distribution of the cell-adhesion protein DE-cadherin in the Drosophila follicular epithelium and show that spot adherens junctions are enriched near tricellular junctions and contain more E-cadherin than the apical adherens junctions, suggesting that spot junctions play a wider role in cell-cell adhesion than previously appreciated. Finally, we examine the organization of Gliotactin, a tricellular septate junction protein relative to E-cadherin using exchange-PAINT. These investigations demonstrate that Intrinsic3D delivers rapid 3D protein mapping in whole cells. Combining Intrinsic3D with existing multiplex and resolution enhancing methods (e.g. exchange-PAINT and RESI) will enable multicolour, 3D in situ spatial proteomics in tissue samples and bridge the gap between SMLM and systems-level cell biology.
affiliations: University of Cambridge (corresponding author)

papers.title: Dynamic membrane organization coordinates protein-O-mannosylation and proteostasis in mycobacteria.
papers.abstract: Integral membrane enzymes operate within molecular environments, yet how these are organized remains poorly understood. Using M. smegmatis as a mycobacterial model, we define the membrane environment of the protein O-mannosyltransferase MtPMT through stratified interactomics combining affinity purification-mass spectrometry under four stringencies with a persistence score. This approach resolves a persistent membrane-associated core of 108 proteins from more transient layers, revealing a hierarchically organized landscape enriched in Sec protein translocation, protein biogenesis and envelope proteostasis machineries. Reciprocal affinity purification and in vivo FRET identify YajC and FtsH as neighbors of MtPMT, while structural modelling supports integration within a Sec-associated assembly. Genetic disruption of factors reduces O-mannosylation activity, demonstrating dependence on platform integrity. The MtPMT-associated network is remodelled during growth, indicating an adaptive system. Loss of POM compromises envelope permeability and stress resilience, linking O-mannosylation to fitness. Together, our results establish protein O-mannosylation as an integrated component of a dynamic membrane platform coordinating secretion, membrane protein biogenesis and proteostasis. Our findings support a model in which mycobacterial membranes contain specialized domains dynamically modulated by physiological state.
affiliations: IPBS CNRS - Université de Toulouse (corresponding author)

papers.title: A two-step organoid screen identifies transient p53 activation as a senolytic strategy for radiation-induced salivary gland dysfunction
papers.abstract: Radiotherapy significantly improves the survival of head and neck cancer patients. However, it frequently damages the salivary glands, causing persistent hyposalivation and xerostomia. Radiation-induced cellular senescence within the salivary gland stem/progenitor cell niche contributes to hyposalivation, suggesting that selective elimination of senescent cells could promote tissue recovery. However, the effectiveness of senolytic compounds is strongly context dependent, varying with tissue of origin and potentially impairing regenerative cells required for functional restoration. Here, we developed a two-step organoid-based screening methodology that integrates the preferential induction of apoptosis in irradiated, senescence enriched, salivary gland organoids with the preservation of stem/progenitor cell regenerative capacity. As a first step, the senolytic activity of candidate drugs was tested to identify drugs that induced apoptosis in senescent cells of irradiated organoids but were not or less toxic to unirradiated organoids. As a second step, the confirmed senolytic compounds were tested for effects on stem cell self-renewal potential. Using this approach, we identified Nutlin3a, an MDM2 inhibitor and p53 activator, as the compound with the most favorable toxicity profile in salivary glands. Last, we confirmed the anti-senescence and pro-regenerative potential of Nutlin3a in an in vivo mouse model of radiation-induced hyposalivation, where localized Nutlin3a delivery resulted in a robust increase in saliva production, as early as two weeks after administration. These findings establish an organoid-based strategy for identifying tissue-adapted senolytic interventions and propose transient local p53 activation with Nutlin3a as a potential approach to mitigate radiation-induced salivary gland dysfunction.
affiliations: University Medical Center Groningen (corresponding author)

papers.title: DLGAP5 promotes vascular cell proliferation and remodeling in pulmonary arterial hypertension
papers.abstract: Background: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) manifests by pulmonary vascular remodeling, caused by hyper-proliferation and apoptosis resistance of resident PA cells, elevated right ventricular (RV) afterload, and death of RV failure. The goal of this study is to determine the role and mechanisms of action of mitotic spindle-associated microtubule regulator DLG associated protein 5 (DLGAP5) in pulmonary vascular remodeling in PAH. Methods: DLGAP5 expression was assessed in human PAH transcriptomic datasets, PAH patients' lung tissues, pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells (PASMCs), and pulmonary artery adventitial fibroblasts (PAAFs). Loss-of-function, molecular, functional, RNAseq, and network analyses were performed. Smooth muscle (SM)-specific DLGAP5 knockdown using adeno-associated virus serotype 6 (AAV6) in mice with SU5416/hypoxia-induced PH was performed. Results: DLGAP5 was overaccumulated in small muscular PAs, PASMCs, and PAAFs from PAH lungs. siRNA DLGAP5 down-regulated cyclin A2, suppressed hyper-proliferation, increased pro-apoptotic BIM, and induced apoptosis in human PAH PASMCs and PAAFs. DEP domain containing 1 (DEPDC1) was identified and validated as a downstream effector of DLGAP5 in PAH PASMCs responsible for hyper-proliferation and apoptosis resistance of human PAH PASMCs. SM-specific DLGAP5 knockdown with AAV6-enTagln-shDLGAP5 reversed DEPDC1 overaccumulation in small muscular PAs, reduced PA medial thickness, RV systolic pressure, mean PA pressure, and RV hypertrophy in mice with SuHx-induced PH. Conclusions: DLGAP5 supports proliferation and survival of human PAH PASMCs and PAAFs through up-regulation of cyclin A2, DEPDC1, and suppression of BIM, and promotes PA remodeling and PH in mice. DLGAP5 could serve as a potential molecular target to attenuate pulmonary vascular remodeling in PAH.
affiliations: University of California Davis School of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Cajal bodies shape the nuclear transcriptome, intron retention and transcripts redistribution in Arabidopsis roots under hypoxia
papers.abstract: Cajal bodies (CBs) are nuclear condensates known for their role in sn- and snoRNA maturation in animal, but their function in plant stress responses remains poorly understood. We compared wild-type (WT) Arabidopsis thaliana with the CB-lacking ncb-1 mutant during hypoxia and reoxygenation, focusing on nuclear retention of transcripts. In both genotypes, hypoxia caused nuclear accumulation of poly(A+) RNA and extensive reprogramming of gene expression. However, the transcriptional response, including induction of hypoxia-responsive genes, was considerably weaker in ncb-1, both during stress and recovery. In nuclear RNA, introns with low (intron retention index, IRX 50%) retention showed opposite, genotype-dependent dynamics. During hypoxia, efficiently spliced introns (IRX < 10%) accounted for over 70% of introns detected in nuclear RNA. Relative to normoxia, this proportion increased two- to threefold in WT but only moderately in the mutant. Together with poly(A+) RNA accumulation, this suggests that largely spliced transcripts, including those of genes involved in protein transport and ribosome biogenesis, are held in the nucleus during stress. Conversely, strongly retained introns, often terminal and located in genes related to hypoxia and other abiotic stresses, were most abundant in WT nuclear RNA under normoxia. Their proportion dropped sharply during hypoxia, and much less so in ncb-1. This indicate that WT plants maintain a nuclear reserve of incompletely spliced stress-related transcripts that are processed upon stress. The mutant also showed reduced interaction between U2 snRNA and U2B'', which leads to splicing defects. Our results indicate that CBs regulate which transcripts are held in the nucleus and how they are processed, contributing to plant tolerance of oxygen deprivation and recovery.
affiliations: Department of Cellular and Molecular Biology, Nicolaus Copernicus University, Lwowska 1, 87-100, Torun, Poland (corresponding author)

papers.title: SETD3 ACTIN HISTIDINE METHYLTRANSFERASE REGULATES INTESTINAL EPITHELIAL BARRIER INTEGRITY AND MUCOSAL INFLAMMATION
papers.abstract: Intestinal epithelial barrier is a key feature of the healthy gut, and disruption of this barrier is a driver of mucosal inflammation. Integrity of the intestinal epithelial barrier is controlled by tight junctions (TJs) and adherens junctions (AJs) associated with the underlying actin cytoskeleton. Posttranslational modifications of actins affect the cytoskeletal assembly and dynamics, however whether such modifications regulate epithelial barriers remains unknown. SETD3 methyltransferase methylates actins at the His73 residue, thereby enhancing filamentous (F)-actin polymerization and turnover. This study examines the role of SETD3 in regulating structure and function of normal intestinal epithelial barrier, as well as its involvement in barrier disruption during mucosal inflammation. siRNA mediated knockdown of SETD3 in DLD-1 and HCA-7 human intestinal epithelial cells (IEC) resulted in several functional and morphological cell abnormalities. These include increased permeability of the IEC barrier, diminished assembly of the perijunctional F-actin belt, increased cell size, and delayed TJ reassembly during calcium switch. Consistently, SETD3 knockout (KO) mice displayed increased intestinal permeability and decreased labeling intensity of apical {beta}-actin as compared to wildtype controls. Furthermore, SETD3 KO mice showed increased cell stemness and proliferation in colonic epithelium without defects in AJ/TJ assembly and secretory cell differentiation. In addition, SETD3 KO mice developed more severe disease symptoms during dextran sodium sulfate (DSS)-induced colitis, which were accompanied by accelerated mucosal erosion and increased macrophage, T cell and neutrophil infiltration into colonic tissue. Overall, our data suggests that SETD3 acts as a novel positive regulator of the intestinal epithelial barrier and plays a protective role during intestinal mucosal damage and inflammation.
affiliations: Lerner Research Institute Cleveland Clinic (corresponding author)

papers.title: An amyloid-β/APP regulatory layer in human brown adipocyte recruitment identifies repurposable drugs for thermogenic fat expansion
papers.abstract: Brown adipose tissue (BAT) increases energy expenditure but is scarce in adults, yet most strategies focus on activating existing thermogenic adipocytes rather than recruiting new ones. We integrate human single-nucleus transcriptomics with protein-interaction and knowledge-graph analyses to identify stage-specific, druggable programmes governing brown adipogenesis. This pipeline resolved four ordered transcriptional states and three transitions, revealing an amyloid-{beta}/APP regulatory layer and nominating APP as a central signalling hub. Most prioritised compounds altered differentiation or metabolic phenotype, several substantially. Phenserine (APP-lowering) and sacubitril (neprilysin inhibitor) promoted differentiation through distinct mechanisms and stages and could be combined sequentially for benefit. Phenserine increased differentiation across three human models and, in mice, expanded BAT mass and increased thermogenic capacity. Together, these findings reveal targetable control points in human brown adipocyte recruitment, nominate repurposable drugs for BAT expansion, and establish a generalisable framework coupling single-cell transcriptomics with network-based drug repurposing across staged biological systems.
affiliations: University of Cambridge (corresponding author)

papers.title: AI-assisted quantification of the clonogenic assay
papers.abstract: The clonogenic assay is the foundational standard for evaluating cellular radiosensitivity, yet its manual quantification is limited by labor-intensive processing, high inter-observer variability, and a reductive binary scoring system. Here, we present and validate a deep learning-based segmentation pipeline for the automated, high-throughput quantification of mammalian cell survival across diverse radiation qualities (photons, protons, and carbon ions). By benchmarking against expert consensus using Bland-Altman analysis, we demonstrate that this AI framework consistently operates within natural human error margins. Crucially, transitioning to automated whole-well image-based analysis enables the extraction of continuous multidimensional data, including colony area, density, and cellularity. This phenotypic profiling successfully identified and quantified high-cellularity colonies formed by radioresistant BxPC-3 cells under particle irradiation. Coupled with rapid image acquisition platforms, this methodology significantly reduces processing bottlenecks while standardizing the derivation of relative biological effectiveness (RBE). By advancing beyond binary survival metrics to continuous morphological profiling, this framework provides a vital new analytical dimension for investigating structural mechanisms of radioresistance.
affiliations: Department of Radiation Oncology, Mayo Clinic, Jacksonville, United States (corresponding author)

papers.title: Transient 5-azacytidine exposure elicits persistent myogenic-like transcriptional remodeling in zebrafish fibroblasts: implications for cultivated seafood
papers.abstract: Fibroblasts are readily obtained and expanded and may provide an alternative cell source for cultivated seafood if their latent myogenic potential can be accessed. We examined whether transient exposure to 5-azacytidine (AZA), a cytidine analogue known to convert mouse embryonic fibroblasts into myoblasts, elicits a persistent muscle gene program in embryo-derived zebrafish (Danio rerio) Z3 fibroblasts. Cells were exposed to 0, 2.5, 5 or 10 M AZA for 48 h and maintained in drug-free medium for 3 weeks. RNA-seq identified 744 genes that increased and 670 that decreased consistently across the concentration series. Increased genes encompassed myogenic regulators, fusion factors, sarcomeric components and excitation-contraction machinery, whereas decreased genes were enriched for extracellular-matrix and adhesion functions. In a separate six-dose RT-qPCR experiment (0-20 M AZA) with three biological replicates per concentration, all 19 selected muscle genes were significantly increased at 1.25 M, the lowest concentration tested, whereas 9 of 12 extracellular-matrix/fibroblast genes were significantly decreased. Several muscle genes plateaued or declined at higher concentrations, and multinucleated myotubes were not observed. A separate 5-aza-2'-deoxycytidine (decitabine) series showed a comparable muscle-associated response at 0.25 M. These findings indicate that zebrafish fibroblasts retain access to a myogenic-like transcriptional program, and they provide a model for identifying food-compatible approaches to control fish-cell lineage plasticity for cultivated seafood.
affiliations: School of Marine Biosciences, Kitasato University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Endothelial gain of PIEZO/TRPV mechanosensors drives cavernous malformations
papers.abstract: Vascular disease often begins as a failure to read mechanical force. Cerebral cavernous malformations (CCMs) are leaky, brain-invading capillary clusters that cause stroke and seizures and arise from endothelial loss of the CCM complex. They form exclusively in low-flow vessels but existing models cannot explain this selectivity. We previously established that CCM-mutant endothelium inverts its adhesive balance, weakening cell-cell junctions while building matrix-degrading adhesions. The mechanosensors imposing this switch are unknown. Here we show that the mechanosensitive Ca2+ channels PIEZO1, TRPV2 and TRPV4 are overexpressed in the endothelium of CCM lesions in a 42-patient cohort, and that lesion volume scales with their expression level. Mechanistically, PIEZO1 partners with TRPV4 to destabilise cell-cell junctions and with TRPV2 to reinforce cell-matrix adhesions; silencing TRPV4 restores junctional integrity and abolishes KLF4 induction, whereas silencing TRPV2 or inhibition with tranilast abolishes matrix degradation and invasion. In vivo, trpv4 knockdown or inhibition with GSK2798745 restores atrioventricular canal morphogenesis in ccm2-mutant zebrafish. Gain of mechanosensory channel function is thus a causal step in CCM pathogenesis, upstream of the KLF program. Combined therapeutic targeting of TRPV2 and TRPV4 with inhibitors validated in humans offers a route to therapy.
affiliations: INSERM U1209 CNRS UMR5309 UGA (corresponding author)

papers.title: A possible role for the kinetochore COMA complex in sensing the damage in stn1-sz2, a mutant of the Cdc13-Stn1-Ten1 telomeric complex
papers.abstract: Telomeres, the ends of linear chromosomes, form a cap composed of specific telomeric DNA associated with specialized proteins that ensures efficient protection against chromosome degradation and, consequently, overall genome instability. Three main complexes have been implicated in chromosome end protection, namely telomerase, shelterin, and the CST complex (CTC1/Cdc13-STN1-TEN1). In a recent study, we uncovered mutants of the S. cerevisiae CST in which damage was sensed both by the two major spindle checkpoints and the major DNA damage checkpoint. In the best-studied of these mutants, stn1-sz2, the stability and organization of the mitotic tubulin spindle was profoundly affected, as were the organization of the centrosomes and the kinetochores. Here, we find that the stn1-sz2 mutant is hypersensitive to deletion mutants of two members of the kinetochores, Ctf19 and Mcm21, which correlated with mis-localization of their associated subunit in the COMA complex, Okp1, during anaphase. Defects in interactions between the kinetochores and the tubulin spindle are entirely sensed by the SAC (spindle assembly checkpoint). Here, we find that some of the stn1-sz2 damage is recognized by the Mad2 checkpoint protein independently from the SAC. The data presented here contribute to a better understanding of the damage in stn1-sz2, the prototype of novel mutants of telomeric CST characterized by mitotic-spindle-damage in addition to the classical telomeric-DNA-damage.
affiliations: CNRS (corresponding author)

papers.title: A regenerative fibroblast competence field supports multiple cell fates in adult skin regeneration
papers.abstract: Adult mammalian wounds typically restore tissue integrity through fibrotic repair rather than regeneration of the original architecture. Here, we compared small non-regenerative and large regenerative skin wounds to investigate how fibroblasts acquire regenerative competence and enter alternative cell-fate programs. Integrated single-cell RNA sequencing identified a transient signaling and extracellular-matrix-remodeling niche enriched in large wounds, together with NCAM1-associated competent fibroblast states. Time-resolved analysis positioned these states within a root-like fibroblast manifold connected to hair dermal-condensate, endothelial, pericyte and glial-associated fate-entry programs. Inferred cell-cell communication networks revealed shared matrix and adhesion signals, superimposed with branch-associated inputs, including VEGF signaling toward NCAM1-positive endothelial-transition cells. Lineage tracing showed that PDGFRA- and NCAM1-expressing lineages contributed to vascular- and nerve/glial-associated regenerative compartments. Functionally, partial NCAM1 perturbation reduced vascular organization while increasing hair follicle neogenesis, whereas stronger inhibition impaired both outcomes. These findings identify NCAM1 as a regulator of regenerative competence and fate specification within a regenerative competence field rather than a marker of a single terminal lineage. We propose that regenerative wounds activate an NCAM1-associated fibroblast competence field whose quantitative modulation biases competent fibroblasts toward alternative outcomes.
affiliations: Department of Pathology, Keck School of Medicine, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: Ref(2)P/p62 protein pleomorphism confers tissue-specific function
papers.abstract: Protein structure dictates function and proteins often perform the same function in different cell or tissue-type. Here, we report that in Drosophila melanogaster, the broadly expressed protein Ref(2)P, an orthologue of mammalian p62/SQSTM1, performs mutually exclusive functions across tissues - autophagy in midgut and mitochondria-associated proteostasis in muscle. These functional differences arise from tissue-specific secondary and tertiary structures adopted by the same Ref(2)P polypeptide, rather than protein abundance, isoforms, post-translational modification, or binding-partner availability. The tissue-specific structures are cell autonomous and resistant to environmental perturbation. Deletion of a short intrinsically disordered region converts muscle Ref(2)P to a midgut-like structural and functional state. However, this forced switch causes muscle dysfunction, linking tissue-specific physiology to alternative structural states of the same polypeptide. We posit that Drosophila Ref(2)P exemplifies a mechanism for tissue-specificity, protein pleomorphism, in which the intrinsic structural plasticity of a protein and the physicochemical/molecular environment of a tissue enable a broadly expressed protein to adopt tissue-specific structure and function.
affiliations: Stowers Institute for Medical Research (corresponding author)

papers.title: Notch1 and Notch2 receptors mediate the prosensory functions of the Notch ligand Jagged1 in the mammalian cochlea
papers.abstract: Mechanosensory hair cells in the cochlea of the inner ear are essential for sound detection. Previous studies have shown that loss of the Notch ligand Jagged1 (JAG1) disrupts maintenance of prosensory progenitors, from which hair cells and their surrounding supporting cells derive. However, the molecular and cellular mechanisms by which JAG1 regulates prosensory progenitor maintenance are poorly understood, and the Notch receptors that mediate this function in the developing cochlea remain unknown. To address this, we generated Jag1 conditional knockout mice and characterized their prosensory deficits using transcriptomic and phenotypic analyses. We show that JAG1 loss abolishes prosensory expression of CDKN1B (p27Kip1) and reduces expression of essential neurotrophic factors, thereby disrupting the stereotyped pattern of cell-cycle exit and innervation within the prosensory domain. Furthermore, conditional knockout of Notch1 and Notch2 (Notch1/2) receptors in supporting cells phenocopied the Jag1 deletion phenotype, showing both a severe reduction in outer hair cell formation and a disrupted pattern of cell-cycle exit and innervation, thereby confirming their essential roles in mediating the prosensory functions of JAG1.
affiliations: Johns Hopkins University (corresponding author)

papers.title: A new mouse model for a high-risk AMD variant, ARMS2A69S
papers.abstract: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is the leading cause of irreversible central vision loss in older adults. The highest genetic risk for AMD maps to Chromosome 10q26. However, due to strong linkage disequilibrium between two genes, ARMS2 and HTRA1 located in this region, it has been difficult to determine whether one or both genes contribute to the AMD-disease risk. Functional studies of ARMS2 have been hampered due to the lack of animal models, as orthologs are only found in the higher primates and the gene is absent in rodents. To model ARMS2 biology in vivo, we used CRISPR-Cas9 to insert the complete human ARMS2 gene carrying the A69S risk variant (rs10490924), into a region of homology between humans and mice, on mouse Chromosome 7, 3.5 kb upstream of Htra1, preserving its native promoter, spacing, and orientation. We also generated a mouse model bearing its wild-type counterpart ARMS2A69 (ARMS2WT). RNA analysis revealed tissue- and cell-type-specific pattern of ARMS2 expression enriched in neural tissues, testis, and eye, and within the eye, in retinal horizontal cells and the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). ARMS2 expression was consistent with human expression data and unaltered by the A69S mutation. By 12 months, ARMS2A69S mice develop AMD-relevant phenotypes including increased fundus spots, A69S-specific thinning of the outer nuclear layer, and reduced scotopic ERG amplitudes. Transcriptomic profiling of postnatal day 14 retina and RPE-enriched fractions revealed reduced mitochondrial oxidative-phosphorylation genes, corroborated by reduced retinal mtDNA copy number and lower maximal respiration, alongside preliminary results that suggest sphingolipid remodeling in the RPE. This humanized model links the ARMS2 A69S variant to mitochondrial dysfunction and provides an in vivo platform for defining AMD mechanisms and testing therapies.
affiliations: The Jackson Laboratory, Bar Harbor, Maine (corresponding author)

papers.title: piRNA loss unleashes episodic transposition bursts
papers.abstract: In Metazoa, transposon expression is suppressed by the piRNA pathway, and disruption of this pathway leads to rampant transposon expression. However, it remains unclear whether increased transposon expression results in actual transposition, and if so, which and how frequently transposons mobilize upon piRNA loss. Here, we developed a framework to track transposon copy accumulation across generations on a single set of nonrecombining haploid genome in the Drosophila male germline, with or without the piRNA biogenesis factor HP1D/Rhino. Single-fly Nanopore DNA sequencing revealed that multiple transposon families mobilized after 10-45 generations of piRNA loss. Among them, the most prolific across all replicates was copia, producing dozens of new insertions that were distributed across chromosome arms. With genomic DNA collected at every generation, we validated and dated each copia insertion, revealing episodic bursts of transposition that deviated strongly from a Poisson process. Using phylogenetic analysis, we further showed that multiple copia loci--both autonomous and nonautonomous copies--can mobilize. Interestingly, two additional transposon families, mdg3 and invader3, also mobilized episodically, but with distinct timing and magnitude, highlighting the stochastic nature of transposition bursts. Because we did not observe a single transposition event for these elements in controls, our results provide direct evidence that the piRNA pathway tightly suppresses germline transposition. More importantly, our findings argue that disruption of the piRNA pathway does not simply elevate transposition rates, but it instead unleashes punctuated and stochastic bursts of transposon movement that may radically reshape the timing and magnitude of mutational input during evolution.
affiliations: Cornell University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Nascent transcript O-MAP reveals the molecular architecture of an RBM20-regulated single-locus subnuclear compartment organized around the TTN RNA
papers.abstract: Eukaryotic gene expression is regulated by highly organized subnuclear compartmentalization, yet the molecular architecture of locus-specific nuclear microenvironments remains difficult to dissect. Here, we adapt oligonucleotide-mediated proximity-interactome mapping (O-MAP) to map genomic loci, RNAs, and proteins within discrete nuclear neighborhoods, using a cardiac-specific RNA factory organized around nascent TTN RNA as a model. We find that the TTN-associated microenvironment is embedded within a developmentally regulated hub of chromosomal interactions, including cis-interacting active domains and trans-interacting poised and repressed domains. In addition to chromatin contacts, the factory contains diverse RNAs in a pattern consistent with substantial post-transcriptional recruitment and is enriched for RNA-metabolic and chromatin-regulatory proteins. These include the splicing factor RBM20 and chromatin-scaffolding factor SAFB, which exert opposing effects on factory-associated gene expression. Disruption of factory architecture through loss of TTN RNA or RBM20 leads to widespread splicing defects and mislocalization of transcripts. Notably, many splicing defects caused by RBM20 loss are attenuated by TTN RNA depletion, indicating that TTN's unbound transcript exerts toxic gain-of-function effects on RNA metabolism in the absence of RBM20. Collectively, this work establishes O-MAP as a powerful approach for biochemically dissecting single-locus compartments and reveals how coding RNAs can influence nuclear architecture and gene regulation.
affiliations: University of Washington (corresponding author)

papers.title: Quantification method affects replicability of eQTL analysis, colocalization, and TWAS
papers.abstract: Expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) mapping, colocalization, and transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS) are widely used to contextualize GWAS loci, yet the impact of upstream RNA-seq processing choices on these analyses remains critically unexplored. Two poorly characterized decisions include the transcriptomic reference annotation used for quantification of short-read RNA-sequencing samples, which defines transcript composition and structure, and the quantification method itself. Through a comprehensive analysis spanning 48 tissues in GTEx and seven widely studied and diverse phenotypes, here we find that these choices substantially affect eQTL detection and gene expression prediction with significant downstream impact on colocalization and TWAS results. Concordant results across pipelines are further enriched for longer genes, genes with more isoforms, and greater expression heritability. Our findings demonstrate that seemingly minor methodological decisions substantially affect these common analyses, highlighting the need for standardized practices to ensure reproducible genetic association studies.
affiliations: University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: From mountaintops to metacollections: using genomics to evaluate ex situ conservation collections. A case study from tropical montane cloud forest plants in Australia
papers.abstract: A core aim of ex situ conservation is to represent wild genetic diversity in managed living collections. For the climate-threatened tropical montane cloud forest (TMCF) flora of northeast Australia, an ex situ metacollection of plants and seeds has been established by the Tropical Mountain Plant Science (TroMPS) project. In this study we used reduced-representation sequencing (DArTseq) of wild, herbarium, and ex situ material alongside provenance information for ten species, to pursue two central aims: to characterise landscape-scale genetic structure across species' ranges, and to evaluate how well the assembled metacollections represent that wild diversity. Analyses revealed consistent patterns of genetic differentiation among mountain top populations across multiple species, reflecting the isolating influence of lowland gaps between upland habitats, with the degree of differentiation varying among species. These results provide the first genetic baseline for Australian TMCF flora and reinforce the importance of treating individual mountain top populations as distinct units for conservation management. Additionally, the project provided valuable insights into the logistical challenges of coordinated multi-institutional collecting, informing strategies for metacollection design more broadly. Evaluation of the metacollection revealed both strengths and gaps in representation across species, providing evidence to refine the current holdings and guide future targeted collecting to strengthen their long-term conservation value.
affiliations: Research Centre for Ecosystem Resilience, Botanic Gardens of Sydney, NSW 2000, Australia (corresponding author)
