Megakaryocytes from Lepr-cre; Cxcl14 fl/fl mice expressed lower levels of genes that encode granule proteins as compared to control mice, leading to the release of platelets with fewer -granules and defective thrombus formation/growth. CXCL14 promoted platelet formation by remodeling lipid metabolism in megakaryocytes, increasing fatty acid transporter expression and enabling megakaryocytes to take up more polyunsaturated fatty acids from circulation. A high fat diet rescued the formation of proplatelet-forming megakaryocytes and platelets, as well as platelet function, in Lepr-cre; Cxcl14 fl/fl mice. CXCL14 protein was sufficient to promote platelet formation by megakaryocytes in vitro and in vivo. LepR+ cells thus create a perisinusoidal niche for thrombopoiesis by producing CXCL14, which regulates lipid metabolism and terminal differentiation in megakaryocytes.
affiliations: Howard Hughes Medical Institute, University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: Functional Deorphanization of Tumor-reactive TCRs Uncovers a Landscape of Shared, Immune Dominant Antigens across Cancers
papers.abstract: Single-cell sequencing has charted the clonal landscape of tumor-infiltrating T cells, but the antigens that drive these responses remain largely undefined, limiting rational immunotherapy design. Here, we introduce TWISTAR, a platform that systematically deorphanizes single-cell-derived TCRs against tumor transcriptomes. By directly validating TCR engagement, TWISTAR exclusively recovers functionally immunogenic antigens. Applying TWISTAR to melanoma, breast, and hepatocellular carcinoma patients responding to immune checkpoint blockade, we uncover that tumor-reactive TCRs recognize a broad repertoire of immunogenic targets beyond neoantigens, including peptides derived from unannotated coding sequences and novel transcripts. Many of these antigens are shared across patients and cancer types, revealing communal targets. Furthermore, we observe immune dominance, consisting of multiple clones converging on few immune dominant epitopes. Together, these findings reveal an unexpectedly broad landscape of tumor immunogenicity, expanding opportunities for the development of pan-cancer vaccines.
affiliations: VIB KU Leuven (corresponding author)

papers.title: A novel adenovirus 19K/IX protein enhances infection by attenuating proteasomal degradation of tyrosine-ubiquitinated capsid protein IX
papers.abstract: Human adenoviruses (HAdVs) are double-stranded DNA viruses that cause a wide range of diseases, including respiratory, ocular, and gastrointestinal infections. HAdVs rely extensively on alternative splicing to expand their coding capacity and regulate gene expression during infection. Using replication-competent epitope-tagged HAdV-C5 viruses, we investigated the function of a newly identified alternatively spliced viral transcript, 19K/IX, derived from the E1B19K and pIX genes. We show that the 19K/IX protein binds to and stabilizes the minor capsid protein IX (pIX), thereby attenuating its proteasomal degradation and enhancing the production of infectious viral progeny. Mechanistically, we demonstrate that pIX degradation is mediated by non-canonical ubiquitination of the conserved tyrosine residues Y14 and Y49, which confer pIX subnuclear localization and partially mediate its interaction with the PSMC3 subunit of the 26S proteasome. Collectively, our study identifies 19K/IX as a novel regulator of HAdV-C5 infection and suggests that non-canonical tyrosine ubiquitination contributes to the regulation of capsid protein IX stability.
affiliations: Uppsala University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Epigenetic regulators partition the genome by evolutionary and developmental constraint
papers.abstract: Many epigenetic regulators play essential roles in animal development, but precisely how they function across different cell types without clear sequence preferences remains a foundational challenge. Here, we employed single-cell RNA sequencing to survey the mutant phenotypes of 30 essential regulatory pathways across over 450 gastrulation stage mouse embryo replicates, including essential factors associated with repressive chromatin states, RNA surveillance/processing, and other genomic roles. We then use this integrated manifold to partition mutant responses into a developmentally-resolved interaction network, revealing a hierarchy of heterochromatin-associated interactions that act orthogonally to Polycomb Repressive Complex-mediated control of embryo patterning. Compared to the embryo proper, we find that the developing placenta and yolk sac can accommodate broad swings in repetitive element expression, a resilience in keeping with the relative evolutionary recency and phenotypic plasticity of these tissues. Dense temporal sampling of Human Silencing Hub (HUSH) mutant embryogenesis further supports the notion that the gastrulating embryo is particularly constrained and depends on multiple layers of insulation, including the need to suppress evolutionarily young genetic elements to stably license highly conserved, phylotypic programs. In combination, our work highlights the power of single cell-resolved developmental genetics to contextualize the roles of epigenetic regulators, which restrict genomic action to support robust cellular identities and embryological forms.
affiliations: Max Planck Institute of Molecular Genetics (corresponding author)

papers.title: Complex folding kinetics of multi-domain proteins disentangled with periodic forces by magnetic tweezers
papers.abstract: Force spectroscopy enables direct investigation of the interplay between free energy and transition kinetics in proteins and nucleic acids. However, multi-domain proteins often display multiple intermediate structures with diverse stabilities and kinetics, making equilibrium conditions difficult to achieve and out-of-equilibrium experiments challenging to interpret. We introduce a single-molecule force spectroscopy assay using periodic forces and high-resolution magnetic tweezers to bridge different stabilities, selectively enhance intermediate populations, and rigorously analyze multi-domain protein folding kinetics at quasi-equilibrium. By applying well-defined periodic square force functions with tunable steady states, we first validate our framework on the two-state folder {lambda}6-85, demonstrating that periodic force experiments can reproduce equilibrium kinetics. Extending this approach to the multi-domain protein mimic (Protein L), we show that tuning force, frequency, and amplitude enhances populations of distinct intermediate states. Finally, we dissect the entangled states of the hybrid two-domain protein {lambda}-L, where a 100-fold difference in domain kinetics precludes equilibrium analysis, by expanding from a two-state to a three-state periodic force protocol to direct intermediate populations. Our assay and analysis framework open new possibilities for deciphering complex multi-domain folds and their multi-dimensional folding pathways.
affiliations: TU Dresden (corresponding author)

papers.title: State-selective nanobodies to probe Guanylate-binding protein coat assembly and function
papers.abstract: Cell-autonomous immunity against gram-negative bacterial pathogens relies on Guanylate-binding proteins (GBPs). GBPs are interferon-inducible guanosine triphosphate hydrolases that coat cytosolic bacteria and promote non-canonical inflammasome activation. GBP coat assembly is initiated by GBP1, which binds bacterial lipopolysaccharide and recruits further paralogs in a hierarchical and nucleotide-dependent manner. Dissecting the contributions of individual GBPs has remained challenging because the seven human paralogs are structurally similar and undergo nucleotide-driven conformational changes that are difficult to resolve in cellular and biochemical experiments. Here, we developed a nanobody toolbox for the state-selective probing of human GBP coat assembly. We identify eight nanobodies with distinct paralog, domain, and conformational specificities and define their binding profiles and epitopes using complementary biophysical assays and cryogenic electron microscopy. We further demonstrate the utility of selected nanobodies by demonstrating their functionality in membrane reconstitution assays and in infected cells. A dimer-disrupting nanobody blocks progression of GBP-coat assembly from soluble GBP1 assemblies to LPS-associated coats, suggesting a stage-specific structural transition during coat formation. In contrast, a dimer selective nanobody binds assembled coats without measurably perturbing their organisation and is robustly recruited to GBP1-positive bacteria in infected cells, indicating that this dimer interface remains intact and accessible in coat-associated GBP1. Together, these nanobodies establish a set of state-selective reagents to distinguish, perturb, and probe GBP assemblies in structural and cellular studies.
affiliations: Delft University of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: MOSAIC: Learning Graph Node Embeddings from Spectrally Isolated Dominant Subspaces of Accumulated Diffusion Operators
papers.abstract: Graph embedding transforms complex networks into low-dimensional representations for analysis and downstream machine learning. Existing methods often rely on eigenvalue ordering, random-walk sampling, or neural optimization. We introduce MOSAIC, Multistep Operator Spectral Accumulation with Isolated Components, an unsupervised framework that constructs an accumulated diffusion operator from successive powers of a graph transition matrix. MOSAIC uses Krylov subspace analysis to identify dominant spectral components according to their convergence behavior. This approach emphasizes persistent and spectrally separated diffusion modes rather than selecting embedding coordinates solely by eigenvalue magnitude. We evaluated MOSAIC using a biomedical graph projection derived from the Data Distillery Knowledge Graph that contained 5,171 human genes and 10,147 phenotypes. Across embedding dimensions from 16 to 128, MOSAIC achieved node-type classification AUROCs from 0.9863 to 0.9926 and exceeded FastRP, Node2Vec, HashGNN, and GraphSAGE. For gene-phenotype link prediction, validation and test associations were withheld before embedding generation. Under progressive removal of all edges or specific edge classes, MOSAIC retained more node-label information than FastRP, including after extreme graph sparsification. In a focused DICER1 analysis, 106 of 137 documented phenotype associations received scores above 0.90, demonstrating concordance with known pleiotropic biology and prioritizing additional relationships for independent evaluation. These results support MOSAIC as a fully unsupervised framework for learning informative graph representations. Although demonstrated using a biomedical graph projection, MOSAIC is domain independent and can be applied to other complex networks
affiliations: The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia / University of Pennsylvania (corresponding author)

papers.title: The GndA microprotein promotes cell growth during heat shock in Escherichia coli
papers.abstract: Hundreds of bacterial small open reading frames (sORFs) encoding microproteins of fewer than fifty amino acids have recently been identified. Biological functions have been ascribed to an increasing number of microproteins, some of which play roles in bacterial stress responses. In this work, we provide evidence that GndA, a frameshifted 36-amino acid microprotein encoded in an internal open reading frame overlapping the 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase (6PGD) coding sequence (CDS), functions in the response to heat shock. We demonstrate independent contributions of GndA and 6PGD to cell growth at high temperature. GndA is hydrophobic and associates with the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex and respiratory complex I (RCI). Consistent with a role in cellular homeostasis, GndA mutations alter the transcriptional response to heat shock. These results demonstrate that GndA promotes bacterial cell growth at high temperature independently of the 6PGD protein that it overlaps. GndA thus expands the paradigm of bacterial microproteins that function in cellular stress responses.
affiliations: Yale University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Gag proteolysis drives HIV-1 envelope conformational closure through the gp41 cytoplasmic tail
papers.abstract: HIV-1 must present a fusion-competent envelope glycoprotein (Env) to enter host cells while concealing the very conformation targeted by broadly neutralising antibodies (bnAbs). How the virus resolves this conflict has remained unclear. Using a minimally invasive nanobody-labelling strategy targeting Env's V4 loop, we combine single-virus FRET, fluorescence lifetime cross-correlation spectroscopy, and DNA-PAINT super-resolution microscopy to resolve Env conformation on individual, intact virions from the primary isolate JR-FL. We show that immature virions predominantly display an open Env conformation, while Gag maturation drives acquisition of the tightly closed, fusion-competent State 1 that harbours the principal bnAb epitope. Truncating the Env cytoplasmic tail abolishes this regulation, identifying the gp41 tail as the conduit linking Gag lattice maturation to Env's conformational fate. We further show that bnAb b12 preferentially binds open Env on immature virions, supporting a decoy mechanism that shields mature virions from immune recognition, with direct implications for HIV-1 vaccine design.
affiliations: King's College London (corresponding author)

papers.title: Integrating cell-state and enhancer constraints discriminates models of PU.1 regulation during hematopoietic differentiation
papers.abstract: Distinct PU.1 levels are associated with progenitor, B-cell, and macrophage states during hematopoietic differentiation. A previous dynamical-systems model attributed these levels to multistability generated by PU.1 autoregulation coupled to feedback between PU.1 abundance and cell-cycle progression, but its predictions were not quantitatively evaluated against the motivating measurements. Here, we test this mechanism using reported measurements of PU.1 abundance, its synthesis rate, and cell-cycle duration, and develop progressively more mechanistic alternatives. The original growth-feedback model neither represents the two reported progenitor groups nor reproduces the nonmonotonic relationship between PU.1 abundance and cell-cycle length. Even with experimentally measured cell-type-specific growth rates, PU.1 autoregulation alone does not reproduce the observed PU.1 abundance and synthesis rates across cell states. Reproducing the cell-state measurements requires an additional cell-state-dependent input to PU.1 production. Guided by enhancer regulation, we model positive feedback between PU.1 and C/EBP and constrain it with reporter measurements, but this architecture cannot jointly reproduce the reporter and cell-state datasets. Adding RUNX1 permits data-consistent stable states when high effective cooperativity in PU.1-dependent C/EBP activation is allowed. Thus, combined dynamical and cis-regulatory constraints support additional regulation of PU.1 production beyond autoregulation, cell-type-specific dilution, and C/EBP feedback. The RUNX1-extended architecture provides one biologically grounded realization and generates experimentally testable hypotheses for differentiation networks.
affiliations: Rice University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Conformational dynamics of ND2 antiporter-like subunit in intact and truncated complex I
papers.abstract: Respiratory complex I is a large redox-driven proton pump and contributes to the proton motive force required for ATP generation in mitochondria and bacteria. It has been extensively studied with structural and biochemical approaches leading to enhanced understanding of its three- dimensional architecture. Despite significant progress in deciphering its catalytic function, the redox-coupled proton pumping mechanism remains unclear and extensively debated. The three membrane-bound antiporter-like subunits ND2, ND4 and ND5 are responsible for pumping protons from the negatively charged side (N-side) of the membrane to the positively charged side (P-side). Emerging evidence supports the role of ND5 subunit in releasing pumped protons to the P-side of the membrane, but the question whether ND2 and ND4 also contribute to proton release remains unanswered. Here, we performed atomistic molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of an intact and a truncated model of complex I in which ND5 and ND4 subunits are removed in-silico. The simulation data reveals a previously unobserved conformational change in the P-side region of ND2 subunit that occurs much more easily in a truncated model of complex I, as also estimated based on free energy calculations. The conformational change, in part triggered by the artificial exposure of ND2 subunit to lipid bilayer, results in a local hydration of the region, similar to what has been observed in recent cryo-EM structure of plant CI:CIII2 supercomplex. We discuss the functional relevance of observed conformational transitions and identify residues that can be manipulated with biochemical approaches to shed light on proton pumping by complex I.
affiliations: University of Helsinki (corresponding author)

papers.title: Plunge freezing tweezers with ultrasonic excitation for reducing preferred particle orientation in cryo-EM
papers.abstract: Preferred particle orientation, which results from the adsorption of proteins to the air-water interface, is a frequently encountered issue in single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). Particles then present only a limited number of views, which are oversampled during data acquisition at the expense of throughput, while other views may be missing altogether. In severe cases, a high-resolution reconstruction becomes unattainable. We have recently established that ultrasonic excitation of the sample during vitrification improves the angular distribution by detaching particles from the air-water interface and reshuffling their orientations. Here, we describe an implementation of this principle for a plunge freezing apparatus, in which the ultrasonic transducer is integrated into the head of the pair of tweezers holding the sample, and show that this design is able to reduce preferred orientation. We demonstrate this for hemagglutinin, the canonical example of preferred orientation, and show that the fraction of side and tilted views increases with the excitation amplitude. This allows us to obtain a complete reconstruction of the trimer at 2.5 [A].
affiliations: Ecole Polytechnique Federale de Lausanne (EPFL), Laboratory of Molecular Nanodynamics, CH-1015 Lausanne, Switzerland (corresponding author)

papers.title: Toll-like receptor expression across histological states of Epidermodysplasia Verruciformis
papers.abstract: Epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV) is characterized by susceptibility to cutaneous {beta}-human papillomaviruses, persistent viral lesions and an increased risk of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC). We investigated whether expression of Toll-like receptors 3, 4, 5 and 9 (TLR3, TLR4, TLR5 and TLR9) differs across histological states within EV. Immunoreactivity was quantified by digital H-score using QuPath in 97 specimens from 28 patients, comprising 13 lesion-free skin samples, 15 flat warts and 69 cSCCs. Prespecified comparisons evaluated flat wart versus lesion-free skin, cSCC versus non-neoplastic tissue and invasive versus in situ cSCC, with invasive tumour differentiation assessed secondarily. Patient-clustered generalized estimating equations and false-discovery-rate (FDR) correction were used for inference. After correction for multiple testing, TLR9 H-scores were higher in flat warts than in lesion-free skin ({beta}=60.58; q=0.0332). Compared with non-neoplastic tissue, cSCC showed lower TLR3 ({beta}=-81.40; q=0.00745), higher TLR4 ({beta}=55.59; q=0.04793) and lower TLR9 expression ({beta}=-34.80; q=0.03412). TLR5 showed a nominal increase in cSCC that did not meet the FDR threshold. None of the four receptors differed significantly between invasive and in situ cSCC, and no differentiation trend remained significant after FDR correction. These findings show receptor-specific differences in TLR expression across histological states of EV, particularly involving TLR3, TLR4 and TLR9, although the diagnostic and prognostic significance of these tissue patterns remains to be established.
affiliations: Department of Dermatology, University of Sao Paulo Medical School, Sao Paulo, Brazil (corresponding author)

papers.title: A Nanomechanical Fingerprint of Centromeric Methylation Co-Localization in TNBC Chromosomal Instability
papers.abstract: Centromeric heterochromatin is maintained by a self-reinforcing loop between DNA methylation (5mC) and histone H3 lysine 9 trimethylation (H3K9me3), yet whether this coupling is preserved at the level of individual chromosomes in cancer has been inaccessible to conventional epigenomic assays, which average signals across cell populations and cannot resolve single-chromosome heterogeneity. Here, we use antibody-functionalized atomic force spectroscopy to simultaneously map 5mC and H3K9me3 at the centromeres of individual metaphase chromosomes from non-tumorigenic, luminal, and triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) cell models. Co-localized 5mC/H3K9me3 sites are mechanically stiffer than sites carrying either mark alone across the panel, revealing a cooperative biophysical signature of epigenetic crosstalk. Luminal chromosomes acquire the highest mark density, co-localization, and stiffness, whereas TNBC chromosomes show reduced density and diminished, though not absent, co-localization and stiffness, converging toward the low baseline of non-tumorigenic epithelium. TGF-{beta}1-induced epithelial-mesenchymal transition reproduces this attenuated phenotype in luminal cells, linking it directly to a process central to TNBC aggressiveness. These biophysical parameters classify cancer versus non-tumorigenic chromosomes with near-perfect, cross-validated accuracy, and further resolve the two TNBC subtypes using colocalization-derived features alone (macro-F1 = 0.933). These results establish the mechanical consequence of epigenetic mark co-localization as a single-chromosome-resolvable signature of centromeric organization, attenuated in aggressive breast cancer, and demonstrate a force-spectroscopy platform for mechano-epigenetic profiling of cancer chromosomes.
affiliations: Shiv Nadar University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Transient tubular membrane injury is converted into persistent fibrosis through a macrophage-fibroblast relay
papers.abstract: A central unresolved problem in acute kidney injury (AKI) is how a transient epithelial insult is converted into persistent fibrotic repair that drives progression toward chronic kidney disease. Although tubular, immune and stromal responses are individually well recognized, the mechanistically continuous relay linking these three compartments has remained unresolved. Here we define a directional information-conversion pathway spanning injured tubular epithelial cells, macrophages and fibroblasts. Time-resolved single-cell profiling identified a TREM2/SPP1 macrophage state that emerged as post-ischemic repair became fibrotic. Tubular injury remodeled phosphatidylserine (PS) species, increased oxidized PS and PS externalization, and generated a membrane-lipid context for TREM2 sensing, supported by PS masking, defined liposomes and orthogonal binding assays. Structure-function analysis separated R47-dependent phospholipid recognition from K183-dependent DAP12 coupling, linking membrane damage to SYK activation and NF-kB/AP-1-driven Spp1 transcription. Macrophage-derived SPP1 then activated ITGAV/ITGB1-associated FAK-SMAD2/3 signaling, fibroblast contraction and matrix production. Crucially, repair-phase SPP1 neutralization and post-injury Cx3cr1-lineage Trem2 deletion attenuated fibrosis, with delayed Trem2 deletion protective in both ischemic and obstructive injury. Human single-cell, spatial, urinary and tissue analyses showed cross-species and cross-scale convergence. These findings resolve how transient tubular membrane damage is successively transformed across three cellular compartments into persistent, yet interruptible, fibrotic repair.
affiliations: Renmin Hospital of Wuhan University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Generating Structural Ensembles of Disordered Proteins with Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Generative models of protein structures have accelerated scientific discovery. However, the leading structure-prediction models are trained primarily on crystal structures, limiting their ability to sample the conformations of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs). All-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations can probe the diversity of IDP conformational ensembles, but these simulations are slow and costly. Leveraging the speed of generative models and the accuracy of MD, we develop Zephyr, an SE(3) equivariant diffusion model trained on simulated IDP ensembles. The model generates the structure of a single protein sequence in two phases: a coarse-grained structure is first sampled and heavy atoms are subsequently denoised onto this structure. We evaluate our method on two fronts: ensemble accuracy and sampling efficiency. Across five test systems, the model reproduces key geometric and energetic metrics of the MD ensembles, while sampling at least 63 times faster.
affiliations: University of Toronto (corresponding author)

papers.title: Red states modulate energy localization between the antenna and trap in PSI
papers.abstract: The core antenna of the photosystem I (PSI) complex of oxygenic photosynthesis operates at near perfect quantum efficiency, making it one of the most efficient energy conversation devices in nature. The presence of low energy or red chlorophylls (chls) is nearly universal in this core antenna, and these red chls are known to extend the light harvesting capacity and control the rate of energy migration in PSI. Surprisingly, the significance of the structural position of the red chls in PSI remains unknown. In this study, we introduced mutations that generate specific red sites in the PSI core antenna, consistent with those observed in natural species. Using CryoEM, we characterized the structural changes at these red sites. Using transient absorption spectroscopy, we measured the effects of red chlorophyll at specific sites on energy transfer and trapping in PSI to identify their functional significance. While one site funneled energy to the reaction center, the other slowed equilibration in the antenna. These opposing effects indicate different functions are associated with the different red chlorophyll location, reconciling previous seemingly incompatible suggestions as to their functional role.
affiliations: Arizona State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: High-Throughput Morphological Profiling of Patient-Derived Human Liver Organoids for Hepatotoxicity Hazard Identification and Compound Prioritization
papers.abstract: Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) remains a major challenge in drug development because existing in vitro models poorly predict clinical hepatotoxicity. We coupled patient-derived human liver organoids (HLOs) with high-content imaging and automated machine learning (ML) to detect hepatotoxicity-associated phenotypes by morphological profiling. HLOs from six DILI patients and one healthy donor (n = 7) retained donor-specific baseline phenotypes in hepatocyte maturity, metabolism, and morphology. ML models trained per line on MAD-robustized, well-level-aggregated median features achieved compound-level AUROCs of 0.88 (95% CI 0.86-0.90) to 0.91 (95% CI 0.89-0.93) and balanced accuracies of 0.81-0.84 in distinguishing 54 hepatotoxicants from 20 non-hepatotoxic controls. Averaging predictions across all seven lines at an optimized threshold gave 94.4% sensitivity (95% CI 84.6-98.8%) and 85.0% specificity (95% CI 62.1-96.8%), substantially outperforming HLO cytotoxicity assays and cancer cell line profiling. Lines were moderately-to-highly concordant (Pearson r = 0.66-0.85), and benchmark concentration modeling revealed reproducible inter-line differences in phenotypic sensitivity (median 4.0-fold, several compounds exceeding 20-fold). Exposure anchoring of benchmark concentrations to human-equivalent plasma concentrations, using in vitro mass-balance dosimetry and curated plasma free fractions, placed organoid points of departure within 100-fold of clinical Cmax for 60 of 66 compounds (23-fold residual offset, 95% CI 12-45), and placed two of the three misclassified negative controls an order of magnitude above clinical Cmax. Sulindac injury signatures were significantly enhanced by TNF co-treatment, demonstrating capacity to detect pro-inflammatory-mediated DILI. This platform preserves inter-line variability while enabling reproducible, scalable multi-line consensus hazard classification; because compounds were tested over a common nominal concentration range, the readout defines hepatocellular hazard, which must be combined with exposure as an independent input to estimate clinical DILI risk.
affiliations: Department of Medicinal Chemistry, College of Pharmacy, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI, 48109, USA; Department of Internal Medicine, Gastroenterology and (corresponding author)

papers.title: Integrating Developmental Neurotoxicity Prediction with Adverse Outcome Pathway Reasoning
papers.abstract: Experimental assessment of developmental neurotoxicity (DNT) is costly, time-consuming, and difficult to scale across large chemical inventories. New approach methodologies (NAMs), including computational approaches based on machine learning, deep learning, and large language models (LLMs), offer new ways to screen and prioritize chemicals. However, these emerging computational approaches have largely focused on predicting toxicity endpoints, with less attention to the mechanisms underlying those predictions. For DNT assessment, understanding this mechanistic basis is equally important. In this study, we integrated LLM inference with the adverse outcome pathway (AOP) framework to connect DNT predictions with plausible mechanisms. We constructed an AOP-informed benchmark linking ChEMBL target-activity measurements for 5,861 compounds to 14 AOPs representing five neurodevelopmental outcomes and evaluated ten LLMs for the prediction of molecular initiating events (MIEs), key events (KEs), key event relationships (KERs), and adverse outcomes (AOs), as well as the generation of mechanistic explanations. Explanation quality was evaluated using both a naive LLM judge and a rubric-based LLM judge. Across the zero-shot models, the highest observed macro-F1 scores were 0.818 for MIEs and 0.463 for AOs, but only 0.056 for KEs and 0.034 for KERs, identifying downstream pathway reconstruction as the principal challenge. Few-shot prompting substantially improved performance, with Gemini 3.8 Flash under four-shot prompting achieving macro-F1 scores of 0.956 for AOs, 0.813 for MIEs, 0.492 for KEs, and 0.457 for KERs. Both LLM-judge configurations indicated improved mechanistic explanation quality with few-shot examples, although strong outcome prediction did not consistently ensure recovery of the recorded pathway. Our results demonstrate the potential of AOP-informed LLMs to support DNT assessment by linking predicted neurodevelopmental outcomes to plausible biological mechanisms and enabling predictions to be evaluated at both the outcome and pathway levels.
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (corresponding author)

papers.title: A Kiss-and-Ride Mechanism for Lipid Exchange at Membrane Contact Sites
papers.abstract: Lipid transfer proteins (LTPs) mediate non-vesicular lipid transport at membrane contact sites, yet how transient membrane tethering contributes to lipid transfer remains poorly understood. Here, we use the single-domain yeast phosphatidylserine transporter Osh6, a member of the oxysterol-binding protein-related protein family, to investigate tethering-dependent lipid transport. We show that Osh6 can access two transport modes depending on membrane composition: conventional shuttling between membranes and a tethering-dependent mode in which the opposing membrane facilitates cargo extraction from the donor membrane. Combining lipid transport and membrane-tethering measurements with kinetic analysis, lipid partitioning, and in vivo complementation, we provide evidence for a transient membrane-bridged intermediate during lipid transfer. Productive phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate (PI4P) extraction destabilizes this bridged state, allowing cargo-loaded Osh6 to disengage and continue the transport cycle. We term this mechanism kiss-and-ride, in which transient membrane contact facilitates cargo extraction ("kiss") before the cargo-loaded protein disengages ("ride"). Consistent with this model, PI4P transport is preserved in a lidless Osh6 mutant with impaired membrane dissociation, whereas phosphatidylserine transport is strongly reduced, revealing distinct mechanistic requirements for the two cargoes. Together, our findings reveal a tethering-dependent transport mode in a cup-like LTP and suggest that membrane contact sites can actively shape the mechanism of lipid transport rather than merely bringing donor and acceptor membranes into proximity.
affiliations: Institute of Organic Chemistry and Biochemistry of the CAS, Prague (corresponding author)

papers.title: A Novel ACLY Inhibitor Induces Transcriptional and Metabolic Reprogramming to Overcome Tyrosine kinase inhibitor Resistance in Lymphoma
papers.abstract: Background: Metabolic plasticity contributes to therapeutic resistance in T-cell lymphoma, but the metabolic dependencies underlying tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) resistance remain poorly understood. ATP citrate lyase (ACLY), which converts citrate to cytosolic acetyl-CoA, links glucose metabolism to lipogenesis and acetylation-dependent regulation. We hypothesized that ACLY represents an actionable metabolic vulnerability in lymphoma. Methods: Structure-guided drug discovery and biochemical screening were used to identify the novel ACLY inhibitor VCB1. VCB1 was evaluated against recombinant human ACLY and in TKI-sensitive and TKI-resistant lymphoma models. Antitumor activity was assessed by proliferation, cell-cycle analysis, apoptosis, and immunoblotting, followed by integrated transcriptomic, metabolomic, and lipidomic profiling. Results: Our xenograft study showed that ACLY dependence in ALK+ALCL. We discovered novel ACLY inhibitor VCB1 directly inhibited recombinant ACLY with uM potency (IC, 0.9 uM) and strongly suppressed lymphoma cell growth. In ALK inhibitor-sensitive SUPM2, VCB1 showed an IC of 0.299 uM and retained potency in lorlatinib-resistant SUPM2-LR1000 cells (1.62 uM), whereas BMS-303141 was substantially less active (17.46 and 22.07 uM). VCB1 similarly inhibited BTK inhibitor sensitive and resistant mantle cell lymphoma cell growth (IC, 0.28 and 0.278 uM), compared with BMS-303141 (30.5 and 37.01 uM). Multi-omics profiling revealed suppression of de novo lipogenesis, including ACACA, FASN, and PPARGC1B, together with extensive remodeling of triglyceride, phospholipid, cardiolipin, ceramide, and acylcarnitine species and increased expression of fatty-acid oxidation genes. VCB1 activated the integrated stress response (ISR), inducing ATF4, PPP1R15A, DDIT3, DDIT4 and SESN2, while disrupting purine and pyrimidine metabolism and reducing nucleotide biosynthetic genes, including CAD, DHODH, UCK2, and ATIC. VCB1 further activated an ACLY/ISR/CHAC1 axis associated with reduced GCLC/GCLM expression, glutathione depletion, and a decreased GSH/GSSG ratio, indicating impaired redox homeostasis. TKI-resistant cells exhibited distinct lipid-metabolic remodeling consistent with metabolic plasticity. VCB1 also altered immune-regulatory programs involving PDCD1, TIGIT, CD247, CD226, NFATC2, and inflammatory cytokines. Functionally, VCB1 induced cell cycle arrest and apoptosis. Conclusions: ACLY represents an integrated metabolic and signaling vulnerability in lymphoma. VCB1 suppresses lymphoma growth across TKI-sensitive and resistant models by disrupting lipid and nucleotide metabolism, metabolic adaptation and ISR and redox homeostasis supporting ACLY inhibition as a therapeutic strategy for TKI-resistant lymphoma.
affiliations: Fox chase cancer center (corresponding author)

papers.title: A Novel NO Donor 3A72 Activates Mitochondrial-Associated Endoplasmic Reticulum Membrane Structures to Induce Ferroptosis in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer
papers.abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) remains a major clinical challenge due to a lack of effective interventions and severe drug resistance. Disrupting tumor metabolism using nitric oxide (NO) donors to drive ferroptosis represents a promising therapeutic strategy. Here, we developed 3A72, a novel furan-coumarin-based NO donor with potent anti-TNBC efficacy. In vitro and in vivo studies demonstrated that 3A72 significantly suppresses TNBC cell proliferation and restricts xenograft tumor growth. Notably, its efficacy matches the first-line drug paclitaxel but with enhanced safety and reduced systemic toxicity. Mechanistically, 3A72 induces ferroptosis in triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) cells via a synergistic dual-pathway mechanism. Initially, 3A72 releases intracellular NO to trigger cytoplasmic calcium overload, followed by high-affinity binding to both inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptor (IPR) and acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain family member 4 (ACSL4). Binding to IP3R provokes mitochondrial calcium overload and a massive burst of reactive oxygen species (ROS), while concurrent ACSL4 activation drives essential membrane phospholipid remodeling. Crucially, our transcriptomic and structural predictions reveal that while ACSL4 exhibits a broader distribution across organelle membranes, its functional association with IP3R spatially converges at the endoplasmic reticulum membranes associated with mitochondria (MAMs). This subcellular niche closely couples IPR-mediated ROS generation with ACSL4-driven lipid remodeling, accelerating lethal malondialdehyde (MDA) accumulation and triggering irreversible ferroptosis. Overall, these findings highlight the MAMs calcium-lipid metabolic hub as a promising structural scaffold for antitumor drug development.
affiliations: Fudan University, School of Pharmacy (corresponding author)

papers.title: A Novel Biofilm Amyloid Ligand for Caspase-11 Drives Hyperactivation in Dendritic Cells
papers.abstract: Bacterial biofilms drive persistent infection and chronic inflammation, yet host sensing of biofilm-derived ligands remains poorly understood. Here we identify curli amyloid, an integral component of Enterobacteriaceae biofilms, as a novel activator of the non-canonical inflammasome in human and mouse dendritic cells (DCs). Curli both primes and activates the inflammasome, directly binding caspase-11 to engage NLRP3 and drive robust IL-1{beta} maturation without pyroptosis, establishing curli as a previously unrecognized trigger of DC hyperactivation. Mechanistically, this non-lytic signaling is marked by limited gasdermin D oligomerization without mitochondrial localization and NINJ1-dependent membrane rupture. Functionally, curli-hyperactivated DCs show enhanced migration to the draining lymph nodes in vivo, suggesting consequent augmented adaptive immunity. Finally, curli-containing biofilms also elicit IL-1{beta} secretion without cell death, identifying bacterial amyloid as a central driver of non-lytic inflammasome activation during immune recognition of biofilms.
affiliations: Laboratory of Dendritic Cell Biology, Division of Innate Immunity, Department of Medicine, University of Massachusetts Chan Medical School, Worcester, MA, 01545 (corresponding author)

papers.title: Acetylated PLIN2 coordinates the innate immune system and oxylipin synthesis on lipid droplets to propagate inflammation
papers.abstract: Research has implicated lipid droplets (LDs) and their associated proteins in inflammation and the innate immune response. The key LD protein Perilipin 2 (PLIN2) is tightly correlated with lipid storage and inflammation, but little is known about the mechanisms underlying its proinflammatory effects. Here, we show that PLIN2 is required for the inflammatory response to mitogens and the recruitment of pro-inflammatory proteins to the surface of LDs. PLIN2 directly binds arachidonic acid and interacts with key oxylipin synthetic enzymes such as PLA2 and COX2 to promote LD-localized oxylipin synthesis and propagate inflammatory signaling. Moreover, LPS induces PLIN2 hyperacetylation, and acetylation-dead PLIN2 mutants lose their proinflammatory properties in the presence of an inflammatory stimulus, as if PLIN2 were ablated. Thus, acetylated PLIN2 forms a key metabolon on LDs that is essential for the response and amplification of proinflammatory signaling.
affiliations: Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Longitudinal linear-epitope profiling of SLE identifies novel antigens associated with disease and disease activity
papers.abstract: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is the prototypical systemic autoimmune disease defined by the production of autoantibodies directed against diverse self-antigens. Antinuclear antibodies (ANA) are central to SLE diagnosis, and anti-double-stranded DNA (anti-dsDNA) antibodies are clinically used to track disease activity. However, these biomarkers provide only partial insight into the full spectrum of autoimmune changes in patients. To expand the known landscape of SLE autoreactivity shared among patients and associated with disease activity, we performed an unbiased characterization of 1,268 SLE plasma samples from 695 SLE patients and 301 healthy controls using phage immunoprecipitation and sequencing (PhIP-seq). This technique preferentially displays linear epitopes, and thus provides a complementary set of autoreactivities to previously discovered autoreactive targets. Despite the marked clinical heterogeneity of SLE, machine learning applied to this data surfaced a shared, reproducible signature that robustly discriminates between SLE and healthy controls in two validation cohorts. Autoreactivities in SLE were significantly enriched for RNA-binding protein targets. Autoreactive proteins containing Basic Acidic Dipeptides (BAD) repeat domains, features associated with biomolecular condensate formation, distinguished patients with high disease activity (by SLEDAI score) from patients with no disease activity. Among all shared autoreactivities, a peptide derived from YTHDF2 emerged as the most prevalent target across SLE cohorts occurring in ~25% of SLE patients and displayed striking sequence similarity to a peptide derived from the Epstein Barr virus (EBV) lytic switch protein BZLF1. Competition assays demonstrated higher-affinity binding to the viral peptide, supporting a model in which antiviral humoral responses to EBV may drive secondary epitope spreading toward molecularly mimicked self-antigens. Remarkably, orthogonal validation using the Luminex bead platform containing a panel of only 10 peptides, including BZLF1, demonstrated strong discrimination between SLE and healthy controls (AUC = 0.95). Together, these findings identify a rich, greatly expanded landscape of autoreactivities in SLE, candidate biomarkers associated with high disease activity, and provide mechanistic insight linking EBV-driven immunity to epitope-specific autoimmunity in lupus.
affiliations: University of California, San Francisco (corresponding author)

papers.title: The helminth-derived effector protein HpBARI trimerises to selectively target membrane bound ST2 receptor
papers.abstract: The ST2 receptor is activated by the alarmin cytokine IL-33, inducing and controlling immune responses. ST2-mediated signalling contributes to protection from parasitic infection, but is also involved in asthma, inflammatory bowel disease, fibrosis and allergic inflammation, making inhibitors of ST2 desirable. While signalling is mediated by membrane-associated ST2 on immune cells, extracellular fluids also contain a soluble form of ST2 which acts as a decoy, soaking up IL-33. An effective ST2-targeting therapeutic will selectively target membrane-associated ST2. The intestinal helminth H. polygyrus bakeri suppresses ST2-mediated signalling to reduce helminth clearance from the gut, with the effector HpBARI2 directly binding to and inhibiting ST2. Here, we present the structure of the ST2:HpBARI2 complex. HpBARI2 forms a stable, planar trimeric structure, with three vertices each binding a single ST2. HpBARI2 occludes the IL-33 binding site of ST2 and constraints the receptor in a conformation incompatible with recruitment of signalling co-receptor IL-1RAcP. The trimeric valency of HpBARI2 results in preferential binding to multiple membrane-associated ST2 molecules rather than the soluble decoy receptor. Therefore, HpBARI2 combines steric blockade, conformational restriction and multivalent binding to potently and selectively inhibit ST2 signalling in the context of soluble ST2. This insight will guide design of improved therapeutics which target ST2.
affiliations: University of Oxford (corresponding author)

papers.title: CHAIR an antigen-resolved antibody-reactome resource for healthy adult immune aging
papers.abstract: Antigen-recognition histories accumulate across adult life, but existing human aging resources largely emphasize host-state measurements rather than antigen-resolved humoral memory. We present CHAIR, the Chinese Healthy Aging Immune Resource, which integrates self-antigen, human virome and toxin/virulence-factor PhIP-seq with routine clinical measurements and T/B/NK phenotyping in clinically screened adults aged 20-94 years. The resource framework includes 1,008 unique PhIP-seq samples, 995 clinical records, 977 T/B/NK records and 853 participants with all three layers. Across modeled spaces comprising 23,584 self-antigen targets, 210 virome targets and 1,258 virulence-factor source targets, most measured antibody-reactivity architecture was consistent with broad preservation within domains, whereas age- and sex-associated signals were concentrated in focal targets and modules. Together, CHAIR provides a traceable, antigen-resolved reference framework based on clinically screened adults for investigating focal humoral remodeling across healthy adult aging.
affiliations: Shanghai Center for Systems Biomedicine, Key Laboratory of Systems Biomedicine, Ministry of Education, Tong Ren Hospital, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shangha (corresponding author)

papers.title: Early-life adversity alters the adult blood proteome primarily in female mice
papers.abstract: Background: Early-life adversity (ELA) is one of the strongest predictors of poor mental and physical health later in life, increasing an individual's risk for disorders ranging from depression to metabolic syndrome. However, whether and how ELA shapes immune memory through adulthood, subsequently affecting susceptibility to immune-associated diseases such as autoimmunity, remains elusive. Methods: To address this question, we employed a translationally and ethologically relevant mouse model of resource deprivation, the limited bedding and nesting model, to study the long-term effects of ELA on the immune system. ELA was induced by limited bedding and nesting material in the cage during postnatal days (P)2-9, which provokes fragmented and unpredictable maternal behavior in the dams, and results in chronic stress in the pups. Nucleic acid Linked ImmunoSandwich Assay (NULISA) was used to survey the proteome of adult (~P90) mice of both sexes that experienced ELA vs. control conditions. Results: Using a novel proteomic method, we detected significant upregulation in the levels of IL-17A in the adult blood, primarily in females. Within females, ELA also upregulated IL-13 and CCL3. Three proteins, HGF, PDGFA, and WNT16, were significantly downregulated in ELA mice of both sexes. Conclusions: Being a hallmark proinflammatory cytokine, IL-17A is found to increase in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), as well as in animals with lupus-like diseases in virtually all reports. Importantly, autoimmune diseases like SLE have a higher prevalence in women than men, and our data support this sex bias. Together, our data suggest that ELA shapes long-term immune function in a way that may increase risk for autoimmune diseases, with promise for the development of more targeted and personalized therapies for autoimmunity.
affiliations: Georgia State University (corresponding author)

papers.title: NAD+ modulation by nicotinamide riboside enhances CD8+ T-cell metabolic fitness and effector function during Trypanosoma cruzi infection and improves parasite control
papers.abstract: Chagas disease, caused by the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi, remains a major health concern, with effective immune control relying heavily on CD8+ T cells. However, the metabolic factors that regulate CD8+ T cell function during infection are not well understood. Acute T. cruzi infection induced metabolic remodeling in parasite-specific and effector CD8+ T cells, characterized by increased reliance on glycolysis, altered mitochondrial homeostasis, oxidative stress, and increased CD38 expression. Nicotinamide riboside (NR), an NAD+ precursor, improved mitochondrial function, reduced mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mROS) and CD38 expression, decreased apoptosis, and enhanced CD8+ T cell effector responses in vitro and in infected mice. In vivo, NR treatment increased intracellular NAD+ levels in CD8+ T cells and improved parasite control during acute infection, reducing parasitemia and skeletal muscle parasite burden. Furthermore, transient NR supplementation was associated with persistent metabolic and functional changes in memory CD8+ T cells during chronic infection. These findings identify NAD+ metabolism as a modulator of CD8+ T cell metabolic fitness during T. cruzi infection and support its further investigation as a host-directed strategy to enhance parasite control.
affiliations: Universidad Nacional de Cordoba Facultad de Ciencias Quimicas (corresponding author)

papers.title: Photoprotective Bioactive Pigment Produced by Bacillus altitudinis MIM2 Isolated from Mundra Port, Kutch, Gujarat, India
papers.abstract: Melanins are ubiquitous black or brown color pigments exhibiting a wide variety of bioactivities. They are stable and insoluble in nature. Melanin are industrially important pigment currently used in cosmetics, medicine and pharmaceuticals, industries. Bacteria mainly produce three types of melanin namely, Eumelanin, pheomelanin and pyomelanin which is usually extracellularly secreted. This makes the downstream processing of bacterial melanin easier. Stress conditions like salt stress, radiation stress etc. triggers the bacteria to produce melanin and several bacterial species were found to produce melanin under different stress induced conditions. In this present study we had isolated melanin producing bacteria from saline sediment sample of Mundra port, Kutch region of Gujarat state of India. The melanin producing bacteria was characterized using staining, biochemical and molecular methods. The melanin produced was extracted and analyzed using physicochemical techniques. The extracted melanin had shown good anti-bacterial and radical scavenging activity. To our knowledge, this is the first report on Bacillus altitudinis producing melanin.
affiliations: Atmiya University, Rajkot (corresponding author)

papers.title: Mechanistic Insights into Human Cathelicidin LL-37-Induced Activation of a Broadly Conserved Bacterial Signaling System
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) represent a promising class of therapeutics against bacterial pathogens. While their direct bactericidal mechanisms are well-characterized, how bacteria sense and respond to these peptides at sublethal concentrations remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate the activation of the Escherichia coli PhoQ-PhoP signaling system by the human antimicrobial peptide LL-37 and its derivatives (KR-12 and RI-10). We demonstrate that these peptides exhibit variable antimicrobial potency but surprisingly similar abilities to activate the PhoQ-PhoP pathway, indicating that signaling function is separable from bactericidal activity. Notably, sublethal concentrations of these peptides induce significant cell elongation, a phenotype dependent on PhoQ and mediated by the upregulation of QueE, which interferes with bacterial cell division. Contrary to the previous model suggesting peptides activate PhoQ passively by displacing its inhibitor MgrB, we observed enhanced cell elongation in {Delta}mgrB strains across all tested peptides, including RI-10, lacking antibacterial activity. Our findings suggest peptides actively stimulate PhoQ through a mechanism independent of MgrB dissociation, providing a more refined understanding of the peptide signaling through the PhoQ-PhoP system. These insights into bacterial adaptation mechanisms against host-derived peptides may guide the development of peptide therapeutics with enhanced efficacy against drug-resistant pathogens.
affiliations: Waksman Institute of Microbiology, Rutgers University (corresponding author)

papers.title: A nucleocapsid-tagged fluorescent pangolin coronavirus enables authentic-virus neutralization assays and localizes the antiviral activity of cepharanthine to viral entry
papers.abstract: Replication-competent coronaviruses carrying a fluorescently tagged structural protein are rare, and the only well-developed example tags the membrane (M) protein. Using the highly attenuated pangolin coronavirus GX_P2V(short_3UTR) as a backbone, we assembled a full-length cDNA clone by multifragment in vitro ligation and recovered GX_P2V-mBJ-N, a recombinant virus in which the bright monomeric green fluorescent protein mBaoJin is fused to the N terminus of the nucleocapsid (N) protein. The equivalent C-terminal fusion was not viable. GX_P2V-mBJ-N is infectious in Vero E6 cells but is attenuated and genetically unstable in the absence of exogenous N; supplying wild-type N in trans allows propagation to high titer with the fusion intact. Because mBaoJin is translated as part of N, fluorescence reports viral antigen synthesis directly, and infection can be quantified in a plate reader without immunostaining or plaque reduction. We applied the reporter virus in two settings. First, sera from ten healthy blood donors were titrated in parallel against GX_P2V-mBJ-N and a vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV)-based GX_P2V pseudovirus. The two assays agreed on rank order, but pseudovirus titers were about 10-fold higher overall and diverged by at least 70-fold in one donor, showing that the two formats are not interchangeable for individual samples. Second, time-of-addition experiments identified entry as the principal target of cepharanthine (EC50, 0.20 M under continuous treatment), whereas preincubation of virions with 25 M drug had no effect, excluding direct virion inactivation. GX_P2V-mBJ-N provides a practical authentic-virus platform for coronavirus serology and antiviral pharmacology.
affiliations: Beijing University of Chemical Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Novel but stable endosymbionts have contrasting effects on aphid dispersal and plant feeding damage in the cereal pest Diuraphis noxia
papers.abstract: Endosymbiotic bacteria can affect many ecological attributes of their insect hosts, including (in herbivorous insects) how they interact with plants where they feed. This raises the issue of whether deliberate endosymbiont introductions could be used to decrease crop damage caused by insect pests. Here we investigate how transinfecting Rickettsiella viridis and Regiella insecticola endosymbionts into a novel pest aphid host, the Russian wheat aphid (Diuraphis noxia), influences population growth, alate production, dispersal ability and crop damage. Both the Rickettsiella (originating from pea aphids) and Regiella (from green peach aphids) were stably maintained in their new host where they had contrasting effects. Rickettsiella increased the severity of aphid feeding damage on wheat and barley, resulting in greater leaf loss, chlorotic streaking, and higher aphid populations, whereas Regiella reduced aphid population growth and the severity of feeding damage by aphids. Their effects on dispersal morphology also differed: Regiella had no detectable impact on alate incidence, while Rickettsiella consistently suppressed wing formation in small cages, and in larger mesocosms with multiple wheat plants, this endosymbiont suppressed dispersal. Endosymbiont-mediated changes in feeding damage did not involve the main plant immune response pathways: transinfected and wild type aphids induced similar levels of jasmonic acid, jasmonic acid-isoleucine, and salicylic acid in plant tissues, even though these plant defenses were strongly activated during aphid feeding. Novel endosymbionts can therefore modulate the severity of plant feeding damage by aphids as well as influencing aphid dispersal. Potential applications in controlling pest D. noxia populations are discussed.
affiliations: The University of Melbourne (corresponding author)

papers.title: RSV & rhinovirus coinfection order dictates outcome via type III interferon-mediated interference in infant respiratory epithelium
papers.abstract: Coinfection with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and rhinovirus (RV) is the most frequently detected coinfection in infants, yet mechanisms governing viral interference and disease outcome remain poorly understood. Although infection order is a key determinant of coinfection outcome involving RSV, influenza, rhinovirus, and SARS-CoV-2, its role in RSV/RV coinfections has not been defined. Using infant-derived human nasal organoids at air-liquid interface, we demonstrate that coinfection order fundamentally determines the outcome of RSV/RV interactions. An initial RSV infection almost completely inhibits secondary RV coinfection, whereas primary RV infection only partially impairs a subsequent RSV coinfection. These distinct outcomes are accompanied by divergent temporal antiviral and pro-inflammatory responses. Mechanistically, we identify type III interferons as a sufficient mediator of RSV-induced restriction of RV, establishing a host-driven mechanism of viral interference. In contrast, partial impairment of RSV following RV infection occurs through an interferon-independent mechanism. Despite marked differences, RSV/RV coinfections do not exacerbate epithelial injury or innate immune responses beyond that induced by RSV alone, indicating RSV is the dominant driver of pathology in coinfections. Collectively, our data establishes coinfection order as a critical determinant of RSV/RV outcome and reveals novel and mechanistic insight into critical viral-host interactions in the infant nasal epithelium.
affiliations: Baylor College of Medicine (corresponding author)

papers.title: Structural mechanism of metal-induced DNA release by an ArsR/SmtB transcriptional regulator
papers.abstract: Metal-responsive transcriptional regulators must couple metal coordination to DNA release at the DNA-binding interface. However, the pathway connecting these states remains poorly understood. Here, we define this mechanism for the ArsR/SmtB-family repressor CadC from Listeria monocytogenes by combining crystal structures of apo, DNA-bound, and cadmium-bound states with biochemical and in vivo analyses. The DNA-bound structure reveals how CadC dimers bind sequence-specifically to operator DNA, via coordinated major-groove, wing and backbone interactions, with high-affinity binding depending on operator architecture. Cadmium is coordinated at the 3N sensor by an unusual Cys3-Met ligand set and stabilizes a DNA-incompatible conformation through remodeling of DNA-contacting elements and steric incompatibility between the ordered N-terminus and DNA. Mutational analyses show how these structural transitions link to metal-dependent transcriptional control in Listeria cells. We show that CadC binds zinc and supports zinc-responsive transcription in bacterial cells, and that host zinc availability modifies CadC-dependent infection phenotypes. Together, results reveal how metal coordination is converted into DNA release through coupled allosteric remodeling and steric exclusion, establishing a mechanism for signal-dependent transcriptional switching in ArsR/SmtB metalloregulators.
affiliations: i3S - IBMC (corresponding author)

papers.title: Restoring Antibiotic Sensitivity via Metabolic Pathway Manipulation in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
papers.abstract: Stopping antimicrobial multidrug resistance (AMR) is essential to maintain the efficacy of current treatments and sustain modern medicine, but current control relies on a coordinated One Health approach involving stewardship, infection prevention and other control measures, without direct actionable mechanisms against resistance itself. Here, integrating proteomics and metabolomics with high-throughput Caenorhabditis elegans infection models, we show that unique synergy of biotin biosynthesis inhibition with metformin uncouples virulence from bacterial viability shutting down major Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA) virulence mechanisms that impair host survival. Under directed evolution induced by central carbon metabolic stress, laboratory and clinical PA strain isolates acquire mutations in the MexAB-OprM multidrug efflux pump, leading to reversal of the AMR phenotype and restored susceptibility to multiple legacy and last-resort antibiotics such as meropenem. Our findings reveal a previously unexploited vulnerability in PA, its co-dependence on biotin biosynthesis and energy metabolism for virulence and resistance. This work establishes a conceptual framework in which metabolic co-targeting can abolish pathogenesis and drive reversal of antimicrobial resistance. It lays the foundation for first-in-class, non-antibiotic PA-selective anti-virulence and resistance-reversing therapies, key to extending the lifesaving duration of existing antibiotics.
affiliations: Imperial College London; Cluster of Excellence Cellular Stress Responses in Aging-associated Diseases (CECAD) (corresponding author)

papers.title: Host Cellular Remodeling, Not Viral Transcriptional Inhibition, Drives Quorum Sensing Signal-Mediated Evasion of Viral Lysis in Gephyrocapsa huxleyi
papers.abstract: Bacterial infochemicals can profoundly alter phytoplankton physiology, yet how these compounds influence viral infection outcomes remains poorly understood. The bacterial quorum sensing molecule 2-heptyl-4-quinolone (HHQ) enables the globally abundant coccolithophore, Gephyrocapsa huxleyi, to evade virus-induced mortality following infection by Emiliania huxleyi virus (EhV). HHQ reduced infectious virus production at 24 hours despite largely intact viral gene transcription, as revealed by RNA sequencing of host and viral responses during EhV-201 infection. Host transcriptomics instead revealed rapid and progressive HHQ-dependent physiological remodeling evidenced by changes in protein encoding genes associated with vesicular trafficking, and cytoskeletal organization. Transcriptional responses further implicated endolysosomal sorting, membrane remodeling, and protein modification as potential barriers to productive infection. These findings indicate that HHQ-mediated evasion of virus-induced mortality occurs downstream of viral entry and transcription, through remodeling of host processes required for virion assembly, maturation, trafficking, and release.
affiliations: Haverford College Department of Biology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Selected plasma-associated molecular species remodel the ABCB1 linker with effects retained under structure-derived tethering
papers.abstract: Multidrug resistance mediated by P-glycoprotein/ABCB1 remains a major limitation to chemotherapy, and cold atmospheric plasma has been reported to restore drug sensitivity in resistant cancer models. However, the molecular pathways connecting plasma-associated species to P-glycoprotein regulation remain unclear. Here, we used a two-stage reduced-model strategy to test whether selected plasma-associated molecular species can noncovalently remodel the intrinsically disordered NBD1-TMD2 linker of human ABCB1 and whether phenotypes detected in an unconstrained screening model persist when linker terminal geometry is restricted to a structure-derived range. We first screened the free linker against H2O2, NO, or O2 at three molecular loadings and then repeated the same perturbations under terminal tethering, yielding sixty 100-ns all-atom molecular-dynamics trajectories. The free linker showed species- and loading-dependent chemical susceptibility: high-loading H2O2 produced a coherent restriction-oriented phenotype, whereas low-loading O2 drove a pronounced compact, low-exchange redistribution. Chemical responsiveness was not eliminated by tethering. High-loading H2O2 retained a compact, low-exchange phenotype, and high-loading O2 narrowed the projected conformational ensemble and reduced selected exchange modes. In contrast, the strong low-loading O2 response was largely suppressed, indicating dependence on conformational routes enabled by unconstrained terminal motion. Across conditions, responses were spatially heterogeneous; total species-linker attraction did not predict remodeling magnitude, whereas intramolecular H-bond-network reorganization tracked conformational restriction more closely. Together, these simulations establish chemical susceptibility of the ABCB1 linker while distinguishing mechanically persistent from free-motion-dependent responses. The persistent phenotypes provide candidates for testing in full-length transporter simulations and functional assays of ATPase-transport coupling and drug efflux.
affiliations: Amirkabir University of Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: Promoter-targeted duplex RNAs activate TCF4 expression
papers.abstract: Pitt-Hopkins syndrome (PTHS) is a severe neurodevelopmental disorder caused by haploinsufficient expression of transcription factor 4 (TCF4). Increasing expression from the remaining functional TCF4 allele could provide a mutation-independent strategy for patients with diverse pathogenic variants. We integrated genomic datasets with strand-specific RNA analysis to identify transcribed regions of the TCF4 promoter suitable for targeting by activating double-stranded RNAs (dsRNAs). Screening of overlapping promoter-targeted dsRNAs identified a hotspot for increased TCF4 expression. Activation was retained by a lead dsRNA containing extensive 2'-fluoro, 2'-O-methyl, and phosphorothioate modifications used in therapeutic oligonucleotides. Anti-AGO2 immunoprecipitation showed association with RNA transcribed from the targeted promoter region. dsRNA-mediated activation was associated with increased RNA polymerase II occupancy. These findings establish promoter-targeted dsRNAs as chemically tractable starting points for increasing TCF4 expression and support their investigation as a mutation-independent strategy for haploinsufficient disease.
affiliations: The University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: BRN2 suppresses stress-induced hair greying
papers.abstract: Adult stem cells maintain tissue homeostasis and regenerative capacity, but mechanisms preserving their integrity under stress remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify BRN2 (POU3F2), a POU-domain transcription factor, as a regulator of melanocyte lineage homeostasis and response to genotoxic stress. Single-cell transcriptomic analyses identified Brn2 among transcription factors preferentially active in melanocyte stem cells (McSCs), with BRN2 activity declining with age in human hair follicle melanocytic cells. Melanocyte-specific Brn2 deletion increased melanocyte differentiation and accumulation in the hair bulb, while downregulating DNA-repair and chromosome-maintenance programs. Despite these changes, Brn2 loss caused neither spontaneous hair greying nor detectable McSC depletion under steady-state conditions. Following ionizing radiation, however, Brn2-deficient cells showed altered DNA-damage responses, reduced mitotic signatures, increased p53 and p21, and enhanced melanocytic differentiation. Irradiated Brn2-deficient mice developed rapid, dose-dependent, permanent hair depigmentation associated with McSC and melanocyte depletion. Thus, BRN2 links POU-dependent transcriptional control to stem-cell resilience under genotoxic stress, preserving melanocyte regenerative capacity and protecting against irradiation-induced hair greying.
affiliations: Institut Curie (corresponding author)

papers.title: A stress-responsive morphogenetic program coordinates uterine luminal remodeling during early pregnancy
papers.abstract: Successful embryo implantation requires coordinated interactions among the endometrial epithelium, stroma, and the embryo, yet the underlying mechanisms have not been fully understood. Using three-dimensional histological reconstruction combined with single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, we identify a previously unrecognized phase of luminal architectural reorganization preceding embryo attachment. Within a narrow peri-implantation window, the luminal epithelium rapidly remodels from a highly folded structure into a flattened, organized architecture that is spatially associated with embryo positioning. This morphogenetic transition is accompanied by activation of stress-responsive signaling across the epithelial and stromal compartments. Functional analyses show that uterine-specific deletion of the stress-responsive MAP kinase p38 disrupts luminal remodeling, leading to persistent epithelial folding, failed embryo attachment, and infertility despite normal hormone levels and embryo development. In contrast, epithelial-specific deletion of p38 causes only mild uterine abnormalities, indicating that epithelial p38 loss alone is insufficient to account for the severe implantation phenotype. Although combined progesterone and leukemia inhibitory factor supplementation rescues embryo attachment in p38-deficient uteri, luminal disorganization, abnormal stromal responses, and impaired pregnancy progression persist. These findings identify a uterine p38-dependent, stress-responsive program that supports luminal remodeling and epithelial-stromal communication required for implantation competence.
affiliations: The University of Tokyo (corresponding author)

papers.title: Developmental Convergence Across Diverse Genetic Architectures in Childhood Apraxia of Speech
papers.abstract: Childhood apraxia of speech (CAS) is a neurodevelopmental disorder of speech-motor planning and programming, associated with literacy, academic, and psychosocial difficulties. We performed whole-exome sequencing in 11 families comprising 21 affected and 15 unaffected individuals with phenotyping spanning speech, language, cognition, literacy, and motor function. We identified 60 prioritized variant observations representing 22 unique variants across 20 genes with family-based segregation analysis assessed in informative relatives; 5 arose de novo. Our cohort included multiple affected siblings and extended relatives, with several families carrying multiple prioritized variants, suggesting cumulative or oligogenic susceptibility. Speech and literacy impairment co-occurred with oral-motor, feeding, and fine-motor difficulties. BrainSpan co-expression analysis identified MECP2 and ANK2 as the genes with the highest observed connectivity in the sampled postnatal network. Exploratory analysis of the KOLF2.1J perturbation atlas in undifferentiated human induced pluripotent stem cells identified a positive LMO3 expression-response score following NIPBL repression and opposing LMO3 and ANK2 response directions within a cohesin-associated perturbation cluster. These observations motivate testing in human neural cells. Functional enrichment, protein-association, and developmental-expression analyses supported shared biological themes involving chromatin regulation, neuronal signaling, and extracellular-matrix organization. Among six families, multiple affected relatives shared prioritized variants across a unique set of several genes, demonstrating multilocus candidate profiles whose individual and combined effects may contribute to CAS susceptibility. We propose four novel CAS candidate genes: LMO3 and PCDH10, previously linked to human accelerated regions, as well as MYCBP2 and PTPRS. Our work provides multiple testable hypotheses for future variant-specific functional validation in speech-motor development.
affiliations: The Johns Hopkins University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Adaptive introgression in subdivided populations leaves distinct genomic footprints under global and local selection: a case study in Ciona intestinalis
papers.abstract: Adaptive introgression, the transfer of beneficial alleles between species through hybridization, is increasingly recognized as an important source of adaptation to novel environments. However, the theory of adaptive introgression has primarily been developed for a single panmictic population, whereas many empirical examples involve spatially subdivided populations. In such systems, a low-frequency adaptive allele may either represent the leading edge of an adaptive travelling wave or occur in a subpopulation where the introgressed allele is locally selected against. We developed a simple prediction based on the relationship between adaptive allele frequency and introgressed tract length. Simulations predict a positive correlation during an ongoing sweep of an unconditionally beneficial allele, but no correlation under local adaptation. Tract erosion provides a recombination clock for time since introgression, which also determines the distance travelled by the adaptive wave and hence allele frequency in the former, whereas allele frequency is determined by local selection in the latter. We tested this prediction in a well-characterized case of adaptive introgression, in the sea squirt Ciona intestinalis, using haplotagging to reconstruct phased genomes and local ancestry. We found no relationship between adaptive allele frequency and introgressed tract length, providing additional support for a model of local adaptation rather than ongoing global selective sweep.
affiliations: Institute of Evolutionary Sciences of Montpellier (ISEM), CNRS (corresponding author)

papers.title: Disease-associated mutations directionally modulate epigenetic age in iPSC-derived tissues
papers.abstract: Reprogramming somatic cells into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) resets epigenetic age, creating a major challenge for modeling age-associated cellular states and limiting the use of iPSCs in aging research beyond the genetic component. Recent work has shown that healthy organoids can re-accumulate age-associated epigenetic states over extended culture; whether disease-associated genetic states can directionally reshape these trajectories after reprogramming remains unknown. Here, we present a reproducible, in-vitro approach to re-establish epigenetic aging trajectories using iPSC-derived organoid systems, as quantified by multiple epigenetic clock models. We first demonstrate that epigenetic age progressively increases with serial passaging in a lung organoid model (alveolospheres). We then show that disease-associated mutations in multiple models drive additional, cell-intrinsic shifts in epigenetic age, implicating disease state as an independent modulator of epigenetic clocks. Together, these findings reinforce that iPSC-derived organoids recapitulate epigenetic aging trajectories over time, while highlighting disease state as a potent and potentially tractable modulator of epigenetic age in vitro. By enabling more faithful modeling of age-associated cellular states, this approach expands the utility of iPSC-based systems for dissecting the molecular mechanisms that regulate human aging.
affiliations: Center for Regenerative Medicine (CReM) of Boston University, and Boston Medical Center (corresponding author)

papers.title: Germline hypomethylation shapes dynamic CpG reservoirs in ape genomes
papers.abstract: CpG dinucleotides are essential substrates for DNA methylation and genome regulation, yet paradoxically, methylated CpGs are lost through deamination-associated mutations. How CpG-rich sequences persist and are replenished during evolution remains unresolved, as previous sequencing technologies left structurally complex regions inaccessible. Here, leveraging complete telomere-to-telomere ape genomes, we show that peri/centromeric satellites are reservoirs of hypomethylated CpGs in sperm, and likely oocytes. This peri/centromeric hypomethylation extends into adjacent euchromatin, revealing novel centromeric hypomethylation extension domains enriched for segmental duplications, recently duplicated genes, and testis- and brain-biased expression. More broadly, young structural variants are CpG-rich and germline-hypomethylated, whereas older sequences are methylated and CpG-depleted. These findings link rapidly evolving centromeric regions to distinctive germline epigenetic state, CpG evolution, and structural and transcriptomic evolutionary innovation.
affiliations: University of California, Santa Barbara (corresponding author)

papers.title: Distinct sequence grammars of nucleosomal and linker DNA shape mutational and methylation landscapes in cancer
papers.abstract: Nucleosomes regulate DNA accessibility and thereby influence gene expression, DNA repair, and mutagenesis. Although DNA sequence strongly determines nucleosome positioning, the higher-order sequence grammar underlying nucleosome organization and its relationship to cancer-associated mutational and epigenetic processes remain poorly understood. We developed DeepND, an interpretable deep learning framework that distinguishes nucleosomal from inter-nucleosomal DNA and identifies sequence features associated with nucleosome architecture. Our interpretable framework enabled analysis of sequence patterns and identified 210 sequence motifs of 2-16 bp length that were significantly enriched or depleted in nucleosomal DNA, substantially extending the previously characterized nucleosomal motifs. These motifs revealed distinct sequence grammars within nucleosomal footprints and linker regions, including patterns associated with inward- and outward-facing minor grooves. Forty-four of these motifs showed cancer-type-specific enrichment or depletion of somatic mutations, and six motifs were associated with differential DNA methylation levels. In lung and endometrial cancers, mutations exhibited a significant ~10-bp periodic enrichment pattern across distinct minor-groove orientations, consistent with differential sensitivity of mutational and DNA repair processes to nucleosomal rotational positioning.
