We further identified sequence-specific methylation patterns consistent with reduced accessibility of nucleosomal DNA to DNA methyltransferases, including differential methylation at inward- and outward-facing CpG motifs. Together, these findings provide a sequence-resolved characterization of nucleosome-level organization and its link to cancer-specific mutational processes and epigenetic landscapes.
affiliations: University of Toronto (corresponding author)

papers.title: Genetic exchange drives relatedness of large linear and circular extrachromosomal elements of archaea
papers.abstract: Archaeal extra-chromosomal elements (ECEs) play key roles in archaeal host biology and evolution, yet little is known about their diversity and interactions with each other. Here, we report 42 complete 66 - 165 kbp genomes: 23 "Klingons", 8 "Romulans" and "Romulan-like elements", and 11 "Ferengi", three new families of archaeal ECEs from diverse terrestrial environments. Methylation patterns, phylogenetics and gene sharing analyses suggest that Klingons and Romulans associate with Candidatus Methanoperedens and Ferengi are likely hosted by Candidatus Bathyarchaeaota. Like known archaeal viruses and plasmids, these ECEs both have circular genomes and replicate bi-directionally, unlike the linear Borg and mini-Borg ECEs that also replicate in Methanoperedens. The new ECE genomes all encode genes for methylation, glycosylation, protein degradation, and novel TnpB-like enzymes, which may interact with novel CRISPR-like arrays. All genomes also encode proteins with strong structural similarity to archaeal viral capsid proteins, and some are predicted to multimerize into pentameric or hexameric subunit capsid-like arrays and thus may encapsulate themselves. The three new ECE families share gene content with each other and with Borgs and mini-Borgs, often concentrated in specific genomic regions. Discordance among single gene and genomic phylogenies suggests that apparent relatedness of the five distinct ECE types stems from extensive horizontal gene transfer, rather than evolution from a common ancestor. The three new families of ECEs broaden our understanding of the diversity of archaeal ECEs and highlight the role of horizontal gene transfer in modulating the archaeal and archaeal ECE gene pools.
affiliations: Innovative Genomics Institute, University of California, Berkeley 94720, CA, USA (corresponding author)

papers.title: The mammalian genome is punctuated by regularly spaced nucleosome islands
papers.abstract: Nucleosome positioning plays a fundamental role in regulating DNA accessibility and cellular activity, yet the precise rules by which mammalian sequences instruct this organization have remained incomplete. Prior work has established that intrinsic sequence preferences dictate nucleosome architecture in yeast, but in mammals, this sequence code is modulated by chromatin state and cell-type-specific factors. Here, we train a deep-learning model on genome-wide maps from mouse embryonic stem cells to predict nucleosome occupancy directly from the primary DNA sequence. Our model accurately predicts in vivo occupancy and captures shared biological signals while effectively denoising assay-specific technical biases. Through in silico mutagenesis, we identify specific nucleosome positioning regions comprised of short 5-to-20-base-pair motifs concentrated within dense regulatory windows. Furthermore, we demonstrate that repetitive DNA elements play a major role in establishing these highly organized nucleosome arrays on a genomic scale. Specifically, CCCTC-binding factor motifs embedded within short interspersed nuclear elements, zinc-finger-bound motifs within long interspersed nuclear elements, and microsatellite repeats act as potent organizers of nucleosome phasing. Together, our findings extend the concept of sequence-encoded nucleosome architecture to mammalian genomes and reveal that regularly spaced nucleosome islands are shaped by short, recurrent sets of DNA motifs that couple local sequence to chromatin structure.
affiliations: MNHN (corresponding author)

papers.title: Pangenome and transcriptome analyses reveal extensive diversity and breeding signatures in the oat GDSL-esterase/lipase gene family
papers.abstract: Lipolytic enzymes play critical roles in plant development, growth, and stress responses. In oat (Avena sativa), they are of particular interest because lipid hydrolysis contributes to rancidity and reduced grain quality, yet little is known about genomic variation in oat lipolytic enzymes. Here, we investigated genomic and expression diversity of the GDSL-esterase/lipase gene family using pangenome, transcriptome, and genome-wide association analyses. Across 22 A. sativa and two A. sterilis genome assemblies, we identified 7,775 GDSL genes (~324 per assembly), revealing wide conservation of ancestral orthologs alongside extensive copy-number variation among homoeologs and paralogs. Transcriptome profiling across 20 genotypes and six tissues demonstrated preferential expression in embryo and root, with tissue-specific patterns highlighting candidates for specific functions, such as seed lipid metabolism. Associations with structural variants further uncovered candidate mutations underlying expression variation among accessions. Comparisons of cultivated and wild oat detected loci with signatures of breeding-based selection, suggesting that GDSL genes have contributed to diversification of the cultivated gene pool. Using 629 whole-genome sequenced accessions, we also identified associations between GDSL regions and agronomic traits, particularly plant height and effective tiller number. Several regions showed patterns consistent with selection, highlighting candidate loci for further investigation of agronomic variation. Together, our results reveal substantial genomic and transcriptional diversity within the oat GDSL gene family and identify candidate genes and genomic regions for improving seed quality and agronomic performance. More broadly, our study demonstrates how pangenomic resources can be used to investigate gene-family diversity and function in complex polyploid crops.
affiliations: Natural Resources Institute Finland (Luke) (corresponding author)

papers.title: The limits of Bayesian estimates of divergence times in measurably evolving populations
papers.abstract: Bayesian inference of divergence times for extant species using molecular data is an unconventional statistical problem: Divergence times and molecular rates are confounded, and only their product, the molecular branch length, is statistically identifiable. This means we must use priors on times and rates to break the identifiability problem. As a consequence, there is a lower bound in the uncertainty that can be attained under infinite data for estimates of evolutionary timescales using the molecular clock. With infinite data (i.e., an infinite number of sites and loci in the alignment) uncertainty in ages of nodes in phylogenies increases proportionally with their mean age, such that older nodes have higher uncertainty than younger nodes. On the other hand, if extinct taxa are present in the phylogeny, and if their sampling times are known (i.e., `heterochronous' data), then times and rates are identifiable and uncertainties of inferred times and rates go to zero with infinite data. However, in real heterochronous datasets (such as viruses and bacteria), alignments tend to be small and how much uncertainty is present and how it can be reduced as a function of data size are questions that have not been explored. This is clearly important for our understanding of the tempo and mode of microbial evolution using the molecular clock. Here we conducted extensive simulation experiments and analyses of empirical data to develop the infinite-sites theory for heterochronous data. Contrary to expectations, we find that uncertainty in ages of internal nodes scales positively with the distance to their closest tip with known age (i.e., calibration age), not their absolute age. Our results also demonstrate that estimation uncertainty decreases with calibration age more slowly in datasets with more, rather than fewer site patterns, although overall uncertainty is lower in the former. Our statistical framework establishes the minimum uncertainty that can be attained with perfect calibrations and sequence data that are effectively infinitely informative. Finally, we discuss the implications for viral sequence datasets. In a vast majority of cases viral data from outbreaks is not sufficiently informative to display infinite-sites behaviour and thus all estimates of evolutionary timescales will be associated with a degree of uncertainty that will depend on the size of the dataset, its information content, and the complexity of the model. We anticipate that our framework is useful to determine such theoretical limits in empirical analyses of microbial outbreaks.
affiliations: Institut Pasteur (corresponding author)

papers.title: π-MSNet: A large-scale, AI-ready and continuously reprocessed proteomics data resource
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping proteomics workflows, delivering remarkable gains in both peptide identification sensitivity and quantitative performance. However, the potential of deep learning models in proteomics has not been fully exploited due to the scarcity of large-scale, high-quality and consistently labeled datasets. Here, we present {pi}-MSNet, a large-scale, AI-ready and continuously reprocessed mass spectrometry (MS) data resource. Using a uniform identification and quality control workflow, it comprises over 737 million peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs) obtained from 2.16 billion MS2 spectra, and 11 million precursors from 45,583 LC-MS/MS runs across 12 instrument types and 55 diverse species. Through community collaboration, the data are shared via international, interactive, and continuously reprocessed web resources. {pi}-MSNet provides an AI-ready data framework for efficient training and systematic benchmarking of multiple models across four representative tasks (e.g., MS2 prediction, retention time prediction, collisional cross sections prediction, and de novo peptide sequencing). In particular, by retraining multiple models on {pi}-MSNet, we achieved consistent performance improvements over their original versions. These improved models were subsequently integrated into the {pi}-MSNet agent to enable interactive, deployment-free use. Through SDRF (Sample and Data Relationship Format) metadata, open-source cloud analysis workflow, and a community-driven interactive data portal that supports continuous data submission, {pi}-MSNet serves as a continuously updating, AI-ready resource for reproducible benchmarking, robust model training, and accelerated AI innovation in proteomics.

papers.title: Kidzoi Enables Cell-Type-Specific Regulatory Activity and Variant Effect Prediction in Kidney
papers.abstract: Sequence-to-function (S2F) deep learning models predict genome-wide functional profiles directly from DNA sequences and have significantly advanced our understanding of gene regulation. However, existing S2F models are fundamentally constrained by their initial training datasets, and no single model encompasses the full spectrum of cell types, clinical conditions, and cellular states, while training new models de novo is nontrivial. Here, we develop Kidzoi, a kidney cell-type-specific S2F model obtained by transfer learning from the pretrained model Borzoi using single-nucleus chromatin accessibility data from human kidney tissue. Kidzoi accurately predicts cell-type-specific chromatin accessibility and improves regulatory variant effect prediction by 10-23% over existing models. Furthermore, Kidzoi effectively prioritizes genome-wide association study (GWAS) fine-mapped causal variants associated with kidney function (estimated glomerular filtration rate based on both creatinine and cystatin C; eGFRcr-cys) while resolving their cell-type specificity. Systematic ablation of flanking sequence indicates that a local context of 32-64kbp, representing only 6-12% of the full model input, is sufficient for accurate variant effect prediction. Finally, we show that a multi-task model achieves comparable performance to single-task models at a substantially reduced computational cost.
affiliations: Boston Children's Hospital & Harvard Medical School (corresponding author)

papers.title: Mitigating Class Imbalance in Graph-Structured Data via Hierarchical Learning: Insights from Protein Binding Site Prediction
papers.abstract: Learning from imbalanced data remains a major challenge for graph neural networks (GNNs), as minority nodes are not only rare but also structurally marginalized within the graph. We address this issue with CLARA, a hierarchical learning framework that decomposes node classification into two stages: a coarse subgraph-level classifier that selects regions likely to contain minority instances, followed by a fine-grained node-level predictor within these regions. This design improves sensitivity while maintaining scalability, filtering out irrelevant areas and focusing learning on topologically meaningful neighborhoods. Experiments on benchmark graph datasets demonstrate substantial gains over established imbalance-handling methods, with CLARA reaching an F1-score of 88.3\%. The same strategy achieves significant improvements in protein-ligand binding site prediction, underscoring its broad and consistent effectiveness across both biological and general graph learning tasks.
affiliations: Universidade Federal de Vicosa (corresponding author)

papers.title: WrapEvoFS enables auditable feature compression with regret-constrained representative locking
papers.abstract: WrapEvoFS provides a deterministic, auditable rule for choosing one feature set from repeated stochastic searches. It retains candidates within a prespecified development-score gap, selects the most representative set by feature overlap, and records the decision before held-out evaluation. A corrected genetic objective preserves score ordering lost through zero truncation. In a fully nested four-class cancer analysis, all 30 locked signatures met the 0.01 tolerance, and 11 differed from the highest-scoring candidate; every changed selection increased mean feature overlap within the eligible pool. Paired differences in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve against recursive feature elimination with cross-validation all had 95% intervals crossing zero. No selector dominated matched comparisons on feature count and predictive performance, and one-time evaluation of frozen signatures at held-out centers yielded heterogeneous effects. WrapEvoFS standardizes selection within a fixed candidate bank under an empirical score-gap constraint, enabling reproducible reporting of performance, compression, and feature-agreement trade-offs without implying predictive superiority or stability under changes in participant composition.
affiliations: The University of British Columbia (corresponding author)

papers.title: Tracking two decades of global dengue virus lineage dynamics
papers.abstract: Dengue virus (DENV) is genetically diverse, consisting of four antigenically distinct serotypes and extensive sub-serotype variation that can influence epidemiology and control. As DENV continues to expand globally, there is an urgent need to characterize the dynamics of distinct DENV genetic lineages, including their persistence, establishment, and spread. Using a standardized DENV lineage nomenclature system and 37,828 publicly available DENV genomes sampled from 2000-2024, we classified sequences across nine global regions to construct a comprehensive resource of regional lineage distributions over time. We found marked regional differences in lineage diversity, with higher lineage richness in Southeast and East Asia than in the Americas. We further showed that COVID-19-related disruptions were associated with decreased regional lineage persistence and detection of new lineages during 2020-2021, followed by rebounds after 2022 and, in some regions, substantial lineage turnover. Finally, we identified a small set of globally expansive (cosmopolitan) lineages that are over-represented in available sequences, including five first-order minor lineages detected in at least seven of nine regions: 3III_B.3, 2II_F.1, 2II_A.1, 1III_A.3, and 1I_K.3. Together, these results demonstrate how standardized lineage classification enables global tracking of emerging DENV diversity and supports targeted genomic surveillance.
affiliations: Department of Epidemiology of Microbial Diseases, Yale School of Public Health, New Haven, Connecticut, United States of America (corresponding author)

papers.title: Biology-guided machine learning for robust anatomical correspondence across biodiversity datasets
papers.abstract: Three-dimensional imaging is rapidly increasing the scale of biological morphometric datasets, but establishing automated anatomical correspondence remains a major bottleneck. Conventional point-cloud registration methods transfer landmarks efficiently, yet poor initialization or high morphological variation can produce geometrically plausible but biologically implausible deformations. Here, we developed a statistical-shape-model (SSM)-regularized coherent point drift (CPD) estimator for automated morphometric landmark transfer. It replaces the unconstrained non-rigid CPD update with optimization in SSM coefficient space and regularizes coefficients by inverse population covariance, so deformations along low-variance biological modes are penalized more strongly. We compared pose-matched conventional CPD, SSM-CPD, and SSM-CPD with refinement in leave-one-out atlas experiments on laboratory mouse skulls (N=249), primate molars (N=115), and squamate vertebrae (N=254) under aligned, mildly perturbed, and severely perturbed initialization. We evaluated these formulations in terms of landmark accuracy, failure-tail behavior, runtime, and preservation of morphometric structure. Under severe perturbation, we also evaluated an integrated recovery procedure that optimizes the starting template, recovers global pose, and then applies SSM-CPD with refinement. Severe misalignment produced widespread failures in pose-matched conventional CPD, whereas SSM regularization reduced median error from 13 - 21% to approximately 1 - 3% of the target bounding-box diagonal. This improvement was highly consistent for skulls and molars. In the morphologically complex vertebral dataset, however, low median error concealed a substantial minority of catastrophic failures (28% of vertebrae above a 6% error threshold), which integrated recovery reduced to 4%. Across datasets, automated landmarks preserved the major axes and pairwise relationships of morphometric shape space, and local CPD refinement improved covariance preservation. Embedding learned biological variation directly into registration broadens the range of starting conditions and anatomies for which automated landmark transfer remains reliable. Our results also show that failure tails and downstream morphometric fidelity must be assessed alongside median accuracy when automated landmarking methods are evaluated.
affiliations: Florida Museum of Natural History (corresponding author)

papers.title: Lorentz Tangent Diffusion Adapter for Multi-label Prediction of Protein-Protein Interaction Types
papers.abstract: Protein-protein interactions shape cellular organization and disease processes, but their prediction remains difficult because known interaction networks are incomplete, noisy and highly uneven across proteins. Hyperbolic graph learning is well suited to the hierarchical structure of such networks, yet most methods emphasize learning hyperbolic embeddings and pay less attention to how these embeddings are propagated and decoded for type prediction. Here we introduce the Lorentz Tangent Diffusion Adapter (LTDA), a post-embedding module for PPI type prediction, that is, for predicting which of several interaction types a candidate protein pair undergoes. LTDA learns relation-specific protein representations on the Lorentz manifold, projects them to tangent space, applies lightweight graph diffusion, and decodes the diffused representations directly in tangent space. This design uses the tangent space as a prediction-oriented interface between hierarchical representation learning and interaction classification. On SHS27K and SHS148K under BFS and DFS splits, LTDA consistently improves over representative PPI methods and a reproduced HI-PPI baseline, with average gains of 1.41 percentage points in Micro-F1, 3.21 in AUPR, 1.31 in AUC and 1.25 in accuracy. Ablation, degree-bin and biological-evidence analyses indicate that the gains are not explained by simple smoothing or hub correction. LTDA therefore shows that post-embedding adaptation can make Lorentz representations more effective for PPI type prediction.
affiliations: Jingdezhen Ceramic University (corresponding author)

papers.title: GalaxyMemMD: an end-to-end Galaxy toolset for reproducible membrane embedding, molecular dynamics simulation, and analysis of membrane proteins
papers.abstract: Membrane proteins play crucial roles in cellular signaling, transport, and pharmacological regulation, yet their structural and functional characterization remains challenging due to experimental limitations. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations have become indispensable for probing membrane protein behavior at atomic resolution; however, executing these simulations at scale remains a significant bottleneck. Existing tools excel at system preparation for individual cases, but none offer a complete, high-throughput pipeline spanning embedding, simulation, and analysis across multiple membrane compositions, and rarely integrate modern structure prediction and molecular docking frameworks. Here, we present GalaxyMemMD, a fully automated, open-source Galaxy framework that provides a direct, scalable alternative to existing preparation-only tools. GalaxyMemMD integrates every stage membrane embedding, system preparation, MD execution, and downstream analysis into a single reproducible pipeline. Leveraging Galaxy's HPC-ready job scheduling, GalaxyMemMD natively supports high-throughput parallel simulations across multiple membrane compositions and protein variants, including AlphaFold-derived structural inputs and downstream molecular docking workflows, without repeated manual setup. We validate GalaxyMemMD across six structurally diverse membrane proteins four GPCRs, one ion channel, and one beta-barrel demonstrating consistent system preparation, while the benchmark analysis shows stable embeddings, and reproducible trajectory-level production workflow. Across these benchmarks, GalaxyMemMD matches the setup quality of established tools, therefore serves as both a practical alternative and a capability extension for the membrane protein simulation community.
affiliations: Cleveland Clinic Research, Cleveland Clinic (corresponding author)

papers.title: Disease-associated protein states accessible to 8-oxoguanine transcriptional miscoding without genomic mutation
papers.abstract: 8-Oxoguanine (8-oxoG) is a common oxidative DNA lesion that can alter coding output during transcription without changing the underlying DNA sequence. When present on the template strand, 8-oxoG can direct RNA polymerase II to insert adenine, generating a transient coding-sense C>A error restricted by the genetic code to 18 directional amino-acid substitutions. Mapping these substitutions onto ClinVar identified 3,910 disease-associated protein states across 1,333 genes, representing 5.7% of evaluable pathogenic or likely pathogenic missense states. In 211 cases, transcriptional miscoding and the corresponding genomic disease variant affect different nucleotides within the same codon yet converge on the same amino acid substitution, allowing the disease-associated protein state to arise while the implicated genomic nucleotide remains wild type. Accessible states were enriched among genes with post-mitotic expression and neurological disease annotation, particularly in neuronal signaling pathways. Published oxidized-guanine maps supported 2,146 accessible genomic coordinates, while human proteogenomic data contained 78 exact codon-compatible protein states not explained by sample-specific transcript sequence. Together, these analyses define a chemically constrained set of disease-associated protein states accessible through 8-oxoG transcriptional miscoding without permanent genomic mutation.
affiliations: Florida International University (corresponding author)

papers.title: G4SCOPE identifies sequence features and epigenetic contexts of chromatin G-quadruplexes
papers.abstract: Cancer-associated epigenetic remodeling involves a complex interplay between DNA secondary structures and covalent cytosine modifications, yet predicting endogenously folded, chromatin-constrained G-quadruplex (G4) dynamics remains challenging. Here, we develop G4SCOPE, a multi-task deep learning framework that models chromatin-associated G4 occupancy and reconstructs quantitative high-resolution CUT&Tag profiles directly from primary DNA sequence alone. We initially trained G4SCOPE on genotype-stratified G4 enriched cut&tag landscapes generated across an isogenic series of human breast epithelial cells (WT, TP53-/-, TP53-/-;BRCA1-/-, and TP53-/-;BRCA2-/-). G4SCOPE integrates convolutional motif learning with transformer self-attention to decode long-range sequence contexts. The model robustly distinguishes chromatin-associated G4s from GC-matched loci with intrinsic in vitro folding potential, generalizes across distinct breast lineages, and transfers accurately to an independent K562 cellular context. Strikingly, genotype-resolved mapping reveals a profound divergence in genome maintenance states: BRCA1 deficiency indicated a global inflation of chromatin-embedded G4 density, whereas BRCA2 loss was associated with systemic, chromosome-wide structural depletion. Furthermore, unsupervised clustering of model-derived latent sequence representations identified distinct biological G4 subclasses that occupy unique regulatory class genomic environments associated with distinct local 5-methylcytosine and 5-hydroxymethylcytosine landscapes. Together, our framework decodes the primary sequence grammar governing cell-based G4 occupancy and demonstrates that sequence-defined G4 topologies harbor intrinsic and distinct local epigenetic features.
affiliations: BC Cancer Research Institute, 675 W10th Avenue, Vancouver, V5Z 1L3, Canada (corresponding author)

papers.title: AtaA as a Self-Immobilizing Scaffold for Enzymatically Active Surfaces through Oxidative Tyrosine Coupling
papers.abstract: Protein nanofibers are hold great promise as genetically programmable scaffolds for constructing functional material interfaces. AtaA, a giant trimeric autotransporter adhesin from Acinetobacter sp. Tol 5, forms an elongated architecture from the bacterial cell surface, enabling the cells to adhere directly to a wide variety of abiotic surfaces. However, the potential use of AtaA as a scaffold with additional biological functions remains largely unexplored. In this study, we investigated the use of AtaA as a self-immobilizing scaffold for constructing enzymatically active surfaces via horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-catalyzed tyrosine coupling. We prepared a recombinant AtaA nanofiber fragment (NhNs-AtaA) and its derivative containing two tyrosine-containing loop structures (YL-NhNs-AtaA). Both recombinant proteins retained their adhesive properties. Treatment with HRP and H2O2 generated high-molecular-weight products from both proteins, and dityrosine fluorescence emission indicated the formation of tyrosine-derived covalent cross-links. Y-Loop insertion further increased the consumption of monomeric AtaA and promoted the formation of high-molecular-weight products. The removal of arginine, which was included during purification, further increased the loss of monomeric AtaA in both constructs, indicating that intermolecular protein association influenced productive AtaA cross-linking. NhNs-AtaA and YL-NhNs-AtaA were combined with Y-tagged bacterial alkaline phosphatase (BAP-Y). HRP-mediated coupling generated high-molecular-weight products consistent with the cross-linked AtaA-BAP-Y conjugates and enabled the retention of BAP activity on AtaA-coated surfaces without prior chemical modification. Although Y-Loop insertion enhanced polymerization in solution, it reduced AtaA adhesion and consequently lowered surface-bound phosphatase activity, revealing a trade-off between cross-linking reactivity and native adhesive function. These findings establish AtaA as a self-immobilizing protein nanofiber scaffold for constructing enzymatically active surfaces, and suggest the potential extension of this strategy to other AtaA-based interfaces.
affiliations: Nagahama Institute of Bio-Science and Technology (corresponding author)

papers.title: The Alzheimer's Disease-associated gene CD2AP regulates permeability of endothelial cells and transendothelial migration of immune cells
papers.abstract: Variants at the CD2AP locus, which encodes a branched-actin regulator, are associated with late-onset Alzheimer's disease (AD), and CD2AP-deficient mice show increased blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability. CD2AP is enriched in endothelial cells, but its function there is poorly understood. In endothelium, branched actin networks maintain cell-cell junctions and are also required for immune cells to cross through individual endothelial cells (transcellular transendothelial migration, TEM). We previously showed that the Arp2/3 activators N-WASP and WAVE2 contribute to these processes, but the capping protein (CP)-interacting proteins involved are unknown. Here we tested whether CD2AP, a CP-interacting protein recruited to cell-cell contacts, regulates both junction integrity and TEM. In primary human microvascular endothelial cells, shRNA knockdown of CD2AP increased TNF-induced monolayer permeability, measured by transendothelial electrical resistance, and altered VE-cadherin junction morphology. Unexpectedly, on soft hydrogels the same knockdown reduced TEM of NK-92 MI cells, lowering the proportion of transcellular events. Thus, loss of CD2AP weakens the endothelial barrier yet impairs a distinct, actin-dependent route of immune-cell passage. These findings suggest that CD2AP risk variants may affect the BBB through more than permeability, and they identify endothelial immune-cell trafficking as a testable link between CD2AP and AD.
affiliations: Washington University (corresponding author)

papers.title: Coiled-coil homo-oligomerization and disaggregase Hsp104 act in parallel to stabilize orphan septins
papers.abstract: Multiple septin family proteins co-assemble with strict subunit stoichiometry into hetero-oligomers. In the absence of native septin partners, purified septins aggregate in vitro, and "orphan" septins are found in pathological aggregates associated with neurodegenerative diseases. Cytosolic chaperones bind the septin GTPase domain to promote on-pathway septin folding but it was unclear how cells manage orphan septins to maintain subunit stoichiometry. Most septins have C-terminal domains (CTDs) that form heteromeric coiled coils within or between septin complexes. Here we present evidence that orphan yeast septins are protected from proteasomal degradation by forming transient coiled-coil homodimers and trimers and, in parallel, by the disaggregase chaperone Hsp104. Septins unable to undergo CTD-mediated homo-oligomerization require Hsp104 to accumulate to super-stoichiometric levels. We show that septin-encoding mRNAs differ in copy number per cell and subcellular localization, creating opportunities for transient subunit imbalances. These findings reveal a novel role for coiled coils and the proteostasis machinery in the fidelity of higher-order septin assembly.

papers.title: SEEKER: A genome-scale library-on-library screening platform for deciphering T cell recognition of antigen
papers.abstract: Decoding which antigens activate a given T cell receptor (TCR) is a central challenge in immunology. We present SEEKER, a functional genome-scale library-on-library screening platform built on three elements: a Jurkat-derived T-APC cell (TAPCell) that combinatorially expresses one TCR and one peptide-MHC drawn from separate libraries together with an NFAT activation reporter; encapsulation of single TAPCells in a thermos-reversible hydrogel for isolated clonal expansion, so recognition is read out as intraclonal activation; and dual-asymmetric PCR that links TCR- and pMHC-encoding sequences into a heritable unit, enabling progressive hit enrichment over screening rounds. SEEKER interrogates ~10^8 TCR-pMHC combinations per run without prior knowledge. Screening joint-infiltrating CD8+ T cells from HLA-B*27+ ankylosing spondylitis patients against proteome-wide libraries validated 53 TCR-peptide pairs, uncovered extensive cross-recognition of self and common viral epitopes, and revealed highly polyreactive T cells recognizing up to 80 autoantigens, implicating virus-triggered poly-autoreactivity in multi-organ autoimmune diseases.

papers.title: Validation of a high throughput fluorescent Capillary Electrophoresis Sodium Dodecyl Sulfate method for monoclonal antibody size heterogeneity assessment
papers.abstract: Fluorescent capillary gel electrophoresis (CGE) with sodium dodecyl sulfate (CE SDS) provides a powerful, high sensitivity alternative to ultraviolet (UV) based detection for characterizing therapeutic monoclonal antibodies (mAb). Regulatory and standards organizations, such as the United States Pharmacopeia (USP), include only UV based CE-SDS methods, hindering adoption of alternative detection methods. There is growing opportunity to expand beyond exclusively UV based CE SDS methods. In this study, we present an analytical validation of a light-emitting diode (LED) fluorescence-based parallel CE SDS method for both non reduced and reduced analysis of therapeutic antibodies. Using the NISTmAb reference material as a model system, size heterogeneity critical quality attributes (CQAs) including monomeric purity (non-reduced conditions), percent glycosylation (reduced conditions), and percent thioether (reduced conditions) were assessed. The fluorescence method demonstrated high specificity and precision with relative standard deviation (RSD) values 0.99 for both non reduced and reduced analyses. These results highlight the high sensitivity, stable baseline performance, and suitability of LED fluorescence-based parallel CE SDS as a validated, higher throughput alternative to traditional UV based methods for mAb quality control (QC).

papers.title: Antibodies targeting a conserved cryptic epitope at the influenza hemagglutinin head-stem interface via distinct binding modes
papers.abstract: Influenza A virus continues to pose pandemic threats, as demonstrated by the recent global spread of highly pathogenic H5N1 strains. Consequently, the development and characterization of vaccines targeting zoonotic influenza subtypes have become a major focus of the field. In this study, we characterize two broadly reactive antibodies previously isolated from H5N1 vaccinees. Although they have distinct immunoglobulin germline gene usage and binding modes, cryo-EM analysis shows that both antibodies share a highly conserved cryptic epitope at the interface of the hemagglutinin (HA) head and stem domains. The antigenicity of this epitope is influenced by natural amino acid variation at residue 293 of HA subunit 1, and its access is facilitated by acid-induced conformational change of HA. Nevertheless, both antibodies are non-neutralizing and possess only marginal protective efficacy against seasonal and H5N1 viruses in vivo, thus representing suboptimal vaccine responses. Overall, our findings expand the interactions of cross-reactive antibodies with an under-characterized HA epitope and provide insights for next-generation influenza vaccine design.

papers.title: Time-resolved functional rotation crystallography probes protein dynamics during enzymatic catalysis
papers.abstract: Kinetic crystallography (KX) encompasses methods designed to characterize structural changes associated with protein dynamics and function. Here, we present Time-Resolved Functional Rotation Crystallography (TR-FRX), an integrated KX workflow combining room-temperature rotation crystallography on single crystals, nanolitre ligand delivery, and optional in crystallo optical spectroscopy using conventional synchrotron instrumentation. In TR-FRX, biochemical function is initiated by dispensing a nanolitre volume of ligand onto a single crystal while X-ray diffraction data are collected continuously. The resulting dataset is divided into sequential subdatasets, yielding a series of structural ensembles each averaged over the duration of their data collection time window. Together, these structural ensembles provide an overview of protein dynamics during ligand or substrate binding. We first applied TR-FRX to hen egg-white lysozyme in order to monitor N-acetylglucosamine binding and visualise associated local solvent reorganization. We then applied it to crystals of Chloroflexus aurantiacus malate dehydrogenase, first demonstrating by in crystallo spectroscopy that they are catalytically active, then revealing by X-ray diffraction ligand-associated solvent reorganization and active-site conformational changes over time windows ranging from hundreds of ms to tens of seconds. TR-FRX provides an accessible single-crystal workflow for establishing conditions in which ligand associated structural changes can be followed at room temperature, thereby generating preliminary data to guide future time-resolved serial crystallography experiments aimed at determining the structure of reaction intermediates.

papers.title: Mechanochemically-reprogrammed stem cell exosomes reconcile the biogenesis internalization trade-off for pulmonary fibrosis therapy
papers.abstract: Matrix stiffness serves as a pivotal biophysical cue of extracellular vesicle (EV) function and cellular uptake, yet the mechanical cues that enhance EV function may not simultaneously favour cellular uptake. Through comparative analyses across pulmonary cell populations, we identified macrophages as the predominant EV recipients in our experimental system and as a functionally relevant effector population in pulmonary fibrosis. Herein, we developed a mechanochemical reprogramming strategy to coordinate the immunomodulatory function of mesenchymal stem cell (MSC)-derived EVs with their uptake by macrophages. We found that soft-matrix conditioning of MSC-derived EVs enhanced immunomodulatory activity and promoted an anti-inflammatory macrophage phenotype. By contrast, increasing matrix stiffness upregulated ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1), increased EV membrane cholesterol, and enhanced macrophage uptake. Guided by these complementary mechanical responses, we combined soft-matrix conditioning with ABCA1 modulation to generate mechanochemically programmed MSC-EVs. This strategy preserved the immunomodulatory advantages associated with the soft matrix while enhancing macrophage uptake and increasing EV production. In a murine model of pulmonary fibrosis, mechanochemically reprogrammed EVs produced higher and more persistent EV-associated signals in lung tissue and were preferentially associated with pulmonary macrophages. Treatment promoted anti-inflammatory and reparative macrophage responses and was accompanied by reduced pulmonary inflammation and fibrotic remodelling. Together, these findings establish a mechanochemically reprogrammed strategy that coordinates MSC-EV immunomodulatory function with macrophage uptake while increasing EV production, providing a framework for engineering EV-based therapies for pulmonary fibrosis.

papers.title: Interplay of mechanics, growth and viral infection dynamics in a spatially expanding bacterial colony
papers.abstract: We investigate the dynamics of the spread of the infection due to a phage- during the range expansion of an E coli colony. We find a rich panoply of spatio-temporal dynamics at large colony-level length scales, arising due to the interplay of mechanical forces, growth and viral infection dynamics at smaller cellular length scales. Strikingly, the phages "surf" the front of the growing bacterial colony by hitchhiking on E coli that are advected due to the growth of bacteria in the colony, resulting in an anisotropic spread of the phages. We identify microscopic processes - of the phage release during lysis (occurring on short millisecond timescales at length scales close to that of a single bacterium) and local nematic alignment of the rod-like E coli bacteria (occurring on timescales comparable to the bacterial growth rate and the length scales of a few bacterial cells) - that enhance the advective effects driving the hitchhiking behavior. Combining our experiments with a mathematical model, we explain the multiple spatio-temporal dynamical regimes - from the coexistence of uninfected bacteria, resistant (lysogenic) cells and phages, to fixed points where the entire population turns resistant or remains uninfected. Our work broaches a new frontier in the investigation of eco-evolutionary processes arising from the mechanical and ecological forces due to the interactions between viruses and their hosts.

papers.title: Cellular Density Homeostasis Is Governed by an Anisotropic Attractor and Predictive Feedback Control
papers.abstract: Cell density is a fundamental biophysical property of living cells, yet the dynamical architecture underlying density homeostasis remains unknown. Here, we reconstruct the geometry, dynamics, and control structure governing cellular density regulation from single-cell mass-volume measurements acquired during recovery from osmotic perturbation. We identify a persistent anisotropic attractor in mass-volume state space that permits coordinated density-preserving fluctuations while strongly suppressing density-changing deviations. Optimal transport analysis reveals directed recovery trajectories confined to this attractor, enabling inference of an effective density-restoring control law. Density deviations are associated with coordinated changes in biomass accumulation and volume expansion that together generate an effective density-restoring control law. Moreover, density error contains significant predictive information regarding future corrective behavior, revealing an information-rich component of cellular regulation. Together, these findings establish cellular density homeostasis as an emergent dynamical control process and demonstrate how attractor reconstruction, optimal transport, and information theory can be combined to uncover the organizing principles of biological homeostasis.

papers.title: Structural basis of selective phospholipid recognition and local membrane deformation by CTL1
papers.abstract: The physiological function of the human choline transporter-like protein CTL1 (SLC44A1) remains elusive despite its implication in key pathophysiological processes. Here we combine cryo-electron microscopy, native mass spectrometry, lipidomics, molecular dynamics simulations and functional assays to characterise the molecular basis of phospholipid recognition by CTL1 and explore its potential molecular role. High-resolution structures of CTL1 in both monomeric and dimeric states reveal a broad amphipathic cavity and an extracellular domain that accommodate multiple phospholipid species, identifying phosphatidylethanolamine, phosphatidylserine, phosphatidylinositol and phosphatidic acid as endogenous CTL1 ligands. Molecular dynamics simulations show spontaneous phospholipid recruitment into these conserved binding sites accompanied by membrane thinning, curvature and local phospholipid reorganisation, with membrane deformation being enhanced upon dimerisation. Functional analyses in mammalian cells and in reconstituted proteoliposomes failed to detect CTL1-mediated choline transport, supporting a function distinct from canonical choline uptake. Together, our findings suggest that CTL1 acts as a phospholipid-binding protein capable of locally deforming the membrane and provide a structural framework linking phospholipid recognition to membrane organisation. These results offer new insights into potential mechanisms underlying the altered phospholipid homeostasis associated with CTL1 dysfunction in neurological diseases and cancer.

papers.title: Rational design of intrinsic transcription terminators with programmable strength
papers.abstract: Intrinsic terminators are widely used in synthetic biology and metabolic engineering, yet their strength must be selected empirically from characterized libraries. We therefore developed a framework for designing intrinsic terminators with programmable strength. TK, designed to maximize termination strength, exceeded both B0010, a widely used standard, and the strongest terminator in a 582-member reference library when assayed in parallel. To establish that these gains reflect intrinsic termination rather than cellular context, we developed a cloning-free in vitro transcription assay using fluorescent light-up aptamers; TK again ranked highest. The framework improved the canonical T7 terminator and recovered strength rankings across three other bacterial species. Designs were generated using an interpretable sequence-to-function model trained from primary-sequence descriptors alone. The framework is available as open web tools, TerSP for strength prediction and TerFac for target-driven design. Model interpretation revealed previously unreported determinants, including a preference for compositionally diverse hairpin stems.

papers.title: IgG sequencing maps systemic antibody binding to oral commensals and pathobionts in health and periodontitis
papers.abstract: The oral cavity harbors one of the body's most diverse microbial communities, which continuously seeds the bloodstream and gastrointestinal tract, particularly in periodontitis, a disease in which both barrier permeability and microbial burden increase. Despite this constant systemic exposure, overt bacteremia from oral organisms is rare, suggesting an active surveillance system that contains this reservoir. Here, we apply IgG-sequencing to comprehensively map mucosal and systemic antibody recognition of the oral microbiome across paired oral fluid and serum from healthy individuals and patients with periodontitis. We find that IgG-binding is only weakly predicted by microbial abundance, suggesting taxon-specific and largely conserved IgG-binding of commensals, many of them streptococci which dominate antibody recognition irrespective of disease state. Periodontitis broadens the repertoire of IgG-bound taxa to include particular disease-associated pathobionts while preserving robust targeting of health-associated symbionts. Comparison of salivary and serum antibody profiles further uncovers a subset of commensal streptococci, including species implicated in infective endocarditis, that acquire disproportionate systemic IgG binding in periodontitis. Together, these findings establish a taxon-level atlas of humoral immunosurveillance at a major mucosal-microbial interface and reveal how periodontal disease reshapes systemic antibody recognition of both pathobionts and commensals.

papers.title: Cytokine-mediated activation of exhausted T cells
papers.abstract: CD8 T cell exhaustion during chronic infection and cancer is marked by impaired effector function and limited responsiveness to stimulation. While memory CD8 T cells can be activated TCR-independently by IL-12 and IL-18, it remains unclear whether exhausted cells, despite diminished TCR responsiveness, retain this cytokine-driven effector capacity. Here, we show that IL-12 and IL-18 stimulation induce robust IFN{gamma} production in exhausted CD8 T cells from chronic LCMV Cl13 infection, exceeding responses to antigen-specific stimulation. This activation does not result in upregulation of Tox, suggesting engagement of transcriptional circuits distinct from those promoting exhaustion. Single-cell transcriptomics revealed an innate acting T cell (TIA)-specific gene signature enriched within exhausted populations in chronic infection and tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, particularly at the interface of intermediate and terminal exhaustion. Using heterologous Legionella pneumophila infection, we confirmed in vivo bystander responsiveness of exhausted CD8 T cells, reducing bacterial burden, highlighting their functional capacity. Our findings demonstrate that exhausted CD8 T cells retain inducible effector capacity through IL-12 and IL-18 stimulation, providing new insights into possible routes to activate exhausted T cells.

papers.title: The Lag3 KIEELE motif couples HPK1 to metabolic and functional regulation of Foxp3+ regulatory T cells
papers.abstract: Lymphocyte activation gene-3 (Lag3) is an inhibitory receptor that limits effector T cell activation and function. We previously demonstrated that Lag3 supports regulatory T (Treg) cell function through Myc-dependent metabolic reprogramming. However, the intracellular mechanisms underlying this regulation remain incompletely understood. Here, we generated mice with Treg-specific deletion of the Lag3 KIEELE motif and demonstrated that this motif is required for Treg-mediated suppression of autoimmune inflammation. Loss of the Lag3 KIEELE motif led to enhanced TCR/PI3K-Akt/MEK-ERK signaling and Myc expression, accompanied by increased glycolytic activity and acquisition of effector T cell-like features. We also identified that hematopoietic progenitor kinase 1 (HPK1) and Cbl-interacting protein of 85 kDa (CIN85) associate with Lag3 through the KIEELE motif. HPK1 depletion partially recapitulated the phenotypic changes and impaired Treg suppressive function in vivo. Together, these findings identify the KIEELE motif as a critical link between Lag3-associated signaling machinery and metabolic regulation that sustains Treg suppressive function during autoimmune inflammation.

papers.title: Codon usage bias maps ocean microbiome adaptation to temperature-nutrients regimes
papers.abstract: Microbial communities underpin ocean productivity and biogeochemistry, but their functional adaptation to environmental gradients remains poorly understood. Codon usage bias (CUB), a marker of translational efficiency, constrains growth rate potential, yet its role in functional adaptation across natural communities is underexplored. By analysing 589 metagenome-derived microbial communities from the global ocean, we demonstrate that CUB in 320 metabolism-related gene groups capture genomic adaptation to distinct temperature and nutrient concentrations. We identified four adaptation signatures shaped by distinct temperature-nutrient regimes, revealing how microbes optimize protein synthesis in their ecological niche. This genome-centric approach deepens our understanding of functional adaptation in uncultured marine microbes and provides a framework to inform ocean biogeochemical models and predict microbial responses to climate-driven changes.

papers.title: Evidence of active phage replication during vegetable fermentation and implications for the dynamics of bacterial communities
papers.abstract: Spontaneous vegetable fermentation is driven by the indigenous microbiota associated with the raw ingredients. The process often involves an initial heterofermentative phase followed by a predominantly homofermentative phase, both ensured by lactic acid bacteria (LAB). While microbial dynamics during fermentation are well characterized, phage communities remain poorly understood, despite evidence linking phage activity to LAB succession. We monitored viral and bacterial succession during sauerkraut and carrot fermentations using a metagenomics approach to characterize community dynamics. To further assess the impact of phage PLE001 on bacterial community dynamics, we developed a simplified carrot fermentation model comprising representative strains of Rahnella aquatilis, Leuconostoc mesenteroides and Lactiplantibacillus plantarum. Two consortia were assembled: one containing the PLE001-susceptible strain L. mesenteroides CIM3004, and the other containing also its phage-resistant derivative, CIM3004 BIM. We observed major shifts in the viral community during the first week of fermentation, coinciding with changes in bacterial structure during hetero- and homofermentative phases transition. In the simplified model, phage PLE001 reduced the population of the host during the heterofermentative phase but did not affect overall fermentation dynamics nor metabolite production. These results suggest that bacteriophages contribute to bacterial succession during fermentation, while communities remain resilient to phage infection, preserving fermentation stability.

papers.title: Effects of CO2 on the growth and metabolism of Akkermansia muciniphila
papers.abstract: The human gut is home to more than 100 trillion bacteria, where various environmental factors, such as nutrients and gases, exist and influence them. The levels of fermentation gases in the gut, including CO2, fluctuate depending on the host's diet. However, how CO2, an environmental factor, affects the physiological states of gut anaerobes remains poorly understood, but CO2 is often utilized in their cultivation. Akkermansia muciniphila (A. muciniphila) is widely studied as a beneficial human gut microbe. However, the effects of CO2 on the physiological state of A. muciniphila are not fully understood. In this study, we focused on CO2 as an environmental factor and aimed to clarify how CO2 affects the physiological state of A. muciniphila. Culture experiments showed that compared with the absence of CO2, the presence of CO2 significantly increased the growth of A. muciniphila. The results of the metabolomic analysis revealed distinct metabolic profiles in the presence or absence of CO2. The tracing analysis using stable 13C-labelled CO2 demonstrated that CO2 was incorporated into various metabolites in the TCA cycle, the de novo purine/pyrimidine synthesis pathways, and other pathways. In addition, the activity of pyruvate carboxylase, which catalyses an anaplerotic reaction involving CO2 fixation to supply oxaloacetate (OAA) to the TCA cycle, was significantly higher in A. muciniphila cells grown in the presence of CO2. Moreover, supplementation with OAA increased the growth of A. muciniphila in a dose-dependent manner, mirroring the effects of CO2 supplementation. These findings suggest that A. muciniphila utilizes CO2 for an anaplerotic reaction in the TCA cycle and other pathways involving CO2 incorporation, facilitating metabolic flux to promote its robust growth.

papers.title: Bacterial NDH-1 is a key gut target of metformin mediating its antidiabetic effects
papers.abstract: Metformin is the first-line therapy for type 2 diabetes, yet the mechanisms underlying its glucose-lowering effects remain incompletely understood. Increasing evidence implicates gut microbiota as an important mediator of metformin action, but the bacterial targets of the drug remain poorly defined. Here, we identify bacterial NADH oxidoreductase (NDH-1), the homolog of mitochondrial complex I, as a key target of metformin. Metformin inhibited bacterial growth at millimolar concentrations and, at subinhibitory concentrations, markedly impaired carbohydrate fermentation in Escherichia coli and other NDH-1-containing bacteria. Supplementation with nicotinic acid and Mg2+; restored fermentation, whereas pyruvate bypassed the metabolic defect, implicating impaired NAD+; regeneration and disruption of metabolism upstream of pyruvate formation. Genetic analysis further established NDH-1 dependence: metformin failed to inhibit fermentation in an E. coli delta-nuoF mutant lacking functional NDH-1 but retained activity in an NDH-2-deficient delta-ndh strain. Molecular docking predicted metformin binding within the NDH-1 quinone-binding region, proximal to conserved residues involved in quinone reduction. Consistent with this mechanism, Staphylococcus aureus, which lacks NDH-1, was not affected in carbohydrate fermentation, while several gut-associated probiotic and short-chain fatty acid-producing bacteria, including Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, and Akkermansia muciniphila, lacked detectable NDH-1 homologs, suggesting intrinsic resistance to this metabolic effect of metformin. These findings identify bacterial NDH-1 as a metabolic target of metformin and provide a mechanistic framework for its effects on the gut microbiota. Selective inhibition of NDH-1-dependent bacteria could alter microbial substrate utilization and ecological interactions in the intestine, potentially contributing to the microbiome-mediated component of metformin's antidiabetic effects.

papers.title: A Seed-Derived Multi-Kingdom Synthetic Community Enhances Radish Seedling Protection Against Alternaria brassicicola Abra43
papers.abstract: Seed-associated microorganisms represent a promising resource for developing microbiome-based strategies against seed-borne pathogens. Here, we assembled synthetic microbial communities (SynComs) from cultivable members of the natural radish seed microbiota and evaluated their capacity to protect seedlings against the seed-transmitted fungal pathogen Alternaria brassicicola Abra43. Seven SynComs representing single- or multi-kingdom combinations of bacteria (B), filamentous fungi (F), and yeasts (Y) (B, F, Y, BF, BY, FY, and BFY) were inoculated onto radish seeds. We assessed their effects on disease incidence, seedling growth, microbial community assembly (ITS1 and gyrB gene metabarcoding) and pathogen colonization (metabarcoding and specific qPCR on dhn1 gene for A. brassicicola Abra43). Protection of radish seedlings against A. brassicicola Abra43 strongly depended on SynCom composition. The yeast fraction alone provided little protection, whereas the bacterial fraction partially reduced symptoms and maintained seedling growth despite substantial pathogen colonization, suggesting increased plant tolerance. SynComs containing filamentous fungi markedly reduced A. brassicicola Abra43 abundance, and the full multi-kingdom BFY SynCom provided the most consistent protection, combining reduced disease incidence, restored seedling growth, and low pathogen relative and absolute abundance. Inoculated strains, Alternaria alternata ABAI001 and Plectosphaerella sp. FL19 were enriched in protective SynComs and displayed antagonistic activity against A. brassicicola Abra43 in vitro. Together, these results show that seed-derived multi-kingdom communities can reshape early plant microbiota and that combining bacterial and fungal strains with complementary ecological functions can improve protection against a seed-borne fungal pathogen.

papers.title: A streamlined and abundant Nitrosopumilus population retains vitamin biosynthesis under high purifying selection in the Baltic Sea
papers.abstract: Genome streamlining is expected to favor the loss of costly biosynthetic functions, raising the question of what benefit justifies the continued maintenance of complex pathways in small genomes. Here, we investigated this question in an abundant Nitrosopumilus population from the Baltic Sea that combined a streamlined genome (1.4 Mbp) with substantial biosynthetic capacity for vitamins B1, B7, and B12. We found three lines of evidence that support the biological significance of this retention. First, phylogenomic analysis of 1,077 archaeal species representatives showed that B-vitamin biosynthesis is broadly conserved across ammonia-oxidizing archaea (AOA), indicating maintenance over deep evolutionary timescales. Second, genes associated with B-vitamin biosynthesis tended to be under stronger purifying selection than the genomic background across Baltic Sea metagenomes, consistent with selection preserving these functions in current environmental populations. Third, measurements in the cultured relative Nitrosopumilus maritimus showed B-vitamins and related precursors in both intracellular and extracellular fractions, providing a potential route through which these retained functions could influence metabolite availability beyond the producing cell. Together, our findings suggest that retained biosynthetic pathways in highly streamlined microorganisms reveal functions that are beneficial for the success of a natural population, while also pointing to their potential importance for other community members coexisting within the same environment.

papers.title: Hiding in plain sight: rare Bacillus cereus group species are present among unassembled metagenomic samples in public databases
papers.abstract: Abstract The Bacillus cereus group is a complex of closely related species, which vary in terms of their geographic spread, industrial utility, and pathogenic potential. In addition to encompassing well-known species represented by thousands of genomes (e.g., bioterrorism agent B. anthracis, foodborne pathogen B. cereus, biopesticide B. thuringiensis), the B. cereus group houses "rare" species discovered/first sequenced over a decade ago. Until recently, four rare species (B. manliponensis, B. bingmayongensis, B. gaemokensis, "B. clarus") were each represented by a single unique genome; as such, virtually nothing is known about these species beyond their type strains. We hypothesized that additional representatives of rare B. cereus group species may already be present in public databases as yet-unassembled metagenomes. To this end, we used species-specific markers to identify 7 metagenomic samples in NCBI's Sequence Read Archive, which harbored B. manliponensis, B. bingmayongensis, or B. gaemokensis. Metagenomic assembly and binning yielded an isolate-quality B. manliponensis metagenome-assembled genome (MAG) from avocado orchard soil in Israel, plus a partial B. bingmayongensis MAG from commercial spinach spiked with Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli. For rare species represented by >1 unique genome, we compared our novel MAGs to all available genomes and identified strain- and lineage-specific genomic elements (e.g., sphingomyelinase C and hemolysin BL homologs, variably present in B. manliponensis and B. bingmayongensis, respectively). Altogether, our study indicates that some rare B. cereus group species may be more common and geographically widespread than previously thought, and highlights the utility of culture-independent methods for recovering rare/under-isolated taxa. Impact Statement Individual B. cereus group strains vary in terms of their pathogenic potential and industrial utility. While some strains cause illness in humans and/or animals (e.g., anthrax, emetic intoxication, diarrheal toxicoinfection, non-gastrointestinal illnesses), other strains have important biotechnological applications (e.g., biocontrol, plant growth promotion, production of antimicrobials and other natural products). Because many virulence- and biotechnological-related phenotypes are strain-dependent (rather than species-dependent), phenotypes associated with an individual strain (e.g., a species type strain) cannot be extrapolated to an entire B. cereus group species. Within this context, rare B. cereus group species represent a major gap in our understanding of B. cereus group evolution, ecology, and pathogenicity, as until 2021, each rare species was represented solely by its type strain genome. Here, we aggregate all publicly available genomes/MAGs of rare B. cereus group species and supplement them with their first novel representatives since 2024. Our efforts bring the total number of unique B. manliponensis and B. bingmayongensis genomes/MAGs to >2, allowing us to conduct the first-ever phylogeographic survey and strain-level assessment of functional potential for each species. Overall, our study represents a critical first step toward understanding rare B. cereus group species beyond their type strains.

papers.title: Structure-Informed Stress-Testing of the Standard Numbering Scheme for Class B β-Lactamases Using AlphaFold2
papers.abstract: The standard numbering scheme for class B beta-lactamases (metallo-beta-lactamases, MBLs), the BBL scheme, was proposed by Galleni et al. in 2001 and updated by Garau et al. in 2004 from the small number of MBL structures then solved. Hundreds of additional class B sequences have since been catalogued, but most have never been structurally solved, so whether BBL correspondences hold across this larger diversity has not been directly tested. Following the precedent set for the sibling class D enzymes, we used ColabFold (AlphaFold2/MMseqs2) to model 87 class B families across subclasses B1, B2, and B3 lacking an experimental structure, after validating the pipeline against an eight-enzyme benchmark spanning all three subclasses (RMSD to experimental structures 0.35-0.46 A). Applying BBL zinc-ligand numbering to the 87 models via paired sequence- and structure-based residue-transfer methods, the canonical zinc-coordination motif transferred cleanly in the large majority of families, and 11 of the 16 sequence-level exceptions were accounted for by a literature-supported biological cause (a subclass-appropriate substitution or a previously proposed, unconfirmed fourth subgroup), while two motif-retaining families showed predicted local structural divergence at the active-site loop, flagged by structural superposition, that could not be resolved to exact zinc-ligand numbering and warrants direct experimental follow-up. These results show that the BBL scheme, formulated before metagenomic sequencing or deep-learning structure prediction existed, generalizes robustly into the structural space these technologies have since opened, and identify a small set of variants whose active sites merit experimental attention.

papers.title: Comparative functional genomics of six Pectobacterium species reveals core and unique fitness determinants in potato tubers
papers.abstract: Pectobacterium, a member of the soft rot Pectobacteriaceae (SRP), can cause highly destructive soft rot and blackleg diseases on many important crop and other host plants, particularly potato (Solanum tuberosum). Pectobacterium and its sister genus Dickeya have common virulence strategies, yet a highly diverse "open" pangenome containing many unique and hypothetical proteins. Here, we used randomly-barcoded transposon insertion-site sequencing (RB-TnSeq) on six Pectobacterium species to identify genes involved in bacterial survival and growth in potato tubers, as well as in minimal media conditions containing different single carbon sources. The strains evaluated varied broadly in genomic content as well as host plant and year of isolation. We focused on identifying conditionally essential genes across all strains tested, as well as genes that were important for growth in one or few of the tested strains. These results highlight the importance of many common genes involved in metabolism and maintaining cellular homeostasis, as well as shared and rare virulence traits including polygalacturonate catabolism, genes involved in polysaccharide biosynthesis, immunity proteins, and (for P. brasiliense) self-tolerance of the antibiotic carbapenem. This large dataset of conditionally essential genes, generated across Pectobacterium species during soft rot infection of the agriculturally important plant host potato, can serve as a rich dataset for further hypothesis generation and identification of important and/or novel in planta fitness factors.

papers.title: Regulation of polyphosphate homeostasis in S. cerevisiae by the Sky1 protein kinase
papers.abstract: Eukaryotic cells store inorganic phosphate in the form of long chains called polyphosphates (polyP) that can reach many hundreds of residues in length. In the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, polyP is synthesized by the VTC complex using ATP as a substrate and sequestered at high concentrations in the vacuole. Here, polyP chain length and turnover are regulated by the polyphosphatase enzymes Ppn1 and Ppn2. In the vacuole lumen, polyP plays a critical role in phosphate and ion homeostasis. Beyond the vacuole, minor populations of polyP are thought to impact various cellular functions, including in the nucleus, in part by binding to target proteins. We speculated that polyP metabolism must be tightly coupled to mechanisms of homeostatic control operating elsewhere in the cell. In this work, we report that cells lacking Sky1, a serine-arginine repeat protein kinase, have very low levels of polyP, an effect that is exacerbated by alkaline stress. Under these conditions sky1{triangleup} mutants also display increased expression of a subset of genes from the PHO regulon. Genetic analysis suggests that both phenotypes are linked to an increase in potassium influx via the Trk1 potassium transporter. Loss of Npl3, a known target of Sky1, partially rescues the phosphate homeostasis defects in sky1{triangleup} mutants, although this occurs independently of a well characterized Sky1 phosphorylation site on Npl3. Finally, the loss of polyP in sky1{triangleup} mutants depends on the Ppn1 and Ppn2 polyphosphatases and the Pep4 protease located in the vacuole. Altogether, our work provides novel insights into how polyP homeostasis in the vacuole is coordinated with events occurring throughout the cell.

papers.title: Comprehensive Lineage Tracing Maps the Landscape of Cell Fate Decisions in Mouse Embryogenesis
papers.abstract: A comprehensive cell fate map of mammalian embryogenesis has remained out of reach given the scale, cellular diversity, and non-deterministic nature of development in utero. Here, we use PEtracer to continuously install heritable genetic marks as development progresses, reconstructing lineage trees that resolve ~75% of cell divisions across >1.4 million cells from 16 replicate embryos. We pair these trees with deep transcriptional profiling to resolve cell fate biases, restriction timing, progenitor pool sizes, and lineage relationships throughout embryogenesis. Using this quantitative reference, we uncover strikingly reproducible lineage architecture between replicate embryos and chart the lineage dynamics driving fate specification across diverse tissues. Specific biological insights include the progressive restriction of neural crest fate, the relative contributions of distinct mesodermal origins to endothelium, and the dynamics of axial elongation. This work provides a foundation for a quantitative and predictive understanding of mammalian development.

papers.title: Significance filtering induces denominator selection bias in local genetic correlation: closed-form characterisation, a gate-aware correction, and an applicability diagnostic
papers.abstract: Local genetic correlation is estimated as a ratio of a local genetic covariance to the geometric mean of two local heritabilities. LAVA, the standard implementation, returns that ratio only where both traits clear a univariate heritability test at P < 0.05, a rule its documentation presents as a stabiliser. We show that it is a selection event acting on the denominator, and characterise what it does to the estimates that survive. Under the noncentral Wishart model LAVA's own interval routine assumes, the gate-conditional mean of the estimator is affine in the true correlation, with slope and intercept available in closed form from quantities every run already reports, that is, the components retained, the two univariate P-values, and the sample-overlap correlation. Attenuation is therefore a property of the analysis, not of the method. Across six psychiatric trait pairs the measured slope runs from 0.579 to 0.923 and the closed form predicts each to within 0.007 with nothing fitted to the panel, while within a single pair it runs from 0.371 to 0.971, so no single factor can correct it. Overlap and the filter jointly manufacture correlation where the truth is zero, most where power is lowest. We invert the closed form into a gate-aware correction, which reduces mean absolute bias from 0.247 to 0.026 over 48 simulation cells, and pair it with a diagnostic that decides whether the correction is identified. Three pairs fail it, all three sharing one trait whose local heritabilities are indistinguishable from a complete local null.

papers.title: Defining the spectrum of cellular protection against cadmium stress by Dsup expressed in yeast
papers.abstract: The intrinsically disordered tardigrade Dsup protein has garnered attention for its ability to protect cells and organisms from radiation and oxidative stress. Our lab has previously described Dsups protective effect in yeast, finding that, while Dsup expression comes with a fitness cost, it improves survival under many stressors, including the heavy metal cadmium. While Dsups protection against oxidative stress and radiation is well-established, the mechanism by which it protects against other stressors is underinvestigated. To address this knowledge gap, we screened a collection of 4000 yeast deletion mutants expressing Dsup in the presence of three doses of cadmium to identify synergistic/synthetically lethal genes and processes. We find that Dsup broadly buffers many processes/genes at lower levels of cadmium stress but at higher doses, cells shift to buffering specific genes/processes. These results identify host genetic processes that influence Dsups ability to confer cadmium resistance to organisms.

papers.title: scDEcrypter: Uncertainty-aware differential expression analysis for viral infection in scRNA-seq
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA-seq studies of viral infection are limited by sparse viral reads, under-labeled infected cells, and bystander responses that confound differential expression (DE) analysis. We introduce scDEcrypter, a penalized two-way mixture model that leverages partial infection and cell type labels to estimate latent cell-state probabilities. scDEcrypter provides fast permutation-based approximate p-values for prioritizing infection-associated genes while accounting for the uncertainty in cell-state. In simulations and applications to two viral infection datasets, scDEcrypter improved recovery of infected cell states and identified more biologically coherent infection-associated genes and enriched pathways.

papers.title: Breedbase 2.0 - expanding the functionality for traditional breeding and transgenics
papers.abstract: Breedbase ( is a comprehensive, web-based, open-source breeding management and analysis software for plant breeding that was introduced to address gaps with existing software for plant breeding data. Breedbase is continually improved and developed, with new features being added as required by the breeding community. Since its inception, the capabilities of Breedbase were improved to better serve the diverse data modeling needs of additional crops beyond our original ensemble of cassava, banana, yam, sweet potato, tomato, rice, and wheat. We describe here major updates that have been made in the past 4 years, including (1) improved handling of repetitive measurements; (2) a redesigned experimental treatments interface; (3) a more fine-grained user permission system; (4) improved trial quality control workflows; (5) intercropping support; (6) the addition of a decision meeting feature that helps decision makers make the best selection with the available data; (7) transgenics and tracking tools and finally, (8) an improved field layout tool which consolidates several trials in one field. These new features integrate seamlessly with the previous feature set of Breedbase - making it one of the most feature rich breeding management softwares available.

papers.title: Agent-optimized GPU polygenic scoring at cohort scale
papers.abstract: A polygenic score (PGS) is a unitless weighted sum of allele dosages, interpretable only as a percentile within a reference distribution. Evaluating risk across models requires scoring each individual against a whole reference panel, but current CPU pipelines process targets or models sequentially, making full cross-product calculations prohibitively expensive. We reformulated PGS calculation as a cohort-wide sparse matrix product on a GPU and optimized it via an autonomous coding agent under read-only inputs, cold starts, and strict numerical validation against pgsc_calc. The scorer was "trained" by the agent accessing synthetic data and real 1000 Genomes data. On a synthetic benchmark, the scorer achieved a 10.6-fold speedup during the training course (184.9 s to 17.4 s) and ran 71-fold faster than pgsc_calc. However, on held-out real genomes, the synthetic-trained scorer was 15.3-fold slower than the real-data-trained version and diverged significantly from pgsc_calc (maximum absolute difference of 3.7x10-1 vs. 3.1x10-4). Three replications of the synthetic loop from an identical prompt showed that agent optimization trajectory variance explains 91 to 96% of total wall-clock variance, against 0 to 2.6% for the data sampled and 0.2 to 3.3% for repeated execution. A memory-bounded rebuild then scored all the 3,202 1000 Genome genotypes against all 5,385 models in 6.5 h within a 72 GB memory cap, released here as a frozen scoring manifest with ancestry-stratified reference distributions for the whole PGS Catalog

papers.title: Accurate prediction of protein stability changes from single mutations using self-distillation and antisymmetric constraint strategies
papers.abstract: Computational approaches for accurately predicting protein stability changes upon residue mutations are crucial for protein engineering and design. Sequence-based methods are easier to apply to large-scale proteins since they do not rely on high-quantity structures. However, existing sequence-based approaches struggle to capture structural changes, resulting in lower performance compared to structure-based methods. In this study, we propose DPStab, a sequence-based deep learning solution that accurately predicts protein stability changes upon single residue mutations. DPStab transfers a protein large language model as a core component and incorporates a cross-attention mechanism to capture the contact changes around mutated positions for {Delta}{Delta}G and {Delta}Tm prediction. To address data imbalance and the antisymmetric nature of mutation effects, DPStab employs a self-distillation inference strategy under the supervision of an antisymmetric constraint. Benchmarking demonstrates that DPStab achieves state-of-the-art performance in both {Delta}{Delta}G and {Delta}Tm prediction. Practical evaluations confirm DPStab's capability in accurately ranking protein stability on large-scale datasets and effectively identifying critical structural contacts impacting stability. More experiments on extensive cDNA display proteolysis data demonstrate the significant contributions of self-distillation and antisymmetric constraint strategies.

papers.title: Antibody-Antigen Affinity Prediction with Chain-Aware Protein Language Modeling
papers.abstract: Motivation: Antibody-antigen affinity determines which antibodies advance in therapeutic discovery, repertoire analysis and affinity maturation, but experimental measurements are sparse relative to the scale of sequence libraries.
