FluxAtlas is a pan-cancer metabolic flux atlas that identifies tumor-selective dependencies and prognostic biomarkers
papers.abstract: Kohli et al. apply enzyme- and nutrient-constrained genome-scale modeling to more than 10,000 tumors across 28 cancer types, defining a pan-cancer metabolic-flux landscape. This analysis reveals tissue-specific metabolic adaptations and vulnerabilities, including bile acid-linked redox and lipid rewiring, renal-specific purine dependence, and flux-based survival predictors, such as biotin uptake.

papers.title: MCUB restricts mitochondrial calcium to support metabolic adaptation and homeostasis in glioblastoma
papers.abstract: Sun et al. find that hypoxia-induced MCUB promotes a restricted mitochondrial Ca2+ flux state that supports metabolic adaptation and mitochondrial homeostasis in glioblastoma. Targeting MCUB-dependent calcium gating exerts antitumor effects and enhances radiosensitivity, revealing this mechanism as a potential therapeutic vulnerability.

papers.title: Matrix viscoelasticity amplifies pro-fibrotic crosstalk between cardiac fibroblasts and macrophages
papers.abstract: Matrix viscoelasticity governs cardiac fibroblast-macrophage crosstalk, with soft, viscous environments amplifying profibrotic signaling through dynamic paracrine feedback. Atcha et al. examine how mechanical cues and sequential immune activation synergize to recapitulate post-infarction fibrosis, identifying cytokine networks that may serve as therapeutic targets in cardiac remodeling.

papers.title: Cell volume regulation in metazoans involves phosphorylation of TSC22D proteins
papers.abstract: Lee et al. describe a condensate-based signaling mechanism regulating cell volume homeostasis. TSC22D, WNK, and NRBP proteins form dynamic condensates that modulate WNK-SPAK/OSR1 signaling. WNK-dependent phosphorylation of NRBP1 and TSC22D2 promotes pathway activation and condensate dissolution. These findings support a model where TWN bodies behave as signaling assemblies for osmo-regulation.

papers.title: Increased extracellular fluid viscosity drives M2-like macrophage polarization to promote breast cancer progression and immunotherapy resistance
papers.abstract: Zhang et al. demonstrate that increased extracellular fluid viscosity promotes immunosuppressive M2-like macrophage polarization through integrin/FAK-STAT3 signaling and cytoskeletal remodeling. This viscosity-driven macrophage state accelerates breast cancer progression and reduces the response to anti-PD-1 immunotherapy, linking a physical property of the tumor microenvironment to immune evasion.

papers.title: A bifunctional ARHGEF17-AS1 locus encodes MSEP, a protein that supports mitotic spindle organization
papers.abstract: Mahale et al. identify MSEP, a protein encoded within the ARHGEF17-AS1 antisense locus, and show that it localizes to the mitotic spindle and supports spindle organization through a TPX2-associated pathway. The work reveals distinct RNA- and protein-associated outputs from a single bifunctional genomic locus.

papers.title: Biased connectivity shapes food odor categorization in the Drosophila mushroom body
papers.abstract: Chan et al. show that individual Kenyon cell types in the Drosophila associative learning center, the mushroom body, encode odors according to different principles. Biased projection-neuron input yields food-related odor representations by αβ Kenyon cells that support the categorization of food odors in addition to their discrimination.

papers.title: Next-generation cancer therapeutics
papers.abstract: Cancer therapies have evolved substantially in recent decades; however, there remains a pressing need for new therapeutic options. Our Series on Next-Generation Cancer Therapeutics presents commissioned Reviews and opinion pieces on the latest therapeutic approaches and their implementation in the existing clinical landscape.

papers.title: Unsaturated phospholipids form multicompartment liposomes that extend release of hydrophilic drugs
papers.abstract: Unsaturated phospholipids unexpectedly form multilamellar, multivesicular liposomes that efficiently encapsulate hydrophilic drugs and suppress burst release. These structures enable ultra-slow drug release and produce weeks-long sciatic nerve block with tetrodotoxin in rats.

papers.title: Ultra-slow release of hydrophilic drugs via multilamellar–multivesicular liposomes formed by unsaturated phospholipids
papers.abstract: Maintaining therapeutic drug concentrations at a target site while limiting systemic exposure is difficult for hydrophilic drugs, which rapidly diffuse from the injection site. Liposomes are widely used carriers, yet designs based on rigid, saturated phospholipids aim to reduce membrane permeability but often yield modest loading and substantial burst release. Here we compared liposomes composed of phospholipids of identical chain length but varying unsaturation, prepared under matched conditions. Contrary to the expectation that unsaturation accelerates release, liposomes based on 1,2-dioleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DOPC) showed approximately 3-fold higher loading, 11-fold lower initial release and 4-fold lower release at 7 days than saturated analogues. These effects correlated with the emergence of multilamellar and multivesicular structures and extended across diverse hydrophilic drugs. In a rat sciatic nerve block model, tetrodotoxin-loaded liposomes produced 2–3 weeks of blockade without systemic toxicity, establishing a simple platform for sustained local delivery. Contrary to expectations that unsaturation accelerates release, unsaturated phospholipid liposomes showed 3-fold higher loading and markedly reduced initial and sustained release due to multilamellar–multivesicular structure.

papers.title: CaMKII monomers are sufficient for GluN2B binding, co-condensation, and synaptic potentiation
papers.abstract: Brown et al. demonstrate that full-length but not truncated CaMKII monomers can bind GluN2B. The truncated monomers could still induce synaptic potentiation but only after making them artificially autonomous in a phosphatase-insensitive manner, which is normally achieved by GluN2B binding.

papers.title: Dietary α-ketoglutarate modulates lung adenocarcinoma growth and epigenetic remodeling in a sex-dependent fashion
papers.abstract: Alcaraz Jr. et al. show that dietary supplementation with calcium-αKG modulates lung cancer epigenetics and transcriptional programs in a sex-dependent way, resulting in reduced tumor growth in females but increased tumor growth in males.

papers.title: Placental trophoblasts exhibit iron dysregulation and ferroptosis signaling associated with SARS-CoV-2 restriction
papers.abstract: McColl et al. demonstrate that SARS-CoV-2 impairs placental iron efflux, leading to persistent iron accumulation and impaired maternal-fetal iron transfer, and activates ferroptosis signaling, which may limit viral replication. This uncovers both a novel antiviral role of ferroptosis in the placenta and a new mechanism for adverse pregnancy outcomes associated with COVID-19.

papers.title: Alternate day fasting attenuates metabolic dysfunction-associated arterial thrombotic risk via increasing indole-3-propionic acid
papers.abstract: Feng et al. show that alternate day fasting attenuates metabolic dysfunction-associated arterial thrombosis by gut microbiota reshaping. They identify the microbial metabolite indole-3-propionic acid as a crucial contributor that suppresses platelet activation and thrombosis by maintaining intraplatelet Rho GTPase cycle homeostasis, with reduced circulating levels observed in affected patients.

papers.title: piRNA-mediated silencing of exogenous retrovirus in mouse spermatogonial stem cells
papers.abstract: Shiromoto et al. show that PIWI-interacting RNAs and TRP53 protect mouse spermatogonial stem cells from exogenous retroviral infection. Disruption of this pathway enhances viral expression and germline transmission following testicular infection, revealing a mechanism that preserves genome integrity across generations.

papers.title: Role of the pulvinar in early visual cortical signaling in the macaque
papers.abstract: Using simultaneously recorded population spiking activity in the macaque pulvinar and early visual cortical areas V1 and V2, Xu et al. evaluate signaling motifs among these three structures. They find evidence for a relaying of signals from V1 to the pulvinar and on to V2.

papers.title: Topoisomerase I inhibition yields a CD74high/MHChigh human microglial subtype with enhanced Aβ uptake
papers.abstract: Camptothecin and its analog Topotecan drive human microglia toward a CD74high/MHChigh state with enhanced amyloid-β phagocytosis and altered inflammatory signaling. Using cell, organoid, and zebrafish models, Haage et al. link a transcriptomic microglial subtype to distinct functional properties, uncovering a pharmacological route to model microglial states implicated in neurodegeneration.

papers.title: Structured and target-specific development of cortico-cortical connectivity in the mouse visual cortex
papers.abstract: Jacobs and Ratliff et al. show how V1 wiring to eleven higher visual areas develops in mouse cortex through directed, region-specific targeting: medial areas innervate early and refine gradually into adulthood, while lateral areas overshoot early and prune to adult levels by P24. Feedforward and feedback circuits emerge concurrently.

papers.title: Adipocyte methionine reduction promotes cancer cachexia
papers.abstract: Cancer cachexia is a common wasting syndrome in individuals with cancer that involves activation of PKA in white adipose tissue, but the mechanisms that control PKA activity are unclear. A study now identifies iron-activated MSRA as a regulator of PKA in cancer cachexia, which reduces oxidized PKA and thereby increases PKA activity.

papers.title: An iron-regulated methionine redox axis governs adipose browning and cancer cachexia
papers.abstract: Adipose browning and atrophy are early events of cachexia, a lethal metabolic disorder affecting nearly half of the population with cancer. Here, using individual-derived specimens and mouse models, we identified an iron-dependent pathway that initiates adipose browning in both physiological and cachectic settings. Upon adrenergic stimulation of adipocytes, an influx of iron induces the activity of methionine sulfoxide reductase A (MSRA), an enzyme that reverses the oxidation of proteinaceous methionine residues. Mechanistically, iron coordination by the conserved iron-binding EXXH motif of two MSRA polypeptides serves to dimerize, stabilize and elevate its reductase activity. Iron-bound MSRA dimers in turn promote adipose browning by maintaining the reduced state of select substrates, including the catalytic subunit of protein kinase A. Remarkably, in mouse models, MsrA deletion impairs adipose browning, mitigates cachexia and prolongs the survival of tumor-bearing animals. Thus, as a key nexus of cancer-associated cachexia, the β3 adrenergic receptor–iron–MSRA axis is a promising target for clinical intervention. Chio and colleagues describe an iron-dependent pathway with a role in the induction of cancer cachexia-linked events such as adipose browning and identify methionine sulfoxide reductase A as an important and targetable factor in this process.

papers.abstract: The amoeba Incendiamoeba cascadensis demonstrates that eukaryotic life can withstand temperatures beyond what was thought possible and sheds light on molecular strategies for survival in extreme heat.

papers.title: Linker histone H1.0 loads onto nucleosomes through multiple pathways that are facilitated by histone chaperones
papers.abstract: Akbari et al. investigated the mechanisms of linker histone H1.0 loading onto nucleosomes. H1.0 directly binds nucleosomes and DNA, while DNA-bound H1.0 is mobile but does not load onto nucleosomes. Linker histone chaperones facilitate H1.0 loading through enhancing nucleosome binding, increasing H1.0 mobility, and enabling H1.0 loading through DNA sliding.

papers.title: SDCBP competes with CBL to stabilize PES1 and promote c-Myc translation in ESCC tumorigenesis
papers.abstract: Xiao et al. demonstrate that SDCBP drives esophageal squamous cell carcinoma progression by preventing CBL-mediated ubiquitination and degradation of PES1. Stabilized PES1 enhances pre-rRNA processing and promotes c-Myc protein synthesis. Tumor-targeted delivery of SDCBP antisense oligonucleotides effectively suppresses tumor growth.

papers.title: A USP28-BRD4 axis contributes to the acceleration of breast cancer growth by hyperglycemia
papers.abstract: How diabetes promotes cancer progression remains poorly understood. Li et al. show that high blood glucose stabilizes a cancer-promoting protein, BRD4, through a molecular switch involving USP28 and SIRT1. This USP28-BRD4 axis links hyperglycemia to breast cancer progression and may offer therapeutic insights.

papers.title: A compact Druantia defense clears phage infections via single-stranded DNA recognition and directional duplex unwinding
papers.abstract: Himpich et al. show how the Druantia III-A defense system detects and fends off invading phage DNA. The DruE component recognizes exposed single-stranded DNA and unwinds flanking duplex regions 3′-to-5′, employing unique lock, wedge, and clamp elements, while the DruH component might scaffold DruE and host proteins that dissociate upon infection.

papers.title: The spindle-associated antisense RNA ARHGEF17-AS1 functionally contributes to mitotic spindle integrity
papers.abstract: Mahale et al. identify ARHGEF17-AS1 as a spindle-associated antisense RNA that contributes to mitotic spindle integrity. The RNA associates with RPS3 and dynein, supports extra-ribosomal RPS3 abundance and spindle recruitment, and is linked to RNF10-dependent RPS3 monoubiquitination during mitosis.

papers.title: An amygdaloreticular pathway promotes motor programs of ingestion
papers.abstract: Lafferty et al. show that a collateralized amygdala projection to the hindbrain can drive context-dependent consummatory motor states. Activity in this pathway correlates with the motor action of licking, and stimulating this pathway promotes ingestion-related behaviors toward food and non-food objects, providing a potential mechanism for ingestion beyond homeostatic need.

papers.title: From blunt-force treatment to precision: 25 years of transformation in cancer research
papers.abstract: This issue marks the 25th anniversary of Nature Reviews Cancer. On this milestone we contemplate how our view of cancer has changed over the past 25 years and speculate on what the future holds. This Editorial marks the 25th anniversary of Nature Reviews Cancer. On this milestone we contemplate how our view of cancer has changed over the past 25 years and speculate on what the future holds.

papers.title: Replication stress in cancer: origins, consequences and therapeutic opportunities
papers.abstract: Replication stress, defined as impaired DNA replication leading to genomic instability, is a central feature of tumour development and progression. In cancer cells, it arises from oncogene activation, transcription–replication conflicts, altered nucleotide metabolism and DNA secondary structures that hinder DNA synthesis. These pressures compromise accurate genome duplication and promote chromosomal instability and mutagenesis. Recent advances have clarified the molecular mechanisms that stabilize, remodel and restart stressed replication forks, and highlighted the essential role of the ataxia telangiectasia and Rad3-related protein (ATR)–checkpoint kinase 1 (CHK1) pathway in preventing excessive single-stranded DNA accumulation and catastrophic genome fragmentation. Although replication stress fuels tumour evolution and heterogeneity, it also creates dependencies on replication stress response pathways that can be therapeutically exploited. Inhibitors targeting ATR, CHK1 and WEE1 kinases, which override the G2 checkpoint, are in clinical development, whereas synthetic lethal strategies, including poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibition in BRCA1-deficient or BRCA2-deficient tumours and inhibition of the DNA helicase WRN in microsatellite-unstable cancers, illustrate how replication stress-associated vulnerabilities can be targeted. In this Review, we position replication stress as both a driver of cancer genome evolution and a tractable framework for precision oncology. We emphasize that replication stress in tumours is often chronic and sublethal, shaping genome evolution. We further highlight its integration with oncogenic and metabolic alterations and broader impact on tumour–microenvironment interactions, which create dynamic and context-dependent therapeutic vulnerabilities. Replication stress drives genomic instability, tumour evolution and therapeutic adaptation, yet also creates exploitable vulnerabilities. In this Review, Chen and Zou discuss how chronic replication stress shapes cancer biology and how emerging therapies are targeting the pathways that enable tumour cells to survive it.

papers.title: Tumor growth going FAR with KRAS FARnesylation-induced phase separation
papers.abstract: RAS at the plasma membrane relay signals from cell-surface receptors to intracellular pathways. In Cell, Wang et al. show that farnesylation drives KRAS cytoplasmic condensation, contributing to its maturation. They identify statins as candidates to overcome resistance to KRAS-targeted therapies.

papers.title: Processing of lysophosphatidylcholines by ExoU secreted by P. aeruginosa leads to inflammasome activation and cell death
papers.abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa alters the lipidome of host cells by injecting the toxin ExoU, causing lysophosphatidylcholine accumulation that activates inflammatory pathways and inflammasome-mediated cell death. This response is inhibited by lysophosphatidylcholine acyltransferase 3. In patients with cystic fibrosis, the expression of ExoU is reduced, promoting immune evasion and chronic infection.

papers.title: A splicing factor-cohesin association links RNA processing to cohesin-dependent genome folding
papers.abstract: Using proteomics together with an auxin-inducible degron system, Wu et al. identify proteins proximal to MAU2 and uncover genome-wide roles for CDC5L in pre-mRNA processing and cohesin-mediated genome folding in human cells.

papers.title: A role for the subthalamic nucleus in aversive learning
papers.abstract: (Cell Reports 42, 113328; November 28, 2023)

papers.title: Targeting pro-senescent PTGS2+ macrophages alleviates chondrocyte senescence and osteoarthritis progression
papers.abstract: (Cell Reports 45, 117907; September 22, 2026)

papers.title: Protein Kinase C Epsilon Cooperates with PTEN Loss for Prostate Tumorigenesis through the CXCL13-CXCR5 Pathway
papers.abstract: (Cell Reports 19, 375–388; April 11, 2017)

papers.title: Oligodendrocytes in central nervous system health and disease
papers.abstract: Oligodendrocytes, predominantly known for their role in myelination, play a broader role in regulating the central nervous system, including feeding axons and reshaping neural circuits, with their malfunction in diseases ranging from multiple sclerosis to Alzheimer’s. This review covers oligodendrocyte biology and their therapeutic relevance.

papers.title: Mycn facilitates hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell generation from endothelial cells by inhibiting adhesion signaling
papers.abstract: Wang et al. demonstrate that Mycn expression is initiated in hemogenic endothelial cells to promote hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell generation in mouse embryos. Mycn acts by inhibiting endothelial adhesion signaling to enable the endothelial-to-hematopoietic transition.

papers.title: A Middle East collaborative for undiagnosed diseases
papers.abstract: Undiagnosed disease networks advance the discovery of genes associated with rare diseases. However, a considerable gap in discovery remains, and genomic resources continue to exhibit population bias. A collaborative initiative in the Middle East could harness unique population structure, extensive family lineages and underrepresented genomic diversity to enhance local diagnostic capabilities and facilitate global gene discovery.

papers.title: The many faces of malaria parasites
papers.abstract: In this Journal Club, Elena Gómez-Díaz highlights two studies that established the Malaria Cell Atlas, demonstrating how single-cell transcriptomics can resolve parasite heterogeneity across development, transmission and natural infections to advance malaria research.

papers.title: De novo-engineered guide RNA-directed transposition with TnpB-family proteins
papers.abstract: Schargel et al. engineer TnpB-family proteins into minimal de novo RNA-guided transposition systems. Nuclease-deficient TnpB-family proteins enable three-component DNA integration with high efficiency, target-site immunity, orientation control, and programmable insertion into the bacterial chromosome. In parallel, mutations to the TniQ-TnsC interface in wild-type V-K CAST attenuate off-site transposition.

papers.title: PADI-dependent mitochondrial adaptation drives resistance to KRAS inhibitors
papers.abstract: KRAS-mutant pancreatic and colorectal cancers frequently develop resistance to KRAS(ON) and KRAS(OFF) inhibitors. Here, Gani et al. identify a PADI-dependent adaptive circuit that promotes therapeutic escape through HSPA9/Mortalin citrullination. Pharmacological PADI inhibition restores KRAS inhibitor sensitivity and induces non-lytic apoptosis, revealing a therapeutic vulnerability in KRAS-driven tumors.

papers.title: Antigenic landscape of rabies and related lyssaviruses revealed by cryo-EM
papers.abstract: Callaway et al. solve cryo-EM structures of nine antibodies in complex with rabies virus glycoprotein, illustrating the breadth of the rabies antibody-binding landscape. Two identified antigenic sites, sites V and VI, are unusually well conserved across rabies and related lyssaviruses and are targets for structure-guided antibody and vaccine design.

papers.title: Anticipatory metabolic regulation drives the distinct and improved metabolic state of caloric restriction compared to Fasting-Refeeding cycles
papers.abstract: Velingkaar et al. demonstrate that metabolic adaptation during caloric restriction is driven by more than prolonged fasting. They show that caloric restriction engages anticipatory, circadian-regulated metabolic programs independent of gastric emptying, whereas fasting-refeeding cycles remain nutrient-driven, disrupting circadian rhythmicity while impairing glucose tolerance and promoting hepatic lipid accumulation.

papers.title: Colony morphogenesis regulates sporulation dynamics in bacterial biofilms
papers.abstract: Jones et al. show how the growth dynamics of bacterial biofilms regulate the distribution of dormant spore production within colonies. Cells are rapidly driven to dormancy by a wave of sporulation sweeping through biomass, but increasing the rate of colony spreading proportionally slows the transition to dormancy.

papers.title: Skin commensals shape the clock-ferroptosis axis to preserve barrier function in psoriasis
papers.abstract: Lin et al. show that Lactobacillus is decreased in psoriatic lesions. Lactobacillus plantarum and its metabolite indole-3-lactic acid improve keratinocyte pathology and alleviate psoriasis-like changes in mice through the Clock-ferroptosis axis.

papers.title: The left PBN to aCM pathway mediates pain-related aversion in male mice
papers.abstract: Yan et al. show that in male mice, the left parabrachial nucleus (L-PBN), but not its right counterpart (R-PBN), modulates formalin-induced conditioned place aversion (F-CPA) through direct projections to the anterior central thalamus nucleus (aCM). In contrast, neither L-PBN nor R-PBN is involved in F-CPA control in female mice.

papers.title: Theta synchronization coordinates ventral temporal and medial temporal coding of human face familiarity
papers.abstract: Li et al. reveal how the human brain recognizes familiar faces by coordinating visual perception and memory through theta-frequency synchronization. Their findings show that rhythmic neural activity links feature representations in the visual cortex with memory signals in the medial temporal lobe, providing a mechanistic framework for processing face familiarity.

papers.title: A CsWRKY46-CsPBL9-CsARI1 tripartite regulatory module coordinates H2O2 production and callose deposition in citrus fruit immunity
papers.abstract: Xu et al. reveal a tripartite and interactive rheostat orchestrating self-linked immune responses in citrus fruit, elucidating the poorly understood regulatory mechanisms of callose deposition in plant immunity. Notably, E3 ligase CsARI1 acts as an immune brake via both ubiquitination-dependent and non-catalytic pathways, expanding the functions of RBR-type E3 ligases.

papers.title: Gene regulatory mechanisms downstream of DNA methylation
papers.abstract: Cytosine DNA methylation is a conserved epigenetic modification that regulates gene expression, represses transposable elements and maintains genome stability across diverse eukaryotes. Although major advances have uncovered the pathways involved in the establishment, maintenance and removal of DNA methylation, the downstream mechanisms by which this mark influences transcriptional programmes and shapes chromatin structure are less well understood. Here, we review how specialized reader proteins and transcription factors interpret DNA methylation to preserve methylation patterns, recruit effector complexes, regulate chromatin accessibility and interact with parallel epigenetic systems to mediate transcriptional silencing and activation across mammals and plants. We highlight that robust transcriptional and epigenetic states emerge from overlapping, layered and partially redundant DNA methylation-dependent mechanisms. Together, these insights provide a framework for understanding how DNA methylation shapes the epigenome to regulate development, differentiation and disease progression. In this Review, Buckley et al. discuss how DNA methylation is interpreted in mammals and plants, focusing on the reader proteins and transcription factors that bind to methylated DNA and the downstream mechanisms by which they regulate transcriptional and epigenetic states.

Howard Hughes Medical Institute, University of California at Los Angeles, Los Angeles, USA

papers.title: Cohesin preservation across mitosis contributes to restart transcription via Cdk9-mediated activation of RNAPol2
papers.abstract: Contreras-Pérez et al. address the puzzling role of cohesin on transcription by focusing on the mitotic exit, when cohesin firstly contact chromatin. Combining in vivo labeling, cell-cycle synchronization, and acute protein depletion, authors demonstrate the preservation of cohesin across mitosis and its fundamental role on transcription reactivation of tissue-related genes.

papers.title: A dual-module ECAS complex couples transcription elongation and RNA processing
papers.abstract: Xiang et al. identify ECAS, a chromatin-associated complex that couples an elongation module (AFF4-ELL2-EAF1) to a spliceosome-associated intron binding complex. AQR/XAB2-dependent ECAS functions drive productive RNA Pol II elongation, nascent RNA capping, and co-transcriptional splicing and are required for leukemia initiation, maintenance, and leukemia stem cell function in MLL-rearranged leukemia.

papers.title: Nuclear body assembly by a viral repeat RNA promotes Kaposi’s sarcoma-associated herpesvirus gene expression
papers.abstract: Kaposin is an abundant viral RNA produced by the virus, Kaposi’s sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV). Kleer et al. reveal that kaposin drives nuclear speckle formation adjacent to the viral genome, enhancing viral gene expression. Kaposin is necessary and sufficient for this effect, which requires repeats regions within the RNA.

papers.title: MG53 suppresses IRF7 to reprogram macrophages and promote antitumor immunity in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
papers.abstract: Pei et al. show that macrophage MG53 suppresses IRF7 to promote pro-inflammatory macrophage and T cell responses, while MG53 deficiency drives immunosuppressive polarization. Low-MG53/high-IRF7 TAMs correlate with poor survival in PDAC and CRC. MG53 mRNA-LNP reprograms the TME and suppresses pancreatic tumor growth, suggesting a promising immunotherapy.

papers.title: IL-15 signaling during a critical NK cell developmental window subverts maturation and KIR acquisition
papers.abstract: Ruesch et al. demonstrate that during in vitro human natural killer cell development, early-stage exposure to interleukin-15 paradoxically subverts key aspects of maturation. Their experimental findings mirror those seen in patients receiving hematopoietic stem cell transplants, suggestive of a similar mechanism contributing to delayed natural killer cell maturation in vivo.

papers.title: Fungal lipase LipA disarms macrophages by remodeling their lipidome, enabling full virulence in immunocompetent hosts
papers.abstract: Goldman et al. show that Aspergillus fumigatus lipase LipA remodels the macrophage lipidome, suppressing pro-inflammatory eicosanoid signaling and immune clearance. By depleting host lipid precursors, LipA promotes fungal survival and is required for full virulence in immunocompetent hosts.

papers.title: Temporal CRAC channel blockade modulates the MYC-MXD axis to attenuate autoimmune inflammation
papers.abstract: Temporal CRAC channel inhibition disrupts Th17 cell effector function and metabolic programming. Wu et al. reveal a CRAC-MYC-MXD regulatory axis essential for sustaining Th17 identity, demonstrating that temporal blockade of CRAC channels attenuates pathogenic Th17 responses in both mouse models of autoimmunity and human cells.

papers.title: Albumin uptake through FcRn promotes tumor-associated macrophage maturation and albumin-bound immunotherapy response
papers.abstract: Hu et al. show that myeloid FcRn substantially supports tumor albumin accumulation and Nrf2-dependent macrophage maturation. Circulating albumin is associated with relative macrophage abundance in clinical tumor specimens, and an albumin-conjugated STING agonist leverages this biology to activate tumor myeloid cells and improve antitumor activity in mouse models.

papers.title: Defensive lipid droplets are PUFA reservoirs and suppliers driving bacterial clearance and inflammation
papers.abstract: When infected by bacteria, viruses, or parasites, eukaryotic cells accumulate lipids in organelles called lipid droplets. Bosch et al. investigate the identity and defensive roles of these lipids. In activated macrophages, lipid droplets collect and deliver ω-6 and ω-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids to mediate bacterial phagocytosis and inflammation.

papers.title: Spontaneous lytic reactivation drives a persistent B cell-vector pathway for epithelial dissemination of the Epstein-Barr virus
papers.abstract: Vo et al. reveal that EBV-infected B cells serve as efficient cellular vehicles for viral dissemination to epithelial cells. This contact-dependent transfer requires spontaneous lytic reactivation, genome-containing virion production, and epithelial receptors, including EphA2, DSC2, and R9AP, offering a mechanistic framework for understanding strain tropism and host-virus interactions.

papers.title: Viral infection activates the IRF1-BAK axis to drive mitochondria-derived inflammation
papers.abstract: Ye et al. reveal that BAK is an interferon-stimulated gene up-regulated by the STAT1-IRF1 axis during viral infection, which induces mitochondria-derived inflammation. This mechanism is utilized by RNA and DNA viruses and underlies inflammatory diseases.

papers.title: Choice-selective sequences dominate in cortical relative to thalamic inputs to NAc to support reinforcement learning
papers.abstract: (Cell Reports 39, 110756; May 17, 2022)

papers.title: TCF25 serves as a nutrient sensor to orchestrate metabolic adaptation and cell death by enhancing lysosomal acidification under glucose starvation
papers.abstract: (Cell Reports 44, 116186; September 23, 2025)

papers.title: Bifidobacterium adolescentis-derived nicotinic acid improves host skeletal muscle mitochondrial function to ameliorate sarcopenia
papers.abstract: (Cell Reports 44, 115265; February 25, 2025)

papers.title: Viral mimicry escape as a necessary feature of malignant transformation
papers.abstract: Malignant transformation is driven by disruption of pathways regulating proliferation and cell fate, but these same disruptions can create a collateral vulnerability: loss of transcriptional and epigenetic control over transposable elements and other normally silenced genomic regions. Consequently, emerging cancer cells can accumulate transposable element-derived and other endogenous immunogenic nucleic acids capable of triggering antiviral responses, a process termed viral mimicry. Increasing evidence indicates that viral mimicry can eliminate precancerous cells and shape tumour evolution, positioning it as an intrinsic tumour-suppressive mechanism. Here we highlight how cancer-associated changes in DNA methylation, histone modifications, splicing and RNA processing can lead to the presence of immunogenic nucleic acids that can activate viral mimicry pathways. We outline how cancer cells suppress viral mimicry, including compensatory epigenetic repression, RNA editing, nucleic acid decay and dampening of interferon signalling to enable cancer cell growth. Finally, we highlight the evidence suggesting that escaping viral mimicry is a fundamental process for cancer initiation and progression, and suggest that viral mimicry escape is necessary for cancer transformation and a therapeutic target in combination with immunotherapies. By framing viral mimicry escape as a necessary part of cancer transformation, this Review provides a unifying conceptual model for its translational exploitation. Viral mimicry is the activation of antiviral immune responses by endogenous nucleic acids that have accumulated in the cytosol. In this Review, Chen et al. highlight how cancer-associated epigenetic and transcriptional dysregulation promotes the generation of immunogenic nucleic acids, which can limit tumour progression. They further outline the mechanisms tumours use to suppress these responses, and the evidence that escape from viral mimicry is central to tumour evolution and a potential target for therapy.

papers.title: Molecular residual disease: Charting a new path for treating resectable solid tumors
papers.abstract: Molecular residual disease (MRD), detected via circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) after curative-intent surgery, identifies resectable solid tumor patients at high recurrence risk, thereby enabling enriched trials with larger effect sizes and smaller samples. Yet enrichment narrows the eligible population and thus challenges conventional randomized designs. We propose an MRD Registry as an external control cohort that integrates quantitative ctDNA data with outcomes to validate ctDNA dynamics as response indicators—facilitating efficient MRD-based trial design and accelerating novel therapy development.

papers.title: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: The Vision of Heracles
authors: European Pancreatic Club (EPC) Pancreatic Cancer Think Tank Group
papers.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains among the deadliest malignancies, as tumors evolve faster than therapies. Resistance is ecological, not merely KRAS driven, involving overlooked players like high-grade pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasias (PanINs), peripancreatic fat, stromal mechanics, myeloid-neural circuits, metabolic rewiring, and systemic host responses. We propose precision interception targeting PanIN/intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN) biology, spatial-functional-proteogenomic classification beyond transcriptomics, the Heracles Protocol (measure, prime, strike, and adapt), and integrated technologies from AI pathology to exosomal delivery and CRISPR-based synergy mapping, together making PDAC more tractable.

papers.title: Scherer’s map, remapped
papers.abstract: Scherer’s century-old classification of expansive and infiltrative glioma growth remains foundational to neuro-oncology. In this issue of Cancer Cell, Hoefflin et al. use spatial RNA and protein profiling of IDH-mutant gliomas to reveal hypoxia and necrosis as organizing centers of expansive growth and white-matter tracts as guides and constraints on invasion.

papers.title: Spatial analysis reveals the evolving organization of IDH-mutant glioma
papers.abstract: Hoefflin et al. define organizational principles of IDH-mutant gliomas using multimodal spatial profiling. They identify three spatial archetypes across histological grades and reveal that brain anatomy and hypoxia represent distinct spatial organizing forces, with the white-gray matter junction acting as a functional barrier to invasion.

papers.title: ENPP1 buffers extracellular cGAMP in brown adipose tissue to limit insulin resistance
papers.abstract: Nutritional excess triggers mitochondrial DNA leakage in brown adipocytes, promoting the production and release of the immunotransmitter cGAMP into the extracellular space. Wang et al. discover that ENPP1 acts as a vital immunometabolic checkpoint by clearing this extracellular cGAMP pool, thereby preventing local tissue inflammation, insulin resistance, and diet-induced obesity.

papers.title: Living soil stores defensive memories against herbivores
papers.abstract: Gao et al. show that foliar herbivory creates soil-borne defensive legacy via plant–soil feedback that enables undamaged plants that subsequently grow in the same living soil to recruit parasitoid wasps—a mechanism that holds promise for ecological pest management.

papers.title: Gadd45β is critical for regulation of type I interferon signaling by facilitating G3BP-mediated stress granule formation
papers.abstract: (Cell Reports 42, 113358; November 28, 2023)

papers.title: Making breast cancer innovation deliver for every woman
papers.abstract: Scientific progress is measured at the point of discovery, but patients experience it at the point of delivery. Breast cancer offers a lens through which to examine this gap: advances in biology, diagnostics and treatment have transformed what is possible, yet whether these translate into better outcomes remains shaped by how care is delivered. Despite remarkable advances in our understanding of breast cancer biology and in the diagnosis and treatment of the disease, outcomes remain deeply influenced by where people live, how health systems function and whether care pathways are effectively coordinated. In this Comment, Miriam Mutebi outlines how we can translate innovation into equitable patient benefits.

papers.title: A guide to understanding tumour evolution through the lens of population genetics
papers.abstract: Every cancer carries the history of its own evolution, hidden in its genome. Modern DNA sequencing can catalogue millions of mutations and profile tumours across space and time, but sequencing alone struggles to answer the questions that matter most: when did key adaptations emerge, how strongly were they selected, why do some tumours relapse whereas others do not, and how will the cancer evolve next? The reason is fundamental: sequencing is a snapshot, whereas evolution is a dynamic process. Bridging this gap requires moving beyond descriptive cancer genomics towards quantitative evolutionary inference. In this Review, we argue that population genetics provides the mathematical framework needed to extract evolutionary dynamics from cancer genomes. We show how models of mutation, selection and drift transform allele frequencies from descriptive measurements into quantitative estimates of clonal fitness and evolutionary timings. We discuss how these principles extend to epigenetic inheritance, plasticity and ecological interactions within the tumour ecosystem, and examine the assumptions and limitations for their application to modern sequencing data. By reframing cancer genomes as quantitative records of evolutionary processes rather than catalogues of mutations, researchers have used population genetics to provide a foundation for understanding — and ultimately predicting — the trajectories of cancer evolution. Population genetics provides a quantitative framework for interpreting cancer genomes as records of tumour evolution. This Review outlines how models of mutation, selection and drift enable inference of tumour dynamics from sequencing data, distinguish genetic and non-genetic processes, and support extraction of evolutionary trajectories beyond pattern-based statistical genomics.

papers.title: Lending an ear to the lung
papers.abstract: The unprecedented recent advancement in the field of interoception (sensing self) has introduced neuromodulation as a realistic treatment approach. Shibuya et al. identified an ear-to-lung reflex in which activation of auricular-innervating TRPV1+ vagal sensory neurons functions through neuropeptide CGRPβ to suppress allergic airway inflammation, providing an elegant example of exteroceptive control of interoception and a mechanism for transcutaneous neuromodulation.

papers.title: Chromatin triggers tissue-specific immunity in 3D
papers.abstract: Antigenic and environmental stimuli sensed by innate and adaptive immune cells trigger cognate functions that allow the coordination of the appropriate immune response. In this issue of Immunity, Tzerpos et al. and Jay et al. demonstrate that chromatin architecture dynamics integrate sensory inputs with functional outputs to regulate and direct immune cell responses.

papers.title: Speedy delivery: EV-derived fungal antigens establish oral-gut Th17 crosstalk
papers.abstract: Candida albicans induces Th17 cells, but their origins remain unresolved. In this issue of Immunity, Martini et al. show that the mouth is a reservoir for fungal Th17 cells that adopt pathogenic signatures in the gut during Crohn’s disease.

papers.title: Sensory nerves send lymphoid assembly up in smoke
papers.abstract: Accumulating evidence implicates sensory neurons in tumor progression, but signals linking nociceptive activity to impaired antitumor immunity remain unclear. In a recent issue of Cell, Ho et al. show that nociceptor activation impedes TLS assembly through CGRP, and cigarette smoke engages this neuroimmune axis, promoting tumor growth independently of mutagenic effects.

papers.title: Cyclin E-CDK2 regulates cancer cell transcriptional program and response to immunotherapy through BRD4
papers.abstract: Chu et al. show that cyclin E-CDK2 has a cell-cycle-independent role in transcriptional regulation by phosphorylating BRD4 and controlling its chromatin occupancy. Cyclin E overexpression represses the expression of interferon-stimulated genes in cancer cells through BRD4 and promotes immunotherapy resistance, while inhibition of CDK2 activity enhances responses to immune checkpoint blockade.

papers.title: Live-cell transcriptomics with engineered virus-like particles
papers.abstract: Najia, Le, Borrajo et al. establish “cellular self-reporting,” a technology to export molecular analytes from cells in virus-like particles. The authors demonstrate how mRNA export enables longitudinal transcriptome-wide profiling of living cells by sampling cell media. This platform transcends the destructive nature of conventional transcriptomic analysis methods and reveals gene expression dynamics in complex biological systems in situ.

papers.title: Cross-species single-cell atlas of the striatum defines cell-type and subregion disease vulnerabilities
papers.abstract: Single-nucleus RNA sequencing and spatial validation across human and mouse striatum define principles of neuronal specialization across cell types, subregions, and species. These findings lay the foundation for understanding cell- and subregion-resolved contributions to brain function and disease, including addiction risk, antipsychotic responses, Huntington’s disease vulnerabilities, and pharmacologically relevant species differences.

papers.title: TIME in motion: How response takes shape
papers.abstract: Biomarkers for immune checkpoint inhibitors have largely treated the tumor immune microenvironment as a fixed property. In this issue of Cancer Cell, Lin et al. assemble a longitudinal pan-cancer single-cell atlas and show that the direction of immune-state remodeling during therapy is more informative than baseline composition.

papers.title: Tumor evolution shapes metastatic competence in colorectal cancer
papers.abstract: In this issue of Cancer Cell, Manca et al. investigate the genomic evolution and metastatic tropism of over 7,000 colorectal cancers. Integrating primary tumor location, genomic alterations, and clinical variables, they reveal how distinct patterns of tumor evolution shape metastatic competence and impact organ tropism, offering a framework to refine surveillance.

papers.title: Integrated clinicogenomic analysis reveals the evolution and metastatic tropisms of advanced colorectal cancer
papers.abstract: Manca et al. analyze >7,000 colorectal cancers, integrating next-generation sequencing and clinical data. They define tumor genomics, clonality and dosage of mutations, and metastatic tropisms and their effects on patient outcomes. Incorporating metastatic sites, primary tumor location, and genomics, they develop an organ-specific risk model for metastasis.

papers.title: Tumor immune microenvironment remodeling predicts response to checkpoint inhibitor therapy
papers.abstract: Lin et al. assemble a longitudinal pan-cancer single-cell atlas that tracks how the tumor immune microenvironment remodels during checkpoint inhibitor therapy. They show that the direction of remodeling, rather than the pre-treatment state, predicts response and translate these dynamics into a baseline gene signature that forecasts outcome across cancer types.

papers.title: Endogenous opioid dynamics in the dorsal striatum sculpt neural activity to promote goal-directed action
papers.abstract: Cell-type-specific, time-locked release of the opioid neuropeptide dynorphin in the dorsomedial striatum is both necessary and sufficient for goal-directed behavior. Inputs from the basolateral amygdala trigger dynorphin release that engages retrograde Gi-coupled presynaptic inhibition via the kappa opioid receptor, revealing a rapid neuropeptide mechanism for shaping behavior.

papers.title: Temporal analyses of immune responses in sepsis reveal asynchrony between clinical stage of illness and immune states
papers.abstract: Sepsis lacks effective therapeutic interventions. Fish et al. examine sepsis patients and identify three temporal immune states with distinct resistance, disease tolerance, and resilience program trajectories. Early and late immune responses do not align with clinical stage times, arguing that immunomodulatory approaches for sepsis should be based on immune trajectory.

papers.title: Axes of biological variation in diffuse large B cell lymphoma
papers.abstract: (Cancer Cell 44, 567–585.e1–e12; March 9, 2026)

papers.title: MDMX acts as a pervasive preleukemic-to-acute myeloid leukemia transition mechanism
papers.abstract: (Cancer Cell 39, 529–547.e1–e7; April 12, 2021)

papers.title: DDIAS shields single-stranded DNA in mitosis and promotes vertebrate brain development
papers.abstract: DDIAS is identified as a factor that protects single-stranded DNA during mitosis to maintain chromosome stability, and inactivating mutations in DDIAS are identified in a human neurodevelopmental disorder.

papers.title: Single-allele chromatin tracing reveals cytokine-dependent super-enhancer repositioning in CD4+ T cells
papers.abstract: Cytokine cues reshape how chromatin folds to control immune gene activity. Jay et al. show that cytokine signals reposition the Ets1 super-enhancer toward the geometric center of the locus and sustain Ets1 expression required for helper T cell differentiation, providing insight into how noncoding variants at this locus contribute to immune disorders.

papers.title: Mitotic single-stranded DNA suppression by DDIAS
papers.abstract: Xue et al. identify DDIAS as an effector of the CIP2A-TOPBP1 complex. DDIAS is a single-stranded DNA-binding protein that promotes the repair of single-stranded DNA lesions during cell division. This activity is essential in cells lacking the BRCA1 or BRCA2 tumor suppressors or in cells lacking DNA polymerase ζ.

papers.title: Nicotinamide nucleotide transhydrogenase directly couples redox homeostasis to proline biosynthesis in human glioma
papers.abstract: Vettore and Boufersaoui et al. show that glioma cells require efficient regeneration of mitochondrial NADPH through the enzyme nicotinamide nucleotide transhydrogenase (NNT) to adapt to metabolic and redox challenges in hypoxia. Glioma cells lacking sufficient NNT activity have strongly impaired growth in vitro and in vivo.

papers.title: Metabolic inflammation, obesity, and cancer
papers.abstract: Ginhoux and colleagues review the mechanisms underlying the impact of obesity on cancer susceptibility, progression, and response to therapy. They discuss how metabolic stress reprograms myeloid cells, particularly macrophages, driving chronic inflammation and reshaping tumor microenvironments, and argue for the importance of integrating immunometabolism into cancer research and management strategies.

papers.title: An inflammatory bowel disease-linked lncRNA suppresses transcription factor T-BET expression in T cells to limit intestinal inflammation
papers.abstract: The role of noncoding lncRNAs in human disease is difficult to ascertain. Yang-Fischer et al. identify lnc15 (2310015A10Rik/ENSMUSG00000097729) as a cytoplasmic brake on intestinal inflammation. lnc15 expression is decreased in active human inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), and loss of lnc15 promotes colitis susceptibility in mice. Mechanistically, lnc15 recruits CCR4-NOT to destabilize Tbx21 mRNA, limiting T-BET-driven inflammatory programs.

papers.title: Mutually beneficial interactions between bacteria and Arabidopsis promote phosphorus nutrition and growth
papers.abstract: Over 20% of root-associated bacteria promote Arabidopsis seedling growth under phosphorus (P) deficiency in a host-dependent manner. Further analyses showed that P-deficient plants secrete malate to attract Acinetobacter species to the rhizoplane, where the bacteria utilize plant-secreted nitrogen and carbon sources to fuel P mobilization that benefits both parties.

papers.title: Biological aging and the hidden architecture of early-onset cancer risk
papers.abstract: Across birth cohorts, in a Nature Medicine study, Tian et al. identify larger biological age gaps associated with early-onset lung, colorectal, and uterine cancers across birth cohorts. These findings position biological age as an integrative marker of physiological dysregulation. Future work combining aging clocks and mutational signatures could distinguish tumor-promoting states from tumor-initiating exposures.

papers.title: Canonical and noncanonical autophagy in immunity
papers.abstract: Recent studies have expanded the field of autophagy in immunity to include related but incompletely understood noncanonical autophagy processes. Deretic reviews these advancements in the context of immunity, offering a unifying framework for canonical and noncanonical autophagy processes in the form of membrane atg8ylation as an overarching principle affecting multiple immunological processes.

papers.title: GPCR-Gα13 signaling regulates survival of intestinal intraepithelial CD8+ lymphocytes through migration to cytokine-rich niches
papers.abstract: The intestinal barrier harbors numerous intraepithelial lymphocytes (IELs) that promote tissue integrity and whose dysfunction contributes to disease. Earley et al. studied the G-protein coupled receptor signals regulating IEL movement and function and found that Gα13-Arhgef1 signaling guides CD8+ IEL migration and villous positioning, enabling TGF-β- and IL-15-dependent maturation and survival.

papers.title: Granzyme B Is Critical for T Cell Receptor-Induced Cell Death of Type 2 Helper T Cells
papers.abstract: (Immunity 25, 237–247; August 2006)

papers.title: UV irradiation drives lineage-specific MITF-mediated transcription of PD-L1 to confer immune tolerance to UV-mutated melanocytes
papers.abstract: UVR-damaged melanocytes evade immune attack despite harboring many mutations. Lo et al. show that MITF, a transcriptional regulator crucial to melanocyte identity, directly induces the immune checkpoint molecule PD-L1. This intrinsic tolerance program shields melanocytes from T cells, limiting autoimmune melanocyte destruction and potentially enabling early melanoma immune escape.

papers.title: EGFR-targeting ADCs: From oncogene addiction to antigen-guided drug delivery
papers.abstract: In this issue of Cancer Cell, Li et al. report a first-in-human phase 1 study of SYS6010, an epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-targeting antibody-drug conjugate, in advanced solid tumors. The study highlights how EGFR-directed therapy moves beyond kinase inhibition toward antigen-guided cytotoxic delivery in non-small cell lung cancer.

papers.title: SYS6010, epidermal growth factor receptor-targeting antibody-drug conjugate for advanced non-small cell lung cancer: A phase 1 trial
papers.abstract: Li et al. report results from a first-in-human study showing that SYS6010, an EGFR-targeted antibody-drug conjugate, demonstrates encouraging antitumor activity with a tolerable safety profile in pretreated advanced NSCLC, providing evidence that warrants further clinical development.

papers.title: Convergent evolution of metabolic regulation governs redox adaptation in Toxoplasma
papers.abstract: A protein called TgPRO enables the metabolic adaptation and survival of apicomplexan parasites such as Toxoplasma under oxidative and nutrient stress.

papers.title: Coordinated transcriptional networks program organelle expansion and metabolic flows for high endothelial morphology and function
papers.abstract: High endothelial venules require specialized morphology and PNAd expression to support lymphocyte homing; however, the transcriptional mechanisms coordinating these defining features have remained unclear. Bi et al. identify XBP1-dependent and CREB3L2-associated adaptive ER programs that couple organelle expansion with PNAd biosynthesis to drive HEV specialization and reveal conserved secretory programs shared with intestinal goblet cells.

papers.title: Retraction Notice to: Methionine restriction promotes cGAS activation and chromatin untethering through demethylation to enhance antitumor immunity
The structural basis for LRRK2’s activation and autoinhibition
papers.abstract: Elevated kinase activity in leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) is linked to Parkinson’s disease; this study shows that its ROC GTPase acts as a nucleotide-dependent molecular switch that regulates activation and autoinhibition and reveals how some but not all PD mutations disrupt this regulatory switch.

papers.title: Latent tumor killers awakened
papers.abstract: In this issue of Cancer Cell, Kehl et al. construct a single-cell atlas of bone marrow T cells from patients with bone marrow-resident malignancies, identifying tumor-reactive populations existing in a state of latent competence. A 15-gene signature identifies this subset, which is expanded by immunotherapies and predicts clinical responses.

papers.title: Latent effector T cells mediate immunotherapy responses in the bone marrow microenvironment
papers.abstract: Kehl et al. characterize tumor-reactive T cells in the bone marrow of patients with multiple myeloma and AML. These cells adopt an effector state distinct from exhausted solid tumor TILs. The TFiT classifier stratifies immunotherapy, but not chemotherapy, response, identifying a latent, therapeutically engageable anti-tumor compartment.

papers.title: Ultrarapid deep 3D histology enables intraoperative mapping of glioma infiltration
papers.abstract: ULTRA compresses 3D histology from days or hours to within 30 minutes by leveraging the chemical specificity of stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) microscopy through the synergistic development of rapid tissue clearing and unsupervised AI. The platform enables intraoperative visualization of glioma architecture and depth-dependent tumor infiltration margins.

papers.title: A stress-adaptive lipid kinase axis defines metabolic vulnerabilities in neuroendocrine prostate cancer
papers.abstract: Zheng et al. identify a PIKfyve-ER stress-lipogenesis axis that enables neuroendocrine prostate cancer cells to tolerate elevated basal ER stress through PIKfyve-dependent lysosomal homeostasis and SREBP-driven lipogenesis. Dual inhibition of PIKfyve and FASN disrupts these adaptive pathways, driving terminal UPR activation and apoptosis and providing a robust translational strategy.

papers.title: Gasdermin E couples viral pyroptosis to lethal hepatic lipid accumulation
papers.abstract: Wetland virus activates dual apoptotic cascades to trigger GSDME-dependent hepatocyte pyroptosis, which rewires cellular lipid metabolism and ultimately causes severe hepatic steatosis. Therapeutic targeting of this pyroptosis-metabolism axis alleviates lethal wetland virus infection in mice.

papers.title: Depletion of an immature cord blood NK subset reverses trogocytosis-driven CAR NK dysfunction
papers.abstract: Li et al. identify a previously unrecognized NK cell subset that limits cord blood-derived CAR-NK cell therapy by diverting tumor targeting and promoting self-directed fratricide and show that donor cell composition shapes efficacy while offering a practical manufacturing strategy to improve consistency, persistence, and antitumor activity of off-the-shelf CAR-NK therapies.

papers.title: Tumor-infiltrating plasma cell targets as a source for immunotherapies
papers.abstract: Tumor-infiltrating plasma cells are key responders to immunotherapy. In this issue of Cancer Cell, Meyerhoff et al. show that plasma cells from lung lesions of anti-PD-1-treated patients target citrullinated proteins. Engineering CAR T cells with these plasma cells scFv reveals anti-tumor specificity without adverse effects, identifying therapeutic opportunities.

papers.title: Tumor-infiltrating plasma cell profiling after PD-1 blockade reveals tumor-specific antibodies
papers.abstract: Meyerhoff et al. identify tumor-infiltrating plasma cells as a source of antibodies with therapeutic potential. Their lead antibody, PC-1, recognizes citrullinated antigens on cancer and tumor-promoting myeloid cells and can be repurposed to guide CAR T cell therapy.

papers.title: A self-amplifying nerve-fibroblast circuit drives colorectal cancer progression
papers.abstract: Kobayashi et al. demonstrate that cholinergic signaling induces NTN1 secretion from colorectal CAFs, which in turn enhances intratumoral cholinergic innervation. Increased acetylcholine and CAF-derived NTN1 then accelerate cancer cell growth through tumoral CHRM3 and UNC5B. Blocking CHRM3 or NTN1 may represent a promising therapeutic approach for CRC.

papers.title: Trichoderma swollenin activates AtABCB5-dependent auxin efflux to promote plant development
papers.abstract: The beneficial fungus Trichoderma acts through the secreted swollenin ThSWO, which crosses the plant cell wall and engages AtABCB5, an auxin efflux carrier, at the host cell surface. This effector-transporter module tunes auxin-associated cellular responses, revealing how beneficial fungi co-opt host hormone transport to promote root development.

papers.title: Condensates of the chromatin regulator ANKRD11 restrict hypertranscribed genes to safeguard development
papers.abstract: ANKRD11 restricts hypertranscribed genes by forming biomolecular condensates that spatially sequester elongation factors, with disruption of this condensate-mediated control leading to aberrant organogenesis and underlying the pathogenesis of developmental disorders like KBG syndrome.

papers.title: Robust regulatory interplay of enhancers, facilitators, and promoters in a native chromatin context
papers.abstract: Using an in situ genome-rewriting platform, Zhou et al. demonstrate that precise transcriptional regulation of the NMU promoter is governed by a 3D regulatory hub comprising a core retroviral LTR enhancer, a decoy LTR promoter, and activity-boosting “facilitator” elements.

papers.title: Autophagy maintains high endothelial venule identity and function during inflammation
papers.abstract: High endothelial venules (HEVs) facilitate lymphocyte entry into lymph nodes by displaying peripheral node addressin (PNAd), yet how PNAd is regulated remains poorly understood. Jacobs et al. reveal that autophagy preserves HEV identity and function by sustaining PNAd production. Loss of autophagy impairs lymphocyte recruitment, while targeting this pathway dampens inflammation in mouse models of psoriasis.

papers.title: The transcription factor BACH1 couples chromatin priming and repression to enable macrophage plasticity and adaptation
papers.abstract: Macrophage plasticity and function involve precise regulation of transcriptional programs. Tzerpos et al. find that the transcription factor BACH1 establishes early chromatin accessibility while maintaining transcriptionally repressive states in naive macrophages before activation. This dual activity—termed pioneer repression—regulates macrophage adaptation and inflammatory kinetics in vivo.

papers.title: Activation of the auricular vagus nerve reflex suppresses airway inflammation
papers.abstract: Bioelectronic technologies are being deployed to treat many inflammatory conditions using transcutaneous auricular nerve stimulation. Shibuya et al. employ viral tracing, chemogenetics, and optogenetics to unveil a sensory skin-lung vagal reflex that suppresses allergic airway inflammation. They identify the neuropeptide CGRPβ as a key mediator and provide a rationale for transcutaneous bioelectronic neuromodulation in asthma.

papers.title: Antigen-restricted Candida albicans Th17 cells link oral-gut immunity and adopt pathogenic features during intestinal inflammation
papers.abstract: Martini, Hofmann, et al. identify C. albicans-specific Th17 cells targeting fungal EV proteins that predominantly reside in the human oral mucosa at homeostasis. However, these oral-residing cells exhibit TCR overlap with gut Th17 cells. During intestinal inflammation, C. albicans-specific Th17 cells retain their antigen specificity but acquire pathogenic traits, highlighting how oral immunity impacts intestinal disease.

papers.title: Flavin adenine dinucleotide is an endogenous suppressor for cytosolic DNA and RNA sensors to modulate innate immunity
papers.abstract: Precise control of cytosolic nucleic acid sensing is essential for immune homeostasis, yet endogenous metabolites that regulate both DNA and RNA sensing remain unidentified. Wang et al. identify FAD as a natural brake restraining both DNA- and RNA-triggered innate immunity. FAD deficiency aggravates autoinflammation and senescence. Upon viral infection, reduced FAD relieves this inhibition and enables full antiviral immunity.

papers.title: Transcription factor BHLHE40 expression in group 3 innate lymphoid cells and RORγt⁺ antigen-presenting cells coordinates intestinal immunity
papers.abstract: The ability to maintain tolerance at mucosal barrier surfaces is critical for immune homeostasis. Yang et al. identify Bhlhe40 as a central regulator linking innate and adaptive intestinal immunity. By coordinating ILC3 effector responses with RORγt⁺ antigen-presenting cells, Bhlhe40 integrates inflammatory and microbial signals to balance tissue protection with tolerance, providing insight into mechanisms relevant to inflammatory bowel disease.
